1 Introduction

DOC-1778 · section

1.1 What NeoTeletext is

DOC-1790 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-299, REQ-1643, REQ-1732, REQ-1735

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-299 World System Teletext numbering only (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1643 A teletext page is 40 columns by 25 rows (to be rechecked on main).

NeoTeletext is teletext carried by the web. A viewer opens a channel by its address, reads numbered pages of 40 columns by 25 rows, moves between them by page number and by coloured links, and on some channels types, points and plays. Everything on the screen is a teletext page, coded and drawn by the rules of World System Teletext. It is not a web page: there is no script, no bitmap and no layout engine, and a page's dimensions never change.

What a page means is defined by EN 300 706, which NeoTeletext follows and cites. How pages reach a receiver over the internet is NeoTeletext's own, and is defined here: a static channel is a folder of files on a web server, and a live channel adds one WebSocket that carries teletext packets down and the viewer's input up.

The system. NeoTeletext is made of these parts:

  • The engine, a Rust library that reads, decodes, draws and writes teletext, with its command-line program neottx; every other part builds on it.
  • The browser, the desktop application with which a viewer opens channels.
  • The server, which serves channels and runs the programs behind live channels.
  • The protocol kits and the UI component library, with which a program is written, and the demonstration channels built with them.
  • Channels, static folders of files or live programs, in the channel format defined here.

This document. Its first parts define the protocol, and are normative: a developer can build a client, a server, a channel or a program from them and the standards they link to. The parts that follow describe NeoTeletext's own components, the engine, the browser, the server, and the kits with the component library, and are informative: another implementation of the protocol is not bound to copy them. The tasks and troubleshooting close it.

It is generated from the project's database of requirements and must not be edited. Each item names the requirements it states, so a requirement's number leads to where it is documented, and an item that rests on a standard links to the clause, table or annex in the publisher's own file.

This version is a draft.

1.2 A channel

DOC-1791 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-507

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-507 Channels: a channel is a folder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A channel is a teletext service on the web: a folder at an http or https address whose path ends in /. Its identity is its origin and its folder path, compared exactly, so two folders of one web server are two channels and share nothing. That identity is the boundary for viewer state, redirects and links: a viewer known to one channel is unknown to every other.

A broadcast sends every page round and round and a receiver captures the few it wants. A channel keeps each page at a fixed address and a receiver asks for the few it wants. The files of a channel have fixed names worked out from page numbers, so a folder copied to any web server, or read from a disk, is the same channel.

1.3 A page and a sub-page

DOC-1792 · concept · informative · requirements REQ-300, REQ-304, REQ-418, REQ-1643

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-304 A sub-page is its full page address (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-418 Pages cannot write to the receiver-owned status area (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1643 A teletext page is 40 columns by 25 rows (to be rechecked on main).

A page is addressed by a magazine, 1 to 8, and a page number of two hexadecimal digits, and written as three digits with the magazine first: 100, 1FE. A viewer keys only the 800 decimal numbers from 100 to 899. The hexadecimal numbers are reached by links and mostly carry data.

A sub-page is one version of a page, told apart by its thirteen-bit sub-code, written as four hexadecimal digits from 0000 to 3F7E. A sub-page is a page in every way that matters: it is selected, sent, updated and linked on its own. 3F7F is not a sub-page: in an address it means "no particular sub-page".

A page is always 40 columns by 25 rows, numbered from 0. Row 0 is the header. Columns 0 to 7 of row 0 are the receiver's own status area, which no page can write.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 7.2 Elements of a page; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.1 Page number; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.2 Page sub-code

1.4 Receivers, servers and programs

DOC-1793 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1474, REQ-1501

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1474 The server keeps no channel content beyond per-connection state, one last-sent sub-page per connection, and a short cache of public pages' descriptions (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1501 Every page frame on a live connection carries exactly one sub-page (to be rechecked on main).

A receiver is anything that opens a channel and shows its pages: the NeoTeletext browser, the command-line program neottx, or a microcontroller with a screen. A receiver decodes the same packets a television decoder did, into the same 40 by 25 grid.

A server answers a channel's address. For a static channel any web server will do. For a live channel the NeoTeletext server holds the WebSocket and passes messages between its viewers and a program. It keeps no content of its own beyond the last sub-page it sent each connection and, for a minute at most, what the program said a public page shows the web.

A program is the code behind a live channel, in any language. It runs outside the server, publishes pages, and hears what each viewer selects and types. The kits for Python and TypeScript wrap that protocol.

A generator is anything that writes a channel's files.

1.5 Live and static channels

DOC-1794 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-507, REQ-1462

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-507 Channels: a channel is a folder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1462 Server sends only valid packets downstream (to be rechecked on main).

A static channel is its files and nothing else. A receiver fetches channel.ttx, then a bundle of first sub-pages, then each page's file as it is wanted, with ordinary conditional requests over HTTP. It can be served by any host that serves files, and needs no program.

A live channel says so in channel.ttx. A receiver then opens one WebSocket at the channel's push and fetches no page file: pages, sub-pages and the channel's contents all arrive on that connection as teletext packets, and the selection a viewer makes travels up it. Only a live channel can take a viewer's keys.

The bytes of a page are the same in both. A live connection is a plain stream of 42-byte packets, and what is not a page travels as records inside packets on one data channel, so a recording of a connection plays in any decoder that reads T42.

The smallest channels. A page a viewer can read is a folder holding 100.tti. A page a viewer can use is a channel.ttx of { "name": "Example", "push": { "input": true } } at a folder's address, and a server answering push on that origin with a program that sends page 100 and reads the viewer's keys. A static host cannot serve push, so a channel that takes keys needs a server on its own origin.

1.6 Normative words and how to read this document

DOC-1795 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1734, REQ-1737

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1737 Documentation items are typed topics written in a strict XHTML subset (to be rechecked on main).

The capitalised words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY have the meanings of RFC 2119. They appear only in items marked normative. An item marked informative explains, and no implementation is held to it. In a normative item, a plain statement of what a receiver, a server or a file does has the force of MUST, unless it says otherwise, as with "by default" or "a setting allows".

Every item is marked with what kind of text it is: a concept explains, a reference holds facts to look up, a task is a procedure, and a troubleshooting item pairs a problem with its fix.

An item that a standard defines lists the clauses under "Defined by", each a link to the heading in the publisher's own PDF. Such an item does not repeat the standard: read the clause for the definition, and the item for what NeoTeletext does with it, what it chooses where the standard leaves room, and where it departs. An item that no standard defines says so: it is NeoTeletext's own, and it lists under "Rests on" the places of a standard it relies on, which define what it refers to and not the item.

Offsets of a byte example count from the first byte of the example. A teletext packet here is the 42 bytes a T42 file holds, so offset 0 of a packet is byte 4 of the standard's numbering. Bit numbers run from b1, the least significant bit of a byte, as in EN 300 706.

A passage that begins Not built. describes what is required and is not yet in the code. A receiver or server MUST NOT rely on it. What was decided and never built is in informative items whose titles begin "Decided, not built", so a normative item holds only what can be relied on. An item stating a requirement that the records do not hold as implemented says so at its head, and the document ends with an index of such items: that mark says what the records hold, and not that the work is missing. A section with no text has not been written yet.

1.7 The standards this document cites

DOC-1796 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1733, REQ-1736

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1733 The protocol document links each cited standard clause to its heading in ETSI's own copy (to be rechecked on main).

Four documents are cited, each by its published text at its publisher's address. None is copied here. Each file is pinned by its SHA-256, because a link's page and position belong to that exact file.

DocumentWhat NeoTeletext takes from it
ETSI EN 300 706 V1.2.1, Enhanced Teletext specificationPackets, pages, numbering, presentation at Levels 1 to 3.5, and character sets. The published text is cited, never the final draft.
ETSI EN 300 708 V1.2.1, Data transmission within TeletextThe independent data lines that carry audio and records, and the rules for data broadcasting pages a receiver must not show.
ETSI EN 300 472 V1.3.1, Teletext in DVB bitstreamsHow to read teletext out of a recorded MPEG-2 transport stream.
ETSI TR 100 287 V1.2.1, Code of practice for enhanced TeletextGuidance only: the numbering of sub-pages NeoTeletext's automatic numbering follows.

2 Addressing and the URL map

DOC-1779 · section

2.1 One address does every job

DOC-1907 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1693

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main).

A channel has one URL map. It is complete, so nothing is reachable by an address it does not list. It is fixed, so it is the same for every channel, and a channel cannot rename, move or add to it. It is defined, so each thing has one spelling, and every other spelling is normalised to it or refused.

One address does every job: a viewer's address field, a web visitor, a search engine and a link preview. A receiver never asks a server for a page's address. It goes from <channel>200 to the file 200.tti by rule on a static channel, and to a SELECT of 200 on a live one. Only an ordinary web browser or a search engine requests the address itself.

For a page or a sub-page, the same text is what SELECT carries, so an address and a selection cannot disagree. contents and wall are places of an address only: they are never selected, and a SELECT of either closes the connection.

2.2 The places of a channel

DOC-1908 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-512, REQ-1661, REQ-1693, REQ-1883, REQ-1897

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-512 Channel addresses (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1661 Every part of NeoTeletext supports URIs of at least 8,000 octets (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1883 A channel is a folder (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1897 Viewer addresses (to be rechecked on main).

In this part <channel> means an http or https origin and folder, ending in /, such as https://app.neottx.com/home/. A place is what follows it.

AddressOpens
<channel>The channel, arriving at its initial page
<channel>302Page 302
<channel>302/0002Sub-page 0002 of page 302
<channel>302?name=valuePage 302, with a query for the channel's program
<channel>302/0002?name=valueSub-page 0002 of page 302, with a query
<channel>contentsThe channel's contents
<channel>wallThe wall of pages, with no page selected

Spellings.

  • A page is three hexadecimal digits, the magazine 1 to 8 first.
  • A sub-page is four hexadecimal digits, a sub-code 0000 to 3F7E with no bit outside the thirteen a sub-code has. 3F7F means no particular sub-page, so it cannot name one.
  • Hexadecimal digits are capitals in the one spelling.
  • The words contents and wall are in small letters.
  • A query is name=value pairs joined by &, percent-encoded. A name may not be empty, and a value may.
  • The whole address is at most 8,000 octets.

Where a channel ends. A parser reads the end of the path. A last segment of contents or wall, a last segment that is a page number, or a page number followed by a sub-code is inside the channel, and what comes before it is the channel's folder. Any other address MUST end in /, and is a folder. So a folder named contents, wall or like a page number, such as 100 or 2fa, cannot be a channel: it belongs to the channel above it. Only the end of the path is read, so /100/news/ is a channel.

These are fixed names in the channel's folder, or in a page's folder inside it. A viewer never sees them in an address field, and a file of a page's folder has the path of the address it holds: <channel>602/0101.t42 holds what <channel>602/0101 names. The files of a channel says what each holds.

2.5 What is refused

DOC-1911 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-505, REQ-512, REQ-1693

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-505 The strict address parser (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-512 Channel addresses (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main).

An address outside the map MUST NOT be repaired. It is not opened, and a link carrying it is not a link.

  • A fragment on an http or https address is refused, never ignored: <channel>#302, <channel>302#303.
  • A place the map does not list: 30, 3021, G02, 902, 002, 302/2, 302/3F7F, 302/0080, WALL, contents/1.
  • A query that is not name=value pairs: 302?, 302?name, 302?=value, 302?a=1&.
  • A query after contents or wall.
  • The names receivers use that are not pages: channel.ttx, contents.txt, index.t42, 302/0.sub. The names channel.json, 302-0002.t42 and 302.sub are no names of a channel's.
  • Any other file in a folder named as a place, which is not a channel: 302/100.t42, 302/channel.ttx.
  • Any scheme but http and https.

2.7 The query

DOC-1913 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1388, REQ-1674, REQ-1693

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1388 The page and sub-page a connection has selected are sent with SELECT, which carries no view number (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-1674 When a viewer opens a page of a live channel at an address with a query, the receiver MUST send the query in SELECT (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main).

An address has one query, and it goes with the selection. A receiver sends it in SELECT, and a program receives it, as written, in selected, or in connected for a selection made before the program was told of the connection.

A query belongs to that one selection: choosing another page, by any path, leaves it behind. It stays in the address, so a copied address, a bookmark or Reload sends it again. It MUST NOT go on the push connection's own address. A static channel has no program, so the query stays in the address and does nothing, as a static host ignores one.

The server does not interpret a query. It is untrusted text from the viewer: bytes 0x21 to 0x7E with no #, so no space, at most 8,000 bytes, percent-encoded as it came, and its percent-encoding is not checked.

A live channel on the NeoTeletext server answers exactly this, and nothing else. The server serves no channel's files: a live channel's pages, contents and sub-pages travel on its connection. Only GET and HEAD reach the small page or a redirect, and another method there is answered 404.

A place with a final /308, to the same place with no final /, in the case it was asked, keeping its query

A static channel answers whatever its host answers, and a receiver asks it only for the names receivers use.

2.9 Redirects, local files and links from outside

DOC-1915 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-510, REQ-1693

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-510 Redirects within the channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main).

Redirects. An HTTP redirect of a channel's channel.ttx moves the channel, and the reader keeps the place it was opening. A program's redirect names a place of its own channel, or a whole address of this map. The two are different things: the first is an HTTP response, and the second a record on the connection.

Links in a page. A link resolves through this map, never through anything a page says about files. A page link, from X/27/0, is NNN in the same channel; name:mpp goes through services; an alias through aliases; and a contents.txt x entry names a channel or a file of one.

Local files. A file: address names a real file, so a path cannot also name a page in it: a file takes the places of this map after #, as file:///tmp/news.tti#200. This is the one use of #. Arriving normalises to the initial page, and a file: address is never split by the file-name rule: each local file is its own channel.

Links from outside. A neottx:// link wraps a whole address of this map and adds nothing to it: neottx://https://h.example/home/302 opens https://h.example/home/302.

Outside the map. The browser's built-in page neoteletext:home is not in a channel.

3 The transport and the session

DOC-1780 · section

3.1 One WebSocket for each viewer's tab

DOC-1916 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-1337, REQ-1501

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1337 The push socket alone: never multiplexed with fetches, a connection of its own over HTTP/1.1 or a stream of its own on a channel's HTTP/3 connection (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1501 Every page frame on a live connection carries exactly one sub-page (to be rechecked on main).

A live channel holds one WebSocket for each tab that shows it. The WebSocket is a pipe, not a request: moving between pages does not open a new one. A viewer's selection is a web request that stays open inside it, answered with a page and then that page's changes until the next selection replaces it.

Each tab has its own WebSocket, decoder and store, never shared with another tab, even one on the same channel. So the server sees one WebSocket as one view with one selection. There is no cookie and no session spanning WebSockets: a WebSocket lasts until it closes, and the tabs of one viewer are one viewer to the channel only through viewer state, whose key they share (connections and viewer state).

What may be shared is the transport. A tab's WebSocket travels either on a TCP connection of its own, opened by an HTTP/1.1 upgrade, or as a stream of its own on an HTTP/3 connection over QUIC (opening the connection). The tabs of one receiver that show the same channel, in the same jar (an ordinary window's, or a private window's), may share one such HTTP/3 connection, each tab's WebSocket a stream of its own on it. Such a connection carries the push WebSockets of that one channel and nothing else: never a fetch, never another channel's WebSocket, and never a tab of another jar. Sharing it changes nothing the server or the channel's program sees of a WebSocket: each still has its own opening, its own HELLO, its own selection and its own changes. What it changes is that when the shared connection is lost, every WebSocket on it ends together, and each tab comes back for itself with RESUME.

What travels down is a T42 stream and nothing else, so a recording of a WebSocket plays in any decoder. What travels up is a compact binary stream of the viewer's input, of which SELECT is the one message every receiver needs.

The order on a WebSocket is: its opening (an upgrade, or an extended CONNECT on a stream), HELLO, WELCOME, the server's viewer-state challenge and the receiver's answer, the first selection, its page, and from then on input and changes.

3.2 Opening the connection

DOC-1917 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-524, REQ-1337, REQ-1339, REQ-1895, REQ-6927, REQ-6966, REQ-6983, REQ-6984

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-524 Input messages are sent together and never held for a timer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1337 The push socket alone: never multiplexed with fetches, a connection of its own over HTTP/1.1 or a stream of its own on a channel's HTTP/3 connection (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1339 Input travels in binary frames (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1895 A channel's live connection is at its folder's push (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6927 Push protocol 11 adds capability bit 26, MAGAZINE_SOUND_CAP, without which a receiver is sent no magazine music and no page magazine-music setting (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-6983 [WEB] The user agent reads Alt-Svc on a descriptor's answer for an h3 entry and its port, strictly and within bounds, reports what it named and keeps it while it is fresh (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-6984 [WEB] The user agent can open its push connection as a stream its port presents already opened, with the push state machine after the handshake unchanged (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

The connection's address is the channel's address with push added, and with the scheme wss for an https channel and ws for an http one. It carries no query and no page. A receiver opens it only when channel.ttx has a push member. ws is allowed, and a receiver MUST say that it is not secure wherever it says where keys go.

Two ways to open it. Whichever is used, what follows the server's acceptance is the same WebSocket, and nothing else travels with it: the receiver's fetches of the channel's files never share its transport connection.

  • An RFC 6455 upgrade over HTTP/1.1, on a TCP connection of its own (with TLS for wss) that carries that one WebSocket and nothing else. Every receiver can open it this way, and it is the way back whenever the other cannot be used.
  • An extended CONNECT over HTTP/3 (RFC 9220), on a stream of its own of an HTTP/3 connection over QUIC that carries only push WebSockets of this one channel, for tabs of one receiver's one jar. It is open to a receiver only for a wss address, only when the answer that brought channel.ttx named HTTP/3 in Alt-Svc (RFC 7838 section 3) on the channel's own host and the push address's own port and is still fresh, and only after the server's HTTP/3 SETTINGS carried SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL (0x08) with the value 1 (RFC 9220 section 3). A receiver MUST send no early data (0-RTT) on that connection. When the connection cannot be made, or the setting is missing, the receiver opens the HTTP/1.1 upgrade instead.

A server MAY also accept the same extended CONNECT over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441, after its SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL of section 3), and the NeoTeletext server does, but a receiver MUST NOT open its push WebSocket over HTTP/2, since an HTTP/2 connection is the one its fetches would use.

What every opening carries.

  • A subprotocol's name is neottx. and a version of the input protocol. Versions 10 and 11 are spoken, so the names are neottx.10 and neottx.11.
  • A receiver MUST send Sec-WebSocket-Protocol with every name it speaks, the newest first: Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: neottx.11, neottx.10. A receiver of version 10 sends neottx.10 alone.
  • A receiver MUST send Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13.
  • A receiver MUST NOT send Origin. A web page's script always sends one, so a receiver cannot be written in a web page.
  • A receiver sends no Cookie header, and a User-Agent. It asks for no extension.

The HTTP/1.1 upgrade is a GET of the push address's path with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade and Sec-WebSocket-Key, as RFC 6455 section 4.1 says.

The extended CONNECT is a request with :method CONNECT, :protocol websocket, :scheme https, :authority the push address's host and port, and :path its path, with no query (RFC 8441 section 4). It carries the fields listed above, written in lower case as HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 require (sec-websocket-protocol, sec-websocket-version, user-agent), and no Upgrade, Connection or Sec-WebSocket-Key (RFC 8441 section 5).

The server's answer. One rule holds for every host, and for both ways of opening. The rows are checked in this order, and the first that applies answers.

The requestAnswer to an HTTP/1.1 upgradeAnswer to an extended CONNECT
A :protocol other than websocket(does not arise)501 (RFC 9220 section 3)
Not an upgrade at all426, with neither Upgrade nor Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, with or without Origin(does not arise)
Carries Origin, whatever its value, null included403, whatever it offers. This stops a web page reaching a channel as the viewer, through the viewer's own receiver.403, whatever it offers, for the same reason
Offers no name the server speaks426, with Upgrade: websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Protocol naming the newest one spoken, neottx.11426, with sec-websocket-protocol naming the newest one spoken, and no Upgrade, a field HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not carry
Offers one or more names the server speaks101, with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol naming one of them, the newest the server speaks, Sec-WebSocket-Accept, and no extension200, with sec-websocket-protocol naming one of them, the newest the server speaks, no sec-websocket-accept (RFC 8441 section 5), and no extension

A server of version 11 answers neottx.11 to a receiver that offers both and neottx.10 to one that offers that alone; a server of version 10 answers neottx.10.

What else a host checks. The NeoTeletext server also answers, before it looks at Origin or the offer: 400 to a request on push that carries a query, that is in an HTTP version before 1.1, or that is neither an HTTP/1.1 GET nor an extended CONNECT; and 426 with Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 to one whose Sec-WebSocket-Version is missing or not 13. Another host need not, so a receiver must not rely on being refused for those. A stricter server is allowed.

The connection's version is the version in the name the server answered with. HELLO and WELCOME name that version (the session), a receiver offers in HELLO only the capabilities that version defines (capabilities), and the bytes a viewer-state proof signs name it, so that a proof made under one version is never accepted under another.

The offer is a comma-separated list, on one header line or several, each name matched exactly, since a subprotocol's name is case-sensitive. A server MUST NOT read a receiver's agent text to decide anything: capabilities in HELLO are the only signal. The NeoTeletext server sets no cookie, on the 101 or 200 response or any other; a viewer is known only by viewer state, proved on this connection after WELCOME (connections and viewer state).

The receiver's check. A receiver MUST close the connection and stop when a 101, or a 200 to its extended CONNECT, names no subprotocol, more than one, or one the receiver did not offer, or names an extension. permessage-deflate is never used: private rows compressed in one context with attacker-influenced public rows make a compression oracle. Any other answer to an extended CONNECT is read as the same answer to an upgrade would be (stopping and coming back).

After a 200. The stream carries RFC 6455 frames unchanged, a receiver's masked as over HTTP/1.1, as the stream's data. The stream's orderly end stands for the TCP connection's close, and its reset for an abnormal close (RFC 9220 section 3). Each such stream is one connection to the channel, with its own HELLO, its own selection and its own viewer-state proof, however many share one QUIC connection. When the QUIC connection is lost, every stream on it ends, and each receiver comes back for itself with RESUME.

The wire vectors' version rows of neoteletext-common's wire-vectors.tsv give both versions, both names and the offer.

3.3 Messages on the connection

DOC-1918 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-524, REQ-1066, REQ-1332, REQ-1338, REQ-1462

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-524 Input messages are sent together and never held for a timer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1066 Dead viewer connections found within a bound (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1332 One message per event, never held back (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1338 The round trip measured on the connection (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1462 Server sends only valid packets downstream (to be rechecked on main).

DirectionMessageBound
DownA binary message of whole 42-byte packets. Joined in the order sent, the messages are a plain T42 file, with nothing between packets and nothing added to them. See the downstream record set.A receiver takes at most 65,536 bytes a message by default, and the server cuts what is longer. A cut falls before a sub-page's header where it can, and otherwise at a packet.
UpA binary message: a piece of the input streamAt most 8,192 bytes
UpA text message: the push subscription, subscribe all, or subscribe and page numbers. The engine's receiver sends it when the connection opens. The NeoTeletext server ignores every text message, and a new receiver need not send one: what a connection is sent is its selection.Small

A server MUST NOT send a text message. A receiver discards one, applies nothing of it, and counts it as one invalid packet. A binary message that is not whole packets is discarded whole, and counts as its length divided by 42, rounded up. Neither closes the connection.

Writing. Each event is its own message, written as it happens. Messages waiting at the same moment are written together, in one write and one TLS record where the transport allows, and nothing is held back to be grouped. Input is never sent in TLS early data or a TCP Fast Open SYN, which could be replayed.

The heartbeat. A receiver pings a connection silent for 25 seconds, and treats one that does not answer within 10 seconds as lost. The server pings a connection silent for 35 seconds, 25 and 10 together, so a live receiver's own ping comes first, and drops one that answers nothing within 10 seconds, without a close. Either side answers a ping with a pong, and any byte heard counts as a sign of life.

The round trip. A receiver measures the connection by ping and pong, at most once a second while keys go to the channel, and not from acknowledgements, which measure only the channel's receipt.

3.4 Close codes

DOC-1919 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-1036

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1036 On SIGTERM or SIGINT the server closes viewer connections with a restart close code and exits cleanly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A close code says whether to try again, in two published ranges, so that a code nobody has defined yet needs no change in a receiver.

CodeNameMeaningA receiver
4000CLOSE_BROKE_PROTOCOLThe receiver broke the WebSocket or the input protocolStops
4001CLOSE_WRONG_VERSIONHELLO named a version the channel does not speakStops
4002 to 4099UnnamedReservedStops
4100CLOSE_RESTARTINGThe server is restartingTries again
4101 to 4199UnnamedReservedTries again
Any other, or no close at all1000 among them, and a connection that simply wentTries again

A protocol error closes the connection, on either side, with a code a receiver stops on. A receiver answers a close with a close, as RFC 6455 section 5.5.1 says.

3.5 Stopping and trying again

DOC-1920 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-1036

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1036 On SIGTERM or SIGINT the server closes viewer connections with a restart close code and exits cleanly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Stopping. A receiver that stops MUST NOT reconnect until the viewer opens the channel again. It stops on a close code of 4000 to 4099; on an upgrade answered with a status of 400 to 499 other than 429, which trying again would meet again; and on a 101 without the subprotocol it asked for.

Trying again. After any other loss, a 429 and a status of 500 or above among them, a receiver waits a random time in the upper half of a ceiling, and connects again. The ceiling starts at 1 second and doubles to at most 60 seconds, so the waits are 0.5 to 1 second, then 1 to 2, then 2 to 4, and so on. The randomness is so that the viewers a restart sent away do not all come back at once, and the upper half so that none comes back at once by chance.

The ceiling goes back to 1 second once a connection has shown itself healthy, by bringing packets or a pong. A connection that merely opened has not.

A reconnection is a new session, unless it resumes one. Its receiver sends HELLO again, and SELECT, so the channel sends its page again.

3.6 The session

DOC-1921 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-205, REQ-1471, REQ-1481, REQ-6927

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1471 The server holds a viewer's connection event for the first SELECT and sends the program one connected event (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1481 A selection the program does not answer in time ends with DENIED 503 and the connection stays open (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6927 Push protocol 11 adds capability bit 26, MAGAZINE_SOUND_CAP, without which a receiver is sent no magazine music and no page magazine-music setting (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

  1. When the connection opens, a receiver sends HELLO with the connection's version, the one its subprotocol named (opening the connection), and its capabilities.
  2. The channel answers with WELCOME: the same version and the subset of the capabilities it will use. A channel that cannot speak the version HELLO names closes the connection with 4001, and a receiver refuses a WELCOME that names another version than its HELLO.
  3. The receiver then sends RESIZE, FOCUS_IN or FOCUS_OUT, and SELECT when it shows a page of the channel, and from then on the viewer's input that the page's rule table reports, inside RULE_EVENT (a page asks for input with its rule table).

A receiver MUST send no input before WELCOME. A channel that has not answered within WELCOME_TIMEOUT, 10 seconds, is taken not to take input, and the receiver says so.

The first SELECT. The server holds its connected to the program until the connection's first SELECT, for at most FIRST_SELECTION_WAIT_MS, 1,500 ms, so that a shared link goes straight to its page with no initial page before it. A SELECT of nothing also ends the hold. A receiver that does not set the SELECT capability is not waited for, and is shown the program's answer for the initial page.

A selection's ending. Every selection ends with a page, or with DENIED, within PROGRAM_REPLY_LIMIT_MS, 5,000 ms, of the SELECT. After that the server sends DENIED 503 itself, with the channel's program running or not, and at once when no program is running. So a receiver needs no timer of its own for a selection. A later page for the same selection is still shown: the selection stands, and the program has come back. A selection a newer one replaced has no ending of its own, and what the program sends for it is dropped.

Protocol versions. Versions 10 and 11 are spoken, and a connection speaks the one its subprotocol named; every other version is refused. Version 11 is version 10 with three additions, and nothing else differs:

  • capability bit 26, MAGAZINE_SOUND (capabilities), and what that capability lets a channel send;
  • the PAINT record, record type 35, which says how one generation of a page's ReGIS or NAPLPS picture is painted: its line speed and its default paint rate;
  • the rule table's trigger 22, painted, which fires when a picture or a numbered drawing has been painted whole (rules, triggers, keys and targets).

A receiver of version 11 connects to a channel of version 10, which never agrees the bit and sends neither the record nor the trigger. A channel of version 11 serves a receiver of version 10, which never offers the bit. On a connection of version 10 a channel MUST NOT send a PAINT record, and MUST NOT send a rule that has trigger 22 among its triggers: a receiver of version 10 reads past a record type it does not know, but refuses whole a table that holds a trigger it does not know. The channel sends that connection the page's table without every such rule, the rest of the table as its program gave it, and reads the rule numbers of that connection's reports against the table it sent. So a painted page works on a receiver of version 10, its picture drawn at once and its rules on painted never firing.

Version 3 added the stamp to input events, 4 the REDIRECT record, 5 a query in SELECT, 6 SELECT's payload as the address's text, 7 the subprotocol and the close codes and a query in a REDIRECT's place, 8 viewer state's messages, and 10 the page rule table (RULES, RULES_QUERY and the six command records, types 21, 22 and 28 to 33), the animation records (types 23 to 27), the local sound and cue points, and the rule that the viewer's input travels only inside RULE_EVENT. Version 9, the rule table's first form, was never deployed and is not kept.

A reconnection is a new session for every page: HELLO again (or RESUME, which restores the session's identity and nothing of a page), nothing of any page's local state held, no RULE_EVENT that was unacknowledged sent again, and the input count from zero. The channel sends the selected page again when it receives SELECT, its rule table with it.

3.7 Capabilities

DOC-1922 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-205, REQ-222, REQ-1556, REQ-6523, REQ-6761, REQ-6769, REQ-6879, REQ-6927

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-222 Gone: a receiver sends action 3 when the pointer leaves or a contact is cancelled (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1556 A PAGE event (0x0A) from any receiver MUST be refused as a protocol error; receivers state selection with SELECT alone (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-6761 Capability bits REGIS_CAP (23) and NAPLPS_CAP (24, NAPLPS on the raster from line 20), and DRAWING_LINKS and REGIS_CURSOR naming NAPLPS objects too (PAR-1, PAR-2, RAS-9) (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6879 The push protocol's capability bit 25, SNAPSHOT, and the snapshot request a receiver sends: HELLO then one SELECT, closed at once when WELCOME does not agree it (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-6927 Push protocol 11 adds capability bit 26, MAGAZINE_SOUND_CAP, without which a receiver is sent no magazine music and no page magazine-music setting (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

The caps field of HELLO and WELCOME is a bit set. A sender uses a new flag bit, field, core type or extension type only when both sides set its capability. There are no input modes, and no capability asks for input: what of the viewer's input a channel is sent is decided by each page's rule table, and the viewer's input travels only inside RULE_EVENT. Bits 0 to 15 were input modes until 27 October 2026, and are reserved, never set, and ignored when a peer still sets them.

BitValueCapabilityMeaning
1665,536NoneRetired, PAGE. Never set, and a protocol error when set in HELLO or WELCOME.
17131,072CURSORThe receiver draws the channel's cursor record.
18262,144NoneRetired, provisional echo. Never set, and ignored when a peer still sets it.
19524,288AGENTHELLO carries the user agent string. In HELLO only, never in WELCOME.
201,048,576TOUCHThe receiver reports touch: MOUSE's device bits and TOUCH. Without it touch is reported as the mouse, the first contact alone.
212,097,152RESUMEA lost connection's session may be resumed.
224,194,304SELECTThe receiver shows teletext pages and sends SELECT. A channel that sets it sends the one sub-page selected, never a page's sub-pages together.
238,388,608REGISThe receiver draws a sub-page's ReGIS picture from the REGIS record (type 14), with DRAWING_LINKS and REGIS_CURSOR naming its numbered drawings.
2416,777,216NAPLPSThe receiver draws a sub-page's NAPLPS picture from the NAPLPS record (type 17), with NAPLPS_OBJECTS, and DRAWING_LINKS and REGIS_CURSOR naming its objects, on the 480 by 460 dots from line 20 of the teletext raster (teletext rows 1 to 23), every NeoTeletext coordinate of the page being a dot of that raster.
2533,554,432SNAPSHOTThe connection is a snapshot connection: it asks for one page as a stranger sees it and nothing else. Offered only with SELECT, and with REGIS and NAPLPS as the receiver draws them, never with CURSOR, TOUCH, RESUME, AGENT or MAGAZINE_SOUND. A channel that agrees it creates no viewer, sends no STATE_CHALLENGE, tells its program of no connection (it may ask its program to draw the page for no one in particular, snapshots, for a program), answers one SELECT and closes.
2667,108,864MAGAZINE_SOUNDThe receiver plays the channel's music and a magazine's, and applies a page's two music switches. A channel that agrees it may send a CONTROL record that names a level of music, the blocks of that music's live sound, and the PAGE_MUSIC record of a page's switches. Defined by version 11 alone, and never agreed with SNAPSHOT.

A receiver that does not set SELECT has no selection of its own: it is shown the program's answer for the channel's initial page. Cursor records are the one exception to the rule above: they carry the acknowledgement, so they go to every receiver, and CURSOR says only that the receiver draws them. WELCOME's capabilities are a subset of HELLO's, and a receiver refuses a WELCOME that sets any other.

A receiver offers REGIS or NAPLPS only when it draws that picture language. A channel sends a sub-page's picture records in a language only to a receiver that agreed that language's bit. A receiver MUST drop every NAPLPS record (type 17) and NAPLPS_OBJECTS record (type 25) that arrives on a connection whose WELCOME did not agree NAPLPS, before it draws anything of them, and count each as dropped; the sub-page is then its teletext page. The two bits raise no version: a reader of HELLO reads past bits it does not know and agrees none of them, and a receiver that offers neither is never sent either in WELCOME. The wire vectors input hello_pictures and record welcome_pictures of neoteletext-common's wire-vectors.tsv offer and agree both, with CURSOR and SELECT.

SNAPSHOT raises no version either, for the same reason. A channel that does not know it agrees it in no WELCOME, and a receiver that offered it MUST then close the connection at once, before it sends SELECT or answers anything, so that such a channel creates no viewer and tells its program nothing. The wire vectors input hello_snapshot and record welcome_snapshot offer and agree SNAPSHOT with SELECT, REGIS and NAPLPS.

MAGAZINE_SOUND is what version 11 adds to version 10 (the session). A receiver offers it only on a connection of version 11, and a channel agrees it only when it was offered. A WELCOME that agrees SNAPSHOT and MAGAZINE_SOUND together MUST be refused as a WELCOME with an undefined bit is: a snapshot connection draws one page and plays nothing. A channel MUST NOT send a CONTROL record that names a level of music, the blocks of that music's sound, or a PAGE_MUSIC record on a connection whose WELCOME did not agree the bit. A receiver takes music of the channel or of a magazine only after WELCOME agreed it: until then, and on a broadcast or from a file, it MUST refuse a CONTROL record that names a level of music and a PAGE_MUSIC record whole, count each, start nothing and leave the audio channel's sequence of commands as it was; receiving one on such a connection is a protocol error, on which a receiver may close the connection. The wire vectors input hello_magazine and record welcome_magazine offer and agree it under version 11 with CURSOR and SELECT.

A pointer's gone, MOUSE's action 3, needs no capability, and is given to the page's rule table whatever a session agreed.

The NeoTeletext server agrees CURSOR, SELECT, TOUCH, REGIS and NAPLPS, each only when the receiver offers it, and never RESUME; on a snapshot connection it agrees SNAPSHOT with SELECT and the picture languages offered, and nothing else. It does not yet agree MAGAZINE_SOUND to any receiver, and sends no music of a channel or of a magazine. A receiver that did not agree a picture's language is sent that picture drawn as Level 1 mosaics on the sub-page's teletext, so that it shows something. A program hears a pointer's gone as the lost release of what the pointer held (what a program hears of input), and hears no TOUCH event.

3.8 Resuming a session

DOC-1923 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-224, REQ-1335

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-224 Resumption: receiver keeps and resends unacknowledged input messages (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-1335 Numbered events, resent after a reconnection (tested, not recorded as met on main).

A WebSocket cannot resume: what was in flight when TCP died is lost silently. When both sides set RESUME, a session outlives its connection, so no key is lost when a connection drops and none reaches the channel twice. Events are numbered implicitly, by the input count both sides keep, and nothing is added to any event.

  1. The token. A channel that sets RESUME in WELCOME gives the session a token of 16 bytes from its cryptographic generator, new in every WELCOME.
  2. The receiver keeps every message of input units it sends, as sent, until an acknowledgement covers it, at most RESEND_BYTES, 16,384 bytes, and 256 messages. A message of no input units is never acknowledged and never kept. When what is kept would pass either bound, the session can no longer be resumed.
  3. The channel holds a session whose connection was lost for at least RESUME_HOLD_MS, 32,000 ms, past the first five retries, with its input count taken. It may drop it sooner under load, and MUST drop it after giving the session to another connection.
  4. On a lost connection the channel releases everything held, so a resumed session starts with nothing held.
  5. A reconnection's first message is HELLO, with RESUME after it: the token and the last acknowledgement taken. In a resumed session HELLO counts nothing.
  6. The channel answers with WELCOME: resumed, with the input count taken, when it holds a session of that token with no connection of its own and the count is at or after the acknowledgement. Otherwise new, and the session begins again from HELLO, nothing of the old resent.
  7. The receiver sends again, before anything else and in the order first sent, every message it keeps that came after the count taken, whole messages only. The count taken is always the end of a message it sent, and one that is not is a protocol error. Then RESIZE, the focus and SELECT, so that the channel sends the selected page again.
  8. The channel drops what it has already taken, so a message that reaches it twice is acted on once.

The count is 16 bits and wraps, compared by RFC 1982 serial arithmetic. The token is a secret of the connection, and goes only on the session's own WebSocket.

Not built. The engine's receiver does all of this (its ResumableSession). The NeoTeletext server does not set RESUME, so a reconnection to it is always a new session, and a RESUME sent to it is ignored.

3.9 Connections and viewer state, which replaced cookies

DOC-1924 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1471, REQ-6704, REQ-6713, REQ-6725, REQ-6727, REQ-6731, REQ-6733, REQ-6734, REQ-6735, REQ-6744, REQ-6745

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1471 The server holds a viewer's connection event for the first SELECT and sends the program one connected event (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6704 The server keeps no session and sets no cookie: a connection lasts until it closes, and the program is told gone for it (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6725 Channels cannot relate one another's handles: one key per channel identity in the browser, and each channel's handles derived under a key of that channel alone (not implemented on main); REQ-6727 The server verifies every viewer-state proof itself, by strict Ed25519 over the signed bytes, under each public address configured for the channel (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6731 The server derives each viewer's handle per channel by HMAC-SHA-256 under a channel key made from a server secret kept once in viewer-handle.key (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6733 What a program is told of viewer state: connected carries viewer and remembered, and viewer_began, viewer_left, state_refused, viewers_reset and gone (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6734 What a program may ask of viewer state: request_state, end_state and offer_remember, and nothing else; the cookie message is removed (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6735 The server refuses a program's viewer-state request the viewer has not given: has_viewer, no_gesture, unknown_viewer and the existing refusals (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6744 The protocol's documentation item for viewer state states, as normative text binding every channel author, what a handle may be used for (not implemented on main); REQ-6745 Decided, not built: a future sign-in binds an account on the server to the key identifier of the connection's viewer, one key a device (not implemented on main).

No cookies. NeoTeletext has no HTTP cookies. A receiver sends no Cookie header and ignores every Set-Cookie and Clear-Site-Data, on a page's fetch, a descriptor's fetch and the push upgrade alike; the NeoTeletext server sets no _session cookie and keeps no session key; and the SET_COOKIE record, push record type 8, and the program's cookie message are withdrawn. Nothing a channel writes is stored in or parsed by a receiver.

A connection is a tab. Each browser tab's push connection is a connection of its own, with one selection, and the server keeps no session that spans connections. When a connection closes, the server gives the program the releases of whatever it held that a rule reported, marked lost, tells it the selection left its page (left), and tells it gone: the connection will not come back. A program forgets the connection then. The continuation of a dropped connection is the input protocol's RESUME (resuming a session), which no server offers yet. A program's state for a connection lives in the program: the server is not a database.

A viewer is a handle. When a channel needs to know that two connections come from the same viewer (a poll that counts one vote a viewer, choices a viewer made, a viewer's language), it uses viewer state. The browser makes a key pair for one channel when that channel asks for state and the viewer agrees, and proves possession by signing a fresh challenge from the channel's server on the channel's own push connection; the key never leaves the browser. The server verifies every proof itself and gives the program an opaque handle, 32 hexadecimal characters derived for that channel alone, in connected and viewer_began (from the server to a program), with whether the viewer chose to be remembered. A program asks with request_state, may ask the browser to offer "remember me" with offer_remember, and ends a viewer's state with end_state (from a program to the server); it can never choose, set or extend a handle, a key or a lifetime. A handle reveals nothing to another channel and cannot be replayed. neottx and other receivers that keep no state answer every challenge that they keep none, and are a new viewer each time.

What a program may do with a handle. Use it only to provide what the viewer asked for on this channel, never for advertising, profiling, analytics beyond aggregate counts or sharing with anyone; delete what it keeps for a handle at end_state and at its store's limits; and say on its privacy page what it keeps. The full design, its messages on the push connection and its security analysis are neoteletext-common's docs/viewer-state.md.

Not built. Login is not designed: a program sees connections and handles, and no identity beyond them.

3.10 What is legal when

DOC-1925 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-205, REQ-1481, REQ-1555

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1481 A selection the program does not answer in time ends with DENIED 503 and the connection stays open (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1555 Every input event except focus and session events carries a page and sub-code stamp (to be rechecked on main).

In this stateA receiver may sendA channel may send
Upgrade answered, no HELLOHELLO, first and onceNothing a receiver must act on: pages wait for the program's answer, which waits for SELECT or the first selection's bound
HELLO sent, no WELCOMENothingWELCOME, or a close of 4001. A receiver waits at most 10 seconds.
Welcomed, no selectionRESIZE, FOCUS_IN or FOCUS_OUT, SELECT. A resumed session's messages go first. No RULE_EVENT, since no page and so no rule table is on screen.Index, cursor and control records, and nothing of a page's content until the program answers
A selection awaiting its endingThe session's own events, a new SELECT included, which replaces it, and a RULE_EVENT the rule table of the page still on screen reports, dropped if its stamp no longer matchesThe selection's page, or DENIED, and records. A later change to an older selection is dropped.
A selection ended with a pageThe session's own events, and every RULE_EVENT that page's rule table reportsThat page's changes, its rule table, records and a REDIRECT
