After a closeNothing on that connectionNothing. A new connection is a new session.

The viewer's input is never sent at the top level of the stream: it travels only inside RULE_EVENT, and only as the page's rule table asks. Anything else on the receiver's side is a protocol error, or dropped when the stamp says so. A stamped event sent before any selection is dropped and counted by the NeoTeletext server, which does not close the connection for it.

Not built. The NeoTeletext server does not yet hold a receiver to this order. It answers a second HELLO with a second WELCOME, and closes nothing for raw text, RESIZE or another event before HELLO, nor for a SELECT, or a MOUSE of a device other than the mouse, whose capability was not agreed. A receiver keeps to the order all the same, and another server may close.

3.11 What overload does

DOC-1926 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-208, REQ-1356, REQ-1462, REQ-1557

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-208 The rate: a sender sends at most 120 input units in any second (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1356 Never behind the network (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-1462 Server sends only valid packets downstream (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1557 Server checks input page stamp against the connection's selection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Each message type has one rule for when it cannot keep up, and nothing is merged or dropped beyond them.

MessageThe rule
A key, a button, a contact's down and up, PASTENever dropped by the channel, and limited to 120 input units a second by the receiver, which never drops a release to keep to it
A moveThe latest of a contact's replaces the unsent one, at most 60 a second, and it waits while the socket has 1,024 bytes or more unsent
The wheelUnsent deltas are summed
HOVERGoes as a control is crossed, and counts nothing
COMPOSEHeld to the rate as one unit
SELECTA later one replaces an earlier, whose answer is dropped. The engine's receiver does not hold it to the rate: it counts no units, and the rate counts units.
A page frame, a record, a sound or raw packetsAn answer to a replaced selection is dropped by its number. A connection's queue on the server holds 256 messages of every kind, and what will not fit is dropped, the newest first, so a receiver that far behind can miss a change until the next whole frame.
LOGA receiver passes on at most 16 for each page frame it takes, and 16 before the first
Lines to a programAt most 4,096 lines wait for a program. The newest beyond that are dropped, and the server's log says so.
A move to a programAt most 60 a second for each connection, and one waiting for each connection, which a newer move replaces until the program takes it. It takes none of the room for lines, so moves never cost a program a key (the pointer's moves).

An invalid packet costs a count and no more. A receiver reports the count at most once in 20 seconds, and the server reports input dropped for its stamp at the same pace.

Not built. A policy for each source: the oldest whole record dropped for live audio, the latest of an audio command kept, and a close for raw packets that must not lose data. Nothing ever drops part of a page frame, but a slow connection loses the newest sound as it loses anything else.

3.12 The required core, and what is not understood

DOC-1927 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-200, REQ-201, REQ-1476

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-200 Input is sent as one ordered stream of raw UTF-8 text and 0xFF-framed events (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-201 Input protocol unsigned varints: shortest encoding, at most 5 bytes, 32 bits (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1476 The server and a program MUST exchange only the closed set of exactly typed messages, with no view field (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver that does this much works on every channel: the upgrade with its subprotocol; HELLO, and WELCOME; SELECT, having set the SELECT capability; a page's packets; and stopping or trying again on a close. It need read no record but WELCOME to show a page, and DENIED to say why none came.

A channel's required core is: WELCOME; a page frame or DENIED for every SELECT; and closing with the codes of this part.

Everything else is optional, and each kind of thing has one rule for what is not understood.

WhatA reader of one it does not know
A core event, 0x01 to 0x3FA protocol error: it has no length to step over
An extension event, 0x40 to 0x7FSkipped by its length
Type 0x00, or 0x80 to 0xFFA protocol error
A flag bit of an eventA protocol error
A capabilityIgnored, and not agreed in WELCOME
A record type on data channel 12Skipped by the type byte, not counted
A control messageSkipped by its length, or ignored when withdrawn
A field or a type of a program's messageRefused whole, with a refused message: the program protocol is exact, as its two ends are released together
A member of channel.ttxThe file is refused

3.13 Decided, not built: the socket options of the path

DOC-2127 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1349

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1349 Every socket on the input path sets TCP_NODELAY (not implemented on main).

Not built in full. Every socket on the path of an input event is to have TCP_NODELAY, whatever terminates TLS in front of the server included, and the server's own sockets are to have TCP_THIN_LINEAR_TIMEOUTS on Linux. Nagle's algorithm would otherwise hold a small write until an earlier one is acknowledged, and a lone lost segment would wait for a doubling retransmission timeout.

Today the server sets TCP_NODELAY on each viewer's socket and the receivers set it on theirs. The server does not set TCP_THIN_LINEAR_TIMEOUTS, and the terminator in front of a deployed server has not been checked.

3.14 The return channel: how every hop keeps input and its answer fast

DOC-2275 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1333, REQ-1336, REQ-1340, REQ-1341, REQ-1342, REQ-1344, REQ-1345, REQ-1357, REQ-1365, REQ-1368, REQ-1372, REQ-1373, REQ-1374

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1333 No timer-driven sends on the return channel, except pointer moves, the server's deadlines and a page rule table's reports on its 60-tick clock (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1336 Push WebSocket stays open and is pinged after silence (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1340 Input and answers travel only on the push WebSocket over TCP and TLS (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1341 The server sends a session's queued data in priority order (not implemented on main); REQ-1342 Bound unsent data in each client socket's kernel buffer (not implemented on main); REQ-1344 Only the sub-page that changed (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1345 The server's relay from a channel program never loses a partly read line when another event wins the wait (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1368 Every contact on the open page is the page's while keys go to its channel, given to its rule table and sent only as the table's rules report it (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1372 Show the system keyboard while a cursor record asks for typing (not implemented on main); REQ-1373 Touch devices show an on-screen remote whose keys send KEY like keyboard keys (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-1374 Contacts checked by the trusted core (to be rechecked on main).

The return channel is the path of an input event from the viewer's hand to the program that answers it, and of the answer back to the screen: the browser's interface, its trusted core, the page's rule table in its decoder, the fetcher, the WebSocket, the server, the program on its standard input, and back. It is built for the least delay and the fewest bytes. The rules below are how NeoTeletext's own parts meet that; the wire rules every implementation follows are in the upstream protocol, the page rule table and the downstream record set.

  • No round trip for what the page answers itself. A page's rule table lets the receiver answer an event with no message at all: a note on a local sound, a changed look, an object moved. Only what the table reports goes to the channel.
  • One transport. Input and its answers travel on the channel's WebSocket, over TCP and TLS, and on no other transport. No event is marked for a class of service.
  • A warm connection, never replayable. The WebSocket opens with the tab and stays open while the channel's pages are shown, with a ping after 25 seconds of silence. A reconnection resumes the TLS session where the server allows it, and no event travels in TLS 0-RTT early data or in a TCP Fast Open SYN, either of which an attacker could replay.
  • Nothing waits on a clock. No hop sends an event or an answer on a timer: each acts the moment its input arrives, because a hop that sends on a tick adds half a tick to every event on average. A rule table handles each event the moment it arrives, applies its group's commands at once and makes its reports at once; only what time drives (a timer, a sequence, a condition becoming true) waits for the table's tick of one sixtieth of a second (handlings). The pointer's moves, at most 60 a second, are the one paced stream. The server has three deadlines that are not ticks, each set by the one thing it waits for and cancelled by it: a lone acknowledgement after 250 milliseconds (the input count), a selection's ending after 5,000 milliseconds with DENIED 503 (the DENIED record), and the hold of the connected event a program is sent for a new connection, for at most 1,500 milliseconds while the connection's first SELECT is awaited, so that a shared link goes straight to its page; a SELECT ends the hold at once.
  • The trusted core paces and gates. In the browser, the pacing of the pointer's moves is the trusted core's: the interface passes each change of the dot as an intent, and a move waits in its contact's slot until its sixtieth of a second ends. Before another event is taken the waiting moves go first, early at most once in each period, so whatever the interface sends, the page receives at most 60 paced and 60 early moves a second for a contact, 120 in all. The trusted core numbers touch contacts, keeps their slots and refuses a contact the interface invents, a move or end for a contact not begun, or one too many. It builds every report itself, from its own copy of an event it gave the page (the gate).
  • Touch is not held for gestures. A contact's beginning and end are taken when the system reports them, never held to recognise a gesture, and every contact on the open page is given to its table, as TOUCH and pens says. The browser has no gestures of its own on such a page.
  • Only what changed. An answer sends only the sub-page it changes, never every sub-page of the page, since a page may have 8,190.
  • No line lost in the server's relay. The relay between the server and a program reads each direction in a task of its own for the relay's life, so a partly read line from the program is never dropped when input for the program arrives, and neither direction waits for the other.

Decided, not built.

  • The server is to send what it has queued for a session in order of priority: acknowledgements and answers to input first, then audio, then the program's other page frames, keeping order within each class. Today each connection has one first-in, first-out queue.
  • Each viewer's socket is to keep only a bounded amount of unsent data in the kernel, with TCP_NOTSENT_LOWAT where the platform has it, so the rest waits in the session's queue where an answer can still overtake it. Today the server sets only TCP_NODELAY (see the socket options of the path).
  • On a touch device, a page whose cursor record asks for typing is to bring up the system's keyboard, its text given to the page's table as raw text and COMPOSE; and the browser is to show its own remote, the digits, the four Fastext colours, the arrows, OK and page up and down, each giving the table the KEY the keyboard's key would. The browser does not yet run on touch devices.

4 The upstream protocol

DOC-1781 · section

4.1 A terminal on a line to a host

DOC-1928 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-200, REQ-1332

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-200 Input is sent as one ordered stream of raw UTF-8 text and 0xFF-framed events (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1332 One message per event, never held back (to be rechecked on main).

A channel that takes input is a host, and the receiver is its terminal. Each page says, with its rule table, which of the viewer's input it wants and what the receiver answers by itself: a note on a local sound, a changed look, an object moved. The receiver handles each event the moment it arrives, applies at once what the table's groups say, and sends the channel at once the events the table reports. The channel decides what they mean and answers by sending the rows that changed. The receiver decides only whether an event of the open page is the page's, the table what leaves, and the channel what it means. Nothing runs in the receiver but the page's table, which binds events to ordinary protocol commands and is not a program: a game, a form, a chat and a shell are the same to it. A channel that feeds an ordinary terminal program translates events into whatever encoding that program asked for.

Each binary message a receiver sends is a piece of one ordered input stream, the concatenation of all binary messages on that connection. At its top level are the session's messages (HELLO, RESIZE, SELECT, RESUME and viewer state's) and the table's reports; the viewer's input travels only inside a report, a RULE_EVENT. Four rules shape it.

  • One message per report, never held back. Nothing waits on a timer but the pointer's moves, paced at sixty a second.
  • As few bytes as possible. Raw text is one byte for an ASCII character, and the commonest events take a few bytes.
  • No guessing. An event starts with 0xFF, which never occurs in UTF-8, so the start of every event is known with no timeout, and its length from its type.
  • Bounded everywhere. Every length has a maximum, and every reader refuses whole what breaks a bound.

The stream is defined so that it also works over any reliable ordered byte stream, such as a microcontroller's serial line. Everything in it is fixed-size or length-prefixed, and can be decoded byte by byte with a few dozen bytes of state.

4.2 Framing and encoding

DOC-1929 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-200, REQ-201

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-200 Input is sent as one ordered stream of raw UTF-8 text and 0xFF-framed events (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-201 Input protocol unsigned varints: shortest encoding, at most 5 bytes, 32 bits (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A message MUST hold whole events and whole UTF-8 characters, so that a channel can read each message alone. Text may be split between messages anywhere between characters. A message is at most MAX_MESSAGE, 8,192 bytes.

NameEncoding
u8One byte
uvUnsigned varint: 7 bits a byte, least significant group first, the high bit set on every byte but the last. 0 to 127 take one byte. At most 5 bytes, and a longer or non-minimal encoding is a protocol error.
svSigned varint: zigzag, (n << 1) ^ (n >> 31), then uv. -64 to 63 take one byte.
struv byte length, then that many bytes of UTF-8, within the field's own maximum.

A field marked ? in this part is present only when its flag bit is set.

A protocol error closes the connection with code 4000. What was read before the close may still be acted on, a message behind the faulty one included. A field over its maximum, a message over its bound and a varint over 5 bytes or not minimal are each one.

4.3 Raw text

DOC-1930 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-200, REQ-201, REQ-6528

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-200 Input is sent as one ordered stream of raw UTF-8 text and 0xFF-framed events (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-201 Input protocol unsigned varints: shortest encoding, at most 5 bytes, 32 bits (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Any byte other than 0xFF begins raw UTF-8 text. Raw text is text that does not come from a key: an input method's committed text, and a phone's. A key is never written as raw text: every key is a KEY event carrying its text.

Where it goes. Under push protocol 10 raw text is the viewer's input, so it appears only in the body of a RULE_EVENT, in place of an input event, when a text rule of the open page's rule table fired on it and its group reported it. A reader of the stream at the top level still recognises raw text by its first byte, and a server MUST treat it there as a protocol error and close the connection with code 4000.

  • Text MUST NOT contain control characters, U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F. Enter, Tab, Backspace, Escape and every Control, Alt, Super, Hyper or Meta combination are key events.
  • Bytes 0xC0, 0xC1 and 0xF5 to 0xFE outside an event, and malformed UTF-8, are protocol errors.
  • A character cut short by the next event, as in E2 82 FF 05, is malformed at once.
  • On a WebSocket a character cut by the end of its message is a protocol error, because a message is read alone. On a byte stream, a character cut by the end of what has arrived waits for the rest.
  • Raw text carries no stamp of its own: the RULE_EVENT that carries it is stamped with the page and sub-code on screen.

Why a reader cannot lose its place. No UTF-8 sequence holds 0xFF, so text can never forge an event. Inside an event, position decides: 0xFF may be a field's byte, and is read as one because every field's length is known from what came before. An extension's payload is taken whole by its length. A flag bit, type or value nobody defined is a protocol error, not something to step over, so there is no resynchronising, and no state in which a reader carries on having lost its place.

4.4 The events

DOC-1931 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-202, REQ-1556, REQ-6528

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-202 Input protocol events: the core events and extensions, each with its fixed layout (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1556 A PAGE event (0x0A) from any receiver MUST be refused as a protocol error; receivers state selection with SELECT alone (to be rechecked on main).

An event is 0xFF, a type byte, then its fields.

Type rangeLayout
0x01 to 0x3FCore events, of fixed layout. An unknown core type is a protocol error.
0x40 to 0x7FExtensions: a uv length, then the payload, at most 8,192 bytes. A reader skips one it does not know. A field that a known extension's payload cuts short is a protocol error, and so are bytes after its last field.
0x00, 0x80 to 0xFFReserved: a protocol error.

The events marked input below are the viewer's input to a page. A receiver gives each to the open page's rule table when the last column says, and sends it only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a rule of that table fired on it and that rule's group applied a REPORT of the firing in the event's own handling. The others are the session's and travel at the top level of the stream.

TypeNameFieldsWhen
0x01KEYThe stamp, flags, key and moreInput: every press, repeat and release
0x02MOUSEThe stamp, flags u8, button u8, col uv, row uv, px? uv, py? uv, mods? u8Input: every press and release over the page, and every move that changes the dot
0x03WHEELThe stamp, flags u8, dx sv, dy sv, col uv, row uv, px? uv, py? uv, mods? u8Input: while the pointer is over the page
0x04PASTEThe stamp, str of at most 4,000 bytesInput: while the page has the keyboard focus
0x05FOCUS_INNoneInput: when the page gains the keyboard
0x06FOCUS_OUTNoneInput: when the page loses the keyboard
0x07RESIZEcols uv, rows uv, pw uv, ph uvAlways
0x08COMPOSEThe stamp, cursor uv, str of at most 256 bytesInput: while an input method composes
0x09HELLOversion uv, caps uv, agent? strFirst, once
0x0ANoneWas PAGE until 31 October 2026. It is unused, so it is a protocol error like any unknown core type.Never
0x40SELECTLength, then the place as textWhenever the connection's selection changes, and at the start of a session
0x41, 0x42NoneReserved. They were TUNE and UNTUNE, never built.Never
0x43HOVERLength, the stamp, flags u8, col uv, row uvInput: as the pointer enters and leaves a control
0x44TOUCHLength, the stamp, flags u8, id u8, col uv, row uv, px? uv, py? uvInput: every contact after the first, when both sides set TOUCH
0x45RESUMELength, token 16 bytes, acked u16 big-endian, exactly 18 bytes of payloadAfter HELLO, in a reconnection's first message
0x4BRULE_EVENTLength, the stamp, the table's generation, the rule, the row, the page tick, a kind, a target and a body: nothing, the input events the rule reported, or a value and its readingWhen a REPORT command of the open page's table is applied
0x4CPAGE_STATELength, the stamp, the query's identifier, and the page's local stateOnce, in answer to a RULES_QUERY record for the open page
0x4DRULES_FAULTLength, the stamp, the table's generation, a code and a countAt most once a second for each fault and page

There are no modes and no channel-wide switch: a page asks for input with its rule table, and a page with no table is sent none. A server MUST treat an input event, or raw text, at the top level of the stream as a protocol error and close the connection with code 4000. A receiver MUST NOT send TOUCH, a MOUSE of a device other than the mouse, RESUME or SELECT unless both sides set the capability it needs.

What a channel learns of the pointer is in where the pointer is, and what the reports of a rule table reveal, and to whom, is in privacy of the rule table.

4.5 HELLO

DOC-1932 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-205, REQ-520, REQ-6927

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-520 The user agent string (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6927 Push protocol 11 adds capability bit 26, MAGAZINE_SOUND_CAP, without which a receiver is sent no magazine music and no page magazine-music setting (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

HELLO is the first event of a session, and is sent once. version is the connection's version of the input protocol, 10 or 11, the one the subprotocol the channel answered with names (opening the connection), and caps is the receiver's capabilities, of which a receiver offers only those that version defines. A value of caps with bit 16 set is a protocol error, and so is any other version.

agent is the receiver's user agent string, NeoTeletext/0.1 (macOS), or product/version (platform) neoteletext/version for another program on the engine: at most 64 bytes of printable ASCII. It is present when caps has AGENT, and is sent only over a transport without HTTP, such as a serial line. Over the WebSocket the channel has it from the upgrade's User-Agent header, so it is not sent twice.

The stream's first bytes are therefore always FF 09, and a channel answers with WELCOME or a close of 4001.

4.6 Selected, active and focused

DOC-1933 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1553, REQ-1554

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1553 A connection's selected page is active: the channel sends it every update for as long as it is selected, whatever the focus or the viewer's input (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1554 Keys reach the selected page only while it holds the keyboard focus (to be rechecked on main).

Three words are defined once, here.

Selected
The page and sub-page a tab shows, named by SELECT. A connection has at most one selection, which is what the channel sends, keeps and compares.
Active
What a selected page is to the program. An active page receives the program's updates, whatever the viewer's input is doing. Only a new selection, a SELECT of nothing included, ends them.
Focused
What a selected page is for the viewer's input, and only for input. A page has the keyboard focus while keys go to it, which FOCUS_IN and FOCUS_OUT tell the channel, and the pointer focus while the pointer or a touch is over its page area, which MOUSE gone ends.

So a page can be active without being focused: in a tab behind another, in a window behind another application, while the viewer types an address, or with the pointer outside it. Losing either focus MUST NOT change the selection or stop updates.

4.7 The stamp

DOC-1934 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1555, REQ-1557

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1555 Every input event except focus and session events carries a page and sub-code stamp (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1557 Server checks input page stamp against the connection's selection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

KEY, PASTE, COMPOSE, MOUSE, WHEEL, TOUCH and HOVER each begin with page uv and sub uv, before their other fields: the page and sub-code on screen in the tab when the event happened. That is what the viewer was looking at, not merely what was selected: between a new selection and the arrival of its page, the old page is still on screen, and a click aimed at it carries the old page.

  • page is 0x100 to 0x8FF. sub is a sub-code 0x0000 to 0x3F7E, with no bit outside the thirteen, and never 0x3F7F, because a page on screen is always a particular sub-page. Anything else is a protocol error, and so is a page of 0.
  • Page 100, sub-code 0000 is the three bytes 80 02 00, and a stamp is four bytes at most.
  • No other event has one. FOCUS_IN and FOCUS_OUT are always acted on, since FOCUS_OUT releases held keys and must never be dropped.

The channel's check. A channel compares each stamp with the connection's selection as last recorded. When the page and sub-code are the same, the event is acted on. When they differ, the event is dropped and nothing of it applied, the drop is counted, at most one log line an interval names the count, and the connection is kept.

A release is never dropped: one whose stamp does not match is still applied, as a release of what the connection holds, so that nothing stays held. So is a pointer's gone. A press with a stamp that does not match is dropped.

The selection stays the only truth: a stamp can only cause a drop, never send input to a page other than the selection.

4.8 Selecting a page

DOC-1753 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1090, REQ-1502, REQ-1693, REQ-2787

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1090 REQ-INT-140: A receiver sends the selected page and sub-page with SELECT (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1502 Each live connection has exactly one selection, made of one page number and one sub-code (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1693 A channel MUST have one complete, fixed, defined URL map, in which a channel is a folder and a place in it is the end of the path (to be rechecked on main).

SELECT is the only message that names a selection. It is an extension, 0x40, whose payload is the place as text, the same text the URL map reads.

PayloadSelects
302The page: sub-code 3F7F, "no particular page sub-code", for a page keyed by its number alone, or a link or bookmark that names no sub-page
302/0002One sub-page: a sub-code 0000 to 3F7E
Either followed by ? and a queryThe same, with the query of the address selected, as written: name=value pairs joined by &, in bytes 0x21 to 0x7E with no #, at most 8,000 bytes
EmptyNothing: the tab no longer shows a page of the channel. As a connection's first selection it counts as none, and the connection is shown the channel's initial page, which is then its selection.

Digits are capitals, in the one spelling of the map. Anything else is a protocol error, as is a query with no page, a ? with nothing after it, and a sub-code of 3F7F. A query belongs to this one selection: a SELECT that does not carry it leaves it behind.

When it goes. A receiver MUST send SELECT whenever the page or sub-page shown in its tab changes, on that tab's own connection, whatever the focus: a page keyed or followed by a link, a sub-page stepped to or chosen from the list. It sends it at the start of each session, after HELLO and after any RESUME, when the tab shows a page of the channel, so a reconnection is sent its page again. It sends an empty SELECT when the tab leaves the channel's pages. It sends one for a page a REDIRECT moved it to. It is sent only when both sides set SELECT, and a receiver that does not set it has no selection and is sent no page of its own choosing.

SELECT counts no input units. A SELECT that repeats a selection that stands, awaited or shown, the same page, sub-code and query, is no new selection: a server does nothing for it and sends no answer. A page selected with 3F7F becomes a sub-page when it is answered, so once page 100 has come as 100/0000, a second SELECT of 100 is a new selection, and only 100/0000 repeats it. A selection DENIED ended no longer stands, so a SELECT that repeats it is a new selection: the server asks its program again, and it has an ending of its own.

What the tab is then sent. Every sub-code a page has is one of its sub-pages, all of them peers, and the page's order is ascending sub-code, 0000 first when present. For a page selection, the tab shows the page's first sub-page in that order, and that sub-page then is the selection, exactly as if the viewer had chosen it: the channel answers with it, the receiver sends no second SELECT, and stepping goes on from it. For a sub-page selection, the tab shows that sub-page alone, and is sent only it and its changes, while the page's other sub-pages change, until it selects something else.

Stepping to the next or previous sub-page is a selection of that sub-code. Sub-pages are never sent with their page, and nothing rotates on a live channel: the sub-page shown changes only when the viewer selects another, or when the program moves the tab, which is itself a selection.

Its ending. Every selection ends with a page or with DENIED, by the deadline.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.6.1 Packets X/27/0 to X/27/3 for Editorial Linking; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.1 Page numbering

4.9 KEY

DOC-1935 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-203, REQ-204, REQ-1350, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-204 Functional codes: every non-character key has one fixed code, 1 to 127 from the protocol's table, only ever added to (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1350 Protocol items give each event as it is now sent (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

The stamp, flags u8, key uv, mods? u8, text? str of at most 32 bytes, base? uv.

flags bitMeaning
0 and 1Action: 0 press, 1 repeat, 2 release. 3 is a protocol error.
2F: key is a functional code, not a code point. A code that names no key is a protocol error.
3M: mods present. It is omitted when 0, and present and 0 is a protocol error.
4T: text present: the key produced text.
5B: base present: it differs from key.
6L: lost, on a release only: the key did not come up, because the page lost the input. A protocol error with any other action.
7Reserved: a protocol error when set.
  • key: for a character key, the Unicode code point of the key without Shift, so Control-Shift-A sends a with Shift and Control; otherwise a functional code.
  • mods: 1 Shift, 2 Alt (Option on macOS), 4 Control, 8 Super (Command, Windows), 16 Hyper, 32 Meta, 64 Caps Lock, 128 Num Lock, as the Kitty keyboard protocol has them.
  • text: the text the press produced, if any, with no control character.
  • base: the code point the same physical key has in a United States layout, so a channel's shortcuts work on any layout.

When a key goes. A receiver gives the open page's rule table every key of the page that the table's triggers ask for: every press, repeat and release, the keys that only modify or lock included, and the dead key. A key reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a key or key_up rule of that table fired on it and its group reported it in that key's own handling (a page asks for input with its rule table); a page with no table is sent no key, and a KEY at the top level of the stream is a protocol error. Inside a RULE_EVENT the bytes are exactly those above, from the FF 01: a release is written as FF 01, the stamp, its flags and key. A channel that only types takes text from presses and repeats.

4.10 Functional key codes

DOC-1936 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-204

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-204 Functional codes: every non-character key has one fixed code, 1 to 127 from the protocol's table, only ever added to (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every key that is not a character has one code, which never changes: new keys are only ever added. Codes 1 to 127 take one byte.

4.11 International keyboards

DOC-1937 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-215

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-215 Text is sent as the Unicode the layout or input method produced (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The protocol carries what the viewer typed, in whatever language and on whatever layout, and leaves its meaning to the channel.

  1. Text is Unicode, after the layout. A key's result is sent as the characters the system's layout produced. A receiver MUST NOT translate text into a teletext character set: the channel maps it onto the sets of the page it draws.
  2. Logical order. Text goes in the order it was typed, which for right-to-left scripts is logical order, never the visual order a page may be drawn in.
  3. Normalized. Text is sent in Unicode Normalization Form C, so that a channel compares what it receives without normalizing it again.
  4. Dead keys. A dead key sends no text: it sends KEY with the functional code of Dead and base. The key after it sends the composed character as text, or both characters when the two do not compose.
  5. AltGr is a level shift, not a modifier. A character typed with AltGr is sent as KEY with that text and no modifiers. A receiver on a system that reports AltGr as Control and Alt held together MUST NOT report it so. AltGr itself is the key AltGraph.
  6. Input methods compose in the receiver: their preedit goes as COMPOSE, and what they commit as raw text. Their own keys have functional codes from 128.
  7. key follows the layout, and base the position. A channel binds a letter by key, and a position, such as a game's movement keys, by base.
  8. Digits. The keypad's keys are their functional codes, with their characters as text. A layout that types native digits sends those characters, and a channel that selects pages by number SHOULD take the decimal digits of any script as the digits 0 to 9.
  9. Lock states and layout changes send nothing of their own beyond the lock bits in mods, so the viewer's choice of language is never announced.
  10. Phones. A phone keyboard's text is text under the same rules, with no modifiers.

4.12 MOUSE and WHEEL

DOC-1938 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-202, REQ-214, REQ-221, REQ-222, REQ-1351, REQ-1355, REQ-1369, REQ-5622, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-202 Input protocol events: the core events and extensions, each with its fixed layout (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-221 The pointer's moves of each contact are paced at most once each 1000/60 ms (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-222 Gone: a receiver sends action 3 when the pointer leaves or a contact is cancelled (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1351 Every move over the page is taken for the page's rule table, and sent only as a move rule reports it (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

flags bitsMOUSEWHEEL
0 and 1Action: 0 press, 1 release, 2 move, 3 goneUnused, and a protocol error when set
2px, py presentThe same
3mods presentThe same
4 and 5The device: 0 a mouse or trackpad, 1 touch, 2 a pen, 3 a protocol error. Set only when both sides set TOUCH, and otherwise 0.A protocol error when set
6 and 7A protocol error when setA protocol error when set
  • button: on press and release, 0 left, 1 middle, 2 right, 3 back, 4 forward, 5 and up others. On move and gone, a bit mask of the buttons held.
  • col, row: the character cell, from the top left of the page: columns 0 to 39, rows 0 to 24. A value beyond them is a protocol error.
  • px, py: the dot of the page image from the same origin, 12 to a cell across and 20 down, sent whenever the receiver knows them.
  • dx, dy: scroll in 1/120ths of a line, positive right and down. A wheel that moves in notches sends at least a whole line, 120, a notch. A trackpad's continuous scrolling is sent as it comes.

When they go. A receiver gives the open page's rule table the pointer's presses, releases and moves over the page and the wheel when the table's triggers ask for them, and a MOUSE or a WHEEL reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT: when a press, release, move, enter, leave or wheel rule of that table fired on it and its group reported it in that event's own handling (rules, triggers, keys and targets). A page with no table is sent none, and a MOUSE or WHEEL at the top level of the stream is a protocol error. A move rule fires only on a move to another pixel, so a press is reported once and an unchanged position is never reported again.

Gone says the pointer has gone and nothing it held was pressed. A receiver gives it to the page's table when the pointer leaves the open page or the page loses the input, after the waiting move, and when the system or the receiver cancels a contact. button is the mask held, and col and row the last position given. What it held is released without a click, and a channel MUST NOT act on it as on a release.

A link the page declares is the receiver's on every page: a click or tap on it follows it, no press, release or contact on it is given to the page's table or sent to the channel, and a press rule on a target under a link does not fire. A drag begun off a link stays the page's when it crosses one. The wheel over a page whose page number has more than one sub-code steps the sub-pages, unless the pointer is inside the target of a wheel rule of the page's table (a page asks for input with its rule table).

4.13 TOUCH and pens

DOC-1939 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-223, REQ-1362, REQ-1363, REQ-1364, REQ-1370, REQ-1371, REQ-1376, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1362 The first contact is the mouse (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1363 MOUSE flags carry the device (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1364 Further contacts as TOUCH (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1371 A pen is sent as MOUSE with device 2 (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-1376 Input protocol items give sizes for tap, second-finger down and two-finger move (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

TOUCH is an extension, 0x44, used only when both sides set TOUCH. Its payload is the stamp, flags u8, id u8, col uv, row uv, px? uv, py? uv, and nothing after.

  • flags bits 0 and 1 are the action, as MOUSE's: 0 down, 1 up, 2 move, 3 gone. Bit 2 says px and py are present. Bits 3 to 7 are a protocol error.
  • id is 1 to 9, the contact's number from its beginning to its end, the lowest free when it begins. 0 or above 9 is a protocol error. At most ten contacts are on the page at once.
  • The first contact down, while no other is down and no mouse button is held, is a MOUSE: a press of button 0, moves with button 0 held, a release as it lifts, device 1. Every further contact is a TOUCH. An eleventh is nothing until one ends. Without the capability, only the first counts, as the mouse.
  • A contact's beginning and end are taken the moment the system reports them, never held to recognise a gesture. A cancelled contact is gone. There is no move for a finger before it is down or after it lifts.
  • A pen is a MOUSE with device 2: touching is button 0, its barrel button button 2, and hovering, where the hardware reports it, moves with no button. Pressure, tilt and a contact's size are not carried.

When they go. A receiver gives every contact that begins on the open page to that page's rule table when the table's triggers ask for the pointer, two fingers and a pinch included, and a TOUCH reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a rule of the table fired on it and its group reported it (a page asks for input with its rule table). A page with no table is sent no contact. The system's gestures from the screen's edges are the system's.

The NeoTeletext server sets TOUCH, and gives a program a reported contact after the first as an input of kind touch, with its action, contact number, cell and dot (what a program hears of input).

4.14 HOVER

DOC-1940 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-220, REQ-1361, REQ-1370, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-220 HOVER: while keys go to a channel, a receiver tells the channel as the pointer enters and leaves each control of the open page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1361 HOVER sent as pointer enters and leaves a control (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

HOVER is an extension, 0x43. Its payload is the stamp, flags u8, col uv and row uv. Bit 0 of flags is 1 when the pointer left the control and 0 when it entered, and any other bit is a protocol error. col and row are the control's first cell, its top left.

It is made as the pointer enters and leaves a control of the open page. Leaving one control for another makes the leave, then the enter. It lets a channel show something as the pointer passes, a row's summary or a help line, without working out from the moves which control the pointer is over. It is made only for a mouse or a pen that hovers, never for a finger.

When it goes. A HOVER reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when an enter or leave rule of the open page's rule table whose target is that control (or any control) fired and its group reported it; a page with no table is sent none, and a HOVER at the top level of the stream is a protocol error. An enter or leave on a ReGIS drawing is carried as DRAWING_HOVER, and on a teletext sprite, a NAPLPS object or a rectangle as the MOUSE move that caused it, with the target named (rules, triggers, keys and targets).

4.15 PASTE and COMPOSE

DOC-1941 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-202, REQ-1384, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-202 Input protocol events: the core events and extensions, each with its fixed layout (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1384 NeoTeletext MUST send a mouse click over a page only when the page's rule table asks for it, and never a click with the browser's modifier (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

PASTE is the whole paste as one event: the stamp, then a str of at most 4,000 bytes. It may contain control characters: a channel treats it as data, never as keystrokes. A longer paste is cut at a character boundary.

COMPOSE is an input method's preedit, as it changes: the stamp, cursor uv, a code-point offset into the text, at most its length, then a str of at most 256 bytes with no control character. An empty string ends composition.

When they go. A receiver gives a paste and a composition made while the open page has the keyboard to that page's rule table, and each reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a text rule of the table fired on it and its group reported it; a page with no table is sent none, and either at the top level of the stream is a protocol error.

4.16 FOCUS_IN, FOCUS_OUT and RESIZE

DOC-1942 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-202, REQ-1643, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-202 Input protocol events: the core events and extensions, each with its fixed layout (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1643 A teletext page is 40 columns by 25 rows (to be rechecked on main); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

FOCUS_IN and FOCUS_OUT say when the open page gains and loses the keyboard. They carry nothing. A receiver gives them to the page's rule table as they happen, and each reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a focus or blur rule of the table fired on it and its group reported it; a page with no table is sent neither, and either at the top level of the stream is a protocol error. Losing the keyboard releases everything held, as held input says, whether or not a rule reports it; a program hears focus and blur only after the connection's first selection.

RESIZE gives the page's text area in cells and the page image in pixels as the receiver draws it. It is the session's, not the viewer's input to a page, so it stays at the top level of the stream: a receiver sends it after WELCOME and whenever the drawn size changes. A teletext page is always 40 by 25, and cols or rows of 0 or above that is a protocol error, so RESIZE changes only when the drawn size does. pw and ph are 0 when unknown. The NeoTeletext browser sends 0, and the server passes no RESIZE to a program.

4.17 The input count and the rate

DOC-1943 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-208, REQ-209, REQ-225, REQ-1334, REQ-1375, REQ-6528

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-208 The rate: a sender sends at most 120 input units in any second (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-209 The cursor record carries the input count the channel has acted on (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-225 Pointer moves, gone, HOVER, COMPOSE, SELECT and RESUME count no input units (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1375 A touch contact's down and up each count as input units (to be rechecked on main).

The input count is how much of the session's input the channel has acted on, and is what a cursor record acknowledges. Under push protocol 10 it counts messages, not the events inside them: HELLO and RESIZE count one each, and a RULE_EVENT counts one whatever it carries (a key, a paste, a move, a composition, two events, a bare firing or a value), so a pointer's move and an input method's composition are acknowledged too. SELECT, RESUME, PAGE_STATE and RULES_FAULT count none. A receiver counts what it sends the same way. In a resumed session HELLO counts nothing.

The count wraps at 65,536 and is compared by RFC 1982 serial arithmetic: an older acknowledgement changes nothing, and one beyond what was sent is ignored.

A message of no input units is never acknowledged. A receiver takes a cursor record wherever it comes. The NeoTeletext server ends every page frame with one, which carries the count, and sends one alone only when no frame has carried the count ACKNOWLEDGEMENT_WAIT_MS, 250 ms, after the first input it covers, and never before a selection is made. So an answered report costs one cursor record, or two when the answer comes after the wait, and a run of reports on a page that publishes nothing costs one for each wait. A receiver waits for none of this before it shows anything. A RULE_EVENT not acknowledged when its connection ends is discarded and never sent again (the lifetime of local state).

The rate. A receiver sends at most MAX_PER_SECOND, 120, input messages in any second, counted over a sliding second, and reads what a RULE_EVENT carries to apply it: one that carries a release (a key's, a button's or a contact's up) always goes, one that carries a move is not held to it, so the pointer can never cost a key, and a bare firing and a value are held to it. Beside that, the receiver's trusted part sends at most 120 reports a second for a page, of which at most 20 may carry no input event, and drops the rest, reporting RULES_FAULT code 3 (the gate).

4.18 Held input

DOC-1944 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-207, REQ-5548

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-207 Held input is released when the page loses keyboard focus (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A key or button is held when it went down and has not come up. It is released whenever the page loses the input, and releasing never deselects the page.

SignalReleases
FOCUS_OUT: the page loses the keyboardEvery held key, button and contact
A pointer's goneThe buttons and the contact it held, without a click
A change of selection, an empty SELECT, the program moving the tab, or the page paused because its tab is no longer the active oneEverything
A connection closing or droppingEverything

A receiver. When the page loses the keyboard, the pointer leaves, the page is paused or the page is closed, a receiver gives the page's rule table a KEY release with the L flag set for each held key, a release marked lost for each held button, and a leave for every target the pointer was inside, each stamped with the page that held it. These are handled at once, whatever the table's budgets, after the events already waiting, so that key_up, release and leave rules fire and no note of a local sound is left sounding. Such a release reaches the channel only when a rule of the table reports it. On a disconnect the receiver drops the page's local state at once and runs no handling (the lifetime of local state).

A channel keeps what each connection holds. On a signal it treats whatever is still held as released itself, and acts on nothing else, because a receiver may have sent nothing: a dropped connection cannot, and a terminal that reports no releases never does. The NeoTeletext server keeps a press as held only when a rule of the page's table reported it and the table of the page on which it was pressed asks for releases of that key, button or contact: a rule with a key_up trigger whose key set includes the key, or a rule with a release trigger that names the button, a contact being the left button. Only the trigger's keys or button are read, not its modifiers, its target or the rule's condition. When a connection closes, or its selection changes, while such a key, button or contact is held, the server gives the program the release marked lost, with that press's rule, row and tick. A press on a page whose table asks for no release of it is not held and no lost release is given for it, so that a program still hears nothing no rule asked for.

The mark. Every such release reaches a channel's program marked lost: true, so a game can tell "the player let go" from "the player left". A real key-up or button-up carries no mark.

4.19 The pointer's moves

DOC-1945 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-221, REQ-1352, REQ-1353, REQ-1354, REQ-1356, REQ-1360, REQ-1366

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-221 The pointer's moves of each contact are paced at most once each 1000/60 ms (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1352 Sixty a second (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1353 A pointer move arriving at least 1000/60 ms after the last sent move goes at once (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1354 Waiting move is written before any other event (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1356 Never behind the network (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-1360 Server passes each connection's pointer moves through one latest-wins slot at most 60 a second (to be rechecked on main).

A receiver takes every move that changes the dot under the pointer while it is over the open page, buttons held or not, and gives it to the page's rule table when the table asks for the pointer's moves, within these rules, which keep the pointer from ever delaying a key.

  • Sixty a second. At most one move in each period of 1000/60 ms. While moves follow each other, the kth period ends at the time of the move that began the run plus k times 1,000,000 / 60 microseconds, counted exactly, so that the average is exactly 60 a second with no drift.
  • At once if it can, the latest kept. A move that comes 1000/60 ms or more after the last goes at once, and begins a run. One that comes sooner waits in one slot, replacing any position waiting there. An unchanged position does not go again, and nothing runs while the pointer is still.
  • Order. Before any other event is taken, the move waiting in the slot is taken first, so a release never comes before the move that ended the drag.
  • Each contact has a slot and a pace of its own, and the moves of several contacts waiting at one moment are taken together.

What leaves. A move reaches the channel only inside a RULE_EVENT, when a move rule of the table fired on it, which it does only for a move to another pixel, or an enter or leave rule fired on it, and the rule's group reported it. Such a RULE_EVENT counts one for acknowledgement and is written like any other message: it is never dropped or replaced while the connection is congested (the input count and the rate).

At the server. A server holds each connection's reported moves to the same pace before its program hears them: at most 60 a second, by the same rule, the latest kept and an unchanged position not sent again. Each connection has one move waiting for the program, which a newer move replaces until the program takes it, so a program that reads slowly is given the latest position and never a backlog. A waiting move takes none of the room for the program's other lines (overload), so no number of moves costs a program a key or a release. Any other event of the connection brings its waiting move to the program first, and no later move overtakes it. The NeoTeletext server on Cloudflare keeps the pace but no slot: a move waits for its program as any line does.

4.20 Where the pointer is, at any size

DOC-1946 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1359, REQ-1377

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1359 Documents state that a channel learns pointer position only over its own page (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1377 Positions are sent as the page image's cell and dot at any drawn size (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver draws a page at whatever size its screen allows, and every position it sends is in the page's own units, so that a channel answers the pointer the same way at every size.

  • The units. The image is 480 by 500 dots, 12 to a cell across and 20 down, from the page's top left. The dot is always inside the cell: px / 12 = col and py / 20 = row, rounded down.
  • The conversion. A receiver takes the pointer's position, subtracts the top left of the rectangle where the image was last drawn, and scales by the image's size in dots over the rectangle's size, rounding down: px = (x - left) × 480 / width, and the same down. The border of the screen colour around the image is not the page. A contact's position is the point the system reports for it, converted the same way.
  • Only the open page, at rest. Positions go only for the page keys go to, while it is drawn where the receiver will keep it: not over a page still zooming, sliding or shown as one of many.
  • Drawn larger, several screen pixels show each dot. A move within one dot changes nothing and is not sent, so a page drawn larger costs no more moves. Drawn smaller, one screen pixel covers more than one dot, so some dots cannot be pointed at and a move may step several dots at once. The cell stays exact until a cell is smaller than a pixel. At a size that is not a whole multiple of the image, the dot sent may be the neighbour of the one drawn under the pointer's tip, and is never another cell's.
  • A channel tests where a click landed by its cell, and treats the dot as finer detail, exact only at the image's own size or larger. A channel MUST cope with no dot at all: a receiver that knows only cells sends none.
  • Double height and double size. The cell sent is the grid cell under the pointer, not the cell where a double-height character begins. A channel whose control spans two rows answers both.
  • A trusted check. A receiver SHOULD refuse a cell outside the page, and a dot outside the image or its cell, before anything is encoded. A position comes from outside and is untrusted, so a server checks it again: the NeoTeletext server drops an event whose dot lies outside its cell, as it drops one whose cell is beyond the page, and its program never hears it.

What a channel learns. It learns the pointer's position over its own open page, its clicks, drags and moves, and the contacts on it, while keys go to it. It learns nothing elsewhere: not over another tab, the receiver's own controls or another window, and nothing while keys do not go to it.

4.21 Controls and links under the pointer

DOC-1947 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-218

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-218 Hover look for the control or link under the pointer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A page says which of its cells it answers itself, in its own packets, so that a receiver can show them as it shows links. The pointer is a hand over them, and a control or a link under the pointer takes a look the receiver draws from the page's own colours, with what Level 2.5 already does to them.

  • Hover: each colour of its cells becomes the same entry of the adjacent colour table, the pairing of the Additional Flash Functions' colour flash: CLUT 0 with 1, 2 with 3. A page chooses its hover colours by defining CLUTs 2 and 3 in packet X/28/0 Format 1 and drawing its controls from them. With Table 30's colours, hover is the half-intensity colour of CLUT 1.
  • Pressed, while a button is held on it or a contact is on it: the hover colours with foreground and background exchanged, as Invert Colour exchanges them. A finger gives no hover look.

The receiver draws both itself, at once, and sends nothing for them, so a page lights under the pointer without the channel drawing a copy of it for each viewer. It draws them whether or not the page has a rule table. A page's rule table may also change a control's look itself, with an animation operation in a group (the animation state).

A control is only where a click lands, and a target a rule can name ({"control": n}). A click on it reaches the channel only when a press or release rule of the open page's table whose target is that control, any control or the page fired and its group reported it, as a MOUSE at its cell inside a RULE_EVENT with the control named as the target; the channel decides what it means. Declaring controls asks for nothing: a page asks for input with its rule table (a page asks for input with its rule table).

4.22 The phone keyboard

DOC-2029 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-98, REQ-1387

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1387 NeoTeletext typing and phone keyboard compile out as Cargo features (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A phone can be the keyboard of a channel. It scans a QR code and sends its keys through the relay of qrkeyboard, another project (qrkeyboard.com), whose protocol 3 a NeoTeletext receiver speaks as the screen. That protocol is qrkeyboard's, and is defined there. This item says what a NeoTeletext receiver and neottx keyboard do with it. A channel need do nothing of its own for a phone: a phone's keys are given to the open page's rule table exactly as the viewer's own keys are, under the rules of international keyboards, and reach the channel only when a rule of that table reports them. A page with no table is sent nothing a phone types.

What a phone's keys become. A phone is a keyboard and no more: its keys carry no modifiers.

From the phoneBecomes
A key of the layout going down, named as W3C KeyboardEvent.key names itA KEY press. A single printable character is that character, in lower case, with itself as text. Any other name is its functional code with no text, so the colour keys are 92 to 95, and a name with no code is Unidentified.
That key coming upA KEY release. Only a key the screen holds is released, and a key held past 15 seconds is released without its up.
Text typed in the phone's boxRaw text, with control characters taken out, in messages of whole characters
A special key of the box: Backspace, Tab, Enter, Escape or an arrow, with a countA press and a release of that key, as many times as the count, at most 10,000

neottx keyboard bridges a phone to a channel that takes input, so that a channel gets a phone keyboard without implementing qrkeyboard: neottx keyboard <ws address> [--relay <address>] [--pin] [--name <name>] [--qr-page <mpp> --qr-output <file>]. It offers a text box, a direction pad and the four colour keys.

  • It connects as a receiver that draws nothing: HELLO with no capabilities, so no SELECT, and after WELCOME a RESIZE of 40 by 25 with its pixels unknown.
  • With no SELECT capability the connection takes the channel's initial page, and a page the channel sends is its selection.
  • It is a receiver, so it holds the rule table of the page the channel last sent (the RULES record the server sends before the page), evaluates it, and sends a phone's keys, its text and the gain of the keyboard only inside the RULE_EVENTs its rules report; a page with no table is sent nothing. It has no pointer and plays no sound, so the table's rules on those do nothing in it.
  • It reads the header of each page the channel sends, and stamps every report with that page and sub-code. It reports nothing before the first page, since a report needs a page to be stamped with.
  • It writes the QR code to the terminal with the warning that anyone who can see it can type, and with --qr-page as a page's mosaics too. neottx qr does that for any text.
  • It keeps no viewer key: when a channel asks to know the viewer, it answers that it keeps no state.
  • A dropped phone may come back for 30 seconds and keep the screen.

The screen's side, which the engine's crate neoteletext-qrkeyboard gives neottx and the browser:

  • It asks the relay for an instance, and shows a QR code of <relay>/app#c=<code>&k=<key>&h=<hash>. The join code, the pairing key when there is no PIN, and the configuration's hash go only in the address's fragment, which a phone never sends. The hash is SHA-256 of the configuration in qrkeyboard's canonical JSON, cut to 128 bits.
  • It pairs by a fresh salt from each end and, with a PIN, SPAKE2 (RFC 9382) on P-256, bound to the code and the hash. Each frame is then sealed with AES-256-GCM under a counter nonce, one key each way, and each counter is taken once and in order.
  • Without a PIN, a phone counts as connected at its first sealed frame that opens, not at its salt, which anyone on the relay can send.
  • A PIN is four digits, and five failed runs lock the screen.
  • A relay's WebSocket on another host than the relay is refused. Frames are at most 1,024 bytes, and an HTTP response's body at most 64 KiB. Keys outside the layout are ignored, and everything the relay and the phone send is untrusted.

In the NeoTeletext browser, a phone's keys go from a keyboard process of their own, which alone holds the pairing secret, to the trusted core and on to the interface, which acts on them as on its own: into a page, where the page's rule table takes them, or choosing pages. They reach the address field only after the viewer puts the caret there with the pointer. One phone at a time. Finish in the strip ends it, and a dropped phone holds the screen for at most 30 seconds. The QR code shows only from the panel, with its warning: whoever scans it has the keyboard.

What the relay learns. It carries sealed frames, so a passive relay or anyone on the network learns a phone keyboard's name, layout, addresses, sizes and timing, and not its keys. The relay's operator also serves the phone its page, so that operator, or whoever compromises the relay's server, can read the PIN and the keys.

4.23 Security and privacy of input

DOC-2033 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1039, REQ-1359, REQ-1378

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1039 Session numbers are never reused, across restarts too (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1359 Documents state that a channel learns pointer position only over its own page (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1378 Keys go to a channel only under all five input conditions, and only as the page's rule table asks (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

What is protected is the viewer's keystrokes and reading habits, the truth of the screen and of a receiver's own controls, a receiver's readers, its own keys, the viewer's keys for channels, and a phone's pairing secret. The attackers considered are a channel's author, a network attacker, a compromised part of a receiver, a hostile relay, anyone who can see the screen, and a stranger who scanned a QR code. A receiver is a terminal: no page can run code, a page's rule table binds events to ordinary protocol commands and is not a program, and nothing on the input path can make a receiver fetch, leave the channel, or do anything but draw and sound.

ThreatAnswer
A page or a channel takes input unaskedA channel is sent only what a rule of the open page's rule table reports, of what the viewer did on that page, and a page with no table is sent nothing. channel.ttx declares nothing of input. Input goes only to the open page of the active tab.
A table, or a compromised decoder, sends what the viewer did not doThe receiver's trusted part builds every report itself, from its own copy of an event it gave that page within the last 4 ticks, at most once for a rule and row, only on that page's own connection, and at most 120 a second (the gate).
A table that is a programA table has no loop, no jump, no conditional inside a group, no multiplication or division and no computed address; it is decoded and evaluated by the engine's crate neoteletext-rules alone, within the limits of the limits, and refused whole when it breaks any.
Keys go somewhere elseThe connection's address comes from the channel's own address, and nothing in the protocol names another.
A keylogger on a plain connectionA receiver says "Not secure" on ws://. wss is the default for any channel worth typing into.
A web page reaching a channel as the viewerAn upgrade that carries Origin is refused, so a receiver cannot be written in a web page. There are no cookies: a viewer is known to a channel only by viewer state's handle, proved on the channel's own push connection.
A compression oracle on private rowsNo permessage-deflate.
A server told apart from a receiver by what it calls itselfNo server reads a receiver's agent text. Capabilities are the only signal.
The channel tracks the pointerIt learns the pointer only through the presses, moves, entries and the wheel its open page's table reports, over that page, and nothing elsewhere.
Fingerprinting by keyboard layoutbase names a key's position, not a layout, and lock states go only in mods. There is no clock beyond the page tick of a report: a channel learns typing rhythm only from arrival times and ticks, and no physical key code.
A paste runs as keystrokesPASTE is one event of known length, which a channel treats as data.
A flood from a channelPushed rows are drawn at the display's rate, records are bounded and checked, a table is held to its per-tick budgets, and a protocol error closes the connection.
A flood from a receiver120 input messages a second at the phone relay, the keyboard process and the receiver's trusted part, which also holds a page's reports to 120 a second, of which 20 with no input event; moves are paced at 60 a second a contact and never cost a key.
A page dresses a control as a link, or the other way roundA control gives a page no power: a click on it reaches the channel only as the MOUSE a rule reports, and a press on a link is never given to the table. A link's destination is shown only outside the page. Controls are bounded and checked like every triplet.
A forged cursor or a forged receiver's controlA receiver draws the cursor in a style no page can draw, only in rows 1 to 23, and its own controls are outside the page.
A compromised part of a receiver typesThe part that draws sends intents, and the trusted part alone encodes and builds every report, for the channel of the page it gave the event to. The part that reads the network holds only that channel's messages, bounded. A keyboard process is a hostile person at the keys: bounded keys, no modifiers, and the rate.
Someone photographs a phone keyboard's QR codeIt shows only when asked for, with its warning. A PIN is offered, and there is one phone.
A session is taken over after a reconnectionA reconnection is a new session for every page, with nothing of any page's local state carried over. With RESUME, only a connection showing the session's token, 128 bits new in each WELCOME, resumes it, and only while no connection holds it. A viewer's identity is viewer state's key, which the browser holds and never sends.
A resumed session acts on a report twice, or loses oneEvery counted message is numbered by the count both sides keep, and the channel drops what it has seen; a report not acknowledged when its connection ends is discarded, never sent again.
A hostile programEvery line it sends is checked whole, its tables by the receiver's own code, its queues are bounded, and one program serves every viewer, so there is no process per viewer to exhaust.
A channel learns what is readAccepted. A selection tells a channel which page and sub-page each viewer reads, as a request tells a web server. A compromised interface could signal what it saw on one channel through what it selects on another.
A stolen viewer identityThere is no cookie to steal. Viewer state is a key pair the browser makes for one channel and proves by signing a fresh challenge on that channel's own push connection; a program sees only an opaque handle derived for that channel.

Privacy. A receiver MUST NOT log keys, and nothing of them persists past the window. A channel learns what the viewer did on its own open page only as that page's table reports it, and nothing elsewhere; what a report and the state query reveal, to whom, and what a channel may do with them is privacy of the rule table. Neither side keeps a page's local state after the page is left or its connection ends. The server's figures identify no viewer. What a phone keyboard's relay learns is in the phone keyboard.

The remaining risks, most serious first: plain ws://, likely where it is used; a compromised interface, unlikely, with a medium consequence; an exploited keyboard process, the same; a QR code photographed on a public screen, medium on both counts; and an imitation of the cursor or of a receiver's controls, medium in likelihood and low in consequence.

5 The downstream record set

DOC-1782 · section

5.1 Downstream is a T42 stream

DOC-1948 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-1480, REQ-1501

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1480 Every program message that reaches a viewer is sent as checked T42 packets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1501 Every page frame on a live connection carries exactly one sub-page (to be rechecked on main).

Everything a channel sends a receiver is teletext. The binary messages, joined in the order sent, are a valid plain T42 file, with nothing between packets and nothing added to them, and no text message is ever sent. A recording of a connection plays in any decoder.

Each message is a whole number of 42-byte packets, of these kinds.

FrameHoldsDelivery
Page frameExactly one sub-page, whole or as changed rowsOnly to the connection whose selection that sub-page is
RecordA record on data channel 12: everything that is not a page, sound among itIn order
Raw packetsPackets a program sent as they are: a recording, or a generated stationIn order, never coalesced

What most viewers read is not the broadcast: page frames give a receiver the pages it selects, and a server never claims otherwise. Raw packets are the opposite: they keep the order a program gave them, nothing in them is coalesced, and a recording played back this way keeps a broadcast's own behaviour, its rotation included.

A page update replaces what it covers, and a row packet belongs to the last header sent. So the unit that can be delayed, dropped or resent is the page frame, never a single packet, and a frame carries its own header so that it stands alone. Over a WebSocket, frames need no sequence numbers: TCP is ordered, and the server knows what each connection was sent. A transport that lost or reordered data would carry its sequence number as a record on data channel 12, never outside the packets, which have no spare field for one.

5.2 Page frames

DOC-1949 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1032, REQ-1065, REQ-1501, REQ-1504, REQ-1553

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1032 Sub-pages pass the wire one at a time, only as a connection's one selection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1501 Every page frame on a live connection carries exactly one sub-page (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1504 A connection's last-sent sub-page is kept, and a later version of the same sub-code is sent as changed rows (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1553 A connection's selected page is active: the channel sends it every update for as long as it is selected, whatever the focus or the viewer's input (to be rechecked on main).

A page frame is exactly one sub-page. No event sends two sub-pages in one frame, of the same page or of different pages. A page with one sub-page is a page whose list has one entry, sent the same way. A frame is at most one sub-page, 3,108 bytes before its LINKS record.

A sub-page is its header, rows 1 to 23, row 24 and the packets X/26 to X/28. The header is in serial magazine mode, C11 set, so the stream is valid teletext.

A whole frame has the erase bit, C4, set, so that a sub-page selected again keeps nothing of an older version a receiver's store may hold. It is in the order of Annex B.2: any M/29 packets, the header, X/27, X/28, X/26, then the rows, a row of spaces not being sent. The first sub-page on a connection, the first after its selection changes, and every sub-page whose page or sub-code differs from the one last sent go whole.

A frame of changed rows is sent only for a later version of the very sub-page, same page number and same sub-code, the connection was last sent. It is the header with C4 clear, then the whole group of packets numbered above 24 when any of them changed, then the rows that changed. A receiver keeps every row the frame does not carry. Should a row be gone from the new version, the sub-page goes whole. Nothing is sent when nothing differs.

The header's text is the sub-page's, sent like any row. The server never rewrites it. Columns 0 to 7 of row 0 are the receiver's.

Links and the cursor follow. In the same binary message, a frame is followed by that sub-page's LINKS record when it has Link Extension links, and then, once the session is welcomed, by a cursor record. A change of links alone is a frame of the header with C4 clear, then its LINKS record.

Keeping the last-sent sub-page. A server keeps, for each connection, the one sub-page it last sent it, in memory only, and takes changes against that. It is dropped when the selection changes and when the connection closes, is never shared between connections, and is never served to anyone.

A selected sub-page that a program sends again goes to the connection whatever its focus: a selected page is active.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.6.1 Packets X/27/0 to X/27/3 for Editorial Linking; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.1 Page number

5.3 What a connection is sent, and when

DOC-1950 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1471, REQ-1472, REQ-1474, REQ-1481, REQ-1502, REQ-6719, REQ-6881

Unfinished.
