A SPRITES or NAPLPS_OBJECTS command is held to the command limit like any other, so a group places a few small sprites or objects; the whole set is sent ahead and a group moves and shows it. The wire vectors command drawing_links_of_regis, drawing_links_of_naplps, regis_cursor_of_regis and regis_cursor_of_naplps of neoteletext-common's wire-vectors.tsv are the four picture commands' bodies, and rules picture_links_group a table whose group holds a NAPLPS picture's links and cursor.

Limits of a group, not of its work. A group MAY run other groups to a depth of at most MAX_GROUP_DEPTH (a group that runs none having depth 1), and no group may run itself, directly or through others. One run of a group, with every group it runs, applies at most MAX_RUN_COMMANDS commands, each RUN counting as one beside the commands of the group it runs, and all of a page's groups together, as framed, are at most MAX_GROUPS_BYTES. Because nesting has no cycle and no condition, the number of commands a run applies is a constant of the table. The receiver checks every command of every group when the table is decoded — its type, its body with the same reader that reads that record from the server, its page, its bindings — and refuses the whole table for any fault; nothing is checked when a group runs, and no limit is put on the work a run does beyond these. The receiver's general budgets, which apply to every command however it arrives, apply to a group's commands exactly as to the server's.

6.7 The six command records: LOCAL_MIDI, VARIABLE, TIMER, REPORT, RUN and SEQUENCE, types 28 to 33

DOC-6685 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6528, REQ-6612

Push protocol version 10 adds six records, types 28 to 33, in the audio profile's record frame on data channel 12 like every record of this part. Each is a command a group of a page's table may hold, and a record a server may send directly for the connections that have the page selected; the bytes are the same either way. Every body begins with the page (2 bytes, 0x100 to 0x8FF) and the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E), which in a group MUST be the table's own page. Every integer is big-endian. A body of any other length than its record's, or with a field out of range, is refused by the record's reader. A record of types 29 to 33 sent directly is an event of the open page, handled at once in arrival order (handlings), whose run has no firing: the row's p and every value of the firing read 0. One for a page with no table, or for a page that is not the open page, is dropped and counted.

LOCAL_MIDI, type 28, 8 bytes: page; sub-code; the audio channel (1 byte, 0 to 3); a status byte; two data bytes. It carries one complete MIDI 1.0 channel voice message with no running status: note off (0x8n), note on (0x9n), control change (0xBn), program change (0xCn, whose second data byte is 0 and is not given to the instrument) or pitch bend (0xEn, whose 14-bit value is data 1, the low seven bits, and data 2, the high seven), n being the part's MIDI channel less one and each data byte 0 to 127. Polyphonic key pressure, channel pressure, system exclusive, system common and system real-time messages are refused. The message is given to the local sound (the local sound) playing on the named audio channel for that page in the view; when no local sound plays there, the command does nothing and is counted. It is never given to a sound whose blocks the server sends. Sent directly it is applied on arrival when the page is the open page of the view.

VARIABLE, type 29: page; sub-code; an operation (1 byte); the variable (1 byte, 0 to 15, or 255 for all sixteen with clear only); an operand kind (1 byte); and the operand:

Operand kindBytes after itThe operand's value
0nonenone (for inc, dec, toggle, clear)
1a signed 32-bit constantthe constant
2a constant; a variable (1 byte, 0 to 15)the constant plus that variable's value as it stands, saturating
3a constant; a property of the firing (1 byte, 0 to 4)the constant plus that value of the firing, saturating
4a value (8 bytes)that value as it stands (set only)
5two signed 32-bit constants low ≤ highthe range (wrap only)
CodeOperationOperand kindsEffect on the variable v
1set1 to 4v becomes the operand
2inc0v + 1, saturating
3dec0v − 1, saturating
4add1 to 3v plus the operand, saturating
5sub1 to 3v minus the operand, saturating
6toggle00 becomes 1; anything else becomes 0
7min1 to 3the lesser of v and the operand: v held to at most it
8max1 to 3the greater of v and the operand: v held to at least it
9wrap5when v > high, low; when v < low, high; otherwise unchanged
10clear00; with variable 255, all sixteen

Every sum is computed without overflow and saturates at −2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647. A body not exactly its operation's and operand kind's length, or that pairs an operation with an operand kind the table does not give it, is refused.

TIMER, type 30, 6 bytes: page; sub-code; an operation (1 start, 2 stop); a timer (0 to 7). A start applied in a handling of page tick t makes the timer running since tick t + 1, replacing an earlier start; a stop stops it. The page timer cannot be named.

REPORT, type 31, 13 bytes: page; sub-code; what (1 byte); a value (8 bytes, all zero unless what is 1). With what 0 it reports the firing: in a run made by a rule of an input trigger, that the rule fired together with the viewer's event exactly as the viewer made it (and, for a pointer trigger, the target it was inside); in any other run, only that the rule or the run fired, with no event. With what 1 it reports one value, as it stands when the command is applied, so that a REPORT after a VARIABLE in one group reports the new value. Each REPORT applied makes one RULE_EVENT (RULE_EVENT), which the receiver's trusted part builds and gates; a report carries an input event only when a rule the viewer's own event fired ran it in that event's handling. Sent directly by a server, what MUST be 1.

RUN, type 32, 5 bytes: page; sub-code; a group (1 byte, a group of the page's table). In a group it runs the named group in place, at that point of the run. Sent directly it runs the group at once, as an event.

SEQUENCE, type 33, 12 bytes: page; sub-code; an operation (1 byte: 1 start, 2 stop); a sequence (1 byte: 0 to 7, or 255 for every sequence with stop only); a start mode (1 byte: 0 next, 1 at a page tick, 2 on a timer's beat); a timer (1 byte: 0 to 7, or 255 for the page timer, in start mode 2; else 0); and ticks (unsigned 32-bit: 0 for next, the page tick for at, the period for beat). With stop, the start mode, the timer and ticks MUST be 0. Its effect is sequences'.

Every record of types 21 to 33 is one of the channel's records, which the audio receiver leaves to the page's evaluator and renderers.

6.8 Sequences: stored steps a receiver plays on its own clock, started at the next tick, at a page tick or on a timer's beat

DOC-6684 · concept · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6613

A table MAY hold 0 to MAX_SEQUENCES sequences, numbered from 0. A sequence is a length in ticks (1 to MAX_SEQUENCE_TICKS), a repeat count (1 to MAX_SEQUENCE_REPEAT, or 0 for until stopped) and 1 to MAX_SEQUENCE_STEPS steps, each a tick offset (0 to the length less one) and a group of the table, in ascending offset, two steps of one offset being run in written order. A sequence is stopped, waiting (to start at a page tick it holds) or running (since a start tick, with a position and a count of passes), and holds the row parameter p its steps' groups run with. Every sequence is stopped when the page opens. It is started and stopped by the SEQUENCE command (groups and commands), in a group or sent directly by the server.

Starting. A start applied in a handling of page tick t replaces any run or waiting start of that sequence, holds the p in force (or 0), and sets the start tick S by its mode:

Start modeNameticksThe start tick S
0next0t + 1: the first tick step after the handling in which the command is applied
1ata page tickthat page tick. A tick earlier than t + 1 has passed: the start tick is t + 1, and the start is counted as late. A tick more than MAX_START_TICKS after t is not started and is counted as skipped (RULES_FAULT code 10); the sequence is left as it was
2beata period P, 1 to MAX_TIMER_TICKSthe named timer's next expiry of period P: the first tick from t + 1 on that is the timer's start tick plus a whole number, at least one, of periods, as an every P trigger on that timer would be due; when the timer is stopped, t + 1

The sequence is then waiting for S. At the tick step of S it becomes running at position 0 and pass 0, and its offset-0 steps run in that tick step.

Playing. At the sequences place of each tick step a running sequence runs every step whose offset equals its position. After the tick step's groups have run, the position goes up by one; when it reaches the length it returns to 0 and the pass count goes up by one; and when the pass count reaches a repeat count that is not 0 the sequence stops. A sequence that a command of the tick step stopped or started again does not advance in that tick step. A stop stops a sequence where it is, or cancels its waiting start; the step groups already run are not undone. A sequence's steps are constants of the table, and its position is a counter, never a division.

A one-step sequence is a run at a tick. "Run group g at page tick T" is a sequence of length 1, repeat count 1 and one step at offset 0, started at T; "run g after N ticks" is a sequence of length N + 1 and repeat 1 whose one step has offset N, started next; "run g on the next beat" is such a sequence started on a beat. A rule that should act only near a beat tests the timer's phase in its condition instead (variables, timers, conditions and values).

The two clocks. The page tick is the receiver's: it starts at 0 when the page opens in that view, counts the tick steps run, slows when the receiver is late and does not advance while the page is paused. The server has no copy of it. It learns it from the tick every report carries and from a state answer, and estimates the present tick as the last one learnt plus sixty for each second since. A program that wants several viewers' pages to act at one moment of its own clock starts a sequence at a page tick in each view, from that view's own estimate, and accepts that a start for a tick already past happens at the next tick step. Nothing is resynchronised.

6.9 Cue points: a numbered point in a playing sound, carried in its blocks and acted on when it is heard

DOC-6686 · concept · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6535, REQ-6614

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6535 The sound helper MUST render a page's local sound in 128-sample blocks so a key sounds within 12 ms, report cue points when heard, and fall silent when its page is paused, closed or disconnected (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

A cue is a numbered point, 0 to MAX_CUE, in the event list of a stored or live synthesizer sound whose blocks the server sends. A rule's cue trigger, which names an audio channel (0 to 3) and a cue number or any cue, fires when that cue of the sound playing on that audio channel is heard; the firing's cue value is the number.

  • In the block. A cue is carried as the Standard MIDI Files 1.0 Cue Point meta event (its "Meta-Events": FF 07 len text is Cue Point, FF 06 len text is Marker) with one byte of data, the cue's number: the four bytes FF 07 01 nn after its delta time. It is the one meta event a block carries. A block holds at most four cues (MAX_CUES_PER_BLOCK of the audio crates); a fifth, and a Cue Point of any other length, is passed over and counted. A receiver that knows no cues passes the event over as it passes over any meta event, by its length, and is unaffected. The highest cue number is the highest data byte a block carries.
  • From a program. A family's event list MAY hold {"event":"cue","number":n,"time_us":…}. When a stored sound is given as a Standard MIDI File, the sound message MAY give cues, a list of at most MAX_CUE + 1 entries {"text":"…","number":n}, each text 1 to 64 bytes: the server turns each Marker and Cue Point meta event of the file whose text equals an entry's text byte for byte into that cue at the event's time, and drops the others. No receiver reads a cue's text. A cue in a local sound's setup is refused, since a local sound has no timeline and so no cues.
  • Heard, not rendered. A receiver renders a sound's blocks ahead of what is heard. When its instrument's event reader passes a cue, the decoder sends the sound output stage a cue mark (the audio channel, the position of the cue in the stream as a count of samples from the stream's start, and the number), which keeps at most 32 marks for each stream. As soon as the output stage has rendered the device buffer that holds a mark's sample it reports the cue heard; the decoder gives the evaluator the cue as an event, handled at once in arrival order, which fires the cue rules. A cue is therefore acted on within one device buffer of being heard. A sound that is stopped, and a page that is paused or closed, forgets its marks.

6.10 The RULES record and the table image

DOC-6589 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6526, REQ-6528

A page's table is one image of at most MAX_TABLE_BYTES bytes, sent in one or more records of type 21, RULES. A server sends a connection a RULES record for a page at every selection of the page, before the program is told (the channel's default table or a record that says the page has no table), and the program's own table at once when it gives one, to each connection that has that page and sub-code selected. Every integer is big-endian. A record's body:

BytesFieldValues
0–1page0x100 to 0x8FF
2–3sub-code0x0000 to 0x3F7E
4–5generation1 to 65,535: one above the last RULES record sent on that connection, starting at 1 and passing from 65,535 to 1; the same in every fragment of one image
6flagsbit 0: a table follows. Clear: the page has no table; total and offset are 0 and the body ends at byte 11. Bits 1 to 7 are 0
7reserved0
8–9totalthe image's length, 12 to MAX_TABLE_BYTES
10–11offsetthe place of this fragment's first byte in the image
12–data1 to MAX_TABLE_FRAGMENT bytes of the image

A fragment with offset 0 begins an image and discards any image still incomplete for that page. Each later fragment MUST carry the same generation and total and an offset equal to the bytes already held; one that does not discards the incomplete image, and the receiver reports RULES_FAULT code 1. When the bytes held equal the total, the receiver decodes the image whole; until then the page keeps the table it had. A record with flag bit 0 clear removes the page's table at once. A table of at most MAX_TABLE_FRAGMENT bytes is one record. Inside an atomic frame the records are held with the rest.

The image begins with a header of 12 bytes: format (2); reserved (0); rectangles R (0 to MAX_RECTS); rows W (0 to MAX_ROWS); rules N (0 to MAX_RULES); groups G (0 to MAX_GROUPS); sequences Q (0 to MAX_SEQUENCES); reserved (0); the bytes of the G groups together, as framed, 16-bit (0 to MAX_GROUPS_BYTES); two reserved bytes (0). Then R rectangles, W rows, N rules, G groups and Q sequences, in that order, ending exactly at the last sequence.

  • A rectangle is 8 bytes: x, y, width, height, each unsigned 16-bit, width and height at least 1. A row is 4 bytes: its parameter p, signed 32-bit.
  • A rule is: a flags byte (bit 0: it names rows; other bits 0); its group (1 byte, below G); when bit 0 is set, its first row and its row count (1 byte each, count at least 1, first plus count at most W); a trigger count (1 to MAX_TRIGGERS_PER_RULE); that many triggers, each its kind byte and body; and its condition. The sum, over the rules, of each rule's row count (1 for a rule that names none) MUST be at most MAX_RULE_ROWS.
  • Trigger bodies. key (1) and key_up (2): flags (bit 0 repeat, kind 1 only; bit 1 by_row, only in a rule that names rows, with K equal to its row count); modifier mask; modifier value; key count K (0 for any key, else 1 to MAX_KEYS_PER_TRIGGER); K keys of 5 bytes, a kind byte (1 character, 2 named, 3 physical) and a 32-bit code. press (3) and release (4): a target (3 bytes: kind, 16-bit number) and a button (0, 1, 2 or 255). enter (5), leave (6) and wheel (14): a target. move (13): a target and flags (bit 0 held). open (7), close (8), becomes (9), text (12), focus (15), blur (16): empty. every (10) and after (11): a timer (0 to 7, or 255) and ticks (unsigned 32-bit). cue (21): an audio channel (0 to 3) and a cue number (0 to MAX_CUE, or 255 for any). Kinds 17 to 20, and key kinds with bit 7 set, are refused. A target's kind is 0 to 3 (kind 0 with number 0, kind 3 below R), or in a rule that names rows kind 1, 2 or 3 with bit 7 set, the number then a signed 16-bit constant to which each row's p is added, checked valid for every row.
  • A value is 8 bytes: space (1 to 8), a, and b, c, d (unsigned 16-bit), every field checked against its space's ranges (values). A condition is a count byte of nodes, 0 (no condition) to MAX_CONDITION_NODES, then the nodes in prefix order, each its code byte and body: and (1) and or (2), a child count 2 to MAX_AND_OR_CHILDREN; not (3), nothing; compare (4), a value, an operator (1 to 6: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=), a signed 32-bit constant and a parameter byte (0, or 0x20 to add the row's p, only in a rule that names rows; 0x21 to 0x23 refused); in range (5), a value, low and high; in set (6), a value, a count 1 to MAX_SET_MEMBERS and that many constants; overlaps (7) and inside (8), two targets. The nodes MUST form exactly one tree that uses every node counted.
  • A group is a count byte of commands, 1 to MAX_GROUP_COMMANDS, then that many command frames: the record type (1 byte, one a group may hold); the bindings B (1 byte, 0 to MAX_COMMAND_BINDINGS); the body's length L (16-bit, 1 to MAX_COMMAND_BYTES); the body, exactly as the server sends that record without the record frame's header and CRC-32; and B bindings of 3 bytes each: item (the operation's place in an ANIMATE record, else 0), field code, source (amounts).
  • A sequence is its repeat count (1 byte, 0 for until stopped), its step count (1 byte, 1 to MAX_SEQUENCE_STEPS), its length (unsigned 32-bit, 1 to MAX_SEQUENCE_TICKS), then each step: an offset (unsigned 32-bit, below the length, not below the step before) and a group (1 byte, below G).

Accepted whole or refused whole. A receiver MUST refuse an image when any field is outside its range, any reserved bit or byte is not 0, any count exceeds its limit, any number refers to a rectangle, row, group or sequence the table does not have, a condition is not one tree, a command's type is not allowed or its body is refused by its record's reader, a binding names a field or a source that is not allowed, the groups run each other in a ring or too deep or a run would pass MAX_RUN_COMMANDS, a row's p does not give a valid target number where a trigger uses it, a by_row key set's count is not its rule's row count, a withdrawn code appears, the image is short, or bytes follow its end. Nothing of a refused table is kept or evaluated: the page then has no table and sends no input, and the receiver reports RULES_FAULT code 1 with the table's generation. A receiver never repairs a table or skips a faulty rule or command. A server checks every image with the same code before it cuts it into records, so no receiver is sent a table it would refuse.

6.11 RULE_EVENT

DOC-6590 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6523, REQ-6528

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

A receiver makes each report of a REPORT command (the six command records) as the input event of extension type 0x4B, RULE_EVENT. After the stamp, which is two varints as on every stamped event, every field is big-endian and of the fixed width given:

FieldForm
stampthe page and sub-code on screen, as every stamped event has them
generation16-bit: the table's
rule1 byte, 0 to 63; 255 when the run was not made by a rule (a record the server sent, or a sequence it started)
row1 byte: the place of the firing row within the rule's rows, 0 to 63; 255 when none
tickunsigned 32-bit: the page tick of the firing
kind1 byte: 0 fired (no event), 1 input, 2 value
target3 bytes: the kind and number of the control, object or rectangle the pointer was inside, for a rule whose pointer trigger named one; else all zero
bodykind 0: nothing. Kind 1: one or two whole input events exactly as push protocol 8 encoded them, each from its 0xFF: KEY, MOUSE, WHEEL, TOUCH, PASTE, COMPOSE, FOCUS_IN, FOCUS_OUT, HOVER or DRAWING_HOVER; and after a MOUSE, TOUCH or WHEEL on a page drawn by the ReGIS renderer, its PICK. In place of an event the body may be one run of raw text (UTF-8, which never begins with 0xFF), for text that came from no key. Kind 2: a value (8 bytes) and its reading (signed 32-bit)
  • Under push protocol 10 the events KEY, MOUSE, WHEEL, PASTE, COMPOSE, TOUCH, FOCUS_IN, FOCUS_OUT, HOVER, PICK, DRAWING_HOVER and raw text MUST appear only inside a RULE_EVENT. HELLO, RESIZE, SELECT, RESUME and viewer state's three messages stay at the top level.
  • A target is carried by kind 1 alone: a RULE_EVENT of kind 0 or 2 that names a target is refused by its reader.
  • A RULE_EVENT counts one for acknowledgement whatever it carries, so a pointer's move and an input method's composition are acknowledged, and a move is never dropped or replaced while a connection is congested. The input session's limit of 120 messages a second looks at what a RULE_EVENT carries: a release always goes, a move is not held to the limit, and a firing with no event and a value are. A RULE_EVENT not acknowledged when its connection ends is discarded and never sent again, on that connection or a later one.
  • An enter or leave on a control is carried as HOVER; on a ReGIS drawing as DRAWING_HOVER; on a teletext sprite, a NAPLPS object or a rectangle as the MOUSE move that caused it, with the target named.
  • The gate. A receiver's trusted part builds every RULE_EVENT itself and enforces, without reading a table, that nothing leaves that the viewer did not do on that page: it gives a page's evaluator the viewer's input only while the page has a table, and only of the classes the table's triggers ask for; it keeps its own copy of each event it gave; for a report of an input event it uses that copy, only when the event was given for that page within the last 4 ticks and has not already been reported for that rule and row; it sends a page's reports only on that page's own connection to its own channel, while the page is open or within 4 ticks of its closing, and never after the connection has ended; and it sends at most 120 reports a second for a page, of which at most 20 may be reports with no input event, dropping the rest and reporting RULES_FAULT code 3.

6.12 The RULES_QUERY record, PAGE_STATE and RULES_FAULT

DOC-6591 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6528

The state query. Record type 22, RULES_QUERY, asks a receiver once for the local state of a page. Its body is 8 bytes: the page (2 bytes), the sub-code (2 bytes) and the query's identifier (unsigned 32-bit, which the server chooses and maps to the program's request number). A receiver that has that page open answers exactly once, as an event handled in arrival order, with the input event of extension type 0x4C, PAGE_STATE; it ignores a query for a page that is not open or is paused, and answers at most one query a second for a page, dropping the rest and reporting RULES_FAULT code 6. After the stamp every field is big-endian and of fixed width:

FieldForm
stamppage and sub-code
identifierunsigned 32-bit, the query's
generation16-bit, the table's; 0 when the page has no table, and then nothing follows but a tick of 0
tickunsigned 32-bit: the page tick the query was handled in, whose state is reported as it stood then
variablessixteen values (signed 32-bit), v0 first
timerseight entries, t0 first, each: flags (bit 0 running) and elapsed ticks (unsigned 32-bit)
sequencesa count (the table's sequences), then for each: flags (bit 0 running, bit 1 waiting; other bits 0), passes (unsigned 32-bit), position (unsigned 32-bit)
targetsa count (0 to MAX_TABLE_TARGETS), then for each control and object the table names by a constant, in the order first named: kind; number (16-bit); flags (bit 0 exists, bit 1 shown, bit 2 cycling); look; frame; x; y (signed 16-bit); layer; order (signed 8-bit): 12 bytes
valuesa count (0 to MAX_TABLE_VALUES), then for each distinct value the table reads, in the order first read: the value (8 bytes) and its reading (signed 32-bit)

"First named" and "first read" follow the rules in rule order and, within a rule, its triggers' targets, then its condition's nodes in order, then the commands of its group in order, and after the rules the groups no rule names, in group order; a value of target state names its target. The answer is at most MAX_STATE_BYTES. The query is for reading a page's values and for debugging, never for restoring a page: after a disconnect there is nothing to read.

Faults. A receiver reports a fault of a page's table with the input event of extension type 0x4D, RULES_FAULT: the stamp, the table's generation (16-bit), a code (1 byte) and a count (16-bit, how many times since the last report). It sends at most one a second for each code and page. PAGE_STATE and RULES_FAULT are no input and count nothing for acknowledgement.

CodeNameMeaning
1undecodablethe table image could not be assembled or decoded and was refused whole; the page then has no table
2—withdrawn; never sent and never reused
3reports_droppedreports dropped by the receiver's report budgets
4events_droppedevents (input events, the server's records the evaluator carries out, cues) dropped at a full queue
5commands_skippedcommands that did nothing for a missing target or sound
6query_droppeda state query dropped
7local_overruna local sound stopped for overrunning its time (count 1 or more), or its small device buffer given up after an underrun (count 0)
8animation_slowedanimation slowed by its budget
9evaluation_latethe page's tick steps and handlings took longer than the ticks' own time, so page time slowed
10queue_fulla sound command dropped at the receiver's sound command budget, a cue mark dropped, or a sequence start more than MAX_START_TICKS ahead skipped

6.13 The local sound: an instrument a page keeps open, played by LOCAL_MIDI commands

DOC-6592 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6527

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6527 The audio crates MUST make synthesizer state readable to page rules and MUST provide the local sound: parameter tables, envelope meter, voice peak, pulled voice (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A local sound is a synthesizer sound that the receiver renders itself, with no blocks from the server and no buffer held ahead, and that a page plays with LOCAL_MIDI commands (the six command records), from its groups or sent directly by the server, so that a key sounds without a round trip and without the 400 milliseconds a stream is buffered for.

  • It is of any family that plays notes, codec codes 13 to 18. The family of codec 12, which is programmed by register writes and has no note messages, has none.
  • Its OBJECT record carries tag 9, one value byte, 1. It is announced as a stored sound of one block of its family, and its one block is the setup: an event list in its family's block form with every event at tick 0, at most 1,005 bytes, applied in order when the instrument is made. It names its banks as other sounds of its family do. It has no timeline and so no cues.
  • A receiver never renders a local sound from blocks and never streams it. When a play command (a CONTROL record, from the server or in a group) starts it on an audio channel, the receiver makes the family's instrument in its sound output stage, applies the setup, and from then on gives it the messages of LOCAL_MIDI commands as they are applied. Stop and gain act on its audio channel as on any sound.
  • A local sound MUST be played with a page scope. It belongs to the page (page number and sub-code) open in the view when its play is carried out; it is silent, with all notes released and its instrument kept, while that page is paused, and it ends, with all notes released, when that page is closed or its connection ends. At most 2 local sounds play at once in a view; a third play is refused and counted.
  • A receiver renders a local sound in blocks of 128 samples at 48,000 samples a second, applying before each block every message queued for the instrument in arrival order, so that a message waits at most one block; its queue holds 256 messages, and one that arrives at a full queue is dropped and counted. While a local sound is open the receiver asks its audio device for a small buffer (about 5.3 milliseconds) and gives it up, reporting RULES_FAULT code 7 with count 0, at the first underrun or overrun. When rendering a view's local sounds takes longer than the time of the buffer it fills for 8 buffers running, the receiver stops them with all notes released and reports fault 7.
  • A receiver without a sound output stage of this kind ignores a local sound's OBJECT, as it ignores a codec it does not have.
  • A server may name the sound's variant with tag 5 as on any sound of its family; an OBJECT that names no variant is of variant 0, and the two forms are the same sound.

The OBJECT of a local sound of codec 14 with handle 1, generation 1 and bank 2, whose setup block is 3 bytes, as it is framed before it is cut into fragments; and the same sound with its variant named:

0201001d010001000000010e070003000003c000010401020804000000030901010e74ec4d
02010020010001000000010e070003000003c00001050100040102080400000003090101648ffdb2

6.14 Privacy of the rule table: what a report and the state query reveal, and to whom

DOC-6593 · concept · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6523, REQ-6540, REQ-6615

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-6540 The page rule table and animation: security analysis applied, privacy rule for channels, fuzz targets, shared wire vectors and tests that name their requirement (not implemented on main); REQ-6615 A page's local state is dropped whole when the page is left or its connection ends, and is keyed on page number and sub-code together; a background tab is paused; nothing is resynchronised (tested, not recorded as met on main).

These rules bind every channel's author. A page here is one page number and one sub-code together: what is said of a page is said of each sub-page alone.

  1. Nothing is sent unless the page asks. A channel receives a viewer's input on a page only through that page's rule table: an input event leaves the receiver only when a rule of the open page's table, fired by that event, runs a group that applies a REPORT of the firing in that event's own handling. A page with no table is sent nothing of what its viewer does, and a group run by a timer, a sequence, a cue or a command of the server's can report no input event at all.
  2. What a report reveals. A report of a firing that the viewer's own input caused carries that event on that page: the key and its modifiers, the text typed, pasted or composed, the pointer's button and position and the control, object or rectangle it was on, the wheel, the gain or loss of the keyboard, with the page tick it belongs to and the rule and row that fired. A report of a value carries one number the table reads: one of the page's sixteen variables (which the viewer's keys and clicks may have changed), a key's or a button's state, a timer, a sequence's state, whether an object is shown and where it is, a value of the firing (the key that fired it, the target, the row, the cue), a sound's level or a synthesizer's state on that page. A bare firing says that a rule fired and when.
  3. What the state query reveals. The answer to a state query carries, once, the page's sixteen variables, its timers, its sequences, for each control and object the table names whether it exists and is shown and its look, frame, position, layer, order and cycling, and the present reading of every value the table reads: what the viewer's actions on that page have made of its local state, at one tick. It is for reading and debugging, never for restoring a page.
  4. To whom. All of these go to that page's own channel, on the connection that page was fetched on, and to no one else: not to another channel, not to another page's channel in another tab, not to any third party. The receiver's trusted part builds every report itself from the viewer's own event and gives it only to that channel's connection. No report carries the viewer's volume or mute, anything of another tab, or anything typed outside the open page's picture.
  5. What a channel may do with them. A channel's program MUST use what a report and the state query give it only to provide what the page offers the viewer, under the same rule that binds its use of a viewer's handle: not for advertising, profiling, analytics beyond aggregate counts, or sharing with any other party. What it keeps of them under a handle is personal data, as the handle is, and is described on the channel's privacy page.
  6. A page asks for no more than it uses. A channel MUST NOT give a page a table that asks for input the page does not use. A channel that runs on the server's default table (default_rules send_all) is sent every input on every one of its pages until its pages have tables of their own.
  7. Nothing of a page is kept after it is left. Neither side keeps a page's local state after the page is closed or its connection ends (the lifetime of local state): the receiver drops the page's table, variables, timers, sequences, waiting events, animation state and local sounds, and discards every report not yet acknowledged when a connection ends; the server forgets the page's table names, generation counter, timelines and unanswered state queries, and keeps no table, animation state or local state for a later or returning viewer. A page in a tab that is not the active one evaluates nothing, sounds nothing and reports nothing.

6.15 A sub-page is a page: the rule table and animation are keyed on the page number and sub-code together

DOC-6687 · concept · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6615

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6615 A page's local state is dropped whole when the page is left or its connection ends, and is keyed on page number and sub-code together; a background tab is paused; nothing is resynchronised (tested, not recorded as met on main).

For the rule table and for animation, a page is one page number (0x100 to 0x8FF) and one sub-code (0x0000 to 0x3F7E) together, with no relationship to any other sub-code of the same page number. Each such page has its own rule table, groups, sequences, rows, rectangles, timers, sixteen variables, sprites, objects, sheet, animation state, frames, timelines and local sounds. Every record of the rule table and of animation (RULES, RULES_QUERY, the six command records, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS, SHEET, FRAME), every program message and every kit call that concerns a page carries both, and every implementation keys what it keeps on both.

  • Nothing is addressed by a page number alone, and nothing means "every sub-page of" or "whichever sub-page is shown". The sub-code 0x3F7F is refused in every record and message of the rule table and of animation; no value of a table reads the sub-code shown.
  • A table for 101/0001 is not evaluated while 101/0002 is open. Going from one sub-code to another is leaving one page and opening another (teletext sprites and the rest of this part follow the same rule): what was local to the one left is dropped, and the one arrived at starts from its own opening state, its open rules firing at its own page tick 0.
  • A server sends a connection a page's table, sprites, objects and sheet for the page and sub-code it has selected, at that selection; a program that wants the same table or sheet on several sub-pages sends it to each.
  • The audio profile's CONTROL record names a page number only: a local sound belongs to the page (number and sub-code) that is open in the view when its play is carried out, and ends when that page is no longer open.

6.16 The lifetime of a page's local state: a close, a disconnect, the program's end and a pause

DOC-6688 · concept · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6615

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6615 A page's local state is dropped whole when the page is left or its connection ends, and is keyed on page number and sub-code together; a background tab is paused; nothing is resynchronised (tested, not recorded as met on main).

A page's local state is its rule table with its groups, sequences, rows and rectangles; its variables, timers, sequences (running or waiting), becomes memory and waiting events; its animation state, sprites, objects, sheet and open frame; its local sounds; its cue marks; and its list of metered values. Exactly four things can happen to an open page, and a receiver and a server MUST treat them so:

  1. The page is closed while its connection stands (the viewer selects another page or another sub-code, follows a link, or closes the tab). The receiver handles the lost releases of every key and button still down, runs the one close handling, lets its reports leave, and then drops all of the page's local state. Coming back to the page later is a new selection: the server and the program send it afresh, and its open rules fire at a new page tick 0.
  2. The push connection ends, for any reason. The receiver MUST at once drop the page's rule table and rule state, stop every local sound with every note released, run no close handling, discard every RULE_EVENT not yet acknowledged, never sending it on a later connection, and keep presenting the last picture as it stood, frozen; the picture's sprites, objects, sheet and animation state are kept only as that frozen picture, evaluated and changed by nothing, until the page is sent afresh. When a connection is made again, the receiver selects the page as a new selection, whether or not the session is resumed (RESUME restores the session's identity and nothing of a page); the page is sent afresh and its open rules fire again. The server, when a connection ends, MUST forget everything it holds for it of any page: the names of its table, its generation counter, its timelines, its open frame, its sheet stream and its unanswered state queries, each of which is refused not_answered to the program.
  3. The program's connection to the server ends (the program stops, fails or is restarted). The server MUST, for every connection of that channel, stop every timeline, end any open frame, and send for the page it has selected a RULES record that says the page has no table (or the channel's default table), which makes the receiver drop the table and with it the variables, timers, sequences and waiting events. It holds nothing over for the program's return; when the program is back it is told of each connection's selection as a new one and sends each page afresh.
  4. The tab stops being the active tab, or the page otherwise stops being the open page while still selected (another tab is brought forward, the overview or a wall is shown). This is not a disconnect and not a close: the page is paused. The receiver handles the lost releases at once, then runs no tick step, handles no event, gives the page no input, makes no report, forgets its cue marks, and silences the page's local sounds with every note released, keeping their instruments. The page tick does not advance. Records the server sends meanwhile are applied as for any page that is shown but not open (animation operations are; records that need the evaluator are dropped and counted). When the page is the open page again, it goes on from the next page tick with every variable, timer and sequence as it was, and open does not fire.

No state is ever carried across a close or a disconnect, by either side, and none is rebuilt: the state query is not used for it, and the server replays no table, animation state, sprites, objects or sheet to a returning viewer. What a late or returning viewer is sent is what the page's program sends on its selection. A program is told of every selection, with its page and sub-code, and sends the page then, its table with it.

6.17 The limits of a page's rule table

DOC-6682 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6608

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6608 The limits of a page's rule table: one set of maximums and per-tick budgets, each a named constant, and a table over any limit refused whole (tested, not recorded as met on main).

Every limit of a page's rule table is a maximum, never a minimum, counts for one page (one page number and one sub-code) alone, and is one named constant of the engine's crate neoteletext_rules::limits, used by that name by the server when it checks a table and by the receiver when it loads one. A table that passes any limit is refused whole, with a refusal that names the limit's constant and its value; it is never accepted in part and never cut short. A receiver holds no limit lower or higher than these.

ConstantValueWhat it bounds

The per-tick budgets. MAX_EVENTS_PER_TICK, MAX_EVENT_COMMANDS_PER_TICK and MAX_EVENT_REPORTS_PER_TICK count against the tick an event is handled in. An event over any of them waits for the next tick in the queue of MAX_QUEUED_EVENTS, and is never dropped while the queue has room; the first event of a tick is always handled. They bound events, not the table: a table at every other limit is never refused for them, and they do not apply to a tick step. There is no limit on the work a run of a group costs beyond these; the receiver's general budgets, which apply to every command however it arrives (painting, animation, the trusted core's report and sound command budgets, a local sound's message queue), are not limits of the rule table.

7 Animation

DOC-6582 · section

7.1 The presentation clock, atomic frames and the FRAME record

DOC-6594 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6529

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6529 The engine MUST time everything shown in 60 ticks a second and carry animation: FRAME, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records, teletext sprites, damage repaint (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

One clock. Every time-driven thing a receiver shows is timed in ticks of one sixtieth of a second on one presentation clock, whose tick n is due n × 50,000 ÷ 3 microseconds after its start: teletext flash, the cursor's blink, NAPLPS WAIT and BLINK, frame cycling, the ReGIS paint rate, the end of an atomic frame, and the tick step of the page rule table (handlings). A phase is a function of the tick alone, so every page of a channel flashes in step and animation is the same on every run. Where the display's refresh is a whole multiple of 60 a second, a receiver MAY phase its clock against the display's frames, moving the clock's start by at most a few parts in a thousand of a tick, so that a tick's picture is in the next frame composed; ticks are still counted and never skipped or repeated.

WhatOn the clock
Teletext Level 1 flash57 ticks shown and 19 hidden, three to one: a cycle of 76 ticks
The unit of the Additional Flash Functions5 ticks, one twelfth of a second; a cycle of 60 ticks
The cursor's blinka half period of 32 ticks
A tenth of a second of NAPLPS WAIT and BLINK6 ticks
The ReGIS paint rateafter n ticks, n × rate × 100 ÷ 60 work units, rounded down

Atomic frames. Record type 27, FRAME, has a body of 8 bytes: the page (2 bytes); the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E; a frame belongs to one page number and sub-code, and 0x3F7F is refused); a mark (1 byte: 1 begin, 2 end); a reserved byte, 0; and an identifier (2 bytes, which an end repeats from its begin). Between a begin and its end for a page, a receiver MUST hold, unapplied and in arrival order, everything that changes what that page shows (the page's teletext packets, and its REGIS, NAPLPS, DRAWING_LINKS, REGIS_CURSOR, LINKS, RULES, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records) and at the end apply them all, in order, and show the result on one tick: no picture between is ever presented.

  • What is held is the bytes, at most 262,144, never a second picture. Sound records and other pages' packets pass as they arrive.
  • A frame ends, and what it held is applied at once, also when: the limit of bytes is reached; 120 ticks, two seconds, pass with no end; a second begin arrives for the page; the page stops being shown; the connection ends. A fault therefore delays a picture and never loses or hides one.
  • At most 4 pages have a frame open at once in a receiver; a fifth begin is treated as having no frame.
  • A ReGIS stream already has its marker, the commit, and nothing is added to it. NAPLPS gets no new opcode: the FRAME record brackets its records, and teletext packets the same way.
  • A whole page swapped in. A frame may hold a whole new page: a teletext page with the erase bit, a new generation of a ReGIS or NAPLPS stream from offset 0, new sprites, objects, sheet and table. A receiver MUST keep presenting the page as it was until everything held has been applied and the new picture is complete, and then present the new page on one tick: no blank, erased or half-drawn page between. A page larger than the limit of bytes cannot be swapped whole and appears as it arrives.
  • A server holds a program's frame for each connection and sends it whole; an open frame is ended when its program's connection ends, and forgotten when the viewer's connection ends.

The begin and the end of frame 7 for page 101, sub-page 0001, each as its one packet:

a1ead05e0000021b00080101000101000007d084693b0000000000000000000000000000000000008574
a1ead05e0000021b00080101000102000007c231c6d5000000000000000000000000000000000000d987

7.2 The animation state, its operations and the ANIMATE record

DOC-6595 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6526, REQ-6529

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6529 The engine MUST time everything shown in 60 ticks a second and carry animation: FRAME, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records, teletext sprites, damage repaint (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

For each page shown — one page number and one sub-code together — a receiver keeps, for at most 32 of the objects and controls of a teletext page, 64 of the drawings of a ReGIS picture and 64 of the objects of a NAPLPS picture, an animation state, which is the receiver's own and which nothing in a page's stream can read. An operation that would give one object more than the maximum a state does nothing and is counted. The animation state is part of the page's local state: it is dropped when the page is closed, kept unchanged while it is paused, and after a disconnect kept only as the frozen picture until the page is sent afresh (the lifetime of local state).

PartValuesWithout it
shownshown or hiddenthe object's own visibility
positionx, y (signed 16-bit), in the renderer's units: cells for a teletext sprite, pixels for a ReGIS drawing (relative to its parent), and dots of the 480 by 500 teletext raster for a NAPLPS object (the top left of its rectangle)the object's own position
layer and orderlayer 0 to 3 and order −128 to 127the object's own
frame0 to 15frame 0
cyclefirst, last, period, once, and the tick it startednot cycling
forced look0 none, 1 hover, 2 pressed, 3 alternativethe pointer decides the look

It is changed by operations, carried by the ANIMATE record, which a server sends directly and a group of the page's rule table holds as a command (groups and commands). Each is a code byte, a target (a kind byte, 1 control or 2 object, and a 16-bit number, not 0) and a body:

CodeOperationBodyApplies to
5shownonecontrols and objects
6hidenonecontrols and objects
7looklook, 0 to 3controls and objects
15moveflags (bit 0 relative); x; y (signed 16-bit, in the units of the position)objects
16orderlayer (0 to 3, or 255 to keep it); order (signed 8-bit)objects
17frameframe, 0 to 15; also stops a cycleobjects
18cyclefirst; last (first ≤ last ≤ 15); period (16-bit, 1 to 3,600 ticks); flags (bit 0 once)objects
19stop_cyclenoneobjects
20resetnone: forgets the object's whole animation statecontrols and objects

Record type 23, ANIMATE. Its body is: the page (2 bytes); the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E: the sub-code 0x3F7F, which once meant whichever sub-page is shown, is refused); a count (1 byte, 1 to 64); a reserved byte, 0; then that many operations. A record the server sends is applied as soon as it is read, between the evaluator's handlings, or at its frame's end; a group's command is applied as its run reaches it, with its amounts resolved (amounts). Either way the whole record is applied together, its effects are seen by the next event's handling and the next tick step, and the picture is drawn at the next display frame from the state then current.

  • A relative move adds to the position in force, saturating at the signed 16-bit bounds.
  • A hidden teletext control is drawn as spaces whose background is its row's full row colour, and takes no pointer event. A forced look on a teletext control draws the hover look for 1 and the pressed look for 2 and 3; on a ReGIS drawing, its hover, pressed and alternative looks; on a NAPLPS object, its hover, pressed and alternative macros.
  • One state, last writer wins. A group's ANIMATE command, an ANIMATE record of the server's and the stream's own change of the same thing all write the same state: a ReGIS commit that sets a drawing's position, visibility, layer or depth forgets that part of the drawing's animation state; a ReGIS deletion, a new stream generation, and a SPRITES or NAPLPS_OBJECTS record forget the state of what they remove or replace.
  • Layers. Every page has exactly 4 layers, drawn in this order: 0 background, the page's own picture; 1 scene; 2 sprites; 3 overlay. Within a layer, objects are drawn by order, lowest first, then by number. A receiver keeps the background's picture apart, so that a moving object never causes the background's pixels to be drawn again.
  • Bounding rectangles. Each object has, as its state stands, one bounding rectangle in the picture's own units, or none while it does not exist or is not shown: a teletext sprite's width and height in cells at its origin, cut to rows 0 to 24 of the page, in dots; a ReGIS drawing's reach with that of its shown children, of the look or frame in force, at its screen position and cut by its clip rectangles and the screen; a NAPLPS object's rectangle in dots, cut to the 480 by 500 raster (it may reach teletext rows 0 and 24, outside the picture's display area on rows 1 to 23, where nothing of the picture is drawn). Collision tests, region tests and pointer triggers on sprites and NAPLPS objects are on these rectangles and never on pixels.
  • Frame cycling. With s the tick the cycle started (t + 1 for an operation applied in, or between the handlings of, page tick t), p its period and c = last − first + 1, the frame at tick t is first + ((t − s) ÷ p) mod c; with once, it is min(first + (t − s) ÷ p, last) and the cycle ends when last is reached. Cycling advances at the end of each tick step. At most 16 objects of a page cycle at once. A frame number beyond an object's frames shows its last. Cycles run on the presentation clock whether or not the page has a rule table.
  • The animation budget. A receiver repaints for animation at most half a picture a tick: 120,000 dots of a teletext page, 192,000 pixels of a ReGIS picture, 120,000 dots of a NAPLPS picture (half the raster it is shown on). When a tick's animation would pass the budget, the receiver slows the animation and nothing else: every operation still changes the state at once, the painting waits, and a cycle's frames whose turn passes unpainted are skipped. The viewer's input, the rule table's handlings, sound and the reports to the channel are never delayed by it. The receiver reports fault 8.

7.3 Teletext sprites and the SPRITES record

DOC-6596 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6529

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6529 The engine MUST time everything shown in 60 ticks a second and carry animation: FRAME, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records, teletext sprites, damage repaint (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A teletext sprite is a numbered placement of teletext objects on a page (one page number and one sub-code), which a receiver draws over the page and can move, show, hide, order and cycle. Record type 24, SPRITES, gives a page all its sprites, replacing any it had; a server sends it directly, and a group of the page's rule table may hold one within its command's limit of bytes. Its body: the page (2 bytes); the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E); a count (1 byte, 0 to 32); a reserved byte, 0; then for each sprite:

BytesFieldValues
0–1number1 to 65,535, distinct within the record
2flagsbit 0 shown; bit 1 detectable (pointer triggers see it); other bits 0
3layer1 to 3 (layer 0 is the page itself)
4ordersigned, −128 to 127
5columnsigned, −39 to 39: the column of the sprite's origin
6rowsigned, −24 to 24: its row
7width1 to 40 cells
8height1 to 25 cells
9frames F1 to 16
10–F object references, 2 bytes eachbits 15 to 13 zero; bits 12 and 11 the source (1 a local object of the page's own packets X/26, 2 an object of its Public Object Page, 3 of its Global Public Object Page); bits 10 and 9 the type (1 active, 2 adaptive, 3 passive); bits 8 to 0 the object number: the fields of an Object Invocation triplet

A reader refuses a record with a repeated number, a reserved bit set, or a source of 0.

  • A sprite moves in whole character cells and is never placed between cells. Its frames are built of what teletext objects hold: characters, mosaics and attributes. A DRCS character an object invokes is not drawn, in a sprite as anywhere.
  • How a sprite is drawn. After a page's own enhancement data has been processed, at Presentation Level 2.5 or above, a receiver draws each shown sprite of the page, in order of layer, then order, then number, by invoking the object of its frame in force exactly as an Object Invocation triplet whose active position is the sprite's origin invokes one. Cells the object addresses outside the sprite's width and height from its origin, outside columns 0 to 39, or outside rows 1 to 23 are not written. An object that is absent draws nothing. Below Level 2.5 sprites are not drawn.
  • The display planes of the standard still rank what is drawn: a Passive object's cells lie over an Adaptive object's, and those over an Active object's and the page's own, whatever the sprites' layers; layer, order and number decide among objects of the same type. A sprite whose frames are Passive objects always lies over the page.
  • A sprite's objects count toward the standard's limits of invocations with the page's own.
  • A sprite changes nothing outside its own cells: its objects set no Full Screen Colour and no Full Row Colour, an Active object's attributes stop at the sprite's right edge, and an enlarged character does not reach past the sprite.
  • A sprite's bounding rectangle is its width and height in cells at its origin, cut to rows 0 to 24 of the page, in dots, 12 by 20 a cell.
  • A teletext page's sprite sheet is its objects: its own local objects, and the object pages it links. The server keeps no page content for a later viewer, so a program sends a page's object pages itself, with the program message object_page, at each selection of the page and before the page (the object_page message). That message carries a page's rows as text, so a page whose sprites need objects defined by triplets defines them as local objects in its own packets X/26.
  • A page's sprites are part of its local state, dropped when the page is closed and, after a disconnect, kept only as the frozen picture until the page is sent afresh.

7.4 NAPLPS objects and the NAPLPS_OBJECTS record

DOC-6597 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6529, REQ-6531, REQ-6643, REQ-6644, REQ-6645

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6529 The engine MUST time everything shown in 60 ticks a second and carry animation: FRAME, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records, teletext sprites, damage repaint (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

NAPLPS keeps no scene: a stream draws on the picture and is forgotten. NeoTeletext adds a layer of numbered objects over it, defined by a record and by no new NAPLPS opcode, so that every stream stays a conforming one. Record type 25, NAPLPS_OBJECTS, gives a page (one page number and one sub-code) all its objects, replacing any it had, or redefines one of them; a server sends it directly, and a group of the page's rule table may hold one within its command's limit of bytes. The objects are part of the page's local state, dropped when the page is closed. Every place, size and move of an object is in dots of NeoTeletext's teletext raster, 480 dots across by 500 lines down, the origin at the raster's top left and y down, the same dots a teletext page and a pointer on it use; the NAPLPS picture's display area is drawn on raster lines 20 to 479, teletext rows 1 to 23, and rows 0 and 24 (lines 0 to 19 and 480 to 499) are the teletext page's own, part of the raster, where nothing of the stream is drawn. Its body: the page (2 bytes); the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E); the generation of the NAPLPS stream the objects belong to (2 bytes; objects for another generation than the one shown are kept until that generation is, and dropped when a later one arrives); a count (1 byte, 0 to 64); a flags byte (bit 0 ONE, bit 1 TITLED, the other bits 0); then for each object:

BytesFieldValues
0–1number1 to 65,535, distinct within the record
2kind1 a macro object, 2 a region
3flagsbit 0 shown; bit 1 detectable; other bits 0
4layer1 to 3
5ordersigned, −128 to 127
6–7, 8–9x, ysigned 16-bit: the raster dot of the top left of the object's rectangle
10–11, 12–13width, height1 to 480 dots, 1 to 500 lines: the rectangle is dots x to x + width − 1 and lines y to y + height − 1
14–15, 16–17origin x, origin ysigned 16-bit: the raster dot at which the macro, drawn where the stream would draw it, puts what is to be the rectangle's top left; 0 for a region
18frames Fa macro object: 1 to 16; a region: 0
19covera region: the colour-map entry that fills it while it is hidden; a macro object: 0
20, 21, 22hover, pressed and alternative lookeach a macro's code, 0x20 to 0x7F, or 0 for none
23label length L0, no label, to 64
24–F frame byteseach a macro's code, 0x20 to 0x7F
thenL label byteswhat a screen reader says for the object: UTF-8 with no control character; never drawn
  • The title. With TITLED, a title follows the last object: a length T (1 byte, 1 to 64) and T bytes of UTF-8 with no control character, the name a page list shows for the picture; it is never drawn. NAPLPS has no command that carries undrawn text, so the title travels beside the stream, in this record, as the objects do. A record without ONE sets the picture's title: the one it carries, or none without TITLED. A picture with no objects that has a title is sent a record of count 0 with its title.
  • One object redefined. With ONE, the count is exactly 1 and TITLED is clear: the record's object replaces the page's object of that number, or is added when it has none (within the 64 objects); every other object, with its animation state, and the picture's title are kept, and the redefined object's own animation state and pointer look are forgotten, as a whole set forgets those of what it replaces. It applies to the objects of its generation as a whole record would.
  • Refused whole: a width outside 1 to 480 or a height outside 1 to 500, a label or a title longer than its bound, bytes that are not UTF-8, a control character, an empty title, ONE with a count other than 1 or with TITLED, a reserved flag set. A record with flags 0 and no labels is byte for byte the record of before labels and titles.
  • A macro object is drawn by executing its frame's macro, or a look's, as the stream last defined it, in a fresh presentation state (default attributes, colour mode 0 drawing in white, and the power-up code sets, touching nothing of the stream's own state), with every point it draws moved by (x − origin x, y − origin y) dots and written only inside the object's rectangle. Inside an object's macro these have no effect: SET COLOR's redefinition of the colour map, BLINK, WAIT, RESET, and the definitions of macros, DRCS characters and textures, which are read and dropped; calling another macro, and text in any set including DRCS characters, work as in the stream. An object's macro cannot read the picture. A macro that is not defined draws nothing.
  • A region is a rectangle of the stream's own picture. Shown, it changes nothing unless its look in force has a macro, which is then drawn at its top left corner and clipped to it; hidden, its rectangle is filled with its cover entry on its layer. It exists so that part of an ordinary NAPLPS page can be clicked and covered.
  • Bounds and picking. An object's bounds are its rectangle as its state stands, cut to the raster (dots 0 to 479, lines 0 to 499). An object is inside a pointer's dot when it is shown, detectable and the dot is in its bounds, on the display area or on rows 0 and 24; where several are, each is. Nothing else of a NAPLPS picture can be picked. Nothing is drawn outside the display area.
  • An object's drawing is bounded: at most 16,384 bytes processed, macro expansion counted; past the bound the object's drawing stops.
  • The objects are composed over the stream's picture in order of layer, order and number; an object the animation state puts in layer 0 is still composed over the stream's picture, before every object of layers 1 to 3.
  • WAIT and BLINK are played on the presentation clock. On a WAIT of w tenths a receiver stops feeding that stream's bytes to its renderer for 6 × w ticks and presents the picture as it stands; bytes that arrive meanwhile are held, at most 262,144, and when more arrive the wait ends at once; a stream's waits together are played for at most 3,600 ticks, one minute, in a generation, after which each WAIT passes without delay. A WAIT does not hold the page's other records, its sound or its rule table. A BLINK is played by the colour map alone, at tick boundaries, with no pixel repainted.

7.5 Sprite sheets and the SHEET record

DOC-6598 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6529

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6529 The engine MUST time everything shown in 60 ticks a second and carry animation: FRAME, ANIMATE, SPRITES, NAPLPS_OBJECTS and SHEET records, teletext sprites, damage repaint (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A page's sprite frames are sent once for that page — that page number and sub-code — and named by number afterwards. A sheet belongs to one page and is never shared with another sub-code of the same page number: a program that wants the same sheet on several sub-pages sends it to each. A teletext page's sheet is its objects and the object pages it links (the object_page message). For ReGIS and NAPLPS, record type 26, SHEET, carries bytes of a page's sheet. Its body: the page (2 bytes); the sub-code (2 bytes, 0x0000 to 0x3F7E); a kind (1 byte: 1 ReGIS, 2 NAPLPS); a reserved byte, 0; a generation (2 bytes); an offset (4 bytes); and data, at most 8,172 bytes.

  • A sheet is one stream of at most 65,536 bytes for a page and kind; a new generation starts it again.
  • A receiver MUST keep the page's sheet while that page is selected, feed it to the renderer it makes for that page before the page's own stream, and drop it with the rest of the page's local state. A new generation of a sheet makes the receiver start the page's renderer again from the new sheet.
  • A ReGIS sheet defines hidden drawings and ends with a commit; the page's stream names them as sources, looks and frames. A NAPLPS sheet defines macros, DRCS characters and textures; the page's stream and objects call them.
  • A sheet draws nothing itself: a ReGIS sheet's drawings that are left visible, and anything a NAPLPS sheet draws on the picture, are a fault a server refuses.
  • A server sends a connection a page's sheets at each selection of the page, as a new stream from their start, since it cannot know that a receiver kept the sheet of a page it left. For each connection it holds only the sheet stream it is sending for the page that connection has selected, so that the whole sheet so far is checked at each message, drops it when the connection leaves the page, and never sends it to a later viewer.

8 Teletext packets and pages

DOC-1783 · section

8.1 A packet on a television line

DOC-2120 · reference · informative · requirements REQ-24, REQ-443, REQ-447, REQ-448, REQ-449

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-24 One packet representation (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-443 Finding the clock run-in (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-447 Framing code: found within two bits of its expected place (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-448 Assembling bytes (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-449 The slicer rejects television lines that carry signals other than teletext (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver that reads television lines, not a stream of packets, finds each packet in the line's samples. This is what the engine's slicer does. A receiver that takes T42 packets from a file or a connection has no use for it, and nothing here binds another slicer.

The clock run-in. The slicer searches for the run-in over a configurable window, by default the whole line. The nominal position is 12.0 microseconds, minus 1.0 and plus 0.4, from the synchronising edge, but capture offsets are often unknown. It matches the alternating pattern of bits 3 to 16 and does not rely on the first two bits, which clause 6.1 warns may be reduced or absent. From the run-in it estimates the levels of 0 and 1, the threshold midway between them and the bit phase to a fraction of a sample, and holds the threshold for the rest of the line.

The framing code. After the run-in it looks for 11100100, in transmission order, within two bit periods either way of its expected place. One wrong bit is accepted only on a line where a packet is expected, and only when the two packet address bytes that follow decode with no uncorrectable error. Everywhere else the code must match exactly. The slicer reports whether a correction was needed, and a strict option asks for an exact code on every line.

An expected line. A line is known by its television line number when the source gives it, and otherwise by its field and its place within the field; a line the slicer cannot place is never expected. Fields are counted from the order of the lines: a line of the other field, or one no later in the field than the line before it, begins a new field. A line becomes expected once three packets with an exact framing code and valid address bytes have been accepted on it, each within 50 fields of the one before, and stays expected until 50 fields, one second, have passed since the last of them. A packet accepted only through the one-bit tolerance neither counts toward the three nor renews the expectation, so noise cannot make a line expected.

Bytes. It then assembles 336 bits into 42 bytes, the first bit of each byte as bit 0. Every input, from any source, becomes this one form: the 42 bytes after the framing code, each byte in transmission order with its first transmitted bit as bit 0, and parity and Hamming bits kept. All decoding works from it.

Other signals. Lines carrying the video programming signal on line 16, wide-screen signalling on line 23, test signals or scrambling data are rejected by the run-in match, the framing code and the packet address's Hamming check together.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 6.1 Clock run-in; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 6.2 Framing code; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 7.1 Elements of a Teletext packet; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 annex P Non-Teletext signals in the VBI

8.2 The packet

DOC-1797 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-166, REQ-1462

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-166 T42 packet streams (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1462 Server sends only valid packets downstream (to be rechecked on main).

Everything a receiver decodes is a sequence of 42-byte packets, bytes 4 to 45 of a broadcast packet: no clock run-in and no framing code, in transmission bit order, with parity and Hamming coding intact. This is the T42 form. A receiver MUST accept it from a file and from a WebSocket's binary messages alike.

NeoTeletext's own transports never carry the clock run-in or framing code, and the signal levels and bit rate of the standard's clauses 4 to 6 apply only to the slicer that reads recorded video.

On a live connection a valid packet has an address that decodes, and is one of a page's packets X/0 to X/28, a magazine's packet M/29, packet 8/30, or a packet of data channel 12. A server MUST send only valid packets. A receiver MUST discard and count anything else, without closing the connection.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 7.1 Elements of a Teletext packet; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.1 Overview of packet types; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 1 Summary of packet types, their function and application; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.2 Hamming 8/4

8.3 Byte coding and error protection

DOC-1798 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-114, REQ-115, REQ-116, REQ-117, REQ-118, REQ-119, REQ-357

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-114 Odd parity check (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-115 Hamming 8/4 decoding (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-116 Hamming 8/4 encoding of 4-bit values (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-117 Hamming 24/18 decoding (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-118 Encode 18-bit values into Hamming 24/18 triplets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-119 Bit reversal (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-357 Reserved bits and bytes are ignored when decoding (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Odd parity, Hamming 8/4 and Hamming 24/18 are as the standard defines them, and an implementation MUST follow its encoding and decoding equations. NeoTeletext's choices are what happens to data that cannot be corrected.

WhereRule
Packet address, bytes 4 and 5A byte that cannot be corrected discards the whole packet and counts it.
Header, bytes 6 to 13The header MUST still end the page in reception. It MUST NOT start a page, and its display bytes MUST NOT feed the rolling header.
Editorial linkThat one link is invalid, and treated as no link.
Packet 8/30The field the byte belongs to is invalid.
Triplet in enhancement dataThe triplet is skipped, and does not move the active position.
Character failing parityBy default it does not replace a character that passed in an earlier reception of the same sub-page, unless the page was erased between them. A cell that never held a character that passed shows a space.

A single error in a Hamming 8/4 protection bit, P4 included, is reported as corrected, and the data is used. The sixteen Hamming 8/4 code bytes are those of clause 8.2. A Hamming 24/18 triplet is an uncorrectable one when the tests of clause 8.3 say so, or when the computed error position is above 24.

Bit-reversal between broadcast order and the order of a transport stream is applied only when reading a transport stream.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.1 Odd parity; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.2 Hamming 8/4; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.3 Hamming 24/18; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.2 Reserved bits

8.4 Packet address bytes

DOC-1752 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-349

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-349 Packet address (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver MUST read a packet's magazine and packet number from its two Hamming 8/4 address bytes, and MUST discard the packet when either byte cannot be corrected.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 7.1.2 Packet address

8.5 The page header

DOC-1799 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-72, REQ-302, REQ-303, REQ-350

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-72 Selecting the character set of a page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-302 Page number structure (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-303 Sub-code structure and range (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-350 Page header (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver MUST read a header's Hamming 8/4 bytes 6 to 13 as the page units and tens, the sub-code elements S1 to S4, and the control bits C4 to C14, keeping a separate validity for the page number, the sub-code and the control bits, and MUST keep the 32 display bytes 14 to 45 with their parity. The three bits of byte 9 and 11 that do not carry the sub-code carry C4, C5 and C6, and MUST NOT be read as part of it.

The national option is 4 × C12 + 2 × C13 + C14, so the three bits of the decoded byte are reversed to form it. Implementations often get this wrong, and two off-air recordings confirm it: the reversed order gives the wrong language.

Bytes 6 to 13 of a header are never displayed. Columns 8 to 39 of row 0 show header bytes 14 to 45.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1 Page header; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.1 Page number; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.2 Page sub-code; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.3 Control bits; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 2 Control bits in the page header

8.6 Display rows, X/1 to X/25

DOC-1800 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-242, REQ-351

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-242 A row that has not been received is displayed as 40 spaces (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-351 Decode display row packets X/1 to X/25 as forty 7-bit characters with parity status (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver MUST read bytes 6 to 45 of packets X/1 to X/25 as 40 seven-bit characters, each with its parity status. On an enhancement page the same packets hold triplets, not characters: see the packets of object pages.

A row not received shows 40 spaces.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.2 Packets X/1 to X/25; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause D.1.1 Missing packets X/1 to X/25

8.7 Enhancement packets, X/26

DOC-1801 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-352, REQ-358

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-352 Decoding enhancement packets X/26: the designation code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-358 Triplet functions at Levels 2.5 and 3.5 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver MUST read byte 6 of packet X/26 as a Hamming 8/4 designation code, and bytes 7 to 45 as thirteen Hamming 24/18 triplets, each split into its 6-bit address, 5-bit mode and 7-bit data, and marked valid or invalid. Every valid triplet is one row or column function of Tables 28 and 29, with reserved modes reported as reserved. One decoding serves Level 1.5, Levels 2.5 and 3.5 and objects.

All sixteen designation codes are processed, 15 included, in the default profile. The SAA5246A profile ignores X/26/15, as that chip does.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.4.1 Packet X/26; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3.1 Use of Packets X/26; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 27 Summary of Packet X/26 Triplet Functions; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets

8.8 Link packets, X/27

DOC-1802 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-120, REQ-286, REQ-316, REQ-353, REQ-359

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-120 Page checksum (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-316 Sub-code 3F7F in links names no particular sub-code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-353 Editorial link extraction from packet 27 designation 0 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-359 Compositional link packets X/27/4 and X/27/5 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

X/27/0. A receiver MUST extract the six links, computing each link's magazine by exclusive-OR of the packet's own magazine with its relative magazine bits, and MUST treat page number FF with sub-code 3F7F as no link. It MUST read the Link Control Byte, including the flag that displays row 24, and the two checksum bytes. The checksum MAY be used to check a page, and an encoder writing X/27/0 MUST compute it as clause 9.6.1 defines, with absent packets taken as spaces.

X/27/1 to X/27/3 are stored without interpretation. X/27/4 and X/27/5 are decoded as the compositional links of Levels 2.5 and 3.5, with a link holding an uncorrectable triplet marked invalid. X/27/6 to X/27/15 are ignored.

Links 1 to 4 of X/27/0 are the red, green, yellow and cyan keys, and link 6 the Index key. Link 5 is never followed by a viewer.
