9.7 No downloaded characters: DRCS is banned throughout NeoTeletext

DOC-2266 · reference · informative · requirements REQ-2196

Dynamically Redefinable Character Sets, DRCS, are characters whose 12 by 10 pixel patterns a service downloads in DRCS and Global DRCS pages (EN 300 706 clause 14; page functions 0100 and 0101 of Table 3, clause 9.4.2.1), and which a page places with a DRCS Character Invocation triplet (Table 29, column mode 01101) or sets up with a DRCS Mode triplet (Table 28, row mode 11000). NeoTeletext wants no form of bitmap graphics, which is what the web is for, so DRCS is banned in every component and every design, not only left out of decoding.

  • Nothing decodes or draws it. The engine, neottx, the browser and every receiver built on the engine show a page that uses DRCS as a receiver without DRCS shows it, as What NeoTeletext does not implement says. Recordings of broadcasts that carry DRCS are still read; their DRCS is ignored.
  • Nothing produces it. No encoder, page writer, converter, kit or library emits a DRCS Character Invocation, a DRCS Mode triplet, a DRCS or Global DRCS downloading page, or a DRCS link, and none offers a call that would. Test input that exists to show DRCS being ignored is read, never produced for a channel.
  • No design relies on it. Characters are drawn from NeoTeletext's character sets and its compiled font, and the mosaics and G3 characters are drawn in code. A script whose characters do not fit sets of 96 codes, such as kanji, is not shown by downloading glyphs.

The standard makes DRCS optional at Levels 2.5 and 3.5, so a receiver without it is a valid receiver. One part of the ban is not built: the NeoTeletext server does not yet refuse a program's page or raw packet that is a DRCS downloading page or carries a DRCS triplet.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 14 Dynamically Re-definable Characters; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.4.2.1 Page Function and Page Coding; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 3 Page function and page coding bits (packets X/28/0 Format 1, X/28/3 and X/28/4); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets

9.8 Extensions to the triplets

DOC-1844 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-216, REQ-217, REQ-283, REQ-2180

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-216 Controls: a page declares the cells it answers itself by triplets of column mode 00101 in its local enhancement data, which change nothing drawn (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-217 Controls are bounded and checked (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-283 Reserved and Programme Delivery Control triplets have no display effect (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2180 [CHR] When a column triplet of packet X/26 has mode 01010, the decoder MUST read the row's own codes in the designated G0 set from its column (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

NeoTeletext adds to the packets of the standard in three places, using values the standard reserves, so that any other decoder treats them as it treats anything reserved.

Column mode 00101, a control. Table 29 reserves this mode. In a page's local enhancement data it declares a run of cells the page answers itself: its address is the first column, D5 to D0 the width, 1 to 40, and D6 joins it to the control on the row above at the same column and width. Its row is the active row, from the Set Active Position or Full Row Colour triplet before it. The mode draws nothing, and a page with controls looks the same everywhere. Its controls travel, are stored and are recorded with its rows, in a page frame, a .t42 file or a TTI page's OL,26 lines.

  • One triplet is one control on its row, so four buttons on a row are four triplets, separate even where they touch. A taller control repeats its triplet on each row below with D6 set.
  • Only the page's local enhancement data declares controls, up to its first Termination Marker or Object Definition. An object declares none.
  • A triplet is dropped and counted, and the others kept, for a row outside 1 to 23, no width, a run past column 39, a cell already in a control, a joined run under no control of its column and width, or more than 32 controls on the page.

Column mode 01010, a row set. Table 29 reserves this mode. In a page's local enhancement data, on the active row, it names a character set for the row's own codes: its address is the column it takes effect from, 0 to 39, and D6 to D0 a whole designation in the coding of Table 32, the group in D6 to D3 and the national option in D2 to D0. From that column to the next row set on the row, or the row's end, a receiver reads the row's alphanumeric codes 2/0 to 7/F as characters of the G0 set the value designates, with its national option, and characters that X/26 places there take that set and its G2 set, as after a Modified G0 and G2 Character Set Designation. A value no table holds falls back as the page's default designation does.

  • Each run starts in its own set, whatever ESC did before it; ESC inside a run switches to the page's second G0 set and back.
  • A later Modified G0 and G2 Character Set Designation on the row changes only the characters X/26 and objects write, as Table 29 says, and does not end the run.
  • The next row starts in the page's default set. Mosaic codes stay mosaics, and the row below double height follows the row above.
  • The triplet leaves the active position where it was, as a reserved mode does. An object's row set does nothing.
  • A receiver that does not know the mode shows the run in the page's own sets, so a page that must read correctly elsewhere uses the standard's means alone.

Designations in Tables 32 to 34. NeoTeletext's own character sets use values the tables reserve.

The behaviour of controls under a pointer belongs to the upstream protocol.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3.2 Active Position; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3.4 Column Address triplets

9.9 Character sets

DOC-1845 · section

9.9.1 How teletext came to have G0 and G2 sets

DOC-2182 · concept · informative · requirements REQ-72

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-72 Selecting the character set of a page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every character set teletext has answers one question: how to show more than 96 characters while every receiver already sold keeps working.

One set for English (1974 to 1976). The first specification, by the BBC, the IBA and the manufacturers' association BREMA (October 1974), used ISO 7-bit ASCII with British national characters such as £ at 2/3. The 1976 Broadcast Teletext Specification, which Ceefax and ORACLE broadcast, fixed one English set of 96 characters. The header bits C12 to C14 were "unallocated".

National options. When teletext spread across Europe, other languages needed letters English lacks. The 7-bit page could not grow, so 13 positions (2/3, 2/4, 4/0, 5/B to 5/F, 6/0 and 7/B to 7/E, holding £ $ @ arrows # ½ ¼ ‖ ¾ ÷ in English) were given over to each language's most needed letters. Each variant is a national option sub-set. The Mullard SAA5050 family made one chip for each option (SAA5050 English, SAA5051 German, SAA5052 Swedish), and a maker chose a language by fitting a chip. Later decoders held several options and used C12 to C14 to pick one of eight within a region. Thirteen positions do not hold Czech, Polish, Turkish, Romanian or the Baltic alphabets, and a page could still use only one option.

Supplementary sets. The World System Teletext specification of 1990 (CCIR System B, SRC-2157) and EBU SPB 492 of 1992 (SRC-2158) kept the Level 1 page unchanged and added packets X/26, instructions each aimed at one cell that a newer decoder applies on top of the page. They defined for each script a primary set, now G0, and a supplementary set, now G2: Latin, Arabic, Cyrillic, Greek and Hebrew. The 1990 register of set codes (Figure 14, page 144) also had entries for Devanagari, Thai, Lao, Korean, Japanese and others; SPB 492 marked those entries reserved (page 116), and they were never carried into today's standard. The Latin G2 set took its accented capitals, symbols and the 15 accent marks of its column 4 from ISO 6937. With G2 a page can place any accented letter: a ready-made G2 character, or a G0 letter with a G2 accent drawn over it.

Level 1.5. Broadcasters whose languages needed more than 96 characters sent only the part that mattered: X/26 packets carrying a few G2 characters and a few accented letters, and decoders were built that understood just that. ETS 300 706 (1997), now EN 300 706, first described this as Level 1.5, which "has evolved in the field due to the language requirements in certain countries". Its G2 repertoire "is not fixed and is determined by the language requirements in the country of use".

Today. EN 300 706 keeps four G2 sets: Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and Arabic. The Hebrew G2 set of the 1992 register has no table, and Table 32 pairs Hebrew G0 with Arabic G2.

Every step kept old receivers working. A Level 1 television ignores X/26 and shows the stand-in the row holds, usually the unaccented letter, so an enhanced page reads plainly on a 1980 set and exactly on a later one.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.1 Overview of designation requirements (Level 1.5: X/26 packets for languages needing more than 96 characters); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 32 Function of Default G0 and G2 Character Set Designation and National Option (Hebrew G0 paired with Arabic G2)

9.9.2 How characters are held

DOC-1846 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-70, REQ-79, REQ-423

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-70 Internal character representation (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-79 Unicode conversion (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-423 Text and terminal renderers emit only allow-listed characters (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Inside a decoder each character is a character set identifier and a seven-bit code, never a Unicode value, with a diacritical mark's number when it has one. Conversion to Unicode happens only at output, because some teletext characters have no exact Unicode equivalent.

Any internal character converts to a Unicode scalar value or a short sequence, or to a documented fallback. Text and terminal output MUST pass an allow-list of printable characters: C0 and C1 controls, DEL and every bidirectional control are removed, and a terminal renderer emits only its own escape sequences.

9.9.3 Selecting a page's character sets

DOC-1847 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-72, REQ-78, REQ-264

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-72 Selecting the character set of a page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-78 The ESC attribute toggles between the default and second G0 sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-264 Default G0 and G2 sets taken from Annex C.4 rule 1 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The national option is always the header's C12 to C14 at Levels 1 and 1.5. The group, bits 11 to 14 of the Table 32 value, comes from the page's X/28/0 Format 1 when present and correct, then the latest M/29/0 of its magazine, then the receiver's configured region, by default 0000.

At Levels 2.5 and 3.5 the national option comes from bits 8 to 10 of the highest-priority designation when one is present, and C12 to C14 otherwise, in the order of Annex C.4 rule 1: X/28/0 Format 1, X/28/4 at Level 3.5, M/29/0, M/29/4 at Level 3.5.

The G0 and G2 sets in force come from Table 32. When the entry is reserved, the same three national option bits are tried in group 0000, and when that is also reserved, English is used. The fallback is counted as a diagnostic.

The designation also sets the default sets used by X/26 characters, and the second G0 set used by ESC through Table 33. With no second set, or designation 1111111, ESC only occupies its cell. The national option bits do not apply to the second set. X/28/1 and M/29/1 never affect character sets.

A Modified G0 and G2 Character Set Designation triplet (mode 01000) selects a pair from Table 34, and reserved values are ignored. It lasts to the end of the row in local data and Active objects, and to the last character cell of the object in Adaptive and Passive objects, or to the next such triplet. It never affects the Level 1 page. At Level 2.5 a designation that would make more than two pairs on a page, counting the default, is ignored. At Level 3.5 there is no limit.

9.9.4 How a page's G0 and G2 sets work together

DOC-2183 · concept · informative · requirements REQ-72, REQ-78

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-72 Selecting the character set of a page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-78 The ESC attribute toggles between the default and second G0 sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A page chooses a pair, not two sets. A page never names its G0 and G2 sets separately. Table 32 lists the allowed combinations, each a G0 set with its national option and the G2 set that goes with it, and a page chooses one row of it. A receiver holds the table; no broadcast can change it. Some rows:

Group, optionG0 setPaired G2 set
0000, 001Latin, GermanLatin
0100, 100Cyrillic 2 (Russian and Bulgarian)Cyrillic
0110, 111GreekGreek
1000, 111ArabicArabic
1010, 101HebrewArabic
1000, 000Latin, EnglishArabic

A page can be "German with Latin G2" but not German G0 with Greek G2, which the table does not list.

Why these pairs. A G2 set completes its G0 set. Latin G2 adds accents, accented capitals and symbols. Cyrillic G2 holds the Latin letters Cyrillic G0 lacks (D E F G I J K L N Q R S U V W Z), so a Russian page can write a brand name; Greek G2 does the same for Greek, with accented Greek capitals. Arabic G2 holds Arabic letter forms and a Latin alphabet with French accented letters, which is why it is also paired with Latin English and Latin French in the Arabic group, where pages mix the two scripts. Hebrew has no G2 set of its own, so Hebrew G0 is paired with Arabic G2.

How the choice is sent. At Level 1 by the header's national option bits C12 to C14, the group coming from the receiver's region. At higher levels by a whole 7-bit value in X/28/0 Format 1 or X/28/4 for the page, or M/29/0 or M/29/4 for its magazine. A second G0 set (Table 33), toggled by ESC, has no G2 of its own: G2 characters still come from the default pair. At Levels 2.5 and 3.5 a Modified G0 and G2 Character Set Designation triplet chooses a row of Table 34 for the characters X/26 and objects write later on the same row; it never changes the row's own codes, and its G0 set has no national option. The exact rules are DOC-1847's.

A row never holds a G2 code. Every byte of a row is a G0 character or a control code, so the rows alone are always a complete Level 1 page. G2 arrives in packet X/26, cell by cell, in two ways:

X/26 instructionEffect on the cell
Character from the G2 set (mode 01111)Replaces the cell's G0 character with a G2 character
G0 character with diacritical mark (modes 10000 to 11111)Draws a mark from column 4 of the G2 set over a G0 letter

The cell keeps its colours and other attributes; only its character changes. The second way reaches any accented letter: 26 letters with 15 marks, more than any 96-character table holds.

Stand-ins. The row holds a stand-in at every cell X/26 changes, usually the plain letter: Muller in the row and a mark triplet on the u. A Level 1 television ignores X/26 and shows Muller; a Level 1.5 one shows Müller.

How many characters a set has. Every set has positions 2/0 to 7/F. A G0 set fills all 96, with the space at 2/0 and the block at 7/F. A G2 set leaves some empty: Latin G2 has 91 characters including the space (2/0, 4/0, 5/9, 5/A, 5/B and 6/5 are empty), Cyrillic G2 93, and Greek and Arabic G2 95. Fifteen of Latin G2's characters, column 4, are marks, mostly drawn over a G0 letter. A few G2 characters repeat G0 ones, such as $, # and the block.

From position to glyph. A font knows nothing of teletext positions: each glyph is labelled with a Unicode code point. A receiver maps each set's positions to Unicode by the standard's tables (DOC-1848), and a marked letter to its precomposed character where Unicode has one, then draws the glyph for that code point (DOC-1851). One glyph therefore serves every set with that character.

9.9.5 The sets of the standard

DOC-1848 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-71, REQ-73, REQ-74, REQ-75, REQ-76, REQ-77, REQ-80

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-71 Latin G0 with national options (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-73 Other G0 sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-74 The G1 mosaic set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-75 The G2 sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-76 The G3 set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-77 Diacritical marks from G2 column 4 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-80 Unicode for the G3 set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every set of clause 15 is implemented as a code table with its Unicode mapping: Latin G0 with all 13 national option subsets of Table 36, the three Cyrillic G0 options, Greek, Arabic and Hebrew G0, the Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and Arabic G2 sets, G1 and G3.

The base forms of Table 35 are used whenever X/26 refers to a Latin G0 character. Four national option glyphs are too small in the standard to identify, and are mapped as below. The Turkish currency sign at 2/3 is mapped to U+20BA.

PositionCharacterUnicode
Polish 5/BZ with strokeU+01B5
Polish 7/Dl with strokeU+0142
English 6/0Long dashU+2014
English 7/CDouble vertical barU+2016

Positions the standard leaves undefined show a space: Latin G2 5/9, 5/A, 5/B and 6/5, and G3 6/E, 6/F, 7/E and 7/F. G3 position 5/F, which shows the background colour, converts to a space.

Mosaics as text. Take n = (code AND 0x1F) OR ((code AND 0x40) shifted right by 1). Contiguous mosaics map as: 0 to a space, 21 to U+258C, 42 to U+2590, 63 to U+2588, and the rest to U+1FB00 to U+1FB3B in increasing n, skipping 21 and 42. Separated mosaics map to U+1CE50 + n.

G3 as text follows Unicode's TELTXTG3.TXT mapping.

Diacritical marks. Column 4 of the G2 set gives the sixteen marks, which the "G0 character with diacritical mark" triplets, column modes 10000 to 11111 of Table 29, place over a G0 character (clause 12.3.4). The standard does not name 4/9 and 4/C, and NeoTeletext treats them as U+0323 and U+0332. A mark is kept on a character of any G0 set, not only the Latin sets. Where the core's composition tables give the base and the mark a precomposed character, that character's glyph is drawn; otherwise the mark's spacing glyph is overlaid on the base. The tables hold every Unicode Normalization Form C precomposition of a Latin letter with the marks, and the further pairs the sets need: the letters of the extended sets, Cyrillic ё and Ё as е and Е with the diaeresis, and Greek Ό as Ο with the acute. In text, the base and combining mark are normalised to Form C. Annex E.10 recommends that authors keep to the Latin sets because older decoders may not cope; it places no duty on a decoder to drop the mark.

9.9.6 NeoTeletext's own character sets

DOC-1849 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-81, REQ-82, REQ-83, REQ-84, REQ-2185, REQ-2188

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-81 Designations of neoteletext's own sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-82 The code tables of neoteletext's own sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-83 Diacritical marks from the page's G2 set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-84 Joining Arabic-script letters (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2185 Japanese rōmaji national option sub-set code table (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2188 [CHR] Japanese kana: Hiragana and Katakana G0 sets code tables (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The feature extended-sets, in the default build and the browser's, adds sets for about 50 languages the standard does not serve, and for Japanese. Each is one byte per cell, read as EN 300 706 defines, and is designated by a value Tables 32 to 34 reserve. The allocation is NeoTeletext's own, so another decoder takes the fallback of Table 32's reserved values, as does a build without the feature. Every new set has Latin English as its second G0 set, switched by ESC, except where the table names another.

0111 101 to 0111 111Cyrillic: Kyrgyz and Mongolian, Tatar, TajikCyrillic
1001 000 to 1001 111Arabic script: Persian and Dari, Urdu, Pashto, Sindhi, Sorani Kurdish, Uyghur, Balochi, Arabic in plain lettersArabic

Every value of group 1100 is reserved: NeoTeletext defines no set there, and a page designating one takes the fallback of a reserved value.

A Level 1 page gets its group from the receiver's region, as for every group. Every G0 set has the space at 2/0 and the block at 7/F.

Marks. A diacritical-mark triplet takes its mark from column 4 of the page's current G2 set when that column holds marks (Latin, Armenian and Vietnamese), and from Latin G2 otherwise. The Vietnamese G2 4/C is U+0309.

Arabic-script sets. Each holds a letter once, and the receiver chooses its form. After a page's grid is composed, each row is passed once from right to left. A letter's previous letter is the cell to its right, and its next the cell to its left, when each holds a letter of the same set. It joins its previous letter when that is dual-joining or join-causing, and its next when it is itself dual-joining and the next is dual-joining, right-joining or join-causing. Joining neither is isolated, both medial, only the previous final, and only the next initial. Joining types are Unicode's ArabicShaping.txt, with lam-alef right-joining. Rows stay in visual order. Digits keep 3/0 to 3/9.

Japanese. The kana sets hold the digits at 3/0 to 3/9 and the same sound at the same code in both: the 75 kana they share fill 4/0 to 7/E, then 2/2 to 2/7, 2/A, 2/F and 3/B to 3/E, in Unicode order. Voiced kana are characters of their own. Hiragana keeps ! + - : ? at their ASCII codes and 「 」 at 2/8 and 2/9; katakana holds ァ ィ ゥ ェ ォ ヴ and ー in those places, ー at 2/D; both put 、 at 2/C and 。 at 2/E. No receiver rule applies.

The code tables of these sets follow.

9.9.7 The code tables of NeoTeletext's own sets

DOC-2028 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-81, REQ-82, REQ-83, REQ-84, REQ-2185, REQ-2188

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-81 Designations of neoteletext's own sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-82 The code tables of neoteletext's own sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-83 Diacritical marks from the page's G2 set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-84 Joining Arabic-script letters (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2185 Japanese rōmaji national option sub-set code table (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2188 [CHR] Japanese kana: Hiragana and Katakana G0 sets code tables (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

These are the code tables of NeoTeletext's own character sets, which no standard holds. A decoder holds them as it holds the tables of EN 300 706. They are written from the engine's own tables, so they cannot differ from what a receiver on the engine does.

Each table gives its set's characters in Unicode. The bytes shown first are those characters in UTF-8, code 2/0 first. Each row after them is a column of the table, named as the standard names a position, column then row, and lists its sixteen cells in order. A cell is the code point in hexadecimal, then the character, so 01B0 ư in the fourth place of column 2 says that code 2/3 of the set is U+01B0. A cell the set leaves empty is a space.

Latin with an option. Each is Table 35 with the 13 national option positions replaced, as an option of Table 36 replaces them. Only those positions are listed. The last is Japanese rōmaji's.

Whole Latin sets, and Cyrillic. A whole set holds its letters itself, so that an X/26 diacritical mark finds them. The Vietnamese G2 set goes with the Vietnamese G0 set. The Cyrillic sets are Tables 38, 39 and 40 with some positions changed, so that letters keep their codes, and use the standard's Cyrillic G2 set.

Arabic script. Each set holds a letter once, and a receiver chooses the form to draw by the joining rule. All of them use the standard's Arabic G2 set.

Other alphabets. Georgian and Tifinagh use Latin G2. Armenian has a G2 set of its own.

Japanese kana. Hiragana and katakana hold the same sound at the same code, and each is the other's second set. Both use Latin G2.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.6 Alphanumeric Character Sets

9.9.8 Text in many languages on one page

DOC-2263 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-2147, REQ-2148, REQ-2149, REQ-2150, REQ-2151, REQ-2180, REQ-2181

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-2147 Text carries its language: page default language, per-run language, Unicode input (not implemented on main); REQ-2149 A page's local enhancement data is refused when it needs more than 208 triplets (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-2150 Author's text with an unshowable character fails page making (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-2151 Character-set mix checked against the page's declared presentation level (tested, not recorded as met on main); REQ-2180 [CHR] When a column triplet of packet X/26 has mode 01010, the decoder MUST read the row's own codes in the designated G0 set from its column (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2181 [CHR] The core holds one table mapping each in-scope language, by BCP 47 tag, to its character-set designation (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A NeoTeletext page carries its text's languages, and the people who write channels write ordinary Unicode. They never choose character codes, character sets, ESC codes or X/26 triplets for text: one encoder, the engine's, turns text and its languages into teletext, and the NeoTeletext server runs it for a program (see From a program to the server).

A page has a default language, and a run of text may name its own. A language is named by its BCP 47 tag, such as ru, el or ar, never by a designation code. The page's language decides its default G0 and G2 sets, which are sent in two places: the header's control bits C12 to C14 (EN 300 706 clause 9.3.1.3 and Table 2), and triplet 1 bits 8 to 14 of the page's X/28/0 Format 1 packet (clause 9.4.2, Table 4; clause 15.2, Table 32). The whole designation is always sent, as TR 100 287 clause 10.3 recommends, because C12 to C14 alone cannot tell English from Polish. A run that names no language is in the page's language.

One table of languages. One constant table in the engine's core maps each language to the 7-bit designation of its G0 and G2 pair, in the coding of Table 32, and to the designation it prefers for the page's second G0 set. A tag is matched on its language subtag and, for a language written in more than one script, its script subtag, ignoring case, region and other subtags: sr, Serbian, gives the Cyrillic set of Table 38, and sr-Latn a Latin national option of Table 36. The table holds one entry for each language the standard's sets serve (Tables 32 and 36 to 44) and each language NeoTeletext's own sets serve, and none for any other. A tag it does not hold gives no set, so text in that language is text the page cannot show, and nothing falls back silently to Latin English. The encoder and the server's list of languages read this table.

The order of means. For each character the encoder uses the first means that shows it: the page's default G0 set as the row's own code; the page's second G0 set as the row's own code after an ESC; a G0 letter of the current set with a diacritical mark from the G2 set; a G2 character; and then, for a character of another set, the means of the page's level below. Where a triplet writes the character, the row holds a stand-in at that cell that a Level 1 decoder can show, and only one column triplet selects a character at any cell (Annex A.3). The same input always gives the same bytes, whether neottx write-text or the server runs the encoder.

What text costs. Two sets cost nothing, because their characters are the page's own Level 1 row codes: the default G0 set (clause 15.2), and the second G0 set of Table 33, reached by the spacing attribute ESC at one cell for each switch (clauses 15.1 and 15.3). Text in any further set is written in one of two ways, by the level the page is written for:

  • For NeoTeletext's own receivers, the default: a row set triplet, NeoTeletext's own column mode 01010 (see Extensions to the triplets), at the first cell of the run switches the row's own codes into the run's set, so a run costs one triplet whatever its length, besides the row's address triplet.
  • For Level 3.5 and below: only the standard's means. A Modified G0 and G2 Character Set Designation (column mode 01000, clause 15.4, Table 34) changes only the characters X/26 and objects write, and not the Level 1 page (Table 29, mode 01000), until the next such triplet or the row's end (Annex C.4 rule 2). So every character of a further set is a triplet of its own: mode 01001, or a marked letter (modes 10000 to 11111) or a G2 character (mode 01111) (Table 29). At Level 2.5 only one pair besides the default may be designated on a page; at Level 3.5 any number may.

One budget. Sixteen packets X/26 of thirteen triplets each (clauses 9.4.1 and 12.3.1, Table 27) give a page 208 triplets of local enhancement data, and every one of these draws on them: row set triplets, Modified Designations, characters of further sets, marked letters, G2 characters, NeoTeletext's control triplets, the Set Active Position triplet that begins each row's column triplets (Table 28), and the Termination Marker after the data (Annex A.3). Triplets are ordered as Annex A.4 requires. Objects (clause 13) are not merged with text. A page over the budget is refused when it is made, with the count, so a developer learns it from the channel's tests and not from a viewer. A translator page with every row in its own language costs about 44 triplets for NeoTeletext's receivers; written for Level 3.5, a page holds roughly 190 characters of further sets.

Right-to-left text is put in visual order, as the standard's Arabic set of Table 44 is laid out, and Arabic letters take their joined forms.

Text a page cannot show. In the program's own text, a character none of the level's means shows in the run's language, such as an emoji or a Chinese character, is refused when the page is made, with the character, its code point and the run, so a channel's tests fail on its own text. Text the program receives from outside, a viewer's typing or a feed, is shown instead: a program marks such a run outside, and each character its language cannot show becomes the language's stand-in, the first of the question mark, the Arabic script's own question mark, a hyphen or a full stop that the language shows, and the page is sent. Each character replaced is written once for each page message to the server's log as the event stand_in, with the page, the code point, the stand-in and the language. The NeoTeletext server has kept both rules since program protocol 10.

The level a page is written for. A page may be written for NeoTeletext's own receivers, the default, which compose Level 3.5 with NeoTeletext's own extensions, or for Level 3.5 as the standard defines it, where no row set triplet and no set that only NeoTeletext's receivers hold is used. A developer who needs a page to read correctly on another decoder chooses Level 3.5. The design also lets a page be written for Level 2.5, 1.5 or 1, each checked against what its level allows; those three are not built.

One recommendation not followed. TR 100 287 clause 10.3 recommends that a service with pages in several alphabets give particular magazines to each language, so that a searching decoder shows rolling headers in the right alphabet. That is guidance for broadcast services, and a NeoTeletext page may mix alphabets freely.

9.9.9 Generated character tables and the core's private-use code points

DOC-2323 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-2164, REQ-2166

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-2164 Generated character tables match their generator's output (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2166 Only the core allocates private-use code points for joined Arabic forms (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Generated tables. Most of the engine's code tables are written by hand from the standards. The Arabic-script tables of NeoTeletext's own group 1001 are not: scripts/arabic-sets.py lays them out and writes them, with the joining type of every letter and the code point drawn for each joined form, between the marker lines // BEGIN generated by scripts/arabic-sets.py and // END generated by scripts/arabic-sets.py in crates/neoteletext-core/src/charset/arabic_script.rs, from Unicode's ArabicShaping.txt, which it downloads and checks by SHA-256. The text between the markers is exactly what the generator writes from its committed inputs and is never edited by hand: a change is made in the generator, which is then run. The generator is to have a checking mode, --check, that compares what it would write with what is committed, changes nothing and fails naming the first difference, run by the push gate from a cached copy of the pinned input, failing and saying what it lacks rather than being skipped when that copy is missing. On 3 November 2026 the script and the committed tables agreed, and the checking mode and its gate step were not yet built. The same rule holds for any table a script generates later.

Private-use code points. A font labels each glyph by a code point, and some glyphs NeoTeletext draws have none of their own in Unicode: joined Arabic-script forms that Unicode gives no presentation form, such as several Pashto letters (ټ ځ څ ډ ړ ږ ښ ګ ڼ). The core gives them code points in Supplementary Private Use Area-A, by these rules.

  1. The core's own. Only the core's tables allocate these code points. A font supplies glyphs at them and never defines what they mean, and a glyph in a font at a code point the core has not allocated gives no character.
  2. Stable and append-only. Once allocated and released, a code point keeps its meaning; a new form takes the next free code point of its range, and a withdrawn form leaves its code point unused, never reused. Each range's allocation is one table in the core, from which glyphs/forms.txt is generated. The Arabic forms are today allocated in sorted letter order, so adding a letter can renumber those after it; making the allocation append-only is still to be done.
  3. Ranges kept apart. Arabic forms take U+F0000 to U+F00FF. U+F0100 to U+F017F are retired, allocated to nothing since 3 November 2026 and never to be allocated again, because fonts made with glyphs there exist and would draw them for a new meaning. A future range starts at U+F0180 or above. A range that would overflow, or any allocation in the retired range, fails the build.
  4. Never text. No private-use code point leaves the core as text: converting a joined form to Unicode gives the plain Arabic letter. Private-use code points exist only between the core's tables and a font's glyphs.

9.9.10 Codes kept free for China's teletext standard

DOC-2324 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-2160

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-2160 [CHR] NeoTeletext MUST NOT give its own meaning to the codes CCST uses (not implemented on livedevelopment).

China's teletext standard, CCST (GB/T 14219-1993), is a complete teletext standard on World System Teletext's transport: GB 2312 characters sent in pairs of bytes, each drawn 24 by 24 across 2 cells and 3 rows, switched with the codes 0/E and 0/F. Chinese is out of NeoTeletext's scope for now, and CCST is the way to add it later as a regional profile. That is possible without conflict only if NeoTeletext never gives the codes CCST uses a meaning of its own. So no NeoTeletext character set, triplet extension or other addition gives any of these a meaning:

  1. the header's control bits C12 to C14 set to 111, which in a CCST region mean a Chinese page;
  2. the codes 0/E and 0/F, which CCST uses to switch between Western and Chinese text, in place of double width and double size;
  3. packet X/25, which CCST uses for vertical parity for error correction, not for display;
  4. packets X/27/4 to X/27/7, which CCST uses to link the pseudo-pages of its downloaded characters;
  5. in packets X/26: column mode 00100, which CCST uses to invoke a character set; bit D3 of column mode 01100, which it uses for half brightness; and bits b6 to b3 of row mode 00000, which it uses for the background and foreground of the whole page;
  6. two-byte codes whose first byte is 7/F, which CCST uses for downloaded characters, and 7F7E, which fills the rows under a Chinese character.

The meanings EN 300 706 itself gives these codes stay as the engine implements them; only new meanings of NeoTeletext's own are excluded. EN 300 706 reserves column mode 00100 and bit D3 of mode 01100, so CCST's use of them does not conflict with the standard, and NeoTeletext must not take them either. On 3 November 2026 no NeoTeletext extension used any of these codes: the control triplet uses column mode 00101, and the row set triplet, which switches a row's own codes into another character set, uses column mode 01010 rather than 00100 for this reason. Each decision that adds or changes a NeoTeletext set, designation or triplet extension states that it uses none of them.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets (Rests on: column mode 00100 and bit D3 of mode 01100, which the standard reserves); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets (Rests on: row mode 00000, whose bits b6 to b3 CCST uses for the page's colours); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 2 Control bits in the page header (Rests on: the control bits C12 to C14 of the page header); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.6 Packets for Page Linking (Rests on: packets X/27/4 to X/27/7)

9.9.11 ReGIS's provided alphabets 100 to 154: NeoTeletext's character sets in a ReGIS picture

DOC-6831 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6764

Text in a ReGIS picture is written only in NeoTeletext's 55 provided character sets, as text in every renderer is (a page brings no letters of its own). ReGIS selects a character set with the text command's alphabet option, T(A n) (VT330/VT340 Programmer Reference Manual, volume 2, chapter 7, "Select Character Set"). The VT340 defines alphabet 0, built in, and alphabets 1 to 3, loadable. NeoTeletext's ReGIS adds alphabets 100 to 154: alphabet 100 + n is provided set n, in the engine's order of its sets (the order of NAPLPS's private designations of the same sets).

  • What a string draws. In a provided alphabet a quoted string's byte 0x20 to 0x7E draws the set's position at that code. Any other byte a string keeps (0xA0 to 0xFF) draws the empty character cell and advances. Position 7/15 of a set cannot be reached from ReGIS. The text control characters BS, HT, LF and CR act as in any alphabet. A quote inside a quoted string is written twice.
  • Drawn as a built-in character. A provided glyph is scaled into the unit cell as a built-in character is, under every text option: size, direction, italic and the writing mode.
  • Not loadable. The load command L MUST refuse a provided alphabet, as it refuses any alphabet past 3.
  • Others ignored. An alphabet from 4 to 99 or past 154 is ignored: the alphabet in force stays.
  • Joined letters. The plain Arabic-script sets 44 to 51 (alphabets 144 to 151) are joined by the renderer: each letter of a string is drawn in the form its neighbours in that string give it, a string being in visual order, so the letter that follows a letter in reading is the one on its left. Joining ends at the string's end, at a change of alphabet and at a text control character. The Arabic set of Table 44 of EN 300 706 (set 18, alphabet 118) carries its letters already joined.
  • The teletext cell. A writer that lays text out on teletext's cell grid in a ReGIS picture writes a character display cell of 20 by 20 pixels and a unit cell of 16 by 20, T(S[20,20])T(U[16,20]), with row r of the page at P[0,10+20×(r−1)]. The VT340 makes a unit cell's width a multiple of 8, a width between two being drawn at the next smaller size (chapter 7, "Unit Cell Size"), so 16 is the multiple nearest the teletext glyph's shaped width of 15 and no narrower.

9.10 Fonts

DOC-1850 · section

9.10.1 The one compiled font

DOC-1851 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-73, REQ-121, REQ-132, REQ-383, REQ-401

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-73 Other G0 sets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-121 The compiled font: Noto Teletext (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-132 The Noto Teletext files and their converter (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-383 Glyph data (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-401 Glyph provenance (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A receiver built on the engine carries one font, Noto Teletext, a conversion of Google's Noto fonts to the 12 by 20 cell. It is compiled in, no feature chooses it, and no other font is compiled in. Each glyph is 12 pixels by 20 lines, the whole cell: capitals stand on lines 2 to 15, ten pixels wide, with the baseline on line 16. It covers every character of the standard's 24 sets, every spacing mark and composed Latin letter, and with extended-sets the sets of the extended sets with their joined forms and marks.

It is the default font of every page and the only font of the receiver's own drawing: row 0's status area, its row 24 messages and any confirmation. It is drawn line for line, and is never rounded.

A character of a supported set that the font lacks is a defect in the font. Until it is filled, the character is composed from a base and a spacing mark where possible, and otherwise drawn as a visible placeholder: a hollow box on the lines a capital stands on. A renderer MUST NOT draw a wrong character in its place.

Mosaics and G3 characters are not font glyphs. They are drawn by rule.

A binary that holds the font carries the SIL Open Font License 1.1 and each source's copyright line.

9.10.2 Loaded fonts

DOC-1852 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-122, REQ-123, REQ-124, REQ-125, REQ-128, REQ-130, REQ-131, REQ-3208

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-122 The font form (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-123 Where fonts come from (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-124 Font library folder and index format (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-125 Font order for characters on rows 1 to 24 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-128 Drawing a loaded font (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-130 The font converter converts exact, reversible BDF cell sizes (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-131 A font's conformance for a character set (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A user may load other fonts. A channel or a page can never name one. A font comes from a local file or from an address the user names, and is parsed only in a confined process. A process that draws may parse a font only when it is itself confined; a process that draws without confinement never parses one, and receives instead the font's bytes, whose SHA-256 it computes itself, and a glyph table whose shape it checks before drawing with it. A font named with a SHA-256 is refused when its checksum differs.

The form. A font is a BDF file of version 2.1 or 2.2, at most 256 kilobytes, with lines of at most 512 bytes, accepted only when: it has FONTBOUNDINGBOX 12 10 0 0 or 12 20 0 0; its properties, at most 64, include CHARSET_REGISTRY "ISO10646", CHARSET_ENCODING "1", and SPACING "C" or "M"; CHARS is at most 1,024, with exactly that many following; every character has an ENCODING that is a Unicode scalar value, never repeated, DWIDTH 12 0, a matching BBX, and a BITMAP of exactly ten or twenty rows of four hexadecimal digits whose last four bits are zero. FONT, SIZE and SWIDTH are checked for form and not used. Anything else refuses the whole file, with its line number.

Which font draws a character. On rows 1 to 24: the user's font for the character's own set, then the compiled font, then the placeholder. neottx render --font fills a slot that comes first. Row 0's status area always uses the compiled font.

Drawing. A 12 by 10 font is drawn with each line repeated, and a 12 by 20 font line for line. In the 12 by 10 cell a 12 by 20 character shows the upper line of each pair. Attributes apply as to any character. Rounding applies only to a 12 by 10 font whose every row is made of identical pixel pairs, a doubled dot matrix, and only while rounding is on.

Conformance. A font conforms for a character set when the file meets the form, every assigned position of the set has a glyph at the Unicode code point the tables give, the space is blank, and every other assigned character has a pixel set. It is decided from the glyphs alone, and a page never depends on it. neottx font sets FONT reports it.

Libraries. A font library is a folder with an index fonts.txt, at most 64 kilobytes and 1,000 lines. An f line names a font, its title and its SHA-256, and a c line its conformance. A font is fetched only when chosen, and conformance is computed again when it loads.

neottx font convert converts a font of another cell only where that is exact and reversible.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.6 Alphanumeric Character Sets

9.10.3 How Noto Teletext is made from the Noto fonts

DOC-2321 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-2163, REQ-2165, REQ-2189

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-2163 [FNT] Noto Teletext is made by one pipeline in a fixed order (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2165 Noto converter draws every glyph whole within the 12 × 20 cell (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2189 Noto Sans JP is a pinned, checked source named jp for the Noto conversion (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The one compiled font, Noto Teletext, is made from Google's Noto fonts by one pipeline in the engine's repository, always in this order. The character tables decide which characters exist; the fonts never do.

  1. The character tables. The code tables in crates/neoteletext-core/src/charset/ are written by hand from the standards and datasheets, except the Arabic-script tables, which scripts/arabic-sets.py writes.
  2. The lists for the converter. cargo xtask glyphs writes, from the tables, required.txt, every character a glyph set must draw, and forms.txt, the code point drawn for each joined form.
  3. The fonts. third_party/noto/convert.py, run with uv run, draws every character of those lists from the pinned Noto sources and writes the font files, the fonts.txt index and the checksums in PROVENANCE.md.
  4. The compiled table. cargo xtask glyphs compiles the files into crates/neoteletext-core/src/glyphs/noto.rs, the files agreeing on every character two of them hold.
  5. The checks. cargo xtask check-noto, in every gate, refuses a font that differs from its recorded checksum, and xtask's tests refuse a stored compiled table, list or G3 table that differs from what they regenerate.

The pipeline runs again from the first step affected, and the commit carries every file it changes, after a change to a character table, to the converter's settings.txt or code, to xtask's generators, or to a source. sources.txt names each source by its address in the google/fonts repository at one commit, with its SHA-256; moving that pin changes the commit and every checksum together, in a commit of its own. third_party/noto/PROVENANCE.md is to state the whole order in one place; on 3 November 2026 it lacked the first step and the Arabic generator.

How the converter draws a glyph into the 12 by 20 cell, for every character of the lists, in each output font settings.txt names:

  1. It takes the glyph from the first source font of the character's script that has it, a script being chosen by the start of the character's Unicode name, with "latin" drawing everything no other script claims; only the pinned sources are used, each checked by SHA-256, and nothing comes from any other font.
  2. It shapes the glyph with HarfBuzz, which chooses it and places marks; Arabic is shaped right to left, each joined form from its presentation form or the core's private-use code point.
  3. It draws it with FreeType in two colours with no antialiasing, at its script's weight and hinting as settings.txt gives them.
  4. It sizes it by reference letters, not by the em: for Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and Hebrew the capitals are 14 lines tall on lines 2 to 15, H is 10 pixels wide, and the baseline is line 16; Vietnamese capitals are 13 lines with the baseline on line 15.
  5. It places the glyph on its script's baseline with its ink centred across the 12 pixels.
  6. It shrinks and never clips: a glyph that would leave the cell, such as an accented capital or stacked marks, is drawn again smaller, narrower when it is too wide and shorter otherwise, until it fits.
  7. It carries Arabic joining strokes to the cell's edges in a joining form, so that letters in neighbouring cells meet.
  8. It writes each font as a 12 by 20 BDF file, refusing one of more than 1,024 characters, and is reproducible: the same sources, settings, lists and converter give the same files byte for byte.

Every glyph is drawn whole in its own cell. These settings are those the October 2026 prototypes found legible: weight 700 merges the three stems of m in 10 pixels and strokes break below 500, hinting beat supersampling, sizing by the em lets the tallest stacked capital shrink every letter, the display pixel is 1.39 times wider than tall so letters are widened to ten pixels, and clipping loses parts of letters.

The Japanese sets. Noto Sans JP, Adobe's Source Han Sans, is the pinned source jp. The hiragana and katakana scripts draw from it at weight 900 with the automatic hinter, sized so that the reference kana あかさたな and アカサタナ are 14 lines tall and 10 pixels wide on the Latin capitals' baseline, because kana at weight 600 had one-pixel strokes and looked faint. The Japanese punctuation that Unicode does not name as hiragana or katakana (the ideographic comma and full stop and the corner brackets) is claimed by the hiragana script. A file of its own, noto-teletext-japanese.bdf, family Noto Teletext Japanese, holds the characters of the hiragana, katakana and rōmaji sets, compiled into the extended table under the feature extended-sets.

Nothing regenerates the fonts regularly, since that downloads the sources.

9.10.4 The X11 misc-fixed 6x10 font kept beside Noto Teletext

DOC-2322 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-2223

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-2223 Engine repository carries the misc-fixed 6x10 font (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The engine's repository carries one third-party font beside Noto Teletext: the X11 misc-fixed 6x10 font, in Markus Kuhn's Unicode version of the classic terminal font, -Misc-Fixed-Medium-R-Normal--10-100-75-75-C-60-ISO10646-1. It is kept so that the IBM PC's code page 437 can be seen in a real terminal font of that style: of its 1,597 glyphs, it has all 160 graphic characters of code page 437, the symbols at codes 1 to 31 and 127 and every character of codes 128 to 255 with the box-drawing and block characters, as well as Latin, Greek, Cyrillic and Hebrew. Its licence is the font's own: "Public domain terminal emulator font. Share and enjoy."

It is a loaded font like any other, drawn by neottx render --font and the engine's application layer. It is not compiled into the core, it is not the default anywhere, and the browser does not carry it: Noto Teletext stays the compiled font and the browser's only font. No glyph from a character-generator ROM is admitted by it.

File in third_party/misc-fixed/What it is
6x10.bdfThe original, byte for byte: 184,612 bytes, SHA-256 bb14d95828990eb3ada68a24d716ae640a674cd75ab6caca17c798e4cb385849, from https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~mgk25/download/ucs-fonts.tar.gz
misc-fixed-6x10-12x20.bdfThe font converted to the engine's 12 by 20 loaded-font form, every source pixel made two by two so the 6 by 10 cell fills 12 by 20 exactly and nothing is resampled: 1,020 characters, U+0001 to U+052F, U+2000 to U+27FF and U+FB00 to U+FFFF, holding every graphic character of code page 437
misc-fixed-6x10-12x20-extended.bdfThe other 577 characters converted the same way (its default glyph, Hebrew, Runic, Latin Extended Additional, Greek Extended and Braille), since one font file holds at most 1,024 characters
fonts.txtThe folder's index as a font library, with each font's conformance as neottx font sets reports it
PROVENANCE.mdIts source, retrieval, size, checksums, licence and the command that makes the files

cargo xtask misc-fixed refuses an original whose SHA-256 differs, reads it with the engine's own bounded font reader, doubles every pixel, splits the glyphs between the two files and writes them with the engine's font writer, needing nothing outside the repository. cargo xtask check-misc-fixed, in the gates, fails when a committed file differs from its recorded checksum or the conversion is not the original doubled.

9.11 Drawing

DOC-1853 · section

9.11.1 Cells and rows of pixels

DOC-1854 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-374, REQ-375, REQ-376, REQ-384, REQ-385, REQ-386, REQ-387, REQ-399, REQ-406, REQ-407, REQ-409

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-374 Raster rendering in the SAA5050 style (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-375 Raster renderer 12 by 10 cell mode (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-376 Scaling and aspect (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-384 Double-height glyphs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-385 Character rounding (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-386 Mosaic geometry (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-387 Diacritic composition in raster output (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-399 Core renderer produces only the two fixed resolutions (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-406 Double width left half shows left six half-dots (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-407 Underline (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-409 G3 glyph data (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A cell is 12 pixels by 20 lines, and a page 480 by 500 pixels. A second mode draws 12 by 10 cells, a page of 480 by 250, with no rounding: the compiled font has 12 by 20 glyphs, so each cell shows the upper line of each pair of its lines, and a loaded 12 by 10 font is drawn as given. A renderer draws only these two sizes. Scaling belongs to the output, and the 12 by 20 cell matches a 4:3 television when pixels are about 1.23 times, 16/13, wider than tall. A helper scales by whole numbers and may stretch the width by 16/13, and neottx does so with --aspect, off by default.

Double height draws each line of the upper or lower half of the glyph on two output lines. Double width draws the left or right six half-dots of the normal line, each twice, after rounding and mosaic geometry. Double size combines them.

Rounding applies only to a loaded doubled dot-matrix font, in the 12 by 20 mode, by the rule the SAA5050 uses: with A the row drawn and B its neighbour, A | ((A >> 1) & B & ~(B >> 1)) | ((A << 1) & B & ~(B << 1)) on half-dot rows, the upper line of a pair taking the row above and the lower the row below, with rows outside the glyph empty. It is never applied to mosaics, G3 or any 12 by 20 glyph.

Mosaics. In a cell of W half-dots by H lines the two block columns are W/2 wide, and the three block rows 3/10, 4/10 and 3/10 of H: 6, 8 and 6 lines, or 3, 4 and 3. A separated block loses its leftmost dot column and bottom line to background: in the 12 by 20 cell, half-dot columns 0, 1, 6 and 7 and lines 4, 5, 12, 13, 18 and 19.

G3 characters are drawn at every level from the project's own geometry, the sextant geometry of Unicode document L2/19-025 as polygons on halves and thirds of the cell, separately for each cell size. Thirds round down to whole lines. Light strokes are 2 half-dots wide and heavy strokes 4. Position 2/F is a one-dot checkerboard, as the words of Table 48 say, not the pattern of its figure.

Underline is one line of foreground on the last dot line of the cell, across the cell: line 19, or line 9 in the 12 by 10 cell. It is drawn for G0, G1 columns 4 and 5, and G2, never for G3, and for a double-height character only on its bottom half. A render option turns it off for a port that draws its own link underline.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause G.2 Character displays; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 47 G1 Block Mosaics Set; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 48 G3 Smooth Mosaics and Line Drawing Set; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.6 Alphanumeric Character Sets

9.11.2 Colours and flash in pixels

DOC-1855 · reference · normative · requirements REQ-377, REQ-380, REQ-381, REQ-395, REQ-398, REQ-402, REQ-403, REQ-404, REQ-408, REQ-413

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-377 Level 1 colours from colour lookup table 0 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-380 Plain text output (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-381 Terminal output with ANSI colour (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-395 Mark a screen row as changed when its content changes (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-398 Renderer produces palette indices, never final colours (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-402 Output colours come from the page's Colour Map (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-403 The resolved colour mode (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-404 Change tracker records rows with flashing or concealed cells (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-408 Invert, flash and conceal when drawing (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-413 Text renderer writes 40 cells per row (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A renderer produces colour indices, never final colours. There are two modes.

The palette mode, for Levels 1 and 1.5: indices 0 to 7 are the eight colours and 8 is transparent. A foreground pixel of a flashing cell with foreground f and background b is 16 + 8 × f + b, and of a concealed cell 80 + 8 × f + b. A palette of 144 colours is then filled for the flash phase and reveal setting, so flash and reveal need no redrawing. A cell both flashing and concealed uses the concealed range while reveal is off.

The resolved mode, for Levels 2.5 and 3.5: Colour Map indices 0 to 31, with flash and reveal applied at render time. For each cell the renderer swaps colours if it is inverted, then applies flash, then applies conceal. The palette mode MUST be refused for a grid that uses a colour outside CLUT 0 or a Level 2.5 flash mode.

Output colours. The Level 1 colours are CLUT 0 of Table 30, each primary 0 or 255 in 8-bit output, and may be replaced by the user. Each twelve-bit entry of a Colour Map converts by multiplying each four-bit value by 17. User colours replace the Table 30 defaults before any page data redefines them. Pictures show as fully transparent pixels where a format allows.

Change. A renderer draws only rows that changed, and a row below a changed double-height row. In the resolved mode a change of flash unit reports exactly the rows whose displayed colours differ, and a change of reveal the rows with concealed cells.

Text output writes each row's 40 cells as UTF-8, with concealed characters as spaces unless revealed, and attributes as spaces. Terminal output takes 24-bit colours from the Colour Map, or the nearest of the eight in 8-colour mode.

Defined by: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.4 Colour Map; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 30 Colour Map; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table C.1 Display Priorities

9.11.3 Decided, not built: the glyph line cache

DOC-2124 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-392

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-392 The glyph line cache (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Not built. No code does this. An optional cache is to hold the finished 12-dot mask for every character, every line of the cell and each field, with rounding and mosaic geometry already applied, generated from the cell raster when the decoder starts or at build time as constant data. For the Latin G0 set with its national option characters and the G1 mosaic set, it needs about 8 kilobytes, or about 4 kilobytes when only one field is drawn. With it, drawing one line of one cell is a table lookup and a colour fill. The cell raster stays the reference, and characters not in the cache, such as G2 and G3 overwrites, fall back to it.

9.12 Where the standard leaves a choice

DOC-2122 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-144, REQ-1639, REQ-1641

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-144 Row resolution at Levels 2.5 and 3.5: the per-cell step (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1639 A damaged triplet met while an Origin Modifier waits discards the offsets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1641 Colour mode selection: for_level at Levels 2.5 and 3.5, palette mode kept by from_config (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The standard leaves these points open. They are the engine's rulings: another decoder may rule otherwise and still read the same pages. Each keeps the work bounded, contains a fault, or takes the reading that never hides displayed text. Objects, Magazine Organization Table links and default objects are behind the feature objects, off by default, and the rulings on them say how they behave when built.

The enhancement processor.

  • A damaged triplet met while an Origin Modifier waits for its invocation discards the offsets.
  • Every permitted invocation counts toward the limit of 127 per object type, whether or not its object is found, so that failed lookups also bound the work.
  • Objects open at once, as Annex A.8 limits them, are counted at the invocation point against the open areas of all earlier objects. An object's area runs from its invocation to the last position any of its moving triplets reaches. The count of successive opens restarts at any character or attribute actually placed.
  • At Level 3.5, a stored Magazine Organization Table lacking packet X/22 or X/24 makes the page fall back to Level 2.5 links, whatever X/27/4 says.
  • X/27/4 and X/27/5 take precedence over the table one role at a time, and a role they do not give comes from the table.
  • Default objects are found through the table's own GPOP and POP pages, and a table link to page FF gives none. A display triplet, which suppresses them, is any character or attribute column triplet, screen or row colour, Address Display Row 0 or invocation met before the first Termination Marker or Object Definition.
  • An object writes only into the 40 columns of the page. Elements outside them are discarded, and the object continues.
  • On a page with neither C5 nor C6 set, both Level 1 box codes are ignored. On a boxed page, one boxed state is shared with the window bit of the Display Attributes triplet, and the later of the two wins.
  • Overlapping Adaptive objects keep one merged attribute record per cell, owned by the latest object to place there.
  • Passive objects apply their attributes in transmission order, as the walk meets them, and a Passive attribute at a discarded position is dropped.
  • Incremental and decremental flash count phases by column from the triplet's column, spaces included.
  • Row 0 is rebuilt only when C7 is clear, always keeping columns 0 to 7. Row 24 is rebuilt only when it is shown and not drawn by the receiver. A page with C10 set, or with an X/28/0 page function other than basic text, keeps its Level 1 rows.
  • A page is taken as an enhancement page, and its rows 1 to 24 are blanked, when its number is xFE or its stored copy carries an X/28 page function of GPOP, POP, GDRCS, DRCS or MOT. A page named only by a link is still shown, so that a wrong link cannot hide a display page.
  • X/26/15 is always processed at Levels 2.5 and 3.5.
  • The lower-row fill cells of double height take the background of the cell above and keep its box membership, with flash and invert cleared.
  • A build counts each kind of fault and the triplets read, and the build recorded last is not counted again, so that the counts measure receptions, not how long a page stayed on screen.

A row, cell by cell. At Levels 2.5 and 3.5 each row is resolved from its Level 1 bytes and the enhancement events on it. For each cell, from column 0 to column 39, in this order:

  1. Apply the set-after attributes recorded at the previous cell.
  2. Apply a set-at Level 1 attribute.
  3. Apply each attribute event of the local enhancement data and of Active objects placed at this cell, in the order of the walk. These win against step 2.
  4. For each Adaptive object whose range on this row includes this cell, start its overlay at its first cell from the underlying record, apply its attribute events here, and use its value for each attribute type it has changed.
  5. Apply the attribute events of each Passive object placed here to that object's own record.
  6. Take the character of the highest display priority: Passive, then Adaptive, then local enhancement data, then Active, then the Level 1 character. Take the attributes from the Passive object's record when it supplied the character; otherwise from the Adaptive overlay when the cell is in an Adaptive object's range, the later invoked object's where two overlap; otherwise from the underlying record.
  7. Record the cell, update the held mosaic from Level 1 characters only, and record the set-after attributes of the Level 1 byte for the next cell.

The row after a row with spacing double height or double size uses no Level 1 bytes, and only its enhancement events are resolved.

Drawing.

  • The palette mode keeps Level 1 output unchanged at every level, and the resolved mode is chosen at Levels 2.5 and 3.5. The palette mode refuses a grid it cannot draw, and the 4-bit format refuses indices above 15 in the resolved mode.
  • The Level 1 Flash code has the SAA5050's timing, 960 ms on and 320 ms off, in both modes and at every level. The twelve-unit cycle applies only to cells set by the Additional Flash Functions command.
  • Underline is drawn on the last line of the cell, for G0 and G2 characters only, on double height only on the bottom half, enlarged to two lines, and not on empty cells.
  • A transparent colour in row 0, columns 0 to 7, shows the picture, never the row colour. Mix mode makes gaps the picture, so a dot hidden by flash or conceal also shows the picture.
  • Borders are the caller's to fill, in the colour given to it.
  • Still images are drawn in the on phase of every flash.
  • A pixel of a G3 glyph is set when its centre, nudged upwards by an infinitesimal amount, lies inside the shape, which makes mirrors and complements exact. Positions 2/E and 3/E are drawn at half-dots 1 to 2 and 9 to 10, 4/8 to 4/B are straight diagonals, and diagonal strokes are two half-dots wide. The generated glyphs are used at every level.
  • An eight-colour terminal shows each primary when it is above half intensity.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3 Non-spacing attributes and additional characters; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13 Objects; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13.2 Display priority order; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13.8 Default Objects; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13.9 Object example; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 14 Dynamically Re-definable Characters; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15 Character sets and their designation; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 10.6.1 Page Format; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 annex A Page addresses; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 annex C Decoding Rules; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.4 Addressing order for enhancement triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.8 Number of objects per page; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause C.2 Rules for determining priorities of spacing and non-spacing attributes; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table C.1 Display Priorities

9.13 Testing a decoder against the standard

DOC-2121 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-189, REQ-461, REQ-464, REQ-466, REQ-468, REQ-469, REQ-470, REQ-472

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-189 Authoring test pages for Levels 2.5 and 3.5 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-461 Hamming 8/4 decoding of all 256 byte values (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-466 Level 1 attribute test coverage (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-468 Level 2.5 and 3.5 enhancement tests (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-469 Reproduce the worked examples of EN 300 706 for Levels 2.5 and 3.5 (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-470 Object tests (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-472 Enhancement processing bounded in work and memory (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The standard's own tables and worked examples test a decoder. The engine's tests are built on these, and anyone writing a decoder can use the same list.

  • Hamming 8/4. All 256 byte values against clause 8.2: each of the 16 valid codes decodes to its value, every single-bit error of a valid code is corrected, and every double-bit error is reported as uncorrectable.
  • Characters. The Unicode mapping of every character set and national option against Tables 35 to 48, transcribed once into test data, with every difference explained or fixed.
  • Level 1. Every spacing attribute with its set-at or set-after timing, and every example of Annex G: boxing in G.3.1, separated mosaics in G.3.2 and hold mosaics in G.3.3. Also hold with size changes and with mode changes, double height with its ignored lower row, conceal ended by a colour attribute, New Background after a colour change, and blast-through with national options.
  • Levels 2.5 and 3.5. Every row mode of Table 28 and column mode of Table 29, at both levels, with each class of data value, reserved values included.
  • Worked examples. The three contention examples of Annex C.2, which give red, blue and yellow. The object example of clause 13.9 for each of the Active, Adaptive and Passive types, with the word colours of its notes 1 to 8: its "pink" is CLUT 2 entry 0, red 15, green 0, blue 5, because the standard gives no index. All rows of Table C.1, the precedence lists of Annex A.5, the open area of Figure A.1 and the defaults of Table 30. The layouts of clause 12.5.3 show that side-panel data changes nothing.
  • Objects. Every source and type of invocation and every permitted and forbidden pair of invoker and type; every case in which a pointer, a definition or a link is unusable; each limit of Annex A.8, reached and exceeded; the Magazine Organization Table at both levels, with each Level 3.5 packet missing in turn; default objects with and without local display data; and objects placed past column 39, whose elements are discarded.
  • Bounded work. Worst-case pages: every object type invoked to the limits of Annex A.8, nesting to the greatest depth allowed, objects of 507 triplets and all sixteen X/26 packets. Building the grid stays within a stated bound on operations, uses only the memory the caller gave, and never panics.

Test pages at Levels 2.5 and 3.5 are written by function and not by bit pattern. The engine's builder writes every row and column triplet of Tables 28 and 29 by name; local objects, and POP and GPOP pages with pointer tables computed from their objects; a Magazine Organization Table; and every field of X/28/0 Format 1, X/28/4, M/29/0 and M/29/4; and it writes the result as TTI files and T42 streams. A builder and a decoder written from one reading of the standard share its mistakes, so the builder's output is also checked against the standard's worked examples.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.2 Hamming 8/4; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.6 Alphanumeric Character Sets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 15.7 Graphics Character Sets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 annex G Decoding aspects; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause C.2 Rules for determining priorities of spacing and non-spacing attributes; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13.9 Object example; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table C.1 Display Priorities; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.5 Rules for row and screen colours; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 30 Colour Map; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.5.3 Data transmission and addressing; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.8 Number of objects per page

10 Data carriage and audio

DOC-1785 · section

10.1 What NeoTeletext takes from EN 300 708

DOC-1856 · concept · informative · requirements REQ-40

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-40 Broadcast carriage (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

EN 300 708 defines several ways to send data within teletext. NeoTeletext uses one: the programme-independent audio service on an independent data line, which it declares as a user-defined service and fills with its own records. Sound travels that way, and so does everything else on a live connection that is not a page: the records of the downstream record set.

Part of EN 300 708NeoTeletext

Programme-independent audio, user-defined (clause 6.7.3)The one carriage of records.
