JSON-LD declares that element with isAccessibleForFree false, the structured data Google documents for paywalled content. A sub-page's address and an address with a query show the page's description. Everyone gets the same bytes: no request header reaches the answer, so everything a page marked public gives is readable by anyone.

A page whose picture is ReGIS or NAPLPS. picture is either {"kept":"0001"}, the kept picture of the described page with that sub-code, or {"language":"regis" or "naplps","data":base64,"objects":[…] or null}, those bytes, at most 262,144 decoded (MOST_DESCRIPTION_PICTURE_BYTES), with at most 64 NAPLPS objects for NAPLPS. The server draws it as it draws the mosaic fallback, with the renderer and fonts the browser uses, the shown objects composed, no animation and no pointer look, and gives it as the page's PNG in place of content's drawing, at the language's own size: ReGIS 800 by 480; NAPLPS the 480 by 500 teletext raster, as a teletext page's picture is, the picture on its 480 by 460 dots of lines 20 to 479 (teletext rows 1 to 23) and rows 0 and 24 those of the page beneath. Its alt text is the picture's own title when it has one. content still gives the page beneath, and its text. A kept naming nothing kept is refused not_kept, and bytes the receiver's reader would refuse are refused invalid_regis or invalid_naplps. The bounds below and the 64 KiB of the PNG apply to it as to any description.

A program's words. A title or text is escaped for HTML and for the JSON-LD block, so it can never be markup, and the Content-Security-Policy allows the inline image and one fixed stylesheet by its hash, and no script.

Late and unasked. An answer after description_limit_ms reaches nobody who waited, and is taken once, for those who come after, while the not-public answer the wait left stands. A second answer, or one nobody asked for, is refused with not_awaited, so a program cannot fill the server's cache.

Bounds. An answer is kept for a minute, not-public answers and unanswered pages included, one cache for all visitors. A program is asked for at most 20 pages a second, 40 at once after a quiet time, and what is over that is answered as not public and not kept. At most 1,024 visitors wait, and 256 answers are kept. All of these are provisional.

12.16 The rule table's messages

DOC-6600 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-5548, REQ-6532, REQ-6767

Program protocol 16 carries the page rule table between a program and the server. Every message that concerns a page carries both page (three hexadecimal digits) and sub (four), since a sub-page is a page; an audience of "all" means every connection that has that page and sub-code selected when the message arrives. Names exist only between a program and the server: rule, group, sequence, row-set and rectangle names match [a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,31}, are distinct within their kind, and the server turns each into its number (its place in its list, from 0, unnamed groups after the named) and numbers back into names in every message it gives the program; no name reaches a receiver. Variables and timers have no names: "v0" to "v15", "t0" to "t7" and "page" are the same on every page.

rules gives a page its table, or with "table":null removes it (and, where the channel's default applies, puts the default back):

{"type":"rules","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","table":{
  "rects":[{"name":"pad","x":40,"y":300,"width":200,"height":100}],
  "rows":{"keys":[60,62]},
  "groups":[{"name":"note_on","commands":[
    {"type":"local_midi","channel":0,"message":{"event":"note_on","channel":1,"key":{"plus":0,"row":"p"},"velocity":100}}]}],
  "sequences":[{"name":"pulse","length":30,"repeat":0,"steps":[{"tick":0,"run":"note_on"}]}],
  "rules":[
    {"name":"down","on":[{"event":"key","keys":[{"physical":"a"},{"physical":"s"}],"by_row":true},
                        {"event":"press","target":{"object":{"plus":41,"row":"p"}},"button":0}],
     "rows":"keys","run":"note_on"},
    {"name":"typed","on":{"event":"key","keys":"any","repeat":true},"do":[{"type":"report"}]}]}}
  • In a table rules is required (it may be empty); rects, rows (named row sets, each a list of rows, a row being a signed 32-bit integer or a key written as in a key set), groups and sequences default to empty. A rectangle's x, y, width and height are in the units of the page's picture: dots of the 480 by 500 teletext raster on a teletext page and on a NAPLPS page alike, pixels of 800 by 480 on a ReGIS page (rules, triggers, keys and targets).
  • A rule has name and on (one trigger or a list of up to MAX_TRIGGERS_PER_RULE, each tagged by event: key, key_up, press, release, enter, leave, move, wheel, open, close, text, focus, blur, becomes, every, after, cue); when, a condition or null; rows, the name of a row set; and exactly one of run (a group's name) and do (a list of commands, which the server makes into an unnamed group, two equal lists sharing one). echo: true means "after the group, a report of the firing", which the server makes into commands. A key set is "any" or a list of {"char":"a"}, {"name":"Enter"} or {"physical":"a"}; a target "page", {"control":n}, {"object":n}, {"rect":"name"}, or "any" for a control or object in a pointer trigger, and in a rule with rows {"plus":k,"row":"p"}.
  • A condition is {"and":[…]}, {"or":[…]}, {"not":c}, {"read":v,"op":"==","value":n} (a value may be {"plus":k,"row":"p"}), {"read":v,"in_range":[low,high]}, {"read":v,"in_set":[…]}, {"overlaps":[t,t]} or {"inside":[t,t]}. A value is tagged by of: variable, key, button, pointer, keys_down, timer (with phase and its period), target, sound, synth (by family and field name), fired (key, target, row, cue, p) and sequence.
  • A group is {"name":…,"commands":[…]}. A command is a program message without its connections, page and sub: the sound kinds play, stop and gain, local_midi, animate, sprites, naplps_objects, regis_links, naplps_links, regis_cursor, naplps_cursor, variable, timer, report, run and sequence. A picture's links and cursor in a group are its DRAWING_LINKS and REGIS_CURSOR records (groups and commands), a group's links being at most what one record of the command limit holds. In a group, and nowhere else, a field that takes a binding MAY be an amount: {"plus":k,"variable":"v3"}, {"plus":k,"row":"p"} or {"plus":k,"fired":"key"}. A sequence is {"name":…,"length":n,"repeat":r,"steps":[{"tick":k,"run":"group"},…]}.
  • The server sends a table at once to each connection of the audience that has that page selected, and keeps none for later. At every selection it sends first, before the program is told, the channel's default table or a RULES record that says the page has no table; for a selection of 3F7F it does so when the program's answer makes the sub-code known. For each connection it keeps only its selection, the names of the table in force (and of the last four tables it sent, to name reports), the default's use and a generation counter.

The commands as messages. Each command a group may hold is also a message a program sends directly, for the connections named that have the page selected; the server encodes the same record either way:

{"type":"local_midi","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","channel":0,"message":{"event":"note_on","channel":1,"key":60,"velocity":100}}
{"type":"variable","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","op":"add","variable":"v0","value":{"plus":0,"variable":"v1"}}
{"type":"variable","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","op":"wrap","variable":"v0","low":0,"high":3}
{"type":"timer","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","op":"start","timer":"t0"}
{"type":"report","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","value":{"of":"variable","variable":"v0"}}
{"type":"run","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","group":"flash"}
{"type":"sequence","connections":[7],"page":"101","sub":"0001","op":"start","sequence":"pulse","at":{"beat":{"timer":"t0","ticks":30}}}

variable's op is set, inc, dec, add, sub, toggle, min, max, wrap or clear (with "all"); set alone may take {"read":v}. A report sent directly MUST report a value. run has no at. sequence's at, with start, is null (the next tick), {"tick":n} or {"beat":{"timer":…,"ticks":n}}, and with stop is absent or null. A run or sequence names a group or sequence of the table the server last sent that connection for that page; it goes to each connection whose table has the name, and one refused with unknown_name names the others.

What a program hears. A report of a firing with an input event comes as the input message, its event unchanged, with rule (the rule's name), row (the place of the firing row in the rule's row set, or null), tick (the page tick it belongs to) and target (the target the pointer was inside, or null). A report of a firing with no event, and a report of a value, come as rule_event, whose rule is null when no rule made the run:

{"type":"rule_event","connection":7,"page":"101","sub":"0001","rule":"hot","row":null,"tick":9031,"event":{"kind":"fired"}}
{"type":"rule_event","connection":7,"page":"101","sub":"0001","rule":null,"row":null,"tick":9031,"event":{"kind":"value","read":{"of":"variable","variable":"v0"},"value":5}}

A report is named by the table of the generation it carries; one of a generation the connection was never sent is given to no program and counted with stale input. A report with no input event is given to the program whatever the connection has selected since, so that a close rule's report arrives; an input event stamped with a page that is no longer the selection is dropped. The server keeps a reported press as held only when the table of the page on which it was pressed asks for releases of that key, button or contact: a rule with a key_up trigger whose key set includes the key, or a rule with a release trigger that names the button, a contact being the left button. When a connection closes, or its selection changes, while such a key, button or contact is held, the server gives the program the release marked lost, with that press's rule, row and tick; a press on a page whose table asks for no release of it gives none. A fault of a table in a receiver comes as {"type":"rules_fault","connection":7,"page":"101","sub":"0001","generation":3,"fault":"evaluation_late","count":12}.

The state query. {"type":"query_state","connection":7,"page":"101","sub":"0001","request":42} asks one connection that has the page selected (else wrong_page), at most once a second for a connection and page (else too_frequent). The answer is page_state, with request, tick, table, variables (always sixteen, v0 first), timers (those running, by designator, with running and elapsed), sequences (every sequence of the table by name, with running, waiting, passes and position), targets and values. With no answer within 10 seconds, or when the connection ends or leaves the page first, the program is given refused with not_answered.

Refusals. A faulty message is refused whole with refused (path, rule, detail, message) and nothing of it is sent. Beside the existing rules: rules_over_limit (a limit the schema cannot state, its constant and value in detail); invalid_rules (a shape fault: both or neither of run and do, a becomes rule without when or with a second trigger, low above high, "any" where one target is needed, a row or by_row in a rule without rows, a by_row set of the wrong count, a row giving a target out of range, sequence steps out of order or beyond its length, a sequence stop with an at or a start without a sequence, a phase without its period or a period without phase); invalid_group (a message type a group may not hold, a play with page, after or for the whole service, an amount where none is allowed or a variable as a target's number, a negative plus on an operation's target, a variable operation paired with an operand it does not take, groups that run each other in a ring, nesting too deep, a run too long); invalid_command (sent directly, something allowed only in a group: an amount, a fired value, a report of the firing, or a variable operation and operand that do not pair); unknown_name; duplicate_name; unknown_parameter (a synthesizer field the family does not have); too_frequent; not_answered. The server checks every table with the receiver's own code before sending it, so no receiver is sent a table it would refuse.

The channel's default table. A channel's entry in channels.json has default_rules, "none" (the default) or "send_all". For "send_all" the server sends, at every selection and whenever the program removes a page's table, a table of twelve rules (thirteen when the entry's wheel is true) that each run one group holding one report of the firing: keys (any key, with repeat), keys_up, text, press and release on the page with any button, move on the page, hover_in and hover_out (enter and leave on any control), drawing_in and drawing_out (on any object), focus, blur and, with the wheel, wheel on the page. With it a page's program receives exactly the input it received before rule tables, each now naming its rule.

12.17 Local sounds in the sound message

DOC-6601 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6532

The sound message has, for each synthesizer family that plays notes, a kind that announces a local sound: synth7_local, synth106_local, synth60_local, synthd_local, synth53_local, synth52_local, synth51_local, synth8_local and synth80_local. Each has the fields of its family's live kind (connections, handle, generation, banks, and the family's own options), and setup: a list of at most 64 of the family's events, each with time_us 0, which the server packs into the sound's one block and refuses with block_full when they do not fit. A cue event in a setup is refused, since a local sound has no timeline.

{"type":"sound","kind":"synth106_local","connections":"all","handle":1,"generation":1,"banks":[2],
 "setup":[{"event":"program_change","channel":1,"program":0,"time_us":0}]}
{"type":"sound","kind":"play","connections":"all","channel":0,"handle":1,"generation":1,"gain":100,"fade_ms":5,"duck":0,"loop":false,"after":false,"page":"101"}
  • A play of a local sound sent directly MUST name a page, with loop and after false, else it is refused with out_of_range, and reaches only the connections that have a sub-code of that page number selected. In a group, a play takes its page from the table and MUST NOT name one.
  • The server sends the sound's OBJECT, which says that it is local, and its one block, the setup; nothing more of the sound is ever sent. The notes come from local_midi commands: those of the page's groups, run in the viewer's receiver, and those the program sends directly (the rule table's messages).
  • A program plays a local sound, or lets a group's play start it, and from then on hears nothing of the keys that play it unless a rule reports them. The sound belongs to the page open when it starts, is silent while that page is paused, and ends when the page is closed or its connection ends; a program that wants it again sends it at the page's next selection.

12.18 Animation's messages

DOC-6602 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6533

Program protocol 16 has these messages from a program for animation. Each has connections, a page and a sub, since a sub-page is a page; a message for the sub-code 3F7F is refused out_of_range. An audience is the connections open when the message arrives, and of them a message reaches those that have that page and sub-code selected.

{"type":"frame","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","mark":"begin"}
{"type":"frame","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","mark":"end"}

{"type":"animate","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","ops":[
  {"action":"move","target":{"object":10},"x":120,"y":80,"relative":false},
  {"action":"cycle","target":{"object":10},"first":0,"last":3,"period":6,"once":false},
  {"action":"hide","target":{"object":20}},
  {"action":"reset","target":{"object":21}}]}

{"type":"sprites","connections":"all","page":"160","sub":"0001","sprites":[
  {"number":1,"shown":true,"detectable":false,"layer":2,"order":0,"column":10,"row":5,"width":4,"height":3,
   "frames":[{"source":"local","kind":"passive","number":0},{"source":"local","kind":"passive","number":1}]}]}

{"type":"naplps_objects","connections":"all","page":"170","sub":"0001","objects":[
  {"number":1,"kind":"macro","shown":true,"detectable":true,"layer":2,"order":0,
   "x":300,"y":200,"width":64,"height":64,"origin_x":0,"origin_y":416,
   "frames":[32,33],"cover":null,"hover":34,"pressed":null,"alternative":null},
  {"number":2,"kind":"region","shown":true,"detectable":true,"layer":1,"order":0,
   "x":0,"y":440,"width":480,"height":40,"origin_x":0,"origin_y":0,
   "frames":[],"cover":0,"hover":null,"pressed":null,"alternative":null}]}

{"type":"sprite_sheet","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","kind":"regis","data":"RChCNDEp…","restart":true}

{"type":"timeline","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","id":1,"loop_ticks":null,"steps":[
  {"tick":0,"ops":[{"action":"show","target":{"object":10}}]},
  {"tick":30,"ops":[{"action":"move","target":{"object":10},"x":8,"y":0,"relative":true}]}]}
{"type":"timeline_stop","connections":"all","page":"150","sub":"0001","id":1}
  • frame. From a begin to its end the server holds, for each connection, everything it would send that changes what the frame's page shows, and at the end sends the begin's FRAME record, what it held and the end's FRAME record together; sound records and other pages' packets pass as they arrive. The server ends a frame that is not ended within two seconds and one that is open when its program ends; a selection of another page drops it, and so does the end of the connection. A frame whose content would pass 262,144 bytes is sent unframed and the program is told frame_too_large.
  • animate. ops holds 1 to 64 operations, show, hide, look, move, order, frame, cycle, stop_cycle and reset, each tagged by action with a target; it is sent as one ANIMATE record. A move of a NAPLPS object is in dots of the 480 by 500 teletext raster. The same message without its connections, page and sub is a command of a rule table's group, where its operations' numeric fields may be amounts (the rule table's messages).
  • sprites holds 0 to 32 sprites and naplps_objects 0 to 64 objects, with the fields and ranges of their records; either may also be a command of a group. A sprite frame's source is local, public or global and its kind active, adaptive or passive; an object's kind is macro or region. An object's x, y, origin_x and origin_y are dots of the 480 by 500 teletext raster, its width 1 to 480 and its height 1 to 500 (NAPLPS objects); a width or height outside them is refused out_of_range. A naplps_objects message is written for the generation of the NAPLPS stream the connection has for the page, or, when it has none, for the generation its next naplps message with restart will begin.
  • sprite_sheet. data is base64 of the next bytes of the page's sheet of that kind, regis or naplps, and restart starts a new generation. A sheet belongs to one page and sub-code. The whole sheet so far is read by the receiver's own renderer at every message: a ReGIS commit that fails, or NAPLPS that changes a pixel, is refused with invalid_sheet, and a sheet over 65,536 bytes with sheet_too_large. A new ReGIS sheet makes the server forget the connection's ReGIS stream of that page, so the program begins that stream again.
  • timeline. It holds 1 to 1,024 steps in strictly ascending tick, 0 to 216,000. The server plays it for each connection of the audience that has the page selected: it sends each step's ANIMATE record when its tick is due, tick n at the first millisecond at or after n × 50,000 ÷ 3 microseconds from the message's arrival, and again from the start every loop_ticks when that is given, every step's tick then being below it. id, 1 to 65,535, names it within one connection and page for timeline_stop, and a new timeline with a playing one's id replaces it. At most 16 play for one connection and page and at most 64 for one connection, else too_many_timelines. A timeline ends for a connection that leaves its page or whose connection ends, and for every connection when the program's connection ends.
  • object_page sends the teletext object pages a page's sprites use (the object_page message).
  • Nothing is kept for a later viewer. The server keeps no sprites, objects, sheet or animation state for a viewer who selects the page later, returns to it or reconnects. A program is told of every selection, with its page and sub-code, and sends the page's sheets, definitions and opening operations then: a page's opening state is what its program sends. The server holds, for each connection, only the sheet stream it is sending for the page selected, and drops it when the connection leaves the page.
  • Refusals, beside the rules every message has: frame_order (an end with no begin, a begin inside a frame); frame_too_large; invalid_animation (an operation outside its range, or on any; a step at or past loop_ticks); invalid_sprites; invalid_naplps_objects; invalid_sheet; sheet_too_large; too_many_timelines; not_ascending. Each record is checked with the receiver's own reader before it is sent.

12.19 The object_page message: a program sends the teletext object pages a page's sprites use

DOC-6690 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6533

A teletext page's sprites take their frames from teletext objects: its own local objects in packets X/26, or the objects of the Public and Global Public Object Pages it links (teletext sprites). The server keeps no page content for a later viewer, so it cannot send a selected page's object pages from memory. A program sends them with the program message object_page:

{"type":"object_page","connections":[7],"page":"150","sub":"0001","object":{"page":"1FD","sub":"0001", … }}
  • connections is the audience, of which the server sends to those that have page and sub selected; page and sub name the page whose sprites use the object page; object is the object page, a Public or Global Public Object Page, written exactly as a page message's sub-page is (its own page number and sub-code, its rows, links, control bits, enhancements and packets) and checked as the server checks a published page.
  • The server sends the object page's packets to those connections at once, keeps nothing of it, and changes nothing of what the connection shows: it is no selection's page. A program sends a page's object pages at each selection of the page, before the page itself.
  • For the sub-code 3F7F the message is refused out_of_range, as every animation message is.
  • The message carries a sub-page's rows as text, whose characters the server encodes with odd parity, so it cannot carry an object page's pointer packets and object packets, which are Hamming 24/18 triplets. A page whose sprites need objects defined by triplets defines them as local objects in its own packets X/26, as the music player's page 111 does.
  • Both kits offer it, as context.objectPage(to, page, sub, objectPage, objectSub, object) and app.object_page(to, page, sub, object_page, object_sub, object), the object given as a screen or content like a published sub-page.

12.20 Picture messages: regis, naplps, their links and cursors, and how the server checks them

DOC-6835 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6338, REQ-6372, REQ-6767

A program gives a sub-page a picture in ReGIS or NAPLPS in place of its teletext page, with these messages. Each names page and sub; sub 3F7F names no sub-page and is refused out_of_range. connections is the audience: connections, as every other message names them, or the string "kept" (kept pictures).

typeFieldsWhat it does
regis, naplpsconnections, page, sub, restart (false when absent), and exactly one of data, exact base64 of the bytes, and parts, 1 to 64 parts (text in pictures)Bytes of the sub-page's stream, sent as REGIS or NAPLPS records. With restart a connection's stream of that sub-page begins again as a new generation from offset 0; without it the bytes are added to the stream the connection has, and are not sent to a connection with no stream of that sub-page. Giving both data and parts is refused duplicate_field, neither missing_field.
regis_linksconnections, page, sub, links: 0 to 64 of {"drawing":n,"target":"…"}, each drawing 1 to 65,535 named onceThe numbered drawings of a ReGIS picture that are links, sent as a DRAWING_LINKS record
naplps_linksconnections, page, sub, links: 0 to 64 of {"object":n,"target":"…"}, each object 1 to 65,535 named onceThe NAPLPS objects that are links, sent as a DRAWING_LINKS record
regis_cursorconnections, page, sub, drawing: 0 to 65,535, 0 for noneThe drawing that is the sub-page's cursor, sent as a REGIS_CURSOR record
naplps_cursorconnections, page, sub, object: 0 to 65,535, 0 for noneThe object that is the sub-page's cursor, sent as a REGIS_CURSOR record

A target is 1 to 8,004 characters in any form a text link's target takes. A link or cursor MAY name a drawing or object not yet defined; the receiver uses it once it exists. naplps_objects (animation's messages) takes the same audience, "kept" among it.

Only to receivers that draw the language. Every record of a picture goes only to a connection that agreed that language's capability bit; any other connection showing the sub-page is given the mosaic fallback.

The server checks with the receiver's reader. The server reads every regis and naplps message's bytes, sent to connections or kept, with the reader the receiver uses, holding one for each stream, before anything is sent:

  • ReGIS whose commit a receiver would refuse is refused invalid_regis.
  • NAPLPS that makes the receiver's reader record a refusal (the processed-byte limit of 4,000,000 bytes, a macro too long, the macros full, a picture description instruction too long) is refused invalid_naplps, its detail naming the refusal and the stream offset of the first. Bytes the reader passes over are not refused: the author's log of the receivers says for the message how many and where the first was. A text part's diacritical mark written while NAPLPS colour mode 2 is in force, which erases the letter beneath it, is logged there too.
  • Links a receiver would refuse are refused invalid_drawing_links for ReGIS and invalid_naplps_links for NAPLPS.
  • A naplps_objects whose frames or looks name a macro the stream has not defined is not refused, since the macro may come later, and is logged once a generation.

A refused message is refused whole: nothing of it is kept or sent.

In a rule table's group. regis_links, naplps_links, regis_cursor and naplps_cursor, without connections, page and sub, are commands a group MAY hold (groups and commands).

The version. These messages and fields ("kept", naplps_links, naplps_cursor, forget_picture, parts, measure_picture_text, description.picture, and from the server measured_picture_text and the refusal rules kept_over_limit, wrong_picture_language, not_kept, invalid_naplps, invalid_naplps_links and invalid_picture_parts) are part of program protocol 16. Version 16 was raised from 15 because every NeoTeletext coordinate on a NAPLPS page became a dot of the 480 by 500 teletext raster, the picture drawn on lines 20 to 479 (NAPLPS objects), a change of meaning that a program built for 15 would not notice; a program built for 15 stops on the start of 16, as every program stops on a version other than its own.

12.21 Kept pictures: the audience "kept" and forget_picture

DOC-6833 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1473, REQ-6766

The server keeps no page content for a later viewer, with one exception: a picture a program sends to the audience "kept". The messages regis, regis_links, regis_cursor, naplps, naplps_objects, naplps_links and naplps_cursor take "kept" in place of connections; every other message refuses it. "kept" means: the server keeps this for the page and sub-code named, sends it now to every open connection whose selection is that page and sub-code, and sends it to every connection that selects it later, for as long as it is kept.

What is kept for one page and sub-code, its kept picture: its language, ReGIS or NAPLPS; its stream, every byte since its last restart, in order; for NAPLPS its objects, the last whole set with each later redefinition of one object applied to it, and its title; its links, the last regis_links or naplps_links; its cursor, the last regis_cursor or naplps_cursor. A kept stream message without restart appends to the kept stream; one with restart replaces it and keeps nothing else of before. A message of the other language without restart is refused wrong_picture_language; with restart it replaces the kept picture.

What a viewer is sent. When a connection's selection becomes a page and sub-code with a kept picture, the server sends it right after the frame of the page that answers the selection, in this order: the stream as records of a new generation of that connection's stream of the language, from offset 0; for NAPLPS the objects with their title as one NAPLPS_OBJECTS record of that generation; the links as DRAWING_LINKS; the cursor as REGIS_CURSOR. Each later kept message reaches every connection showing it, appended to that generation. A connection whose stream of that page and sub-code was begun by a message naming connections takes no kept message until it selects the page again. A reconnection is a new connection and is given the kept picture from its beginning. A connection that did not agree the language's capability bit is given the mosaic fallback instead.

Page content, not local state. A kept picture is what the program gave the page to show, as a published page's rows are. Animation (animate, timelines, frame), the pointer's looks and the rule table's state are a viewer's local state: they are never kept and never sent to a later viewer. A kept NAPLPS object is sent as its definition says.

Bounds. A message that would pass one of these is refused whole with kept_over_limit, its detail naming the bound and its value:

BoundValueOf
MOST_KEPT_STREAM_BYTES1,048,576The bytes of one kept stream since its restart
MOST_KEPT_PICTURES512The pages and sub-codes of one channel with a kept picture
MOST_KEPT_COST33,554,432The cost of all of a channel's kept pictures: each stream's bytes counted twice, for the bytes and its reader's copy of what it holds, plus each companion message's bytes as received

A kept picture is never dropped to make room. All of a channel's kept pictures are dropped when its program ends or starts again, and when the channel's host drops its state.

forget_picture {"type":"forget_picture","page":"200","sub":"0001"} drops the kept picture of that page and sub-code: every connection that was taking it is sent a new generation of its stream with no bytes, its objects, links and cursor gone with it. A page and sub-code with nothing kept is refused not_kept.

12.22 Text in pictures: text parts, their ReGIS and NAPLPS bytes, and measure_picture_text

DOC-6834 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6762, REQ-6767, REQ-6772

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-6762 The picture text encoder: Unicode text to stretches of the provided sets, written as ReGIS or NAPLPS bytes and measured (renderer parity PAR-3 to PAR-6) (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A regis or naplps message MAY give its bytes as parts in place of data: 1 to 64 parts (MOST_PICTURE_PARTS), each either {"data": base64}, bytes as data takes them, or a text part {"text":"…","language":tag or null,"outside":false}. A text part's text is 1 to 1,000 characters (MAX_PART_CHARACTERS) in Unicode normalisation form C with no control or bidirectional formatting character; language is a tag of start.languages, none for Latin English; outside is as a teletext text run's (text in any language). The server writes each text part with the engine's picture text encoder, joins the parts in order into the message's bytes, and then treats them exactly as data: checked, kept when the audience is "kept", and sent as records.

Refusals. A character the language cannot show refuses the message text_unshown with the part's path, such as parts[3].text, unless outside is true, when it becomes the language's stand-in and the server's log says so, as for a teletext text run. A text's other faults use the rules of text: not_nfc, forbidden_character, unknown_language, too_long. A parts list outside its bounds is invalid_picture_parts.

The encoder. A run's text is written in visual order as stretches, each a run of codes 0x20 to 0x7F of one of NeoTeletext's 55 provided sets: the choices the teletext page writer makes for a run, the language's own set and Latin English for what it cannot show; right-to-left runs reversed; the letters of the Arabic set of EN 300 706 Table 44 in their joined forms; the letters of the plain Arabic-script sets 44 to 51 in their base forms, which the picture renderers join. A letter with a diacritical mark its set has no precomposed glyph for is written as the letter and the mark of a G2 set over it.

As ReGIS, for each stretch: T(A100 + set), selecting its provided alphabet; then its codes as quoted strings "…" of at most 1,024 bytes each, a space between two, a " among the codes written twice. A mark follows its letter: the string closed, T(A the G2 set's alphabet ), T(W(V)) and the quoted string of BS (0x08) and the mark's code, written over the letter with the temporary overlay write control; the stretch's alphabet is selected again before its next code. After the last stretch, T(A0). A text part leaves alphabet 0 selected and the text position after its last character, and changes no other text control, writing control or position. Code 0x7F cannot be written in ReGIS, and a stretch holding it is refused. At most 32 bytes a character, 32,000 a part.

As NAPLPS, for each stretch: the 94-character designation of its set into G0 (ESC 2/8, a supplement byte 2/1, 2/2 or 2/3 for sets 16 and up, and the final byte 3/(n mod 16), NAPLPS's private designations of the provided sets), SI (0/15), then its codes. A code 7/15 is written by designating the set's 96-character form into G2 (ESC 2/14, the supplement, the final), SS2 (1/9) and the code, then the supplementary set back into G2 (ESC 2/10 7/12). A mark follows its letter as APB (0/8, active position backward), the G2 set's 96-character designation into G2, SS2 and the mark's code, and the supplementary set back into G2. After the last stretch, the primary set back into G0 (ESC 2/8 4/2). A text part leaves G0, holding the primary set, invoked in the in-use table and G2 holding the supplementary set; a page that draws with picture description instructions after it sends SO again. A mark written in colour mode 2, where a character's field is filled with the background colour, erases its letter: do not write text parts in colour mode 2. At most 32 bytes a character, 32,000 a part.

Where NAPLPS text is placed. A NAPLPS text part is characters only: the server writes no character field and no point of its own. A program that places a text part at the cell of row r (1 to 23) and column c (0 to 39) writes before it, in bytes of its own and after DOMAIN selecting six-byte multi-value operands (2/1 5/4 and six 4/0): TEXT (2/2) with its two format bytes 4/0 4/0 and the character field of 3,276 steps across by 4,452 up, in steps of 1/131072 of the unit screen, a hair under one cell of 12 dots by 20 lines; then POINT SET ABSOLUTE (2/4) at the raster dot (12 c, 20 r + 19), the cell's lower left corner, each axis value rounded down, where a dot (X, Y) of the 480 by 500 raster is the unit-screen point X / 480 across and (479 − Y) × 25 / 14720 up. Each character is then exactly one cell of the engine's Noto Teletext glyphs on teletext row r, a whole row of 40 written as one run. Teletext's double height (EN 300 706 Table 26, code 0/D), a character two rows high from its upper row r (1 to 22), is placed the same way with the character field of 3,276 steps across by 8,904 up, a hair under 12 dots by 40 lines, and the point at the raster dot (12 c, 20 (r + 1) + 19), the lower left corner of the row below, each axis value rounded down: each glyph row then lies on two raster lines, the same pixels as teletext's own double height. The kits' NAPLPS builder writes these with its text call, given the row and column, and rows: 2 for double height.

The wire vectors picture_text regis_greek, regis_arabic, naplps_greek and naplps_arabic of neoteletext-common's wire-vectors.tsv are a Greek and an Arabic text part in each language.

measure_picture_text {"type":"measure_picture_text","request":17,"text":"…","language":"ar","outside":false} asks what a text part costs, and sends nothing to any viewer. The server answers {"type":"measured_picture_text","request":17,"cells":12,"regis_bytes":96,"naplps_bytes":40,"sets":["G0-Arabic"],"stand_ins":0}: the character cells the text advances (a mark takes none), the bytes of each language's writing, the provided sets it uses by their names in order of first use, and the characters that became stand-ins. Both picture languages space text by whole cells, so a text's width is cells times the cell width the picture sets. A text the language cannot show without outside is refused text_unshown, with request carried.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 44 Arabic G0 Primary Set; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 1 Summary of packet types, their function and application

12.23 The mosaic fallback: a picture shown as Level 1 mosaics to a receiver that did not agree its language

DOC-6830 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-6769

A receiver that did not agree a picture language's capability bit (REGIS, bit 23, or NAPLPS, bit 24, capabilities) is sent none of that language's records: not its stream records, not NAPLPS_OBJECTS, and not the DRAWING_LINKS and REGIS_CURSOR of its sub-pages. For every sub-page it shows that has a picture of that language, kept or sent to it, the server sends it instead the sub-page as the program gave it with rows 1 to 23 replaced by the picture drawn as Level 1 mosaics. Rows 0 and 24 and everything else of the page are the program's. Rule tables, sounds and every other record go to it as to any receiver.

How it is drawn. The server draws the picture with the renderer and fonts the browser uses: ReGIS by the ReGIS renderer on its 800 by 480 screen, with the VT340's alphabet 0 font and the provided sets (alphabets 100 to 154) from the engine's compiled Noto Teletext glyphs, its committed numbered drawings composed over the base; NAPLPS by the NAPLPS renderer on its display area of 480 by 460 dots, raster lines 20 to 479 of the teletext raster, which are exactly teletext rows 1 to 23, with its stroke font and the same provided sets, its shown objects composed over it. The picture is turned into colours by its colour map and converted into Level 1 mosaics in rows 1 to 23, 80 by 69 sixels, the whole picture contained in them; for NAPLPS each row's mosaics come from that row's own 20 lines of the picture.

How often. A picture is drawn again from its whole stream when it changes, at most once in FALLBACK_INTERVAL_MS, 500 milliseconds, its last change always drawn within that interval. A kept picture's fallback is drawn once and shared by every connection showing it. A channel draws at most MOST_FALLBACK_RENDERS_PER_SECOND, 20 a second, sustained, over all its pictures: a drawing over that budget is drawn late, never wrong and never skipped. Each drawing is bounded by the renderers' own limits on the work a stream may cost.

Streams sent to one connection. For a stream a program sends such a connection itself, the server keeps the bytes it does not send, at most MOST_KEPT_STREAM_BYTES, 1,048,576, for one connection and MOST_FALLBACK_POOL_BYTES, 16,777,216, for all of a channel's connections together. A stream past either is dropped for that connection: its fallback shows what it had, and the author's log of that connection's receiver says which bound was passed.

Compatibility. A receiver built before the two bits offers neither, so it is given mosaics in place of pictures and is never refused; nothing of the push protocol's version changes.

13 Running a server

DOC-2026 · section

13.1 The administration listener

DOC-2030 · reference · normative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1052, REQ-1054, REQ-1055

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1052 Metrics in the Prometheus text format (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1054 Totals accumulated across restarts (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1055 Health and readiness: /readyz is 200 once every channel's program has answered (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The NeoTeletext server answers an operator on an address of its own, given by --admin-listen ADDRESS. With no such option there is none. It is never the address viewers reach, because figures about viewers stay off the public address, and nothing on it needs a client's or a program's author. A deployment puts it on 127.0.0.1:9464.

PathAnswer
/metrics200, text/plain; version=0.0.4; charset=utf-8: the figures since the process started, in the Prometheus text exposition format, version 0.0.4
/stats.json200, application/json: an object with type, server and channels, each channel by its folder, holding what a program is sent in stats, with invalid_packets, stale_input and stale_answers besides, and all_time: the counters and peaks since the server first ran with its state directory
/healthz200, ok: the process is running
/readyz200, ready, once every channel's program has answered since it started, and otherwise 503, no program answering: and the channels' folders. A program that has started may still be loading, so starting does not count: the server asks each program one describe as it starts, and any answer counts.
Anything else404

Every answer has Cache-Control: no-store. The method is not looked at. /stats.json on the viewers' address answers 404, as anything outside what each address answers does.

Metrics. Names follow Prometheus's conventions: the prefix teletext_, base units, and _total on every counter. Nothing identifies a viewer.

KindNames
Of the processteletext_build_info, with the label version; process_start_time_seconds; process_resident_memory_bytes
Gauges of the serverteletext_connections, teletext_connections_peak
Counters of the serverteletext_connections_total, teletext_messages_sent_total, teletext_sent_bytes_total, teletext_http_requests_total, teletext_program_restarts_total
Gauges of a channel, with the label channelteletext_channel_viewers, teletext_channel_viewers_peak, teletext_channel_ready
Counters of a channelteletext_channel_viewers_total, teletext_channel_proofs_accepted_total and teletext_channel_proofs_refused_total (viewers' proofs of viewer state that verified and that were refused), teletext_channel_page_opens_total, teletext_channel_inputs_total, teletext_channel_keys_total, teletext_channel_pages_sent_total, teletext_channel_subpages_not_forwarded_total, teletext_channel_refused_total, teletext_channel_stale_input_total, teletext_channel_stale_answers_total, teletext_channel_redirects_total, teletext_channel_sound_records_total, teletext_channel_program_lines_sent_total, teletext_channel_program_lines_received_total, teletext_channel_program_lines_dropped_total, teletext_channel_events_total
A histogram of a channelteletext_channel_event_duration_seconds: the channel's time over one event and its effects

13.2 The server's options and what it keeps

DOC-2031 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1041, REQ-1054, REQ-6704, REQ-6965, REQ-6974

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1041 The listening socket outlives a restart (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1054 Totals accumulated across restarts (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6704 The server keeps no session and sets no cookie: a connection lasts until it closes, and the program is told gone for it (not implemented on livedevelopment).

teletext-server is the native server. The channels file says what it serves.

OptionHoldsDefault
--listen ADDRESSWhere viewers connect. A listening socket systemd passes, by the protocol of sd_listen_fds(3), is taken in its place, so that a connection made during a restart waits in the socket. More than one such socket is refused. With TLS, the server also listens for QUIC on UDP at the same address and port.0.0.0.0:8090
--origin URLThe origin viewers reach the server at, which each channel's address is on. With TLS it starts https://, and its port, 443 when it names none, is the port every answer over TCP names HTTP/3 at in Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT": the port viewers reach the server at, which is not the listening port when a proxy relays connections to it. With TLS, an origin from which no port can be read stops the server at start.http://127.0.0.1:8090
--channels FILEThe channels fileNone
--state DIRECTORYWhere it keeps what follows, across restarts$STATE_DIRECTORY, as systemd sets it, or nothing kept
--admin-listen ADDRESSThe administration listenerNone
--log-format auto|json|textHow events are written to standard error. RUST_LOG chooses which.auto
--trusted-proxy ADDRESSThe proxy in front of the server. Without --proxy-protocol, a reverse proxy whose X-Forwarded-For then names each viewer's address for the bound on new viewers from one address. With it, the one proxy allowed to connect over TCP, whose PROXY protocol header is believed in place of X-Forwarded-For.None
--tls-certificate FILE and --tls-key FILEGiven together: a certificate chain and its private key, in PEM. The server then ends TLS itself and needs no proxy: HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 on TCP, and HTTP/3 over QUIC on UDP at the same address and port, each carrying a channel's push and program WebSockets (opening the connection). The files are read once, at start; a file that cannot be read, or a key that is not the certificate's, stops the server there.None: plain HTTP/1.1 on TCP for a proxy in front, no UDP port and no Alt-Svc
--proxy-protocolTakes no value, and is valid only with --trusted-proxy and the two TLS options: given without them, the server stops at start. Every TCP connection must then come from the trusted proxy and start with a PROXY protocol version 2 header, read before TLS, whose source address is the viewer's for the bound on new viewers; any other connection is closed with nothing sent, and X-Forwarded-For is not read on TCP. QUIC is not changed by it: a QUIC connection's viewer address is its peer's.Off

What it keeps. No channel's content. A file in the state directory is written beside its place and renamed into it, so a crash leaves the old file or the new one, and the files and their folder are their owner's alone.

FileHolds
viewer-handle.keyThe secret a viewer's handle is derived from (viewer state), made when there is none. Without a state directory a secret is made for the run alone, so every viewer has a new handle after a restart
viewer-handle.rotatedLeft by teletext-server rotate-viewer-secret, which makes a new secret for the next start: every channel then forgets every viewer, and each program is told viewers_reset when it starts. The file is removed once every program has been told. Rotate only after a breach of a program's data or of the state directory
figures.jsonThe totals behind all_time, written every minute and at shutdown. A file that does not read is kept aside as figures.json.unreadable, and the figures start again.

The files session.key and session.key.previous, which held the keys of the session cookie before viewer state replaced it, are deleted at start if an earlier version left them, and never read.

Stopping. On SIGTERM or SIGINT the server closes each connection with 4100, so that receivers come back, keeps its figures, and exits, within 10 seconds. A program keeps its own state, and is told of each connection when it starts or connects again.

14 The engine

DOC-2255 · section

This part describes NeoTeletext's engine, the Rust library and command-line program in the repository neoteletext-renderer-teletext that every other component builds on: how it is divided, how it reads, decodes and draws teletext, its character sets, fonts and sound, its slicer, its web module, its command-line program neottx, its security, and how it is built and tested. The part is informative: it describes one implementation of the protocol, which another implementation need not copy. What every implementation must do is in the protocol's parts above.

14.1 The engine's crates, layers and compile-time features

DOC-2264 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-23, REQ-33, REQ-154, REQ-163, REQ-164, REQ-1642

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-23 Module structure (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-33 The code is organised into the layers of ARCHITECTURE.md (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-154 The Cargo workspace (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-163 Capability features of neoteletext-core (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-164 Optional C interface crate (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-1642 A build contains only the optional parts it uses (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The engine is one Cargo workspace written in Rust. Its crates are divided by what they may depend on and where they must run, and each optional crate depends only on crates above it in this table.

CrateWhat it holdsWhere it runs
neoteletext-coreThe teletext constants, the error-protection codes, packet decoding, the character tables, the state machines, acquisition and the page store, broadcast service data, Level 1, 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 decoding, navigation, the cell grid, the cell raster and the row rendererAnywhere: no standard library and no allocation
neoteletext-formatsThe streaming readers and writers of every input format, the page encoder, and the page writer of neottx write-textReaders without the standard library; writers and file helpers behind the feature std
neoteletext-slicerThe software data slicer, which turns sampled television lines into packetsWithout the standard library
neoteletext-webThe web protocols, HTTP/1.1 and WebSockets, the bytes a viewer-state key signs, and the reader of the zxnet live feed, written to consume and produce bytes and never to perform input or output itselfWithout the standard library
neoteletext-imageThe pixel-format helpers and the image file writersHelpers anywhere; image writers need the standard library
neoteletext-opusThe Opus decoder of the audio profileAnywhere: no allocation, integers only, no dependency
neoteletext-audioThe audio profile: carriage, records, the sound store, control and the decoders; its feature encode writes soundsWithout allocation, except encode
neoteletext-audio-mixA software mixer for a port whose operating system has an audio outputWith allocation
neoteletext-inputThe input system's records and a receiver's sessionWithout allocation
neoteletext-transportA client's sockets: the reader thread, the TLS pump, blocking writes and the connection through a proxyOperating systems only
neoteletext-qrkeyboardA phone as the keyboard, through the qrkeyboard relayOperating systems only
neoteletext-appThe application layer neottx shares with a windowed viewer: sessions, inputs, the two processes of live mode and sandboxingOperating systems only
neoteletext-cliThe command-line program neottxOperating systems only

A development-tools package, xtask, holds project automation that is not part of the library: the glyph export, the font conversion steps, fetching the test corpus, measuring sizes, writing the byte examples of this document, and the checks of the gates. An optional C interface crate, neoteletext-ffi, with a header generated by cbindgen, a static library, the prefix ttx_ on every identifier, and the only unsafe code of the workspace, is planned for a later phase and does not exist.

The layers. Inside and across the crates the code is organised in layers, each depending only on the layers below it: Foundation; L0, ingress; L1, packet decoding; L2, acquisition; L3, the presentation model; L4, rendering; L5, output adapters; L6, interaction; L7, the web user agent; L8, the platform interface; L9, applications and ports; and the cross-cutting modules for security policy, configuration and trace, which may depend only on Foundation. The core modules depend on one another in the order of the crate table's first row, and Levels 2.5 and 3.5 add the Colour Map, the resolution of objects and the enhancement processor beside Level 1.5 decoding. The web crate may use Foundation, the security policy, the configuration and, from L1, the packet value with its address and kind, and nothing above L1, so it never acquires, stores or presents a page. cargo xtask check-layers enforces the rule for each crate and for each core module against the two tables of section 9 of the engine's ARCHITECTURE.md, which it reads from the document itself, so the document and the check cannot differ; it refuses a module with no row, and the push gate runs it. Two rules cannot be seen by a check of paths and are held by the review of each change instead: that neighbouring layers meet only through narrow boundary types, and that security decisions are made only in the policy module. The web crate depends on neoteletext-audio, which stands below it in the table, with no decision for that yet.

Compile-time features. A build contains only the parts it uses. Crates separate different dependencies or environments, features separate the optional areas within a crate, and the configuration chooses behaviour among what is compiled. Features are additive, one for each area and, within Levels 2.5 and 3.5, one for each capability, never one for each function, and no feature changes what another does. Data types and acquisition are never behind a feature, because Level 1.5 reads the character set designations of X/28/0 and M/29/0, so acquisition stays whole at every level and only processing is optional. A configured level that is not compiled in falls back to the highest compiled level below it. A request a build cannot serve says so with a named event or error, such as FormatNotCompiled or Event::PushNotCompiledIn, and a command of neottx whose area is left out exits with the usage status and says so. The features themselves are listed in each crate's Cargo.toml.

The core's capability features are nonspacing-attributes, objects, level25-32colors, level35-32colors (which turns on level25-32colors) and additional-flash-functions (which needs nonspacing-attributes), each needing level25. A build without one contains neither the decoding nor the drawing of that capability and reads its page data without error. Two profiles name a set of features: modern-classic turns on level15, level25, nonspacing-attributes, render, viewer and objects, and classic turns on level15, render and viewer, the small build a Level 1.5 receiver needs. There is no feature for side panels and none that chooses a font: Noto Teletext is in every build, and extended-sets adds the part of it only NeoTeletext's own sets use. cargo xtask features builds, lints and tests each crate with no optional area and with each area alone, and the workspace tests run with every feature.

14.2 The platform interface: everything a port of the engine supplies

DOC-2267 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-31, REQ-32, REQ-396, REQ-434

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-32 Library contains no display, timing or hardware-specific code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-396 Reference callers (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-434 Porting guide explains MPU isolation of network stack from decoder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A port is the code that runs the engine on one platform: a desktop program, a microcontroller with a screen, a WebAssembly host. Everything a port must supply is gathered into one platform interface, so that the surface a new platform has to write stays small and fixed.

What the port suppliesHow
A data sourceInput bytes in any of the engine's input formats, through the embedded-io reading traits, which both embedded network stacks and the standard library implement
Somewhere to put pixelsThe port calls the row renderer with its own buffers whenever its hardware wants them. It does not implement a callback for pixels: it asks, and the library answers.
A time sourceMonotonic microseconds, for flash, timeouts and reveal, through a small trait of the core
Key inputThe viewer's key presses as the numbered functions of navigation, through a small trait
Optionally, a sleep functionFor platforms that must yield
Optionally, for the web moduleA network transport, a byte stream with or without TLS; random bytes from a cryptographic generator, for WebSocket handshake keys and frame masks, which the library cannot make because it has no access to the operating system
Optionally, for soundAn audio sink that plays what the audio receiver gives it

The boundary with the hardware. The library contains no code that puts pixels on a screen, drives a display or display controller, generates a video signal, depends on display or scan timing, or is written for any particular microcontroller, display, capture card or television. Its pixel output ends when the row renderer has written a row or a line into a buffer the port supplied. Everything after that belongs to the port: whether it keeps a framebuffer, a ring of row buffers or a single row, the order and timing of drawing, display drivers, direct memory access transfers, palettes held in hardware, scan-out, and what to do when the hardware is not ready. Input devices are treated the same way: the port supplies bytes through the data source.

Reference callers. The library includes users of the row renderer and the platform interface that show no pixels on a screen and touch no hardware: the whole-screen convenience loop, the image file writers, and a test harness that calls the row renderer in unusual orders and records the results. Ports for particular screens, operating systems or devices are written by their users against the platform interface, and are not part of the library. The engine's docs/spec/design/porting.md is the porting guide.

Isolating the network on a microcontroller. A microcontroller port can use a memory protection unit, where the chip has one (the Arm Cortex-M memory protection unit, or RISC-V physical memory protection), to keep the network stack apart from the decoder. The library cannot enforce that, because it touches no hardware, and the guidance for it in the porting guide is planned for a later phase and not yet written.

14.3 The rules the engine's core keeps: no allocation, caller memory, no hidden state, determinism, robustness and size

DOC-2270 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-146, REQ-147, REQ-148, REQ-149, REQ-151, REQ-152, REQ-153, REQ-155, REQ-157, REQ-158, REQ-160

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-146 A `no_std` core (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-147 Caller-provided memory (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-148 No hidden global state (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-149 Determinism (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-151 Unsigned integer types for bit manipulation (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-152 Robustness against any input, without panics (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-153 Documented resource use (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-155 Public interface follows the Rust API Guidelines (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-157 Packet-level decoder throughput (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-158 Every teletext constant is defined once (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-160 No floating point in the core, web module and formats (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The core crate, neoteletext-core, is written to run on a microcontroller with no operating system as well as on a desktop computer, because the teletext decoders of the past fitted into small integrated circuits and their software equivalent should fit into a small processor. These rules make that possible.

  • No standard library and no allocation. The core declares #![no_std] and uses neither the alloc crate, nor file or console input and output, nor any clock, nor any operating-system facility. It builds and runs on every target the engine supports, including bare-metal microcontrollers.
  • Memory the caller provides. All of the core's state is kept in values whose storage the caller provides. Every capacity that can be configured, such as the number of stored pages, or the number of sub-pages of a page, is a const generic parameter or a slice the caller supplies, so every store a decoder fills, the page store and both parts of the enhancement store, can be a static value made at compile time. The decoder value itself, which borrows those stores mutably, is a local value of the caller. The size of every state type is reported and bounded by a test and published in the engine's porting guide.
  • No hidden global state. The core has no mutable statics, no statics behind interior mutability and no globals made on first use. Several decoders run independently in one program. A decoder's state is Send, so a port may move it between threads or tasks, and need not be Sync, because one thread uses a decoder at a time.
  • Determinism, with time from the caller. The same input and configuration give the same output. Wherever timing matters, the page-completion timeout, the flash phase, the reveal timeout and packet time stamps, the caller supplies the time as a monotonic count of microseconds.
  • Portable bit handling. Bits are handled in unsigned integer types. Multi-byte values from files and streams are assembled explicitly in the byte order their format specifies, never by reinterpreting memory, and nothing assumes the processor is little-endian, which a run of the tests under Miri on a big-endian target checks.
  • Robust against any input. No packet, file, stream, sample buffer or network message, however malformed, truncated or hostile, causes a panic, an access out of bounds, an arithmetic overflow, an unbounded loop or unbounded memory use. Malformed input is reported through the library's error types and events, and skipped. Builds for bare-metal targets abort on panic.
  • Rules for small processors. In the crates without the standard library: no floating point (the Cortex-M0, M3 and RV32IMC have no floating-point unit), except in the slicer; no atomic operations (the Cortex-M0 and RV32IMC have no compare-and-swap); no division and no 64-bit arithmetic in the code run for each packet or each pixel; no unaligned access; no formatting machinery except in Debug implementations and behind an optional feature; and no deep recursion or large stack buffers. The Opus decoder is the one exception for division and 64-bit products, which bit-exactness with the reference decoder needs and whose cost on the Cortex-M0 was measured.
  • Every teletext constant defined once. Every teletext value, each timing, level, code value, bit pattern, packet length, line allocation and tolerance, is defined in one constants module of the core and read by name everywhere else. Where a value is needed in two forms they stand side by side with the conversion stated, as the framing code does: 0x27 in transmission order and 0xE4 in the bit order of digital television. A test searches the rest of the source for such literal values.
  • Public interface conventions. The public interface follows the Rust API Guidelines. Errors are enumerations implementing core::error::Error, never strings. Configuration is a plain structure with a default and named profile constructors. Every public item is documented, and crates follow semantic versioning, checked with cargo-semver-checks before a release.
  • Throughput. The packet-level decoder, from 42-byte packets to stored pages including Level 1.5, processes at least 17,500 packets a second on one core of a current desktop computer, twenty times the greatest broadcast rate of 35 packets a frame at 25 frames a second. The slicer processes at least ten times the real-time rate of one such stream.
  • Documented resource use. The documentation states the memory of a decoder in its smallest configuration, in the default configuration of neottx, at Level 3.5 with its store of enhancement pages, and for each stored page. A cell grid is 16,100 bytes at every level. The full gate measures the flash size of the Level 1.5 build of the core on thumbv6m-none-eabi, optimised for size with link-time optimisation, and fails above a budget of 64 kilobytes; on 1 November 2026 it was 58,570 bytes, the core with no optional area 25,870 bytes, and every area with the whole font 147,282 bytes.

Not yet published: the largest stack frame of the core.

14.4 What the engine's decoder reports and keeps: packet metadata, events, statistics, configuration and characters that fail parity

DOC-2277 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-25, REQ-27, REQ-28, REQ-29, REQ-30, REQ-243

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-25 Packet metadata fields (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-27 Decoder reports events through a caller-registered callback (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-28 Displaying a page is a pure function (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-29 Decoder statistics counters readable and resettable by caller (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-30 Part E behaviour choices exposed as configuration fields (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-243 Characters that failed parity (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Packet metadata. Every packet given to the decoder comes with metadata: the television line number and field where they are known, a time stamp in microseconds, the input it came from, and, for a packet the slicer recovered from samples, the slicer's quality measures and whether the framing code needed correcting. A value that is not known is marked unknown, never set to zero.

Events. The decoder reports what happens through a function the caller registers. Each event names the page by magazine, page number and sub-code where one applies.

EventWhen
HeaderReceivedA page header arrived, for the rolling header
PageStartedReception of a page began
PageUpdatedA row of a page changed
PageCompletedReception of a page ended
PageErasedA page was erased, because its header had C4 set
UpdateIndicatorA header with C8 set arrived
PageStaleA page has not been received for the configured period
ServiceDataBroadcast service data arrived in packet 8/30
MagazineDataA magazine's own data changed; it is raised only on a change
EnhancementPageChangedA stored object page, enhancement page or Magazine Organization Table changed
DiscardedA packet was discarded, for an uncorrectable address or designation code, or a row with no page being received
TraceA state machine made a transition, when tracing is on

Statistics. The decoder keeps counts the caller can read and reset: packets received for each magazine and each packet number, Hamming 8/4 failures where they discard a packet, Hamming 24/18 failures, parity failures, discarded packets, and pages started and completed.

Not yet built. A triplet that fails Hamming 24/18 and a byte that fails parity are counted but raise no event; the header event carries no sub-code; corrections by Hamming 8/4 and 24/18 are not counted at all; and Hamming 8/4 failures are counted only where they discard a packet.

Displaying a page is a pure function. The displayable cell grid is made by a function with no side effects, which gives the same result every time for the same inputs: the stored page, the stored magazine data, at Levels 2.5 and 3.5 the stored object pages, other enhancement pages and Magazine Organization Tables reached through a read-only lookup, the decoder's configuration, and the viewer's state, which is reveal, mix, zoom, the flash phase and the text of the status area.

Configuration. Every choice of behaviour the engine makes where the standard leaves one is a field of one configuration structure. One function fills it with its documented defaults, and another applies a named compatibility profile, such as saa5246a, which reproduces that chip's 12 by 10 cell. Changing the configuration never needs pages already stored to be received again. The engine's user guide lists every setting and profile.

Characters that fail parity. Every stored character carries a flag saying whether it passed its odd parity check. By default a new character that fails does not replace one that passed in an earlier reception of the same page and sub-page, unless the page was erased in between by C4 or a new sub-code, and a cell that has never held a character that passed is shown as a space. Keeping the last good character is how a receiver builds a clean page out of several noisy retransmissions, on a weak signal or a recovered video recording. The two other policies the configuration offers are always showing a space and showing a visible error mark, the latter for diagnosis.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.1 Odd parity (Odd parity: the check a character fails); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.2 Hamming 8/4 (Hamming 8/4, whose failures are counted); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 8.3 Hamming 24/18 (Hamming 24/18, whose failures are counted); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.2 Use of control bits C4 (Erase Page) and C8 (Update Indicator) (C4, Erase Page, and C8, Update Indicator, which the events report)

14.5 The engine's state machines: the line slicer, a page's lifecycle, the viewer and the two triplet walks

DOC-2280 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-133, REQ-134, REQ-136, REQ-137, REQ-139, REQ-141, REQ-142, REQ-143

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-133 State machines implemented as an enumeration and a single transition function (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-134 Line slicer state machine (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-136 The page lifecycle machine (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-137 The viewer machine (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-139 Level 1.5 triplet walk follows the state table (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-141 Tests for every transition (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-142 Transition trace (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-143 The Level 2.5 and 3.5 enhancement walk (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every part of the engine whose behaviour depends on what came before is a state machine, written as an explicit enumeration of states and one transition function that takes the current state and one event and returns the next state with the actions to perform. In Rust that is an enum of states and a match over the state and the event with no wildcard arms, so the compiler checks that every combination is handled. No state that affects a transition is kept outside the machine's own record, every transition of the engine's tables exists in the code and none that is not, and each machine can be used and tested on its own. The magazine acquisition machine is described with where a page starts and ends; the others are these.

  • The line slicer machine runs once for each sampled line. It estimates the black level, searches for the clock run-in within a window, measures the levels, threshold and bit phase, and rejects the line when the amplitude or the match is below the gate. It then looks for the framing code within two bit periods either way, accepting one wrong bit and marking the packet "framing corrected" when that tolerance is on, reads 336 bits at the bit centres into 42 bytes, and gives the packet only when both packet address bytes decode without an uncorrectable error. That last check is what makes accepting a corrected framing code safe. Each rejection is counted by its reason: no signal, below the gate, no framing code or a bad address.
  • The page lifecycle machine, one for each stored page and sub-page, goes from empty to partial when reception starts, raising "page started"; raises "update indicator" while partial when the header that started the reception has C8 set; stays partial while rows are stored, raising "page updated" for each, which is how a change of content is reported; becomes complete when reception ends, raising "page completed"; erases rows 1 to 28 and raises "page erased" when reception starts again with C4 set, and otherwise merges the new rows with the old; becomes stale when it has not been received for the configured period; and is released when evicted from the store. Every other combination of state and event changes nothing.
  • The viewer machine, one for each viewer, requests the initial page when the decoder starts; takes page numbers digit by digit in the status area, refusing a digit that cannot make a valid page and keeping those already entered; after the sub-page key, takes a decimal sub-code digit by digit in the same way and requests that sub-page of the page shown, as it does for a sub-page the port chooses; shows a requested page as soon as it is in the store; keeps the rolling header and clock while searching; clears "not recently received" when the page shown is updated, while the port marks the changed rows for an update, a flash or a reveal; shows "not recently received" for a stale page; stops and resumes applying updates with the hold key; follows the coloured keys, Index, Home, next and previous page and Back and Forward; follows at once a link to another service already confirmed this session; and asks for confirmation in the status area and row 24 before a link to an unconfirmed other service from a page on screen, followed when the same key is pressed again. Any event or key it does not list for a state leaves the state unchanged.
  • The Level 1.5 triplet walk applies a page's packets X/26 to its cell grid in designation-code order, skipping missing codes, and X/26/15 when the profile says so. It starts at row 0, column 0, ignores a triplet that failed its Hamming 24/18 check, stops at the Termination Marker, moves the row on a row triplet that sets it (row 24 for address 40, otherwise the address minus 40) and the column on a column triplet, and writes a character for a character mode whose data is 2/0 or above.
  • The Level 2.5 and 3.5 enhancement walk walks the page's local enhancement data, the objects it invokes and the default objects, and produces the character and attribute events that the grid resolves. Its state is the current source and a stack of walk records, each holding an active position relative to its source's origin, the origin, any pending Origin Modifier, and the source's attribute plane and display priority. The stack is at most three deep, because of the nesting rules of objects, so no recursion is needed. It skips damaged triplets; ends a source at a Termination Marker, the end of its data or an Object Definition; pushes a record for a permitted and found Object Invocation, within its limits, and counts any other; ignores Full Row Colour and Address Display Row 0 inside Adaptive and Passive objects, where neither colour nor position changes; discards an Origin Modifier that is not followed by an invocation; places nothing for DRCS Character Invocation and Font Style, only moving the column; and places the default objects when the page has no display triplet of its own.

Each machine can report every transition it makes as a trace entry: the machine and its instance, such as "magazine 3", the time, the state before, the event, the actions and the state after. Tracing is switched on and off in the configuration and costs one test a transition when off, and the verbosity option of neottx prints it, because a trace of transitions is the quickest way to find why a real recording decodes wrongly. The tests hold at least one test for every row of every table, checking both the next state and the actions, and feed the decoder pages from the encoder and the broadcast corpus in each non-standard order a service may send, checking that the pages and grids are those of the standard order.

Not yet as described. The viewer is not yet one transition function; a chosen sub-page that goes stale shows no mark in the status area; not every machine reports a trace yet; and the reordering tests are not all written.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.2 Use of control bits C4 (Erase Page) and C8 (Update Indicator) (Rests on: C4 erases a page and C8 marks an update, which drive the page lifecycle machine); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.4 Addressing order for enhancement triplets (Rests on: the order in which the walks take enhancement triplets); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets (Rests on: the row address triplets the walks act on); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 29 Function of Column Address triplets (Rests on: the column address triplets the walks act on); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 13 Objects (Rests on: objects, which the Level 2.5 and 3.5 walk enters and leaves); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 6.2 Framing code (Rests on: the framing code the slicer machine looks for)

14.6 The engine's input formats and readers, and the zxnet live feed

DOC-2284 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-26, REQ-165, REQ-167, REQ-168, REQ-174, REQ-175, REQ-181, REQ-184, TODO-185, REQ-186

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-26 Page files enter as packets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-165 Reader interface (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-167 Accept 43-byte packets with framing code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-168 Bit-reversed packet streams (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-174 Linux sliced data (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-175 Raw sampled video files (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-181 Raw screen dump reading (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-184 Reporting input errors (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); TODO-185 Implement additional input formats (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-186 The live WebSocket feed used by the zxnet teletext viewer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every input format is read by a streaming reader in neoteletext-formats. A reader takes bytes as they arrive, in pieces of any size, and gives packets with their metadata, or pages. Its memory is bounded and does not depend on the size of the file, and it works on regular files, pipes and standard input alike.
