DOC-2261 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-659, REQ-660, REQ-661, REQ-662, REQ-663, REQ-664, REQ-665, REQ-666

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-660 Security comes first (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-661 No executable content; the decoder may evaluate a page's bounded rule table (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-664 The engine's own guarantees are kept (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-665 Limits come from neoteletext (not implemented on livedevelopment).

The NeoTeletext browser is a desktop application for browsing teletext delivered over the web and read from local files. Each tab shows one teletext channel, and every page it shows is a teletext page: it shows nothing else, and it fetches nothing that is not part of a channel.

Security comes first. Wherever a choice trades capability, convenience or speed against security, the browser takes the more secure one, and the trade is written down in the browser's security analysis. No protection is ever weakened or dropped: there is no weaker mode to fall back to, and no setting, switch or environment variable selects one. A process that cannot have every protection its design names is not run at all.

No executable content. The browser never runs code supplied by a page, a channel, a server or a file, and contains no interpreter that outside data can reach. There is one exception, a page's rule table: rules that bind events to groups of protocol commands, each event handled at once in arrival order within per-tick budgets, and what time drives evaluated once per tick of one sixtieth of a second. It may be evaluated provided that it is decoded and evaluated only by the engine's crate neoteletext-rules, in the confined decoder process and never in the trusted core; that it stays within every limit of the limits; that its only arithmetic beyond comparison is the saturating addition and subtraction of signed 32-bit integers in the variable commands and in a command's value held to the field's range, with no multiplication, division, loop within a tick or computed address; that no command changes a table, a group, a sequence or a row, and no command makes a rule fire while it is being applied; and that nothing reaches the network because of it but the reports the trusted core itself builds and the answer to a state query, to the page's own channel on its own connection. The one other exception decided, an interpreter of WebAssembly that would run only the browser's own decoder module on iOS, belongs to the phone versions, which are not built.

The engine does the teletext. Every recognition, decoding and drawing of teletext is done by NeoTeletext's engine, and every reading of web protocols by the engine's web module, neoteletext-web; the browser holds no second implementation of either. The engine's crates the browser uses depend on no user interface or graphics toolkit. The browser depends on the engine by one pinned commit of the engine's published repository, never a copy of its source and never patched locally, and its check script fails unless every one of its workspaces names the same engine commit.

Limits come from the engine. Every limit on fetching, refreshing and input is meant to be a constant defined once in the engine and used by name. This is partly met: two values are written again in the browser instead of named, the fetcher's connection time-out of 10 seconds and the pace of 0.2 seconds at which the trusted core hands a file channel's pages on. The engine's own guarantees are kept in the browser's build: the browser's full gate runs the engine's own full gate at the commit the browser builds against and refuses any unsafe code in the engine's source there, and every commit gate checks the engine's feature rule that the desktop builds leave out the PCM16 and IMA ADPCM sound codecs.

15.2 The browser's processes and their sandboxes

DOC-2262 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-667, REQ-668, REQ-669, REQ-670, REQ-672, REQ-673, REQ-674, REQ-675, REQ-678, REQ-679, REQ-680, REQ-6980, REQ-6981

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-667 Separate processes (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-669 The fetcher has only the network (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-670 The decoder has no network access (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-672 The interface process receives no secrets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-673 Operating-system sandboxes on the desktops (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-674 The fetcher, decoder and trusted core are sandboxed on macOS (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-675 Security does not depend on the interface's code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-678 One fetcher per web channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-679 Background tabs sleep (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-680 A decoder starts with room for 256 pages and sub-pages (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6980 One fetcher process serves every tab of one channel in one jar, and each message between the trusted core and a fetcher names its tab (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-6981 A fetcher's sandbox allows UDP to its channel's own port, for the shared HTTP/3 connection, and nothing else new (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The browser runs as separate processes, each allowed only what its work needs, so that a fault in the code that reads outside data reaches nothing of value.

ProcessWhat it doesWhat it may reach
The brokerStarts every other process, and does for the trusted core the few things a confined process cannot: reading a file the viewer gave, keeping a secret in the system's store, showing the system's file dialog, handing an address to the system's web browser.It is the one process not confined, by design, and it reads only the trusted core's bounded requests.
The trusted coreHolds the browser's state and makes every decision: tabs, history, bookmarks, viewer-state keys, settings, links, and what is sent to a channel.No network, no programs, and only its own settings folder.
A fetcher, one for each web channel in each jar (an ordinary window's, or a private window's)Fetches that channel's resources for every tab of the channel in that jar, and holds each such tab's own push WebSocket and, where the channel's server offers HTTP/3, the one connection those WebSockets share, a stream each. Each tab keeps its own user agent, selection and fetch connection inside it. It fetches nothing of any other channel, and serves no tab of another jar.The network and nothing else: no files, and no other process but through its pipe to the trusted core. Where it may share a connection, UDP to its channel's own port and to no other.
A decoder, one for each channel a tab showsRecognises, decodes and draws that channel's teletext, and reads its sound.No network, no files and no secrets: its pipes alone.
The interfaceDraws every window and passes on what the viewer did.No network on any platform, no file beyond its own resources and fonts, and no secret.
The sound helperMixes and plays the channels' sound.The sound output.
The phone keyboard, while it is openRelays a phone's keys (the phone keyboard).Its relay connection.
The updater and the launcherFetch, check and start new versions.The updater: one port and its staging folder.

How each is confined. Every process but the broker starts from "deny everything" and is given back only what it needs: on macOS a sandbox-exec profile of its own; on Linux Landlock, a network namespace for those with no network, and a seccomp filter, each applied by the process itself before it starts any thread; on Windows a job object with the mitigation policies and an AppContainer, with no capability for the decoder and the interface and the internet client capability for the fetcher. Every layer named for a process is required: a process that cannot have them all does not run. The environment each is given holds only what it needs.

A fetcher's UDP port. A fetcher that may share a connection (sharing is on, no proxy is set, and the channel is served over TLS) is started with its channel's port, 443 when the address names none. On macOS its profile then gains two rules: one that allows UDP to that port, before the rule that refuses localhost, which therefore holds for UDP as for TCP; and one that lets it bind the UDP socket it sends from, on any local port, since the socket is bound before it sends and the profile language cannot name the ephemeral port. No rule lets anything arrive but the connected server's answers. On Linux and Windows nothing is added, since the seccomp filter and the internet client capability already allowed a fetcher's sockets, UDP among them, for the system's resolver, and neither can name a port: there the port is held by the fetcher's own code and the engine's address rule. No other process is given a UDP port.

What the trusted core reads. The trusted core links no web engine, no script engine and no interpreter, and takes only typed, bounded messages from the other processes. Of the engine's crates it links only six, each for a bounded use: neoteletext-core for the standard's page numbers, limits and constants, the local-address rule and each packet's address and header in the console; neoteletext-web for the address parser, the channel address map, a proxy's address and the bytes a viewer-state key signs; neoteletext-input for the input records it encodes and the cursor records it checks; neoteletext-audio to tell the console that a packet carries sound; neoteletext-opus, which comes with that and of which nothing is called; and neoteletext-formats for the recognition of a file's format, which the broker runs in its own process to refuse a file that is not T42 or TTI before the core is given its bytes. It calls nothing else of those crates that reads a network or teletext format. The gate fails unless the core's dependency tree holds exactly those six engine crates.

An attacker in the interface. Every security property holds even if the interface runs an attacker's code, except the integrity of the trusted strip and of strip input, which the interface draws and sends. A test harness sends the trusted core 30,000 hostile messages built at the byte level and shows that it never panics, that no key reaches the interface, that no intent but strip input changes a tab's channel or a setting, and that every helper it starts is of an allowed kind.

Sleeping tabs. A channel's decoder runs only while its tab is awake: while it is the active tab, while its channel holds a push WebSocket, while its sound plays, and for 15 minutes after it was last shown. A tab restored with a session and not yet shown sleeps. What the trusted core gave a decoder is kept, up to 8 megabytes, and given to a new decoder when the tab wakes; a channel whose data grows beyond that stays awake. A fetcher runs while any tab it serves is open, asleep or not, and is stopped when the last of them leaves. The trusted core looks for tabs that may sleep at least once a minute.

A decoder's store. A decoder starts with room for 256 pages and sub-pages and says once when that room is full; the trusted core then starts it again with twice the room, up to 4,096, and gives it what the channel's decoder had been given.

Limits. The broker and the launcher are unconfined by design. The interface's window in its AppContainer on Windows has still to be checked by hand. Android and iOS are not built, and their sandboxes are their own.

15.3 Messages between the browser's processes

DOC-2265 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-681, REQ-682, REQ-683, REQ-684, REQ-685, REQ-686, REQ-687, REQ-688, REQ-2946, REQ-6980

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-681 One framed protocol (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-682 Every message is bounded (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-684 Every message is checked by the receiver (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-686 Message readers are fuzzed continuously (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-687 No interface request or key affects fetching, beyond the active tab's channel's wanted pages, sub-pages and selection, and the filmstrip's anonymous snapshots (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-688 Sender cleans untrusted text in messages (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2946 The fetcher takes only the listed kinds of message besides input messages, each naming its tab (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6980 One fetcher process serves every tab of one channel in one jar, and each message between the trusted core and a fetcher names its tab (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

The browser's processes (its processes and their sandboxes) speak one framed protocol, defined once in the browser's protocol crate, with the engine's framing: one byte naming the kind of message, a length of 32 bits, most significant byte first, and the payload. A process flushes its pipe once for each event it handles, not once for each message.

  • Bounded. Every message, and every field in it, has a fixed maximum size stated in code as a named constant. A message longer than its maximum is refused before its payload is read.
  • Checked by the receiver. The trusted core checks every message from every other process against the state it holds: a known channel, a known tab, sizes within their limits, a palette of at most 32 entries with every index within it, and page numbers from 100 to 8FF. A report of visible pages naming another channel's pages is filtered out, and a tab index out of range is ignored.
  • A fetcher's messages name their tab. A fetcher serves every tab of one channel in one jar, so every message between it and the trusted core, in either direction, is preceded by a 32-bit number, most significant byte first, naming the tab it is for. The trusted core chooses the number when it adds the tab with "tab opens", never reuses it within that process, and takes the tab away with "tab leaves"; these two carry nothing but the number, no address, host, path or page, so a tab added to a fetcher shows the channel the fetcher was started for and no other. A fetcher drops a message for a tab it does not hold, and ends at a "tab opens" for a number it already holds or beyond the most tabs the browser has. The trusted core takes a fetcher's message only for a tab it added to that process and has not taken away, so a message of a tab that has left is not listened to.
  • A malformed message closes its sender. Every reader stops at the first malformed message, or the first kind its sender may not send, and the sender is closed by killing it, never by waiting for it. Every tab it served shows that it failed. A decoder serves one tab, and a fetcher every tab of its channel in its jar; each such tab's page area says so until the tab is reloaded, and no new process is started for that tab until then. The sound helper and the phone keyboard serve every tab, and every tab open then says so in its strip until it is reloaded. A failed updater is shown in the updates panel. A broken interface ends the application.
  • Intents carry no address and touch no viewer key. What the interface sends for the page area, a page intent, never carries an address, never changes a security setting, and never reads, uses, makes, remembers or forgets a viewer key; viewer keys are the trusted core's alone (viewer state in the browser). A click on a cell may start a navigation the page started only to a link the trusted core holds in its own table of the page's links. Every other navigation comes from strip input, message kinds of their own that page intents never use.
  • No intent touches fetching, beyond the active tab's channel. No intent of the interface and no key, however received, causes, delays, reorders or gives priority to a network request, except in four ways, and none of them reaches any channel but the active tab's. First, input messages, bounded, go on the active tab's own push WebSocket while a page of that channel is open and its rule table reports them, and name no address, page file or connection. Second, for a static channel, the trusted core asks the active tab's fetcher for the page its address names when it is opened and for the pages the interface says it shows of that channel, in the page area and the wall's thumbnails, each by page number within the protocol's bounds, each once until it arrives or is refused, and only after the channel's bundle has settled; and for its contents file once when the tab comes to the front. Every such request is spaced by the engine's request rate, a report naming another channel's pages is dropped, and a page behind another tab is asked for from the trusted core's own record of that tab's address, never from a report of the interface. Third, while a page that is one of a set is open, the trusted core asks for the parts of its list of sub-pages and the sub-pages its list's rows, its scrolling and the sub-page shown call for, naming only the page open, a part number checked against the page's count and a sub-code it checked; the fetcher builds the file's name in its own channel. Fourth, the trusted core tells a live channel that agreed SELECT which page and sub-page its tab shows, once for each change of selection, from what it holds of the tab. Otherwise selecting a page shows only what the channel sends or the decoder holds.
  • Text is cleaned twice. Text that came from outside the browser is cleaned by the process that sends it and checked again by the process that receives it, which refuses text still holding a hidden character. This is met for the interface's messages.
  • Fuzzed. Every reader of these messages, of the trusted core, the interface, the sound helper, the broker and the updater, and every reader of the browser's own files, has a fuzz target, run at every push in the full gate.

15.4 How the browser fetches a channel

DOC-2271 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-689, REQ-690, REQ-691, REQ-692, REQ-693, REQ-694, REQ-696, REQ-697, REQ-698, REQ-699, REQ-700, REQ-701, REQ-702, REQ-703, REQ-704, REQ-911

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-690 A response is read only in its role (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-691 Trusted core passes teletext data unparsed to the decoder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-692 Descriptors, contents files and discovery are read in the fetcher (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-693 Discovery reads only link pointers (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-694 Discovery results are checked and shown to the viewer (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-696 Fetcher supported transports (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment); REQ-697 Plain connections are allowed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-698 The local network is refused by default (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-699 Fetcher refuses compressed responses (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-700 Every response has a maximum size (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-702 Minimal user agent on every request (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Each web channel has a fetcher process of its own (the browser's processes), which uses the engine's user agent for every request. What a receiver fetches, and in what order, is the protocol's (live and static channels, the files of a channel); this item says how the browser does it.

Only a channel's own resources. The browser fetches only resources in one of these roles: the channel's descriptor channel.ttx and its settings; its contents file; its teletext data (page files, bundles, the parts of a page's list of sub-pages, single sub-pages, and pushed pages); what the channel pushes on its own connection with a page, which includes a sub-page's ReGIS or NAPLPS picture and a page's sounds; and discovery, once it is built. No font is fetched: every page is drawn in the one font compiled into the engine. The updater's fetches of new versions are the only other requests. A response is read only by the reader of the role it was asked for in. Teletext data passes unread through the trusted core to the decoder of the channel that asked for it, which recognises and reads it. Descriptors and contents files are read by the engine's readers inside the fetcher, and the trusted core receives only typed, bounded results, which it checks again: a contents file gives at most 1,000 entries, each title and section name cleaned and bounded.

A channel's requests. When a channel opens, the fetcher asks first for channel.ttx. A live channel, one whose descriptor names a push connection, fetches nothing after it but that connection: its pages and its contents arrive on the connection. A static channel next fetches its whole bundle index.t42 when it has one, then its initial page, from the bundle when the bundle held it and otherwise from the page's own file. After that a static channel's page file is fetched when it is wanted, never merely because the contents file lists it. A page is wanted when a tab shows it (the page open, or else the page its address names, or else the channel's first page), when it is opened, and when the interface shows it of the active tab's channel, as the wall's thumbnails are; each is asked for once until it arrives or is refused. contents.txt is fetched only when the channel's listing is wanted, which is when its tab is in front of a window, since the page list, the contents view and the overview show it, and then once. Fetching proceeds at the engine's request rate through the agent's bounded queue, and what is held is bounded by the decoder's store, which forgets the oldest; since nothing is fetched merely because a channel has it, there is no separate maximum channel size.

Refreshing. A live channel's pages are refreshed by its push connection alone. A static channel's page on screen is asked for again, with a conditional request, at the interval its descriptor declares in refresh, a whole number of seconds from 5 to 86,400; a channel that declares none is never refreshed. The page on screen is that of every tab in front of a window: a tab on the wall or the contents view, and a tab behind another, ask for nothing.

Transports. The fetcher speaks HTTP version 1.1 and WebSocket, each with and without Transport Layer Security, which it does with rustls and Mozilla's root certificates. It has no HTTP version 2 and no server-sent events. Plain http and ws are allowed, and the strip says "Not secure" for as long as such a channel is shown; nothing falls back to them from https or wss. The live feed of the zxnet teletext viewer, which the engine can read, is not wired into the browser.

Bounds. Every response has the engine's maximum size, time to its first byte, total time and number of redirects. The fetcher asks for uncompressed responses (Accept-Encoding: identity) and refuses any response with another Content-Encoding, so it never decompresses anything. Addresses on this computer and on the local network are refused unless the viewer allows a particular address in the settings (what is refused).

What the fetcher says of itself. It sends no Referer header, and its User-Agent is the engine's minimal profile, NeoTeletext/ followed by the version that changes compatibility and the operating system's family in brackets, for example NeoTeletext/0.1 (macOS), on every request and on the push connection's upgrade.

Redirects. An HTTP redirect from a channel's address to another channel is followed as a web browser follows one, after a notice of one second that says where the tab is going, and the destination replaces the address that redirected in the tab's history. The one exception is a redirect from an encrypted address (https) to a plain one (http), within the channel or out of it: it is refused, first by the engine's agent and again by the trusted core whatever a fetcher says, and the channel fails to open with a sentence saying why (REQ-701 item 5, the engine's REQ-420).

Discovery is not built. As decided, it would read only Link response headers and link elements within the first 8,192 bytes of an HTML response to an address the viewer typed that did not answer with teletext, show each address found, checked by the address rules, as a result, and never move a tab by itself; a chosen result would be followed as any link to another channel is.

15.5 How the browser recognises teletext, and what it refuses

DOC-2273 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-706, REQ-707, REQ-708, REQ-709

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-706 Declared media type not used for acceptance (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-707 Decoder detects teletext response format from content (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-709 Detection is deterministic (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The browser decides what a response is by its content alone, in the decoder of the channel that asked for it (the browser's processes).

  • The declared type is not used. The Content-Type a server declares never decides whether a resource is accepted or refused: page bytes go to the decoder whatever type they were declared as (media types and checks).
  • Content decides. The decoder reads teletext data through the engine's content detection, its AutoReader, which recognises page files and recordings.
  • Detection is deterministic. What detection decides does not depend on how the network split the data.
  • What is not teletext is refused, never shown. A response detection does not recognise produces no page. The fetcher reports each file refused, by its role, with the real HTTP status and nothing the server wrote. The trusted core says so in the channel's log in its own words, and on the page area through the strip's "Failed": for channel.ttx for the whole tab, and for a page's file while it is the page open and has not arrived, so that a failed refresh disturbs nothing on screen. A status that a DENIED record carries reads as that record does (the DENIED record), so a static channel's missing page reads as a live channel's. A bundle or contents file that fails is missed rather than needed: the log alone says so.

15.6 Channels kept apart, and refused certificates

DOC-2274 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-711, REQ-712, REQ-713, REQ-714, REQ-715, REQ-716, REQ-717, REQ-718, REQ-719, REQ-721, REQ-723, REQ-2717, REQ-4848, REQ-6980

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-711 Origin is scheme, host and port (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-713 Channels never share data (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-714 Each tab has its own decoder, page store and, on a live channel, its own push WebSocket, which may share only its transport connection with the channel's other tabs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-718 Caches are keyed by channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-721 Certificate failures (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-723 A refused certificate is explained (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2717 On a live channel each tab has its own push WebSocket, decoder and page store, and may share only the transport connection that carries its WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-4848 A decoder, fetcher or cache serves only one channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6980 One fetcher process serves every tab of one channel in one jar, and each message between the trusted core and a fetcher names its tab (tested, not recorded as met on livedevelopment).

The channel is the unit of isolation. An origin is a scheme, a host and a port, as the engine defines it, and a channel is its origin together with its folder's path (a channel's address and boundary). Every tab, and every visit of a tab to a channel, is given a channel number of its own, and its decoder is keyed by it. A fetcher process is the channel's and the jar's: it serves every tab of one channel in one jar (an ordinary window's, or a private window's), and no tab of another channel or another jar, so no decoder, fetcher or cache ever serves two channels, and an ordinary tab and a private tab never share one. A channel's pages, viewer-state key, caches and history are never visible to, mixed with or sent to another channel's decoder or requests; a fetcher fetches only its own channel, so no page can cause a request carrying credentials to another origin. The decoder's page store and the trusted core's record of frames are keyed by channel, as any later cache must be.

Tabs on one channel. Tabs showing the same channel behave as tabs of one site in a web browser. They share the channel's one viewer-state key in the trusted core, so the channel's program sees the same viewer's handle on each tab's WebSocket; private tabs have keys of their own (connections and viewer state). Each tab has its own decoder and page store, never shared even with a tab on the same channel, and each tab on a live channel opens its own push WebSocket, which alone feeds that tab's store and carries that tab's one selection. The tabs of one jar on one channel are served by one fetcher process, in which each keeps its own user agent, selection and fetch connection, and where the channel's server offers HTTP/3 their push WebSockets share one connection to it, each a stream of its own (one WebSocket for each viewer's tab); a channel's tabs never share a connection with another channel's, even on the same host, so a server cannot link a viewer's channels by it. Closing, reconnecting or failing in one tab touches no other tab's WebSocket, decoder or store. When the shared connection itself is lost, every tab on it loses its WebSocket together, and each comes back for itself.

Keys stay in the trusted core. There are no cookies: no fetcher sends a Cookie header or reads a Set-Cookie. A channel's viewer-state key is made and held by the trusted core alone, for one exact channel identity, and never used for another channel, a folder inside it or another scheme or port. A fetcher passes the trusted core only a challenge its channel's server sent for one of its tabs and gets back only the proof to send; the trusted core takes the channel from the address of the tab the challenge names, a tab it added to that fetcher, never from the fetcher's message. How the browser keeps and shows these keys is described under viewer state in the browser.

The interface holds no channel data. The interface process holds no key and no storage of any kind; it writes no file, and it drops the image of every page its layout no longer shows, so it keeps a channel's pages only while that channel is shown.

Certificates. A Transport Layer Security certificate that fails its checks against Mozilla's root certificates ends the handshake and stops the navigation, with no way for the viewer to go on. The tab's page area then shows the certificate-error screen in place of the channel's pages: the host as the strip shows it, never a name taken from the certificate; what failed, in the trusted core's words, chosen from a fixed list by the kind of failure; that there is no way past it; and the buttons Try again, Go back (when the tab has history) and Close tab, with nothing that opens the channel anyway. The strip marks the channel refused while the screen shows, and the screen goes when the channel's contents next arrive or the tab goes elsewhere. A certificate refused on the shared HTTP/3 connection is not shown on its own: the tab's own HTTP/1.1 connection, opened in its place, meets the same certificate and is refused as above.

15.7 A tab's address, its history and redirects

DOC-2278 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-724, REQ-725, REQ-726, REQ-1686, REQ-1690, REQ-1712

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-724 One navigation history per tab (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-725 User-started and page-started navigations are distinguished (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-726 Trusted strip shows the committed address (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1690 A tab's address names the selected page and sub-page, or the wall, in the URL map's forms (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1712 A redirect enters a tab's Back list by Chrome's rules, per page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

One history a tab. The trusted core keeps one flat list of the places each tab has been, which Back and Forward walk.

Who started a navigation. A navigation the viewer starts in the trusted strip (a typed address, a bookmark, Back, Forward, Home, a new tab) and one a page starts (a Fastext key, a link in a page, a redirect, a discovery result) are recorded as such in the tab's history. Links in pages, and links and Fastext keys to another channel, are recorded as started by the page. No rule yet treats the two differently.

The address names what is on screen. Once a tab has arrived at a channel, its address always names that channel and the page and sub-page the tab has selected, or the channel's wall when it has selected none, in the forms of the URL map (the places of a channel, normalising an address). The address field, the bookmark star, Reload, a copied address, the tab's tip, the saved window and history therefore all agree with what is on screen. Every address is written and read in one place in the browser, native/core/src/address.rs, which reads every http and https address through the engine's reader of the map. The strip shows the committed address until a new place commits, and an address that is refused leaves it unchanged.

Leaving the channel by a redirect. When a redirect takes a tab out of its channel, whether an HTTP redirect or a REDIRECT record naming another channel (the REDIRECT record), the page area is cleared and shows "Redirecting to:" with the destination's whole address, wrapped and centred, for one second before the tab moves. The text is made smaller, down to 5 points, so that an address of the full 8,000 octets is shown complete. Full screen ends for the notice, and anything that replaces the tab's channel in that second drops the waiting redirect.

Where a program's redirect goes in the history. When a channel's program redirects a tab, to a page of the same channel or to another channel, the trusted core places the destination in the tab's Back list by the rules a web browser such as Chrome follows, page by page: a redirect that answers the viewer's input adds an entry; a redirect that comes before the page drew replaces the page's entry; a redirect that comes after the page drew adds an entry and marks the page it left, so that Back passes over it. An HTTP redirect from a server keeps its own rule: the destination replaces the address that redirected.

15.8 How the browser draws a page

DOC-2279 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-730, REQ-731, REQ-732, REQ-733, REQ-734, REQ-735, REQ-736, REQ-737, TODO-738, REQ-801, REQ-905, REQ-1645, REQ-1770

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-731 Trusted core validates every frame (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-733 Unchanged frames are not sent again (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-734 Interface reports visible pages (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-735 Whole-frame replacement (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-737 Pages are scaled and pixel-shape corrected when drawn, not re-rendered (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); TODO-738 Measure frame size and encoding time on real channels (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-801 No teletext underline (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-905 Page palette is the Colour Map of Presentation Levels 2.5 and 3.5 plus the receiver's eight colours, rendered exactly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1645 The browser MUST draw a page in an area of 40 columns by 25 rows at every presentation level (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1770 Every page is drawn in the engine's compiled Noto Teletext font, with no font choice (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A page travels from the decoder to the screen as an image, never as anything the interface interprets.

  1. The decoder draws. The channel's decoder renders a page with the engine into 8-bit palette indices at the page's own raster of 480 by 500 dots, with a palette of at most 40 colours: the page's Colour Map of 32 and the receiver's own eight, which every frame carries (cells and rows of pixels). The page area is always 40 columns by 25 rows at every presentation level: side panels are never supported, so nothing widens it, and no input column above 39 is ever sent (the cell grid). Every page is drawn in Noto Teletext, the one font compiled into the engine, with no choice of font (the one compiled font), and the decoder decodes the engine's extended character sets. Teletext's underline is not drawn on any page; separated mosaics are drawn as before.
  2. Only what is seen. The interface reports which pages its layout puts on screen, and the trusted core has only those rendered and sent, of the active channel alone.
  3. The trusted core checks and encodes. It checks every frame: a known channel and page, the exact raster size, a palette of at most 40 entries and every index within it. It encodes the frame in the browser's own frame form: the palette, the screen colour, and the dots raw, in runs, or as changes against the frame of the same page the interface holds, whichever is smallest; it sends nothing when the frame is identical to the last one sent for that page. Measured on 800 pages of a recorded channel, runs encode in about a tenth of the time of the Portable Network Graphics images used before, and the changes that flashing makes are about a seventh of such an image's bytes.
  4. The interface reads and shows. The interface reads only frames in that form: the dots filling exactly 480 by 500, at most 40 colours, every index within the palette, each count bounded before use. Each new frame replaces the page's whole image, and the previous one stays on screen until the new one is read completely.

Flash. The decoder draws flash at the engine's timing: the Level 1 Flash attribute at the SAA5050's rate of 960 milliseconds on and 320 off, at every level, and the Additional Flash Functions at one second in twelve parts (flash, Additional Flash Functions). Only a shown page that has flashing cells is drawn again for flash, only when its phase changes, and by the decoder's own clock; otherwise a shown page is drawn again only when the engine reports that it changed, or that data every page may draw from changed.

Size and shape. Pages are scaled, and their pixels' shape corrected, by the interface when it draws them, never by rendering again at another size. The View menu has an item that turns the 4:3 aspect correction on and off. While it is on, every page is drawn 16/13 wider wherever it is drawn: alone, on the wall, zoomed, in the preview and in full screen; while it is off, a page keeps its raster's proportions. A press on a page finds the same cell, control or link either way, and the channel never learns the setting.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.2 Spacing attributes (Rests on: the Flash spacing attribute, whose timing the decoder follows); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3 Non-spacing attributes and additional characters (Rests on: the underline attribute, which the browser does not draw)

15.9 What the interface process may receive and do

DOC-2281 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-741, REQ-742, REQ-743, REQ-744, REQ-745, REQ-746

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-741 No network byte reaches the interface process (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-742 Page text is drawn only as text (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-743 No debugging interface in release builds (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-744 Dropped files go to the trusted core (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-745 No unsafe code (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-746 The interface process ends on a malformed message (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The interface process draws every window and passes on what the viewer does, and it is built on the assumption that it could be running an attacker's code (the browser's processes).

  • No network byte reaches it. It receives pages only as images the trusted core encoded (how the browser draws a page), and text only as cleaned, bounded text the trusted core sends. No byte received from the network or read from a file reaches it.
  • Text stays text. Text that came from a page, a channel or a server is drawn only as runs of text, never interpreted.
  • Dropped files go to the trusted core. Files dropped on a window are opened by the trusted core through a decoder; the interface never reads them. Linux takes no drop.
  • No debugging interface. A release build holds no debugging interface reachable from outside the process.
  • No unsafe code. The interface, like every crate of the browser, forbids unsafe code in its own source, with three exceptions, each denying it everywhere else and saying at each unsafe block why it is sound: the dock-menu crate, whose macOS module reaches AppKit through the Objective-C runtime; the web-opener crate, whose Windows module calls the shell's ShellExecuteW to open a web address, and SystemParametersInfoW to read whether the viewer turned the system's animation effects off; and the confine crate, whose modules make the operating-system calls that confine a process and pass it its pipes.
  • A broken message ends it. The interface ends at the first malformed message from the trusted core rather than try to continue.

15.10 The trusted strip and the address field

DOC-2282 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-747, REQ-748, REQ-749, REQ-750, REQ-751, REQ-752

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-747 Every window has a trusted strip (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-748 What the trusted strip holds (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-750 Trusted strip visible in every layout except page-only full screen (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-751 Untrusted text is cleaned before display (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-752 Reload opens the active tab's channel afresh (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Every window has a trusted strip: the browser's own area, drawn by the interface in that window outside the page area, never a window of its own, and showing only the state the trusted core sends. Its input reaches the trusted core as strip input, message kinds that page intents never use (messages between the processes), so nothing a page does can act as the viewer's own choice in the strip.

What it holds. The address field, the channel's identity, whether the channel is encrypted ("Not secure" when it is not), Back, Forward, Reload and Home in that order, the bookmark star, the web-browser prompt that comes before a web: link leaves for the system's web browser, and every setting that affects security, which can be changed only in the strip's settings panel.

Always visible. The strip is visible in every layout, the zoomed page included, except the full screen of the page alone. There it comes back when the pointer reaches the top edge or a key the browser keeps for itself is pressed; full screen ends before anything leaves the channel; and while keys go to a channel, a trusted badge outside the page says so.

The address field. When it is not being edited, it shows the address as the address rules format it, with the host emphasised. When it is edited, its text is sent on Enter to the trusted core, which opens it or says why not. Addresses with a user name or a hidden character are refused, and internationalised host names are refused until they can be shown safely. The design is to hold and show such a name only in its ASCII form, each label beginning xn-- and its Punycode (RFC 5890, RFC 3492), never in Unicode, so that no letter of another script can imitate a familiar host, and to refuse a host given with any character beyond ASCII with a sentence telling the viewer how to type it; that is not built. Why an address was refused is written to the log; showing it in the strip is not built.

Untrusted text is cleaned. Text from pages and channels, such as titles, section names, notices and addresses, has its control characters, bidirectional controls and zero-width characters removed, and is cut to a fixed length, before it is shown anywhere. The address editor never inserts a hidden character.

Reload. The Reload button, Command-R on macOS and Control-R elsewhere, opens the active tab's channel afresh, with a new decoder and fetcher reading its pages again, at the tab's place in its history, which does not change. Reload is strip input carrying nothing: the trusted core decides what is opened, and a reload counts as no visit in history.

15.11 Tabs, windows and menus

DOC-2283 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-753, REQ-757, REQ-758, REQ-759, REQ-760, REQ-765, REQ-766, REQ-767, REQ-770, REQ-771, REQ-6640, REQ-6641

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-753 Tabs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-758 Internal pages (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-759 Developer tools (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-760 Each window has one trusted strip (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-765 Tabs are reordered by dragging (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-767 Keys choose tabs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-770 The version on the tab strip (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-771 The browser's icon (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Tabs. The interface draws a tab strip with a close button on each tab and a new-tab button; the list and order of the tabs, opening and closing them, and restoring them at start are decided by the trusted core. A tab is titled by its channel's name from its channel.ttx, shown as plain text, or by its address's host when the channel gives no name. The middle button closes the tab under it. Every tab is the same width however many there are. A tab pressed and moved more than 4 points is dragged, a mark showing where it will go, and let go it moves there, by strip input the trusted core carries out, keeping the active tab active and saving the session; let go where it started, or after Escape, nothing changes. When the tabs do not fit, the strip shows those that do, always with the active tab, sliding to it when it changes, and a count of the rest. Once the pointer has rested on the tabs for 300 milliseconds, or at once when the count is pressed, a filmstrip slides out from under the strip: one row of still pictures of every tab, taken when the viewer last left each tab, each captioned with its title and page number, which the wheel slides left and right; pressing a picture chooses its tab, and resting on one shows its close and mute buttons. It closes 300 milliseconds after the pointer leaves the strip and the filmstrip, on Escape, or when a tab is chosen. Command-1 to Command-8 choose the first eight tabs and Command-9 the last, and Command-Option-Left and Right the tab before and after, round the ends; away from macOS Control and Alt take the place of Command and Option.

Windows. One interface process draws every window, and each window has its own trusted strip drawn from what the trusted core sent for it. A tab moves between windows only as strip input the trusted core carries out, whether chosen from the menu or dragged off the strip into a window of its own or onto another window's strip, and a channel's frames go only to the window showing its tab. A window's helpers, a decoder for each of its tabs' channels and a fetcher for each web channel, are started when the window opens and ended when it closes, and a private window's helpers are never given another window's channel data.

The version and the icon. Every window's tab strip shows at its right end, before the window's own buttons where the browser draws them, the version the trusted core reports followed by the word BETA, for example "0.1.0 BETA", as a label that does nothing when pressed and is left out where there is not room for it beside one tab, the count and the new-tab button. The owner's art, native/icon/neoteletext-icon.png, is the browser's icon wherever a desktop shows one, every size made from that one file by nearest neighbour and never smoothed, and no program reads the file while running.

Menus. On Windows and Linux, where browsers show no menu bar, the menu button's menu holds New tab, New window, New private tab, New private window, Move tab to new window, Reopen closed tab, History, Bookmarks, the bookmarks bar, Bookmark this page, the phone keyboard, the developer console, the remote control and Settings, each with its shortcut where it has one. Menu items and buttons send the same intents. The native macOS menu bar (NeoTeletext, File, Edit, View, History, Bookmarks and Window) is not built; on macOS the menu button serves.

The browser's own pages and panels. Bookmarks, history and settings are shown from data the trusted core supplies, and settings that affect security are changed only in the trusted strip. The developer tools are the console docked in the window, described under settings, the console and proxies in this part; they show the channel's packets, pages, network requests and notices as text and never a cookie.

15.12 The page area: the page alone, the wall of pages, the overview, the lists and full screen

DOC-2285 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-754, REQ-762, REQ-768, REQ-769, REQ-772, REQ-1558, REQ-1559, REQ-1758

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-754 Page walls and transitions (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-762 Updated pages are shown (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-768 The teletext page alone, full screen (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-769 The overview has a close button that hides it (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1558 Each tab's decoder caches page source as packets as last received, without images (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1559 The wall of pages shows at most 128 tiles (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1758 Page Up, Page Down, Up and Down work in the pages list and the sub-pages list (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Below the trusted strip a window holds the banks of magazines, the pages list and the sub-pages list, the page area and the overview of all pages, with transitions between its views. When the platform's preference asks for reduced motion, every move of the wall (its width, hover, zoom and slide) takes no time, and the docked remote takes its place without sliding. On macOS and Windows the preference is read whenever a window opens or gains the focus. On Linux, where the confined interface reaches no session bus, it is read from the desktop portal's settings once, when the browser starts, so a change is followed at the next start.

The page alone. The page area shows only the current page, the one chosen or else the bank's first, as large as the area fits it at its own proportions and centred, and everything that works on an open page works there. Every window starts this way. The browser's modifier with G (Command-G on macOS, Control-Shift-G elsewhere) toggles to the wall of pages, with its bar of page sizes, and back.

The wall of pages. The wall shows at most 128 tiles, each a page or a sub-page, drawn from the tab's cache of page source at the tile's size. A visible tile with no entry in the cache is filled as any page is loaded: by SELECT for its page and sub-code, 3F7F for a page alone, and the channel's answer (selecting a page). Only tiles on screen are filled, one at a time in the order they appear, each waiting for its frame or the channel's limit before the next, and each held to the input protocol's rate (the input count and the rate). When every visible tile has an entry, or the wall closes, the tab selects page 0 while the wall stays shown, so no page is live. Scrolling fills the newly visible tiles the same way. Opening a page from the wall selects it and shows it at once from its cache entry while the answer arrives. No input goes to the channel while the wall is shown.

The cache of page source. Each tab's decoder keeps, in memory, a record of which pages and sub-pages stand in the engine's store and when each was stored: at most 128 entries, keyed by page number and sub-code, fed by every frame the tab receives, whole or changed rows alike. When the cache is full the entry least recently drawn or shown goes first. An entry older than 24 hours, measured on a monotonic clock, is dropped at the moment it is about to be drawn or shown, and loaded again as any page is; nothing scans the cache in the background. The cache is never written to disk and ends with its tab. It is a feature of the decoder, page-cache, on by default and compiled out of microcontroller builds, where the wall fills every tile each time it is shown.

Updated pages. When a page the channel already delivered arrives again with different content, the window shows that it changed, in the overview, the pages list and the page area, and how long ago.

The overview. The overview of all pages has a close button at its top right corner, with its fold button to the left of it; the View menu shows and hides it. Every window starts with it off, and an address naming a channel's contents shows it. While it is off or folded it keeps no animation and asks for no frames.

The lists. In the pages list and the sub-pages list, Up and Down move one row, and Page Up and Page Down move by one list-height, overlapping by one row; each selects the row it lands on, opening its page or showing its sub-page, and none wraps round at the ends. A key that lands on a sub-page not yet fetched moves there and fetches it. A click on either list gives it the keys until a click elsewhere or Escape, with a ring round the list to show it.

Full screen. A window with an open page can show that page alone, filling the display at its own proportions, in the page's screen colour, with no strip, tabs or panels. It is entered by the system's full-screen key (Control-Command-F on macOS, F11 elsewhere), the menu, or a double click on the page, and left by Escape while keys do not go to a channel, by the full-screen key at any time, and whenever anything needs the window. Page keys, Fastext, links within the channel, sound and typing into a channel all work in it, and the strip comes down from the top edge (the trusted strip).

15.13 Text fields, the clipboard, tips and accessibility in the browser

DOC-2287 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-761, REQ-763, REQ-764, REQ-2019

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-761 Screen reader support for the window on every desktop (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-2019 Every text field takes its platform's keys for moving, selecting and deleting (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Text fields. Every text field the browser draws, now and later (the address field, each field of the bookmark star's popover, and the fields of the history, console, bookmarks and settings panels and of the list of channels that know the viewer), takes the keys its platform's own text fields take for moving, selecting and deleting, and the mouse as text fields take it; with Shift, each moving key selects as it goes. A new field has all of this by being a field, with nothing written for it. The platform rules for Windows and Linux are tested as logic on macOS and have not been tried on those desktops.

The clipboard and input methods. Every field supports cut, copy, paste and select all through the system clipboard, by the Edit menu on macOS and by the browser's modifier with X, C, V and A everywhere; a paste is taken as typing is. Text composed by an input method is inserted when it is committed; showing it while it is being composed is not built.

Tips. Every control drawn as an icon, a symbol or text that may be cut short has a tip: a label naming it, what it does, and its shortcut on the platform where it has one. A tip shows when the pointer has rested on its control for half a second, beside the pointer and inside the window, over everything else; a press puts it away until the pointer leaves the control, and leaving puts it away. Tips are the interface's own words, except a tab's title and address and a bookmark's name, which are shown as the cleaned text they are; a tab's tip shows its title and, on the line under it, its address. While a panel or list is open over the window, only its tips and the strip's show. A link's tip is its complete address (controls and links under the pointer).

Accessibility is not built. The window is to be usable with a screen reader on every desktop, through AccessKit or the platform's own interface, with each page labelled with its cleaned text and its links in the tree; none of this exists yet, so screen readers see nothing of the window.

15.14 Installing, updating and removing the browser

DOC-2288 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-773, REQ-774, REQ-775, REQ-776, REQ-777, REQ-778, REQ-779, REQ-780

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-773 Two independent signatures (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-774 Installation without an administrator (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-775 Supported systems (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-776 Newer version offered, nothing downloaded or staged until accepted (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-777 The updater is confined (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-778 Health check gates commit of a trial version (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-779 Uninstall removes the browser's files (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-780 The release's identity is built in (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Where it installs. The browser installs in the user's own folders with no administrator: per user on Windows (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\NeoTeletext) and Linux (~/.local/share/neoteletext), and on macOS in /Applications for an administrator and ~/Applications otherwise. Nothing it installs needs elevation to update.

Supported systems. Releases are to start on macOS 11 and later; Windows 10 version 1703 and later; and Linux with the C library 2.28 or later, kernel 6.10 with Landlock, and unprivileged user namespaces allowed for the browser's programs, which on a system that restricts them, such as Ubuntu from 24.04, means its AppArmor profile, neoteletext.apparmor, installed once by an administrator. The profile ships with every Linux version and --install says how to install it. The oldest of these systems have not been run.

Updates are offered, never imposed. The browser offers a newer version once in the strip, and in the settings panel while the offer stands, and downloads and stages nothing until the viewer accepts. A staged version starts at the browser's next start, never by restarting it under the viewer. "Check for updates", on by default, stops the updater from starting at all when it is off.

Two independent signatures. A version runs only after the updater has verified it against The Update Framework's metadata and the launcher has verified that the platform's pinned signer signed it: the macOS bundle's designated requirement; on Windows every program's Authenticode signer's public key and the release key's signature of the manifest; on Linux the release key's signature of the manifest and of every file. The launcher also finds the folder holding exactly the files the release's manifest names, each of its length and SHA-256, and a version newer than the current one and not known to be bad. What a build trusts for updates (the update host, The Update Framework's first root and the platform signers) is fixed when it is built, and nothing read while it runs can change it. Until the owner's certificates and release key exist, this is met only with test signers.

The updater is confined. It runs confined as the other helpers are, every layer required: connections to one port only, the update host's or the viewer's proxy's, the system's name resolution, and its staging folder written; no other file written, no program started, and no secret of the viewer's held. Its folder and port are the broker's rules, never the trusted core's word. On Windows its container cannot be told a port, and the host is pinned by Transport Layer Security instead.

The health check decides. A trial version is kept only when, within 30 seconds of its start, its window's first frame has reached the screen, its settings were read or found absent, and no decoder ended in error. Its broker must say started within 5 minutes and be healthy within 47 seconds of that; one that misses either deadline is ended with every process it started. A start that missed the health deadline, or ended badly after started, is a failed start; one that never said started is counted apart, and three of those roll the version back; a clean quit before health is not counted.

Removing it. Removing the browser removes its programs, its update files and its menu entries, and asks before removing the viewer's settings, bookmarks, history and remembered viewer keys.

15.15 Local files, and links and files opened from outside the browser

DOC-2290 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-722, REQ-1671, REQ-1672, REQ-1673, REQ-1698, REQ-1699, REQ-1700, REQ-1701, REQ-1702, REQ-1703

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1671 The browser MUST register the neottx:// scheme with macOS, Windows and Linux (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1672 A neottx:// link from outside opens its one wrapped http or https address at once in a new active tab of the most recent normal window, and carries nothing else (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1673 Windows registrations pass a link or file name only after a marker (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1698 The broker reads a file for the trusted core only when it is granted, named to the broker itself, or declared by the interface within DECLARED_FOR (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1700 A file dropped on the page area opens in new tabs and replaces no tab (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1701 Text beginning with a path form is a path (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1702 A restored file tab is read through its grant (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1703 A file opened from the operating system opens in a new active tab of the most recently active normal window (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A local file is a channel of its own. Each local file opened is its own channel, with no viewer state and no fetcher, read by the trusted core through the broker and decoded by its own decoder; it has no push connection, so no channel can ask for state there (viewer state in the browser). The browser opens T42 and TTI files and refuses every other format with the sentence a viewer sees for anything that is not teletext, "not a channel this browser can open", which is also what a missing file, a secret and a file nobody granted get. A file is loaded at once, with no broadcast pace, within its bounds: at most 64 megabytes, or 4,096 page files for a folder of TTI files, which is a channel too. A link from a file to one of its own pages opens at once; a link to a channel goes there at once, as any link to another channel does; a web: link goes through the web-browser prompt (redirects, local files and links from outside).

Only what the viewer gave. The broker, the one process not confined, reads a file channel or a bookmarks file for the trusted core only when one of these holds: the viewer chose it in the broker's file dialog, or it was read before and its grant still stands, the grant recording the file's canonical path and its identity (device and inode on macOS and Linux, volume and file index on Windows), so a file replaced since is refused; it was named on the broker's own command line or handed over by a second start; or the interface declared it, on a channel of its own to the broker that the trusted core never sees, within 10 seconds of the read: a dropped file, a file macOS asked the application to open, or a typed path or file:// address. Grants are kept for restoring sessions, history and bookmarks in grants.txt, in a folder beside the settings folder and outside the one folder the trusted core writes, at most 4,096 of them, read strictly. A private window keeps no grant beyond its run.

Open File. On macOS the File menu's "Open File…", Command-O; on Windows and Linux Control-O. The platform's own dialog, with no type filter and one selection, is shown by a small program, neoteletext-chooser, which the broker starts for each request and which ends when the choice is made; the browser keeps working meanwhile, and at most one dialog is open. The chosen file opens in the current tab as if its address had been typed. "Open Folder…", Command-Option-O on macOS and Control-Alt-O elsewhere, chooses a folder of TTI files. Importing bookmarks uses the same chooser.

Drops and typed paths. Dropping files on the page, the tab strip or the address field behaves as in Chrome on macOS and Windows: the interface never reads the file, but declares one drop's files to the broker and sends the trusted core one intent. Linux takes no drop. On macOS and Linux, text beginning with / or ~ typed in the address field is a path, and on Windows C:\ and \\server\; a typed path becomes a file:// address without any check that the file exists, and while not being edited the field shows the path with a "File" label beside it. File visits are kept in history, offered as suggestions and restored with the session in normal windows, each read again through its grant; private windows keep and restore nothing.

Files from the system. A file opened by double click, Open With, a drop on the Dock icon or the command line opens in a new active tab at the end of the strip in the most recently active normal window, or a new window if there is none, never a private one; its window comes to the front. The macOS bundle declares .tti; the Windows and Linux installers register .tti, with the Linux media type text/x-teletext-tti. One opening takes at most 16 files. A browser already running receives what a second start names, over a local socket or named pipe the confined processes cannot reach, and checks it again from the start.

The neottx:// scheme. Installing the browser registers one URL scheme with the operating system, neottx, and nothing else, and removing the browser removes it. A link such as neottx://https://app.neottx.com/home/302 carries one whole address of the URL map: the prefix is removed, matched without regard to case, and what remains is read by the same strict rules as every other address. It must be http or https; every other scheme, a fragment, a % in the host, and anything over 8,000 octets are refused, and a non-ASCII host must arrive in its xn-- form. A link carries no switch, setting, private-window flag, profile or action. It opens at once, with no question, in a new active tab of the most recently active normal window, recorded as coming from outside and trusted no more than a link. At most five such links open in any ten seconds, and those beyond are dropped, not queued; a refused link opens nothing, is logged by its reason, and tells the sender nothing. A link inside a page whose target begins neottx:// is not a link. On Windows a launch from a registered link or .tti file is refused unless exactly one argument follows its marker, and every other switch is ignored, so that no link or file name can add command-line switches.

Limits. Much of this has been run only on macOS and Linux and by tests; the Windows code for registrations, the chooser and drops, and opening from an installed bundle, have not been run (they wait on an installed build and the Windows virtual machine).

15.16 How the browser is built and checked

DOC-2292 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-781, REQ-782, REQ-783, REQ-785, REQ-786

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-781 One check script runs every named check (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-782 Strict compilation and linting (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-786 Broadcast content is never committed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

One check script. The browser is checked by one local script, scripts/check.sh, which git hooks run in three tiers and which may not be bypassed. The commit gate, before each commit, checks that the staged code compiles clean: every engine dependency, path and lockfile entry against the engine's one pin, the codec and release-version checks, the lockfiles, formatting, the lists of constructs that may not panic, and Clippy, for the workspaces native and native/tuf; it refuses to run while a part it reads has changes not staged, so what it checks is what is committed. The push gate, before a push of any branch but main, adds Clippy in every feature shape, the check of the dependency trees (the trusted core's engine crates, no interpreter in any program, no toolkit under an engine crate), Clippy for the microcontroller targets, cargo deny's advisory check, and the tests, listing the tests that are ignored. The full gate, before a push to main, adds the engine's unsafe-code check, the engine's own full gate at the pinned commit, documentation tests, release tests, tests with links compiled out, the whole cargo deny check, cargo-machete, the release scripts' identity check and fuzzing, with the Linux build and tests on a Linux host alongside. Nothing is skipped: a missing tool, a tool at another version, or an unreachable host fails the run. The compiler, its targets and every tool are pinned. Until the first release, Windows is not a stage of the script: it is checked by hand in a virtual machine, and the result is recorded with its date in the state of each requirement it shows.

Strict compilation. Rust code builds with unsafe code forbidden (but for the three crates named in what the interface process may do), Clippy's pedantic group enabled and warnings treated as errors; a suppression is narrow, at its site, with a written reason. Every public item is documented, and every crate that reads input from outside its process also denies every construct that can panic.

Dependencies. Lockfiles are committed and their changes reviewed, every dependency pinned to an exact version. cargo deny checks the RustSec advisories in both workspaces at every push, and its whole check, of licences, bans, sources and advisories, in the full gate; cargo audit, which reads the same advisory database, is not run. An advisory may be ignored only narrowly, in deny.toml, with its reason and the owner's decision. Every library compiled into the browser is under a permissive licence and approved by the owner; system libraries linked while running may be LGPL ones linked dynamically and not shipped.

Spoofing review. Every new layout, zoom level or full-screen mode is reviewed to confirm that the trusted strip stays visible and that nothing in the page area can be mistaken for it, and the review is recorded in the browser's security analysis. Nothing a channel controls, and no panel of the browser's, is drawn over the strip, except in full screen with the strip hidden. The strip is drawn after the page area, so only what is drawn after it could cover it.

No broadcast material. Teletext recordings, and the sites built from them for development, are broadcast material and are never committed: they stay in folders git ignores.

15.17 The platforms the browser runs on

DOC-2293 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-787, REQ-788, REQ-789, REQ-790

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-787 Desktop platforms (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-788 Phones (after the first version): decoder isolation per platform (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-790 No graphics processor needed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Desktops. The browser is built and run on macOS, on Linux (tested under X11) and on Windows 11, with every process confined, sound, sessions restored, remembered viewer keys kept and installation and updates working on each. The full gate builds and tests on Linux; Windows is built and tested by hand. Not yet the same everywhere: the Dock menu's counterparts on Windows and Linux, and the XDG Desktop Portal on Linux for handing addresses to the web browser.

No graphics processor needed. Every target draws on the processor alone, with vello_cpu and softbuffer, and links no graphics library; a graphics processor may make drawing faster but is never required. On Linux the browser has drawn under Xvfb, a display with no graphics processor.

Phones are not built. When they are, every requirement not tied to separate processes still applies, and each phone's sandbox is required whole, as the desktops' are. On Android the trusted core is to run in the main application process, the fetcher in a separate service process, the decoder in an isolated service process with a seccomp filter, and the interface as the application's activity, with the sound inside it. On iOS, where there is one application process holding the trusted core, the fetcher, the interface and the sound, the decoder is to have a wall of its own by running inside the wasmi WebAssembly interpreter.

Microcontrollers are not built. The interface's core builds without the standard library and draws through the microcontroller back end, draw-embedded, and a test draws the window into a 1024 by 600 display in memory. The push gate builds and lints both, warnings as errors, for the Arm Cortex-M0 and RISC-V RV32IMC targets, with every optional area and with none. A microcontroller build is to keep pages, page-number and Fastext keys, flash and a simple wall of pages, and to have its own security analysis; no such build of the whole browser exists, and no firmware is linked, because no board is chosen.

15.18 Sound in the browser

DOC-2295 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-791, REQ-792, REQ-793, REQ-794, REQ-795, REQ-796, REQ-797, REQ-798, REQ-799, REQ-800

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-791 Sound follows the engine's audio profile (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-792 Sound is read only in the decoder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-793 Every tab is heard (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-794 Every voice operation is checked twice (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-795 The opened page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-796 Sound output through the engine mixer and cpal (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-797 A tab shows its sound and mute state (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-798 Mute every tab (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-799 The Dock menu (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-800 Live sounds (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A channel carries its sound on EN 300 708 independent data lines of data channel 12 (data channel 12), and the browser plays it as the engine's audio profile says, adding no rule of its own about what plays (what a receiver does with sound): the latest command of each channel wins, and a page's sounds play while that page is open, that is, the page zoomed on the wall or else the page chosen by number or in the list.

Where sound is read. Sound packets are read, put back together, stored and decoded only in the channel's decoder process. The trusted core does not parse them. The sound helper, a confined process of its own, receives only 16-bit samples and voice operations the trusted core has checked. Every voice operation is bounded by the protocol between the processes (a voice channel of 0 to 3, a gain of 0 to 100, a fade of 5 to 10,000 milliseconds, a sample rate of the profile, at most two minutes a sound and 32,768 samples a message) and checked again by the trusted core: a sound must be defined before it is filled or started, samples must lie within it, a live sound takes only its next samples, and a channel may hold at most 32 megabytes of samples in the sound helper, every channel together 64 megabytes, a live sound counting as two seconds at 48 kilohertz. Only the trusted core may tell the sound helper to forget a channel's sounds or mute it.

Every tab is heard. The trusted core passes on every channel's sound tagged with its channel, and the sound helper plays each channel through its own mixer, so a background tab keeps playing, as in a web browser, with the page it had open. When a channel's decoder is gone, the sound helper is told to forget that channel's sounds.

Live sounds. A live sound plays as its blocks arrive, from the newest block when its playing starts, and fades out two seconds after its last block. Each decoder keeps the clock of its live sounds itself, waking only when the audio receiver says it next needs a tick.

Output. The sound helper mixes with the engine's mixer, neoteletext-audio-mix, and plays through the operating system's output device with cpal (Core Audio on macOS, WASAPI on Windows, ALSA on Linux), rendering on the audio thread without allocating. The device runs only while a channel sounds. With no output device, or no sound library on the system, the browser runs silent.

Controls. Page sounds are on by default. The settings panel has a setting that silences every page's sound and a master volume from 0 to 100, applied in the sound helper's mixer. A tab whose channel plays sound shows a speaker before its close button, and a muted tab a crossed-out speaker; a click on it mutes or unmutes the tab without selecting it, and a tab's mute follows it to the next channel it shows. The window's title is the selected tab's, followed by "Audio playing" or "Muted" while it sounds. A button beside the menu mutes every tab, or unmutes every tab once all are muted. On macOS the Dock icon's menu lists the tabs, the selected one ticked and those playing or muted marked with a speaker, then "Mute All Tabs" or "Unmute All Tabs"; choosing a tab selects it.
