Windows' jump list and Linux's launcher menus are not built.

Rests on: EN 300 708 V1.2.1 clause 6 Independent Data Lines (IDL) (Rests on: the independent data lines of data channel 12 that carry a channel's sound)

15.19 Links in the browser

DOC-2298 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-755, REQ-802, REQ-803, REQ-804, REQ-805, REQ-806, REQ-807, REQ-808, REQ-809, REQ-810, REQ-811, REQ-812, REQ-813, REQ-1660, REQ-1670

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-755 Clicks on pages are cell clicks (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-802 Links are drawn by the browser (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-803 The trusted core decides every link (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-804 Page numbers in the text are links (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-805 Links are classified from their targets (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-806 The destination is shown in the strip, told apart from the address (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-807 A click follows what the user saw (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-808 A web: link goes through the web-browser prompt (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-809 The hand-off to the system's web browser (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-811 The web-browser prompt never takes the keyboard focus by itself (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-812 The link-target parser contains no panicking constructs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-813 Controls shown only while keys go to the channel, with the hand pointer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1660 Resting the pointer on a link shows a popover with its complete destination (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1670 Following a link or coloured key to another channel goes there at once, in the same tab, with no question, and Back returns (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

What a link is. Only what a page declares is a link: its Fastext links, the runs of text its TTI Link Extension's LT lines mark, at most eight, and its LK numbers, which change what typing a number does and draw nothing (the TTI Link Extension, the LINKS record). Page numbers in a page's text are not links: the rule that once made them links has been withdrawn, so "Sport 101" on a page is text. The channel's descriptor may add aliases and services, which also count as links.

The trusted core decides every link. It takes the candidates the decoder and the fetcher report, checks each one's row, bounds, overlaps and target, and refuses a malformed link or a target too long, never cutting it. It classifies every link from its target alone, before any request: a page of this channel, another channel (a service the descriptor names is another channel), or a web: page for the system's web browser. The interface receives only where to draw a link and its kind. The trusted core's reader of link targets cannot panic and is fuzzed.

How links are drawn. Teletext's own underline is not drawn on any page, so a link's mark is the browser's alone: a hairline drawn by the interface at the screen's resolution, with a contrasting edge, over the page image the link belongs to, in one style no page can change, and only when one teletext dot is at least one and a half device pixels.

Showing where a link leads. Pointing at or focusing a link shows its destination in the trusted strip in place of the address. Resting the pointer on it shows a popover with the link's complete address, never shortened, drawn below the trusted strip and never over it, scrolled when it is taller than the room below the strip, and in full screen too, where nothing else says where a link leads.

Following a link. A click on a page becomes a cell, a column and a row, worked out from the pointer and the rectangle the page was drawn in, and is sent as an intent with the version of the image it was made on; the trusted core decides from its own table whether the cell is a link. A click follows only the link of the image it was made on, whose target equals what the strip is showing, unchanged for at least 500 milliseconds, so a link that changes under the pointer is not followed. A link to a page of the channel opens at once. A link or coloured key leading to another channel goes there at once, in the same tab, with no question, and Back returns. A web: link goes through the web-browser prompt in the strip, which no click, key or touch in the page area can answer, which never takes the keyboard focus by itself, and which takes Enter only once the viewer has moved the focus into it.

Handing an address to the web browser. Only an https or http address the address rules accept, written out again from its parsed parts, is handed to the system's web browser, by the trusted core through the broker, as one argument with no shell, at most once every two seconds, from the selected tab of a focused window, and logged: by open on macOS, xdg-open on Linux and ShellExecuteW on Windows. The XDG Desktop Portal on Linux is not built.

By keyboard. Tab and Shift-Tab move between a page's links, Enter follows the focused one and Escape leaves them. Links are not yet in an accessibility tree.

Controls and the look under the pointer. A page's controls, which the control triplet declares (controls and links under the pointer), are shown only while keys go to the open page's channel, with the hand pointer over them. The control under the pointer while keys go, or the link under it otherwise, takes the hover look, each colour of its cells moved to the same entry of the adjacent colour table; while the main button that went down on it is held, it takes the pressed look, those colours with foreground and background exchanged. The trusted core draws a look only on a control or link of the latest image of the page open in the active tab, checks every control again (rows 1 to 23, within the 40 columns, on no link's cell or another control's, and no more than the engine allows), and sends the channel nothing for either look.

15.20 How the browser sends input to a live channel

DOC-2301 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-211, REQ-814, REQ-824, REQ-825, REQ-826, REQ-827, REQ-828, REQ-829, REQ-830, REQ-831, REQ-832, REQ-833, REQ-834, REQ-835, REQ-836, REQ-837, REQ-838, REQ-839, REQ-840

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-211 Immediacy: every input event is written to the channel when it happens (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-824 The answer drawn as it arrives (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-825 No hold after an input (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-826 Input before drawing (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-827 One frame queued (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-829 Every move over the page, at most 60 a second, paced by the trusted core (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-830 Gone (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-831 Touch contacts reach the trusted core (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-832 A contact on a link is the browser's (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-833 The dot is checked (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-834 Each channel's input session is a ResumableSession offering RESUME (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-835 The strip's round trip is the push connection's own, measured by WebSocket ping and pong (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-836 One write a moment (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-837 The messages of one moment leave in one write (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-838 Never behind the network (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-839 The round trip measured on the connection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-840 A connection resumed, never replayed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

On a live channel the browser is a terminal on a line to its host (a terminal on a line to a host). The interface sends the trusted core intents, descriptions of what the viewer did; the trusted core gives the open page's decoder, which holds and evaluates the page's rule table, the events that table asks for; the trusted core alone builds each report the table makes and encodes the upstream protocol, and the channel's fetcher writes it to the channel's push WebSocket. This item says how the browser does that; the messages themselves are the protocol's (the events, RULE_EVENT).

The connection. The fetcher receives push over the channel's WebSocket, plain or with Transport Layer Security, with the engine's heartbeat, and a pushed page reaches the decoder and is completed at once. No connection of a fetcher uses TCP Fast Open; all share one Transport Layer Security configuration that keeps sessions so that a reconnection resumes the last session where the server allows, and that never sends early data. The fetcher writes to each socket on a thread of its own, so a socket the network does not drain never holds up its loop. A report that carries a move is written like any other message and is never held or replaced while the connection is congested; a connection that would hold more than 64 of the longest input message unwritten is closed.

Immediacy. The interface writes each input to the trusted core before any frame it causes is drawn, and the decoder handles each event of the open page the moment it arrives, applying its groups' commands at once. The trusted core does not hold back the first frame of a page's content after the viewer's input, and a frame that changes only the look under the pointer does not count towards the page's interval between frames; a page still has at most one frame a field on each of three clocks, its content, the look and the answer to an input. The interface draws a frame of the open page, or of the page under the pointer, as soon as it arrives; a frame that changed nothing never delays the next, and nothing is drawn while nothing changes or moves. Each platform's presentation keeps at most one frame queued. The messages of one moment leave in one write: the trusted core marks every input message of a moment but the last as having more after it, and the fetcher gives them to the engine's agent together, so they leave in one send and one Transport Layer Security record where it allows, each still its own WebSocket message, and nothing is held back for a message that has not come.

The mouse and the wheel. The browser gives the open page's table, when it asks for the pointer, every press and release of the main, middle, right, back and forward buttons over the page, and the modifiers Shift, Alt and Control, never Command, which is the browser's (MOUSE and WHEEL); what reaches the channel is what the table's rules report. The browser keeps its own uses: the middle button closes a tab and opens a suggestion, a bookmark or a history row in a new tab, the right button opens Back's or Forward's list, and with the browser's modifier every button is the browser's. A link the page declares is the browser's on every page: no button pressed on it is given to the table. The wheel over a page with more than one sub-code steps its sub-pages unless the pointer is inside the target of a wheel rule. Every change of the dot under the pointer reaches the table as a move within one sixtieth of a second: the trusted core alone paces the moves, with the engine's pacer, sending a move at once when a period has passed since the last and otherwise keeping the latest waiting until the period ends; a waiting move is taken before any other event, and an unchanged dot is never taken again (the pointer's moves). When the pointer leaves the page, the waiting move goes and then MOUSE with action 3, gone; when the page loses the input the same is done for the pointer and every contact still down. The trusted core refuses any mouse, wheel or contact intent whose dot lies outside the page image of 480 by 500 dots or outside its cell (where the pointer is, at any size).

Touch. On Windows and Linux the browser takes a touch screen's contacts and gives every contact that begins on the open page to the trusted core, which numbers them with the engine's contact table: the first contact while no mouse button is held is a MOUSE with device touch and button 0, and each further one, when TOUCH was agreed, a TOUCH with the lowest free number from 1 to 9 (TOUCH and pens), each given to the page's table. A contact's beginning and end are taken at once, never held for a gesture; its moves are paced as the mouse's, each in a slot of its own; a cancelled contact, or one that leaves the page, is gone. A contact that begins on a link is the browser's and follows the link when it lifts on the same link. The control under the first contact that lies on one takes the pressed look, and a finger gives no hover look, until the contact lifts, is cancelled, leaves the control, or the page loses the input. macOS trackpads give no touch events, and a pen on Windows goes as touch because the windowing library does not tell it from a finger. It has not been tried with a real touch screen.

A lost connection. When a page's push connection ends, the browser drops all of that page's local state at once (its table, variables, timers, sequences and local sounds), discards every report not yet acknowledged, and keeps the last picture frozen until the page is sent afresh (the lifetime of local state). Each channel's input session is the engine's resumable session, which offers RESUME (resuming a session), but the engine's session keeps every unacknowledged message for a resumption, so the browser forgets a session that ever gave a page's table input and makes the next connection a new session from HELLO; a session that gave none resumes as before, sending again every message the channel had not taken, then RESIZE and SELECT. Either way the page is selected afresh and sent again with its table. No server resumes yet.

The round trip. While keys go to a channel the strip shows the push connection's round trip, measured by the fetcher's WebSocket ping and pong at most once a second, in milliseconds to a tenth; acknowledgements give no round trip. The trusted core's and the strip's half and the fetcher's half are each built and tested, and are not yet joined.

15.21 Settings, the start page, the developer console and proxies

DOC-2303 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-841, REQ-842, REQ-843, REQ-844, REQ-846, REQ-847, REQ-848, REQ-849, REQ-850, REQ-851, REQ-852, REQ-853

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-841 Settings are kept between runs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-842 The settings file is read strictly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-843 The settings panel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-844 Sound setting and volume in the mixer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-846 The Home button (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-847 The start page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-848 The developer console (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-849 Fetcher reports exchanges and push events to the trusted core (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-850 Proxies (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-851 The local network through a proxy (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-852 The fetcher takes its proxy only when started (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-853 The input trace (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The settings file. The trusted core keeps the settings in one file, settings.txt, in the platform's place for an application's settings: on macOS ~/Library/Application Support/NeoTeletext/, on Windows %APPDATA%\NeoTeletext\, and elsewhere $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/neoteletext/ or ~/.config/neoteletext/. It is written whole to a temporary file renamed over it, and read at start, a missing file meaning the defaults. It is read strictly: a version line, at most 256 kilobytes, each line a setting's name, a space and a value of at most 2,048 bytes, each value checked by its setting's own rule; a line that breaks a rule or names nothing known is dropped and logged, and the rest stand. At most 16 local addresses may be allowed.

The settings panel. The settings are shown and changed in a panel of the trusted strip, opened by its gear button, Command-comma on macOS or Control-comma elsewhere. Each change is strip input the trusted core checks, and a refused one is said in the panel; a change of a setting that affects security, the proxy or the local addresses allowed, is said in the strip's notice and logged. The interface receives the settings only as the text the panel shows. The sound setting silences every page's sound, and the volume scales it from 0 to 100, in the sound helper's mixer.

Home and the start page. The strip's Home button, Command-Shift-H on macOS and Alt-Home elsewhere, opens the home address in the active tab as a navigation the viewer starts, and a new tab opens the home address. The default home, neoteletext:home, is a channel the trusted core serves itself as teletext, with no network: page 100 tells how to open a channel and lists the bookmarks from page 201, and pages 201 to 299 are one for each bookmark, the Bookmarks bar's first and then Other bookmarks', by name, each folder's name as a heading, each page showing a bookmark's name and address. Choosing a bookmark opens it at once, as the viewer's navigation, with the front page behind it. The pages are built only from addresses the address rules accepted, cleaned.

The developer console. A panel docked at the bottom of the window, opened by Command-Option-I on macOS and Control-Shift-I elsewhere, shows for the active tab's channel four tabs, Network, Packets, Pages and Notices, each keeping its newest 1,000 entries a channel, with pause and clear. The fetcher reports each exchange and each push event to the trusted core, bounded and read by a reader that refuses anything else; the trusted core reads each packet's address with the engine, keeps each tab's entries, and sends the open tab's as cleaned text, at most 200 entries a message, only while the console is open. It never shows a cookie, a form's values, a key typed into a page or the phone keyboard's pairing secret.

Proxies. The fetcher's and the phone keyboard's connections go through the proxy the settings name: an HTTP proxy by CONNECT, or a SOCKS5 proxy with no authentication, sending the host's name. A proxy that refuses, fails or does not answer in time fails the connection, with the reason in the strip's notice, and nothing goes direct instead. With a proxy, an address written as a local IP address, localhost, and names under .local and .internal are refused unless allowed, before anything is sent to the proxy. The trusted core gives a fetcher its proxy as a command-line argument when it starts it, so a change of proxy applies to fetchers started after it, and no message can change where a running fetcher connects.

The input trace. Started with --input-trace, the browser shows over the open page's row 0 each input event the trusted core sends a channel, read back from the message as it was sent, with the count of events sent since the start and, while the same event repeats, how many times, in orange. It never shows what was typed: text, a paste and a composition are shown by their length, and a character key only as a character key.

15.22 History, private tabs and recently closed tabs

DOC-2308 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-854, REQ-855, REQ-856, REQ-857, REQ-858, REQ-859, REQ-861, REQ-862, REQ-863, REQ-864, REQ-865, REQ-866, REQ-867

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-854 Visits are recorded (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-855 History is kept between runs in history.txt, readable and writable by the user alone (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-856 The history file is read strictly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-857 The history panel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-858 History panel receives at most 100 numbered rows (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-859 History can be removed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-861 Private tabs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-862 Recently closed tabs (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-863 Back and Forward lists (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-864 Suggestions in the address field (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-865 History never reaches a channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-866 Hostile titles are cleaned and cut (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-867 History and bookmarks do not slow the start (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

What is a visit. The trusted core records each page a tab shows as one row for each address and local day, with the channel's and the page's titles cleaned, the last visit's time, the day's visits and how many of them the viewer typed. A visit is recorded when the tab draws that page's first frame; a pushed update, a sub-page or a redraw is not one. A page the viewer chooses by three digits, a row of the pages list or a tile of the wall is a visit, and so is a channel's redirect, whichever way it enters the Back list; a page a redirect replaced before it drew never drew, and is no visit. The browser's own neoteletext: pages, private tabs, and everything while "Remember history" is off are not recorded.

The history file. History is kept between runs in history.txt in the settings folder, readable and writable by the user alone on macOS and Linux, appended at each visit and written whole to a temporary file renamed over it at start, at quit, when it holds twice as many lines as rows, and at once after any removal. Rows older than 90 days, beyond 50,000, or beyond a file of 16 mebibytes are removed, the oldest first. The file is read strictly: a version line, at most 16 mebibytes, each line seven fields separated by tabs, each within its bound and rule; a line that breaks a rule is dropped and logged and the rest stand. With 50,000 rows of history and 10,000 bookmarks, the time from start to the first frame grows by no more than 50 milliseconds.

The history panel. A panel of the strip, opened by Command-Y on macOS and Control-H elsewhere and from the menus, shows history newest first under a heading for each day, each row with its time, the channel's title, the page number, the page's title and the address, with a search of addresses and titles. Choosing a row opens it as a navigation the viewer starts, in the active tab, or in a new tab with Shift, the browser's modifier or the middle button. The trusted core sends the panel at most 100 rows at a time, each with a number for that view, and acts on the interface's requests to open or remove rows only by those numbers. Every title is cleaned and cut wherever it is shown, and shown beside the address it leads to, never in the address's place. No history row, title, count or typed address is ever sent to a decoder, a fetcher or the phone keyboard.

Removing history. The viewer can remove a row, the rows selected, every row of a channel, and every row last visited within the last hour, 24 hours, 7 days, 4 weeks or ever; removing everything also empties the recently closed tabs and the record of typed addresses. Removed rows are gone from history.txt before the panel shows them removed. The keys of channels that know the viewer, made within the time range, can be forgotten in the same place (viewer state in the browser).

Private tabs. A private tab, opened by Command-Shift-N on macOS and Control-Shift-N elsewhere, records no history, no typed address and no recently closed entry, and is marked "Private" in the strip and in its tab.

Recently closed tabs. The trusted core keeps the last 25 closed tabs, other than private ones, in memory with their whole Back and Forward lists; Command-Shift-T on macOS and Control-Shift-T elsewhere reopens the most recent where it was.

Back and Forward lists. Holding Back or Forward for half a second, or a secondary click on it, lists at most 15 of the tab's entries that way, nearest first; choosing one moves the tab there.

Suggestions. While the viewer types an address, the trusted core offers at most 8 suggestions, from bookmarks and then from history, each shown with its address as the address rules print it; a completion inside the field comes only from addresses the viewer typed before.

15.23 Bookmarks, and the session kept and restored

DOC-2309 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-868, REQ-869, REQ-870, REQ-871, REQ-872, REQ-873, REQ-874, REQ-875, REQ-876, REQ-877, REQ-878

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-868 Bookmarks and folders structure (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-869 The star is filled when the address is bookmarked (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-870 The bookmarks manager (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-871 The bookmarks bar (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-872 Bookmarks stored atomically in bookmarks.txt (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-873 The bookmarks file is read strictly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-874 The session is always kept (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-875 The session is restored at start (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-876 The session file is read strictly (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-877 Restore previous session is a setting, on by default (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-878 Import of another browser's Netscape bookmark file (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Bookmarks and folders. A bookmark has a name and an address; a folder has a name and an order of bookmarks and folders. The folders Bookmarks bar and Other bookmarks always exist. There are at most 10,000 bookmarks and folders together, 16 folders deep, with a name of at most 256 bytes and an address of at most 2,048.

The star. The star in the strip is filled when the strip's address is bookmarked. Clicking an empty star, Command-D on macOS or Control-D elsewhere, bookmarks the address the strip shows, page included, and opens a popover to change its name and folder, to keep the whole channel instead, or to remove it.

The bookmarks manager. A panel of the strip, opened by Command-Option-B on macOS and Control-Shift-O elsewhere and from the menus, shows the folder tree and a folder's contents, searches names and addresses, and opens, edits, removes (with Undo for ten seconds), adds folders, moves by dragging or by a row's "Move…", and sorts. The trusted core sends it at most 100 items at a time with view numbers and acts only by those numbers. The bookmarks bar, a row of the strip off by default and shown or hidden by Command-Shift-B on macOS and Control-Shift-B elsewhere, shows the Bookmarks bar folder from the trusted core's view.

Importing. The manager's Import reads another browser's Netscape bookmark file as well as this browser's own, into a folder "Imported" under Other bookmarks, its folders kept. The file is read by a decoder process started for it, confined as every decoder is, never by the trusted core; the decoder reports only folders, their ends and bookmarks, each bounded, and the trusted core keeps only addresses its rules accept, cleans every name, and keeps the bounds above. Exporting in that format is not built: this browser's bookmarks are channels, which another browser could open only as web pages.

The bookmarks file. Bookmarks are kept in bookmarks.txt in the settings folder, written whole to a temporary file renamed over it at each change, and read strictly: a version line, at most 24 mebibytes, unique numbers, each folder before its contents so that no cycle can be read, a depth of at most 16, each field within its bound and rule; a line that breaks a rule is dropped and logged with anything inside it.

The session. The trusted core keeps the window's place, size and maximised state and every tab but private ones, each with its Back and Forward list (at most 50 entries, those nearest its place), its place and its mute, and which tab is active, in session.txt in the settings folder, readable by the user alone, written whole after every change of the tabs and within a second of the window's last move or resize, so the session survives however the browser ends. With "Restore previous session" on, which is the default, kept in settings.txt and changed in the settings panel, the browser starts with the kept windows, tabs, lists and active tab, and the command line's addresses open as further tabs, the last of them active; with it off, or with no session kept, the browser starts at the home address. session.txt is read strictly, every field within its bound and rule, what breaks a rule dropped and logged, and every restored address passes the address rules again.

15.24 Viewer state in the browser

DOC-2312 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-715, REQ-716, REQ-717, REQ-879, REQ-880, REQ-881, REQ-882, REQ-883, REQ-884, REQ-886, REQ-887, REQ-888, REQ-889, REQ-6713, REQ-6714, REQ-6715, REQ-6716, REQ-6717, REQ-6718

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-889 The browser sends no cookie header and acts on none it receives (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6717 Viewer state behaves identically on encrypted and unencrypted channels; the Not secure badge is the only difference shown (not implemented on livedevelopment); REQ-6718 Restoring tabs at start restores no visit key: a restored tab proves only with a remembered key (not implemented on livedevelopment).

The browser keeps no cookies: no fetcher sends a Cookie header, a Set-Cookie or Clear-Site-Data changes nothing, and there is no cookie file or cookie panel. What a channel may know of a viewer is viewer state (connections and viewer state); this item says how the browser keeps it.

The trusted core owns the keys. A viewer-state key is an Ed25519 key pair the trusted core makes from the system's cryptographic random source, and no other process ever holds a private key or its seed: not the fetcher, the decoder, the interface or the broker. There is at most one key for each channel identity, used for that exact channel alone, never for a folder inside it, another scheme or another port. A fetcher passes the trusted core only a channel's challenge and gets back only the proof to send; the trusted core takes the channel from the address of the tab that fetcher serves, never from the fetcher's message, and builds the signed bytes itself.

When a key is made. Only when a challenge on the channel's own push connection asks to create one, only when that tab had the viewer's input within the last 7 seconds, only when the viewer has not blocked state for the channel or for all channels, and only once the tab's page has been shown. Otherwise the answer is that there is no key, with the reason. Every key is made as a visit key, held in memory alone and deleted when the browser closes, or sooner when it has gone unused or has lasted too long.

Remember me. A visit key becomes a remembered key only when the viewer chooses "Remember me on this channel" in the browser's own interface, outside the page, where the choice names the channel and is off until chosen; a channel can only suggest it. Remembered keys, and nothing else, are kept in viewer-keys.bin in the settings folder, readable by the user alone, sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305 under a key the broker keeps in the platform's secret store; a copy of the file alone opens nothing, and a file that cannot be opened is discarded with a notice that remembered channels were not carried over. A remembered key is deleted after long disuse or at its absolute limit.

Tabs and private windows. Every ordinary tab showing a channel proves with that channel's one key, so its program sees one viewer on each tab. Private windows have keys of their own, in memory alone, shared by every private tab of a channel, never remembered and deleted when the last private window closes; no key moves between private and ordinary windows. A restored tab proves only with a remembered key: no visit key is restored.

Where a key goes. A proof goes only on the push connection of the channel the key is for, opened by that channel's own fetcher, and nothing derived from a key is ever placed in an address, a query, a redirect, a fetch, a header, the history, the session file, a bookmark, a log line, the developer console or a message to the interface. A redirect or a link to another channel takes nothing of the first channel's key.

The viewer's controls. The settings list the channels that know the viewer, with whether each key is a visit key or remembered, when it was made and last used, and never the key; for each channel, Forget, Remember or Stop remembering, and Block, and for all, Forget all and a setting "Channels may ask to know you", Allow or Never. Forgetting a channel deletes its key at once and tells each of that channel's open connections that the viewer has gone, with nothing that relates the old key to a later one. Clearing history offers to forget the keys made within its time range. While a tab's connection carries a key, the trusted strip may show that the channel knows the browser. Everything here is the same on encrypted and unencrypted channels; the "Not secure" badge is the only difference shown.

15.25 Page controls: page numbers, Fastext, reveal, hold, mix and sub-pages

DOC-2313 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-756, REQ-890, REQ-891, REQ-892, REQ-893, REQ-894, REQ-895, REQ-1505

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-756 Keys work in the tab (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-890 Fastext keys and Index follow their links (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-891 The keys act only while their row is shown (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-892 Reveal (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-893 Hold keeps the open page at its shown version (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-894 Sub-pages: bound on listed and reachable sub-pages (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-895 The interface learns only the minimum about the open page's controls (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1505 A live tab treats each of a page's sub-pages as a page, with its own connection, decoder, store and selection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A viewer works an open page with a television remote's controls, taken by the engine's viewer as the standard describes them (navigation), and kept by the trusted core: the interface learns of the open page's controls only which keys lead somewhere, which of reveal, hold and mix are on, and how many sub-pages there are and which is shown, and every control reaches the trusted core as strip input, which alone tells the decoder.

Page numbers. With the page area focused, three digits choose a page of the channel; when the open page links that number with an LK line, or the channel's descriptor aliases it, the number follows that link instead, and one leading to another channel goes there at once. Up and Down step through the pages. A key only selects; it never causes a fetch of its own.

Fastext. While a page is open, its four coloured links and its index link are followed by r, g, y and c (or F1 to F4) and i, the targets read by the engine from the page's packet X/27/0, which the engine also writes from a TTI page's FL and LN lines. A page of the channel opens at once, at the sub-page the link names; a page of a service the descriptor lists opens at once too, in the same tab, with Back to return. A coloured key or index does nothing on an image of the page whose row 24 was blank or boxed away, and a key is checked against the image the viewer was shown, as a click is. The decoder draws the receiver's row 24 for a page with LN lines, a link to another service blank (row 24).

Reveal, hold and mix. ? shows the open page's concealed text and hides it again (conceal and reveal). H holds the open page at the version it shows, a new version or sub-page not drawn until it is let go. m draws the cells' backgrounds transparent. Each lapses when another page is opened.

Sub-pages. On a live channel each tab treats a page's sub-pages exactly as pages, and everything here is per tab. The tab's sub-page list, its count and the selection's place, such as "3/12", come from the page's SUBPAGES record on the tab's own connection (the SUBPAGES record), in ascending order of sub-code, with 0000 first when the page has it. Stepping to the next or previous sub-page, by Left and Right, the remote or the list's arrows, or choosing one from the list, sends SELECT with that sub-code (selecting a page), and the tab shows that sub-page when it arrives, saying it is loading meanwhile. Selecting a page without a sub-page selects it with 3F7F, and the first sub-page the channel sends becomes the selection, at place 1. The sub-page a tab shows never changes by itself: it changes only when the viewer selects another, or when the channel's program redirects the tab within the channel. A broadcast recording played back keeps the broadcast's own rotation. On a channel of files, every sub-page the engine's store keeps is listed, at most 64, and the latest is drawn as it arrives until the viewer chooses one; the control on the page shows how many there are and which is shown, and returns to the latest when pressed. An address naming a sub-page, such as one ending in 302/0002, sub-page 0002 of page 302 in the channel's URL map (the places of a channel), opens its page there.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.6.1 Packets X/27/0 to X/27/3 for Editorial Linking (Rests on: packet X/27/0, from which the engine reads the Fastext links); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 11.1 Navigation via FLOF (Rests on: navigation by the four coloured keys and the index key); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.2 Spacing attributes (Rests on: the Conceal attribute that reveal shows); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause G.1 Mixed mode operation of decoders (Rests on: mixed mode, which mix draws); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.3.1.2 Page sub-code (Rests on: the page sub-code that names a sub-page)

15.26 The remote control

DOC-2314 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-896, REQ-897, REQ-898, REQ-899

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-896 A remote with every page control (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-897 Docked, floating or away (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-898 The remote never covers the trusted strip (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-899 The trusted core keeps the remote's place in settings.txt (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The window offers an on-screen remote control holding every page control: the page number being entered or shown, the number pad, page up and page down, Fastext's four coloured keys and Index, the sub-page steps and count, and Reveal, Hold and Mix, each lit only while it applies and each with its tip. Its keys send exactly the inputs the keyboard's do (page controls).

The remote docks along the window's right edge, the content narrowing as it slides in and out over 200 milliseconds, or floats over the page area, moved by its title row. Command-Shift-R on macOS and Control-Shift-R elsewhere, the menu, and a handle at the window's right edge show and hide it. A floating remote is kept inside the window and below the trusted strip and the bookmarks bar however it is dragged and however the window is sized, so it can never cover the strip.

Whether the remote is hidden, docked or floating, and a floating remote's corner, are kept by the trusted core in settings.txt as a remote line, read strictly (each number at most 16,384), and restored at the next start; the interface stores nothing.

16 The server

DOC-2257 · section

This part describes the NeoTeletext server, the program in the repository neoteletext-app-server that serves channels to receivers and runs the programs behind live channels: where it runs, how it is divided, how it reaches its programs, what it reports and keeps, its radio, and how it is built. The part is informative: another server of the protocol need not be built like this one. What every server must do is in the protocol's parts above, and how an operator runs this one is in Running a server.

16.1 One runtime and the host that drives it

DOC-2296 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1020, REQ-1022, REQ-1044, REQ-3128

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1020 Native on the common systems (not implemented on livedevelopment).

The NeoTeletext server is written in Rust and runs as a native program on a computer's operating system. Its core is kept apart from everything that touches the operating system, so that the core is tested with its own time and no network, and so that another host could drive it unchanged if one were ever wanted.

The runtime does no input or output. The server's core, the crate teletext-runtime, is a state machine, one for each channel, that reads no clock and holds no socket, file, process, thread or asynchronous executor. It is no_std with alloc. A host gives it events, each with the time: a connection opened, bytes from a connection, a connection closed, a line from the channel's program, a deadline reached, or something loaded from storage. It answers with effects: send bytes to a connection, close one, send a line to the program, wake it at a time, load something, or store something. No host's code is in it. Its tests set their own time and need no network.

HostWhat it isIts state
Native, teletext-nativeOne program, teletext-server, on tokio and hyper, one task for each channel's runtime, for Linux, macOS and Windows on x86-64 and arm64. It serves HTTP and the WebSocket itself, takes a listening socket from systemd when given one, may serve TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 itself or sit behind a proxy, starts the channels' programs, and keeps what lasts in its state directory. How an operator runs it is running a server.Built, and run as a systemd service on Linux. Its builds for Windows and for every pair of system and processor are not yet recorded as made and tested.

How a program reaches its channel. A program is started by the server and speaks on its standard input and output; or it runs as a service of its own and connects to a Unix domain socket the channel names; or, on another machine, it opens a WebSocket to the channel's program door, /<channel>/program, presenting the channel's secret as a bearer token, which the channels file names by secret_variable or secret_file (processes, transports and lines). The same lines of the program protocol travel on all three, and only one program at a time holds a channel. The kits do not yet have a WebSocket transport of their own: a program on another machine reaches the door through a bridge script, scripts/bridge.ts, that runs the program and carries its standard input and output over the WebSocket.

16.2 How many viewers one server holds

DOC-2299 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1023

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1023 Native server holds connections up to host limits (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The native server holds as many WebSocket connections as the computer's memory and its limit of open files allow. Three rules keep each connection cheap:

  • a change to a page every viewer shares costs the channel the same however many viewers it has: the change is made once, and each connection's own task catches up from the channel's log of changes by itself;
  • each connection's idle memory is measured and kept small;
  • a slow connection never makes the server hold more than one version of each page for it: it skips to the newest, and no queue grows.

Measured on 25 October 2026 on the Linux host foundintelquiet4060, which has 20 processor cores, with the server as a systemd service allowed 524,288 open files and the load client, teletext-load, on the same host over loopback addresses. Each connection was sent the clock page, page 105 of 1,092 bytes, once a second. The server used 8.9 MB before any connection.

ConnectionsServer memoryFor each connectionFrom a change to the last viewerSent
10,00095 MB8.6 KB11 to 16 ms10.9 MB a second
50,000440 MB8.6 KB61 to 64 ms54.6 MB a second
100,000961 MB9.5 KB123 to 130 ms109 MB a second

These figures were taken before the program protocol of the present version, and have not been measured again since.

16.3 Programs that start, stop and start again, and what outlasts them

DOC-2304 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1038, REQ-1057, REQ-1058

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1038 The server listens as soon as it has read its channels file (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1057 A channel keeps in its own storage what must outlast its process, each viewer's under their viewer-state handle (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1058 Component state kept when asked, for the component's viewer under their handle (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The server serves before its programs run. The native server listens as soon as it has read its channels file, without waiting for any program. One slow or failing program never keeps the other channels off the air. While a channel's program is not running, each selection on that channel ends with DENIED 503 and the connection stays open (processes, transports and lines). Every time a program starts, the first time and each time after, it is sent start and then connected for every connection open on its channel, so a program started again, for example after its author saved a change to its source, serves its viewers afresh without the server starting again. Lines for a program that is not running are dropped rather than queued, because a queued line would reach the next program before its start, about connections it never knew.

What the server keeps. The server keeps no page: only what each open connection is, the sub-page it last sent each one, a short cache of public pages' descriptions, and, in its state directory, the secret viewers' handles are derived from and its figures since it first ran (the server's options and what it keeps). A program is told of every connection again when it starts, and must keep for itself what its viewers did.

What a channel keeps. A channel keeps in storage of its own what must outlast its process: what every viewer shares, such as polls, guestbooks and halls of fame, and what one viewer owns, keyed by the viewer's handle, never by a connection's number, which the server gives again after it restarts. The storage is SQLite, which both kits' languages have in their standard library: node:sqlite in TypeScript and sqlite3 in Python. The component library's SqliteStateStore is such a store for a TypeScript channel: values kept as JSON with the version of their shape, a value of another version dropped as it is read, what one viewer owns kept until 24 hours after it was last read or written, or 180 days for a viewer who chose to be remembered, at most 262,144 viewers' values, every read and change of one value a single transaction, and not dropped when the program is told gone, which every start also tells. The demonstration site keeps its guestbook, hall of fame and poll in it, and the UI components demonstration its poll, each in a file its --state option names, outside the folder a deploy replaces. The Hackaday channels keep everything in SQLite. A component's own state that is not kept holds only what may be lost, such as a cursor, a scroll position or an animation's frame.

Component state kept when asked. A component of the UI component library may name a key, and the version of its state's shape, under which its state is kept for its viewer in the channel's store, under the viewer's handle, and given back when it is mounted again for that viewer, on any tab, after a restart of the program too; state of another version is dropped. A game or a half-written form then survives a restart without each channel writing its own storage. The copy of a page every viewer shares belongs to no viewer and keeps nothing; a connection with no viewer keeps what is its own for its own life.

16.4 The server's log

DOC-2305 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1046, REQ-1047, REQ-1048, REQ-1049, REQ-1050, REQ-1051

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1046 Structured events (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1047 Levels chosen at start (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1048 Server reports operational events at INFO level (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1050 A program's standard error is logged (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1051 The runtime's reports are events too (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Verified by inspection. REQ-1049 Nothing that identifies a viewer: Inspected 20 November 2026 in neoteletext-app-server at b7ec5f8 (TODO-6711, DEC-6471), read-only, for version 4. Every log write in crates was read: (1) the tracing calls in teletext-native (main.rs, apps.rs, apps/remote.rs, connection.rs, hub.rs, http.rs, state.rs, logging.rs) carry only the channel folder, connection numbers, counts, close codes, reasons, program command and socket path, state directory path, figures and fixed text; no tracing field takes a handle, proof, public key or secret, and there is no request-logging layer (no TraceLayer, no peer or forwarded address is logged). (2) Every runtime event goes through Channel::log and Effect::Log (teletext-runtime channel.rs and channel/*.rs), then logging::runtime in teletext-native and log() in teletext-cloudflare; the texts read are fixed phrases with connection numbers, page and sub-page codes, byte limits and fault names; the only Effect::Log built in viewers.rs says no random bytes were available, and the channel_address event names a channel address, not a viewer. (3) protocol/check.rs refusals (logged as line_refused) carry a field path, a rule name and numbers or one rejected character as U+XXXX or a language tag. Found: no event carries a viewer handle, proof, key or the handle secret. Caveats, not breaches: a program's own log lines and standard error are logged as they come (apps.rs line 405), which the requirement already assigns to the program; the redirect event names the address the program chose; and the stand_in event names one character code from text a program sent. No test asserts the absence; this is an inspection of the code at that commit only.

Everything the native server reports is an event, written one a line to standard error, and nothing else is written to standard error or standard output. An event has a time in RFC 3339 form in UTC, a level, a target naming the part of the server that reports it, a message, and named fields. It is written as a JSON object when standard error is not a terminal, and as text when it is, unless --log-format json or --log-format text says which. One event a line with named fields is what journald, Loki, Vector and Cloudflare's Workers Logs read and search.

Which events are written is chosen when the server starts, by the environment variable RUST_LOG, as targets and levels, such as info,teletext_native::connection=debug. When it is unset or cannot be read, the level is info.

LevelWhat is reported
ERRORA listener that fails; a state directory the server cannot write
WARNA line refused from a program, with the reason; lines for a program dropped because it fell behind, at the first and then at each power of two; a record of what the server kept that it ignored; a viewer-handle secret rotated, for the next start
INFOThe server's start, with its version, listening address, origin, channels and state directory; its stop; each program's start and end, with the reason and the pause before it starts again; what the server kept and loaded, and each retired session-cookie key file it deleted; its figures once a minute, as fields; and each line a program writes to its standard error
DEBUGEach connection's opening and closing, with its connection number, and a connection closed for breaking the protocol

Each event about a channel carries the field channel, the channel's folder.

A program's standard error. Each line a program writes to its standard error becomes an INFO event of the target program, with the field channel. A line longer than 64 KiB is cut there and marked as cut. A program's log message is reported the same way, at the level it names.

The runtime's reports. The runtime does no output, so it reports through an effect that carries a level, a stable event name and its text, and each host writes that in its own way: the native host as a tracing event.

Nothing that identifies a viewer. No event carries a viewer's network address, anything a viewer typed, a viewer's handle, key, key identifier, challenge or proof, or any part of one. A connection's number may be carried. A program's own log lines and standard error are logged as they come, so a program that logs what its viewers type breaks this rule itself.

16.5 Decided, not built: the server's streaming audio and radio

DOC-2306 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1063

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1063 Streaming-audio transcoder outputs Opus at 48 kHz (not implemented on livedevelopment).

The server is designed to transcode streaming audio as a service, as it publishes pages, so that a program can play an internet radio station or a podcast to its viewers without touching a byte of audio. None of it is built: what follows is the design in the server's docs/streaming-audio.md, and the encoder is the owner's to choose.

What it is to do. A program names a source by its address. The server fetches it; decodes MP3, AAC or FLAC with the symphonia library; mixes it to mono; resamples it to 48 kHz; encodes it as Opus in the engine's audio profile (codecs and rates): mono, 16 kbit/s at a constant rate, a 40-byte packet every 20 ms; and sends it as live Opus sounds, the records opus_live and opus_packets make (sounds), to every session the program says is listening. The program hears what is playing, such as the station's title, its levels and its position, and draws its pages from that.

Two kinds of source. A live source, such as an Icecast, SHOUTcast or HLS station, is one stream at the same moment for every listener, transcoded once however many listen. An on-demand source, such as a podcast episode, is fetched by HTTP byte ranges, transcoded once into a cache, and served to each listener from their own position. Stations are to be found through radio-browser.info.

How it scales. The transcoder is to do no input or output, like the runtime: it takes bytes and gives encoded packets and events. A live stream is a ring of encoded blocks, each connection catches up from the last block it sent, and a slow connection skips to the newest blocks, so no queue grows. Opus at 16 kbit/s for each listener is a quarter of the 64 kbit/s of the IMA ADPCM output first designed. The desktop browser plays Opus alone; a receiver on a microcontroller decodes no Opus, and a stream for one would be a second output that this design does not cover.

16.6 How the server is built and checked

DOC-2307 · reference · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1025, REQ-1026, REQ-1027, REQ-1028, REQ-1029, REQ-1030

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1025 One check script runs every gate in tiers (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1026 The strictest workspace lints (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1027 Dependencies by approval, licences allowed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1028 Pinned tools (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1029 The engine imported, never copied (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1030 Every reader of outside input fuzzed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The server is one Cargo workspace in the repository neoteletext-app-server, with two crates: teletext-runtime, the runtime with no input or output; and teletext-native, the native host and the load client teletext-load. It is checked locally, with no continuous integration, as every NeoTeletext repository is.

The engine imported, never copied. Every engine crate the server uses is a git dependency on the engine's public repository at one commit, the same commit in every manifest, with its default features off and the features it needs named. No code is copied from the engine or the browser: what the engine lacks for a server is written once, in the server.

One check script and the git hooks. scripts/check.sh runs every gate in three tiers, and the hooks in .githooks/ run it, so nothing may be skipped and nothing may bypass them.

TierWhenWhat it runs
commitBefore each commitThe engine pin; the check that no server code reads a receiver's user agent text; the lockfiles; formatting; the no-panic lists; Clippy
pushBefore a push of any branch but main, on a clean tree at the commit pushedClippy with every optional feature compiled out, and the tests
fullBefore a push to mainDocumentation tests and the documentation, release tests, tests with optional features compiled out, licences and advisories, unused dependencies, fuzzing, and the steps on the Linux host alongside

The strictest lints. Unsafe code is forbidden. Missing documentation, unused qualifications, Clippy's pedantic group, an allow without a reason, dbg!, todo! and unimplemented! are warnings that the gates make errors. Every crate root carries the same list of what may not panic: indexing_slicing, string_slice, unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, arithmetic_side_effects, unreachable, todo and unimplemented, and the commit gate compares every root's list. A suppression is narrow, at its site, with its reason, because everything the server reads comes from receivers and programs that may be hostile.

Dependencies. Every library has the owner's approval by name, recorded in a decision, and a licence deny.toml allows. Cargo.lock is committed, a program pins each dependency's exact version with its licence and reason beside it, and cargo deny and cargo machete pass.

Pinned tools. The development tools are installed at exact versions into the ignored folder tools/ by scripts/tools.sh, each crate checked against its recorded SHA-256, and the check script refuses any other version.

Fuzzing. Every reader of bytes from receivers, programs or files has a fuzz target in fuzz/: the server's WebSocket frames in any pieces, a channel's input streams and its program's lines with time passing, what the server kept under any key, viewer state's messages, and a program's Opus packets. Every input that ever found a fault is kept in fuzz/regressions/ and replayed first by the full gate.

17 The protocol kits, the UI component library and the demonstration channels

DOC-2258 · section

This part describes what NeoTeletext gives the author of a program: the protocol kits, which speak the program protocol for a program; the UI component library, from which a program builds its pages; and the demonstration channels, which show both at work. The part is informative: a program may speak the protocol without them.

17.1 The protocol kits for TypeScript and Python

DOC-2317 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1043, REQ-1479, REQ-2216, REQ-6537, REQ-6538

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1043 A Unix domain socket, for a program that runs as a service of its own (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1479 Protocol messages are JSON lines, one per line, ended by a line feed (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2216 When a program sends measure, the server answers without sending the page to any viewer (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6537 The TypeScript kit MUST offer program protocol 15's rule table, commands and animation as thin calls generated from the server's schema (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6538 The Python kit MUST offer program protocol 15's rule table, commands and animation as thin calls, the equal of the TypeScript kit (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

A channel's program may speak the program protocol directly, with nothing but a JSON library. The kits save it the work. The protocol is the interface; a kit is a convenience over it. Both kits speak program protocol 16, and offer the same calls, handlers and test harness, name for name (the TypeScript names in camel case, the Python names in snake case), as neoteletext-common's docs/audio/kit-calls.tsv lists them.

KitWhere it isWhat uses it
TypeScript, neoteletext-server-ts-protocol, release 19.0.0A repository of its own, released as a built tarball, not to a package registry: a channel commits the release under its vendor/ folder and depends on it by exact version. It needs Node 22.18 or later, which runs TypeScript files as they are.The reference kit, and the base of the UI component library (release 27.0.0, on kit 19.0.0), the Hackaday channel, the demonstration site, the UI components demonstration, the NAPLPS demonstration and the home channel
Python, neoteletext_appThe folder kits/python of the repository neoteletext-server-channels, run with uv, Python 3.13 or laterThe old Hackaday channel in Python, in the same repository

What a kit does. A program gives it applications. Each is called with what happened (start, joined, request, opened, leftPage, input, ruleEvent, rulesFault, wake, gone, stats, describe, refused, soundBuilt, viewerBegan, viewerLeft, stateRefused and viewersReset) and answers through a context: publish a page for everyone or for one connection, send a connection to a page, end a selection without a page with 403, 404, 429 or 503, retitle a page, give a page its rule table, send a rule table's commands directly, query a page's local state, animate its objects, play a timeline on the server's clock, send a sound, write to the viewer's developer console or to the server's log, ask for a viewer's state, or ask to be woken at a time. Every browser tab is a connection of its own, kept until its gone; there is no server session and no cookie, and a connection may carry a viewer's handle (viewer, remembered, requestState, offerRemember, endState). The kit keeps every page the applications publish, the channel's copy and each connection's own, each sub-page by its sub-code in ascending order, and answers the server for them: one reply to each connected, one page to each selected, the first sub-page in ascending order for a selection of the whole page, and denied 404 for a page no application has published. It copies each selection's request number, so a program never sees it, and gives each selection to the page as a request object. It answers describe with the application's own answer, or says a page is not public.

The rule table. rules(to, page, sub, table) writes a page's rule table exactly as built, for the server to make its inline groups, and null removes it; the server keeps no table, so a program sends it at every selection of the page. The table is typed by the types generated from the server's schema (RuleTable, PageRule, RuleTrigger, RuleCondition, RuleValue, RuleCommand, RuleRow, RuleTarget, Amount), and built with builders that check nothing (physicalKey, characterKey, namedKey, level, variable, plus, row, fired, phase, noteOn, noteOff, and the mode set modes). The six commands are also calls of their own (localMidi, variable, timer, report, run, sequence), and queryState(connection, page, sub) resolves with the page's local state or rejects with the refusal. An input names the rule that reported it, the place of the firing row, its page tick and its target; a report with no input event reaches ruleEvent, and a receiver's fault of the table rulesFault. Every page call names its sub-code, since a sub-page is a page.

Animation. frame, animate, sprites, naplpsObjects, spriteSheet, objectPage, playTimeline and stopTimeline write animation's messages; a Timeline builder makes the steps the server plays, and the kit holds no scheduler.

Pictures. Each kit has a ReGIS builder and a NAPLPS builder whose methods append the language's instructions and give the parts a regis or naplps message takes (picture messages). The NAPLPS builder takes every place in dots of the 480 by 500 teletext raster and writes it at six-byte operands after a DOMAIN that selects them; its rect covers exactly the dots it names; its text, given a row and a column, sets the character field and point that put each character on exactly one cell (text in pictures). Both kits keep a copy of neoteletext-common's docs/picture-examples.jsonl and write exactly its bytes.

Checked on both sides. Every message the TypeScript kit writes or reads is checked against the server's published JSON Schema by validators that Ajv 8 compiles from the schema when the kit is built, in standalone mode, so nothing compiles a schema at run time; the Python kit holds text to the server's rules and leaves the schema check to its tests. A kit then holds a message to the server's rules of text that a schema cannot state: no control or bidirectional formatting character, Unicode normalisation form C, and an author's log line bounded in bytes. A sound, a rule table and every animation message are held to the schema alone: every other rule of them is the server's, and its refusal reaches the refused handler. A message the server would refuse for its text is never written: the call throws an error naming the path and the rule. A line from the server that is not valid is reported and never acted on.

Text and measuring. A kit's screen holds a page's words as Unicode runs with their languages, which the server encodes (text in any language), and a run may be marked as text from outside the program, which the server shows with stand-ins rather than refusing. The kit offers measure as a call that resolves to the measured answer or rejects with the refusal (measuring a page), so that a channel's tests can measure every page they build against a running server and fail before deployment. A kit stops on a start of a protocol version other than its own, 16.

Testing a channel. Each kit's harness drives a channel as the server does, so a channel's tests can join a connection to a page, press keys, fire a rule, answer a state query, read the timeline's sends and read what the connection was sent, without a server. An input given with no rule named comes as the server's default table reports it. Each kit builds the worked examples of docs/rules-examples.jsonl and the timelines of docs/timelines.jsonl and writes exactly their messages.

A program that runs as a service of its own. Both kits connect to the Unix domain socket a channel names in the server's channels file (REQ-1043), on Linux and macOS, when the program is started with that socket's path in the environment variable NEOTELETEXT_SOCKET (DEC-2452); unset or empty, a program speaks on its standard input and output. Over the socket a kit reads and writes the same lines as over its standard streams. When the connection goes it connects again: at once after a connection on which the server said start, and otherwise after a pause of 1 second that doubles up to 30 seconds, the server's own pauses before starting a program again. The server says start on every connection, which ends every connection the program knew, so each socket connection starts afresh while the program keeps what it holds in memory; lines written while no connection is open are dropped. In the TypeScript kit runChannel then never resolves; in the Python kit the module's run(app) does the same.

Not built. Neither kit yet has a transport for a WebSocket of its own: a program on another machine reaches its channel through the server's bridge script (one runtime and the hosts that drive it).

17.2 The UI component library

DOC-2318 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1058, REQ-1723, REQ-2020, REQ-2152, REQ-2153, REQ-2217, REQ-5722

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1058 Component state kept when asked, for the component's viewer under their handle (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1723 Every component in the library and in programs built on it is a class extending Component (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2020 A sub-page or Frame can set the colour of the screen around the page through a screenColour prop (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2152 Components take a language for the page and for any text (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

The UI component library, neoteletext-server-ts-ui-components, is to a teletext page what a component library is to a web page. A page is a tree of components: each renders elements or draws itself, and the library lays the tree out on the 40 by 25 screen, publishes it through the TypeScript kit, routes the keys and the pointer to the component where they land, and publishes a viewer's own copy of a page only while it differs from everyone's. It is released, like the kit, as a built tarball that a channel commits under vendor/, and each release names the kit release it is built on.

Class components only. Every component is a class that extends the library's Component, with its props, its state in state changed by setState, its lifecycle as methods such as componentDidMount and componentWillUnmount, its own timers, and its input handlers onKey, onPointer, onWheel and onHover. h(type, props, ...children) makes an element and accepts only a component class: a function passed to it is a compile-time error. The library has no function components and no hooks, and no channel built on it may add them, so that a component's state, lifecycle and timers stay in one place. A plain function that builds an element from a class is allowed. A test in the library requires the type check to refuse a function, and the check script of the library and of each channel finds no hook and no function component.

What is in it. ComponentChannel is the kit's application for pages of components, each page naming its number, title and root, and whether each viewer gets a copy of their own. Frame is a sub-page with a title band, a hint row and up to four Fastext prompts. Beyond those: layout (rows, columns, layers, grids, panels), text (styles, rich text, news, badges, big letters), navigation (tabs, menus, trees, pagination, a page finder), lists (choosing, picking by a digit or a coloured key, narrowing as the viewer types, scrolling, tables, logs), input (fields, buttons, check boxes, radios, switches, sliders, selects, autocomplete, phone-keypad typing), feedback (progress, spinners, toasts, an audio player), dialogs, charts, time, graphics (mosaics, pictures, painting, maps), documents of several sub-pages, polls, quizzes, wizards and games. A bus carries what one page's components tell another's. The kit's harness tests a channel of components as the server drives it.

Text in any language. A page component takes a language, a BCP 47 tag, and every component that shows text takes an optional language of its own, which defaults to the page's. No component encodes text: components hand Unicode and its language to the canvas, the canvas hands the page's runs to the kit, and the server encodes them (text in any language). The page's own designation is written into its header and into packet X/28/0 Format 1, and a page whose language is not Latin English carries X/28/0 even when it has no controls, so that a receiver never has to guess the page's group of sets, as TR 100 287 clause 10.3 advises. On a page written right to left, components lay out from the right, and the direction of arrows and of next and previous steps is mirrored. Every line of text takes exactly one row, in every language. Marks a component draws for itself, such as a sort mark, a separator, a bullet or a scroll bar, are characters the page's sets can show, or mosaics. The library's control triplets and the encoder's character triplets form one stream, in the order of EN 300 706 Annex A.4, counted against the page's 208 triplets.

The scrolling view. A scrolling view holds any components, in any language, beside a scroll bar drawn in mosaics, and moves with the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home and End, the wheel, and presses and drags on its bar. When it scrolls, each row in view carries its own X/26 triplets, addressed to the row where it now stands, and rows out of view carry none. A child of several rows, such as a table or a double-height line, scrolls as one unit and is never cut at the view's edge. Its position is each viewer's own. Content whose rows in view could exceed the budget at some position is refused when the page is made, not when a viewer reaches that position.

The viewer and the viewer's language. There are no cookies. A component reaches the viewer through the library's services: viewer(connection) gives the viewer's handle and whether they chose to be remembered, or null while the connection has none; wantState(connection) asks, after the viewer's input, that the viewer be given state, once on a connection; offerRemember(connection) asks the browser to offer "remember me"; and forgetViewer(connection) ends the viewer's state and deletes all the channel's store keeps for them. A handle is used only to keep what the viewer asked for on this channel, and is never shown, logged or sent anywhere. language(connection) is the language the viewer chose with a LanguagePicker, when it is one of the server's languages, and the channel's default language otherwise; the choice is kept under the viewer's handle, or for the connection's own life when it has no viewer. A page with no language of its own takes the viewer's, so a LanguagePicker switches a whole channel's language with no other code. One viewer's choice never changes another's page.

The colour around the page. Frame and SubPage take screenColour, a Colour Map entry from 0 to 31. The library writes it as a Full Screen Colour triplet (address 41, row mode 00000), the first triplet of the sub-page's X/26 data, on every sub-page, where it takes one of the 208 triplets, and a value outside 0 to 31 throws when the page is drawn. Without it no triplet is sent and the receiver's default applies.

State kept across a restart. A channel gives ComponentChannel a store, usually the library's SqliteStateStore on a SQLite file of its own, and gives the same store to what it keeps itself, such as a poll's Tally, whose votes and each viewer's ballot it then keeps. A component whose keptAs() names a key and the version of its state's shape has its state, as JSON, written to the store each time it changes, and laid over its own state when it is mounted again for the same viewer, on any tab, after a restart of the program too; state of another version is dropped. Only a viewer's own copy of a page keeps state, since the copy every viewer shares belongs to no viewer (programs that start, stop and start again). Some of the language work above was rebuilt on 3 November 2026 and waits to be checked again.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3.3 Row Address triplets (the Full Screen Colour row address triplet a page's screenColour writes); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets (row mode 00000, Full Screen Colour); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 30 Colour Map (the Colour Map entries 0 to 31); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.5 Rules for row and screen colours (the Full Screen Colour triplet first, once a page, at address 41); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.4 Addressing order for enhancement triplets (the one order of a page's triplets, the library's and the encoder's); EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.4.2 Packet X/28/0 Format 1 (packet X/28/0 Format 1, which states the page's own character sets); TR 100 287 V1.2.1 clause 10.3 Language definition and the preferred use of packets 29/0 (why a page that is not in Latin English carries X/28/0 even without controls)

17.3 The channels: the home channel, Hackaday, the demonstration site and the UI components demonstration

DOC-2320 · concept · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1986, REQ-2021, REQ-2154, REQ-2155, REQ-2218, REQ-2995, REQ-3838

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1986 Both demo sites carry one magazine 8 page per language, each with its own character-set designation (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-2021 Page 505 of the UI components demo opens in blue and lets a viewer change the colour of the screen around the page (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

NeoTeletext's own live channels are programs behind the NeoTeletext server. The channels file that names them, channels.json, is in the repository neoteletext-server-channels, and each TypeScript channel is a repository of its own beside it, built on the TypeScript kit and the UI component library, released into its vendor/ folder, and run by Node 22.18 or later.

FolderChannelWhat it is
homeneoteletext-server-channel-home-www.neoteletext.comNeoTeletext's home channel, what a viewer first sees: on page 100 the channels, numbered from 201; on 200 a directory of every channel on the internet, eight to a sub-page; on 300 what NeoTeletext is; on 400 how to use it; on 500 how to host pages of one's own as a folder of files on any web host; and on 600 how to host a live channel.
hackadayneoteletext-server-channel-hackadayHackaday's whole archive as teletext: its posts in areas and subjects, by year, writer, tag and day; the podcast's episodes and the stories in them, to listen to; and the podcast's game, What's That Sound, with its rounds' clips.
oldhackadayneoteletext-server-channels, folder hackadayThe first Hackaday channel, in Python on the Python kit, kept running.
demositeneoteletext-server-channel-demositeThe demonstration site: what a teletext service can be, with news and live services, pages that answer back, games, adventures, music and pictures, every page made of the library's components.
uicomponentsdemoneoteletext-server-channel-uicomponentsdemoThe library's own demonstration: its components working, a page or so to each, in eight magazines.

The colour around the page. Page 505 of the UI components demonstration, "Screen colour", on the Graphics magazine, shows the colour a page may set outside its display area. It opens in blue, Colour Map entry 4, so the colour shows at once around a black page.
