A radio group offers Level 1's eight colours and a slider all 32 entries of the Colour Map, both changing the same colour; a line of text names the entry, its colour look-up table and its place in that table, and says when it is entry 8, the transparent one. Each viewer has their own copy, and the page sends the choice as the first triplet of its X/26 data, a Full Screen Colour triplet.

One site in every language. The demonstration site is one channel in every language the server lists. A viewer chooses a language with the library's language picker, which keeps it under the viewer's handle, asking for the viewer's state when they choose, and from then on every page of the site, every component's demonstration included, is drawn in that language, its text encoded by the server, right-to-left languages laid out from the right, and every line in one row. The site writes no machine translation: the text a component shows in another language is the language's own text that the site already holds for its language pages, its name in itself, the title and Articles 1 and 3 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and its letters. A link can open the site in one language, because the language page answers a selection that carries the language's tag by choosing that language for the viewer. A viewer area of the site shows what the channel knows of the viewer, and lets the viewer ask to be remembered or forgotten.

The language pages. Magazine 8 of both demonstration channels holds an index of languages and a page for each, numbered alike in both channels. Each language page is to be built at run time from the library's components, in the language it shows: a fixed heading on rows 1 and 2; then a scrolling view down to the row above the prompts, holding the Universal Declaration's title and Articles 1 and 3 in that language, the language's letters, the Wikipedia attribution where the page has it, and a table of every character of the page's sets, the codes 2/0 to 7/F of its G0 set, of its second G0 set where it has one, and of its G2 set, sixteen to a row; then the coloured-key prompts on row 24. There is one page for each language the engine has a character set for, not one for each set, so languages that share a set each have their own, and every set the engine's page writer names is used by at least one page: 73 language pages in 48 sets, on pages 802 to 874 in alphabetical order of the languages' names in English, with the index of languages on pages 800 and 801, and magazine 8 holds nothing else. Arabic has two pages, one in NeoTeletext's plain-letter set and one, Arabic T44, in the standard's own Arabic set of EN 300 706 Table 44. Each page shows the language's name in itself, the Universal Declaration's text where one is to hand, the alphabet's special letters, every character of its sets, and row 24 with links back to the index. Each page carries the whole designation of its set in packet X/28/0 Format 1, because the header's three national option bits alone cannot identify a language, as TR 100 287 clause 10.3 says. A page whose text comes from Wikipedia shows on itself its source, the revision, that the text was changed, and its licence. This replaces ready-made TTI pages cut to each viewer's window by hand, which only keys could move. It was rebuilt on 3 November 2026 and waits to be checked again.

Rests on: EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 12.3.3 Row Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 28 Function of Row Address triplets; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 30 Colour Map; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause A.5 Rules for row and screen colours; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 clause 9.4.2 Packet X/28/0 Format 1; EN 300 706 V1.2.1 table 44 Arabic G0 Primary Set; TR 100 287 V1.2.1 clause 10.3 Language definition and the preferred use of packets 29/0

18.1 Build a static channel

DOC-1873 · task · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-91, REQ-93, REQ-508, REQ-513

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-91 The page checker (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-93 Writing a channel's contents from a local folder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-508 The files of a channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-513 A channel's entry file `channel.ttx` holds its settings as JSON (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

This builds a channel any web server can host, with no program. It needs a folder, a text editor and neottx.

  1. Make a folder. Its name is the last part of the channel's address, unless it is the root of a site.
  2. Write each page as NNN.tti, its name the page number. A page needs a PN line and OL lines, as in TTI page files. Give it a DE line to title it, and start each sub-page of a page with a new PN and SC.
  3. Add links with FL, or the Link Extension's lines.
  4. Write channel.ttx, for example { "name": "Example", "initial_page": "100" }. Leave out push. The file is optional: with none, the channel opens at page 100.
  5. Run neottx check 100.tti 101.tti, with --descriptor channel.ttx when links name other services, and correct what it reports. A row over 40 cells is an error, among others, and it exits with status 4 on an error.
  6. Run neottx contents . > contents.txt in the folder. This lists every page by its title. Add x lines by hand for other channels.
  7. Upload the folder to a web server. Check that a missing file answers 404, not an HTML page with status 200.
  8. Run neottx probe https://example.org/news/. It opens the channel as a receiver does, says what each step found, and exits non-zero on a fault. For a server on this machine, add --allow-local 127.0.0.1.
  9. Open the channel in NeoTeletext at the same address.

A channel of many pages opens faster with a bundle: neottx convert 100.tti --to t42 -o index.t42 writes one page's packets, and a bundle may hold any number of them, up to 256 KiB.

18.2 Build a client

DOC-1976 · task · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494, REQ-1732

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

This builds a receiver that opens a live channel and shows a page. It needs a WebSocket, or a TCP socket to write one on, and the standard's decoding of a packet. The steps were first tried at push protocol 7 with 150 lines of Python and nothing but its standard library, against the NeoTeletext server; the steps on the rule table, 8 and 12, are written from the protocol's items and have not been tried that way.

  1. Fetch channel.ttx from the channel's folder. Read it as the settings. With no push member the channel is static: read its files as opening a channel says, and stop here. With one, note initial_page, and open nothing else over HTTP.
  2. Open a WebSocket at the folder's push, with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: neottx.10 and no Origin, as opening the connection says. Check that the 101 echoes the name. A browser's WebSocket always sends Origin, so it cannot do this.
  3. Send HELLO as one binary message with the capability SELECT: FF 09 0A 80 80 80 02, which is version 10 and capabilities 4,194,304. Add 131,072 if you will draw a cursor. Cursor records come either way: they carry the acknowledgement, so skip them if you draw none. Mask it, as a client's WebSocket frames always are.
  4. Read binary messages. Cut each into 42-byte packets, and discard and count a message that is not whole packets.
  5. Read each packet's two address bytes as Hamming 8/4. Bytes that decode to 12 and 15 are data channel 12: check the CRC-16, gather the fragments by record id and index, and when the last has come, check the frame's CRC-32 and read the type at byte 1. Skip a type you do not read.
  6. Wait for WELCOME, type 5, and check its version. Give up after 10 seconds.
  7. Send RESIZE and SELECT of the initial page, in one message if you like: FF 07 28 19 00 00 FF 40 03 31 30 30 selects page 100. Send no FOCUS_IN, FOCUS_OUT or other input at the top level: it is the viewer's input, and a server closes the connection on it.
  8. Read the RULES record, type 21, that comes before each page: the page's rule table, or a record that says the page has none. Keep it for that page number and sub-code alone, and drop it when the selection changes.
  9. Decode the packets that are not data channel 12 as teletext packets: a header starts a page and erases it when C4 is set, and each row packet replaces its row. Page 100, sub-code 0000, whole, has the header 02 15 15 15 15 D0 15 15 15 02: the two address bytes, then Hamming 8/4 digits, in which byte 5 is S2 + 8 × C4 and byte 9 holds C11 in its lowest bit. Clear the row's parity bit to read its characters. They are not ASCII: the page's national option chooses them, and codes below 0x20 are attributes that show as spaces. Columns 0 to 7 of row 0 are yours to fill, with the page number. Show row 24 only when X/27/0 says to.
  10. Read DENIED, type 12, as the end of a selection that has no page, and say so to the viewer. Do not set a timer of your own: the server ends every selection.
  11. Answer each ping with a pong, and ping a connection silent for 25 seconds.
  12. Send the viewer's input only as the page's table asks. A client that does not evaluate tables sends none, and is still a complete reader of the channel. One that does evaluates the open page's table as the page rule table says and sends each report of it as a RULE_EVENT, under the stamp of the page and sub-code on screen, which are the header's, never 3F7F, with the KEY or other event inside it; a page with no table is sent nothing.
  13. Send SELECT whenever the page shown changes. Read each index and SUBPAGES record if you show lists, and REDIRECT always, because a channel moves a viewer with it.
  14. When the connection closes, stop or try again as its close code says. On trying again, begin at step 2, drop every page's table, and select the page you were showing.
  15. Run the wire vectors through your reader and writer.
  16. Try it against a real server. teletext-server is built from neoteletext-app-server, and neottx from neoteletext-renderer-teletext, each with cargo build.

18.3 Build a server

DOC-1977 · task · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1732, REQ-1882

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1882 `neottx probe` opens a channel as a receiver does and reports each step and how each selection ended (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

This builds a server for one live channel, which any receiver can open. The steps were first tried at push protocol 7 with 200 lines of Python and nothing but its standard library, and checked with neottx probe; steps 9 and 12, which push protocol 10 added, are written from the protocol's items and have not been tried that way.

  1. Answer GET <channel>channel.ttx with 200 and application/json: {"name":"Example","initial_page":"100","push":{}}. The push object makes the channel live and declares nothing of input (channel.ttx).
  2. On a GET of <channel>push, refuse an Origin with 403, and an offer without neottx.10 with 426, naming it, as opening the connection says. Otherwise answer 101, with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, and Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: neottx.10. Do not offer compression.
  3. Answer every other path as what each address answers says, or 404.
  4. Read each binary message whole, unmasking it, and read it as the input stream. A message cut short, an unknown core type, a flag nobody defined, malformed text, and any of the viewer's input (a KEY, MOUSE, WHEEL, PASTE, COMPOSE, TOUCH, FOCUS_IN, FOCUS_OUT, HOVER or raw text) at the top level of the stream is a protocol error: send a close of 4000. Skip an extension you do not know by its length, and ignore text messages.
  5. On HELLO, with any version but 10, close with 4001. Otherwise answer with WELCOME: a record of type 5 whose body is FF 01, the version as uv, and the capabilities it will use, a subset of those offered, as uv.
  6. Write a record as the record frame says: version 2, the type, the body's length, the body, and the CRC-32 of all that, big-endian.
  7. Carry the record as packets of data channel 12: cut it into 34-byte fragments, the last padded with zeros. Each packet is the Hamming 8/4 bytes of 12, 15, service byte 8 and the control byte, with the value 1 for a first fragment and 2 for a last, which are bits 1 and 2 as EN 300 706 counts them; then the record id, the index, the 34 bytes, and the CRC-16 of those 36 bytes, whose polynomial is x16 + x9 + x7 + x4 + 1. Number each record one on from the last, from 0 at WELCOME, modulo 256.
  8. On SELECT, read the place as the map reads it. A SELECT that repeats a selection that stands does nothing, and a page answered with a sub-page has become that sub-page, so the page's own SELECT is new, and one that repeats a selection you ended with DENIED is a new selection. An empty one ends the selection.
  9. At every selection, before the page, send a RULES record (type 21) for that page number and sub-code, its generation one above the last you sent on the connection, from 1: either one that says the page has no table, so that the page sends you nothing of what the viewer does (the row rules_no_table of the wire vectors), or a table's image, such as the default table that reports every key, text, press, release, move, hover, focus change and wheel (the rows rules_default_send_all and default_send_all). Keep nothing of a page's table for a later selection.
  10. Answer every selection within 5,000 ms, with a page frame: a header with C4 and C11 set, such as 02 15 15 15 15 D0 15 15 15 02 for page 100, sub-code 0000, and the page's rows, as one binary message. A header's bytes are Hamming 8/4 and its 32 display bytes, like a row's 40, have odd parity. Or answer with DENIED.
  11. Send a changed sub-page as a header with C4 clear and the rows that changed, for the same page and sub-code only.
  12. Read the viewer's input only inside RULE_EVENT (extension 0x4B): after its stamp, the generation, rule, row, page tick, kind and target, a kind 1 body holds one or two whole input events exactly as their own items encode them, or a run of raw text. Keep what each connection holds of the presses a rule reported, and on a reported FOCUS_OUT, a change of selection or a lost connection, treat it as released, as held input says.
  13. Answer pings, and send a close of 4100 before a restart, so that receivers come back.
  14. Run the third part of the conformance table, what a server answers, and the wire vectors against it.
  15. teletext-server is built from neoteletext-app-server, and neottx from neoteletext-renderer-teletext, each with cargo build. Run neottx probe http://127.0.0.1:8090/example/ --allow-local 127.0.0.1. It opens the channel through the same process as a viewer's receiver, selects the initial page and page 8FC, and ends with result no fault.

18.4 Build a program

DOC-1978 · task · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1476, REQ-1732, REQ-1882

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1476 The server and a program MUST exchange only the closed set of exactly typed messages, with no view field (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1882 `neottx probe` opens a channel as a receiver does and reports each step and how each selection ended (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

This builds a channel behind the NeoTeletext server, in any language, with nothing but a JSON library. Each step was tried with a program of 60 lines of Python.

  1. Make a folder, and write a program there that reads lines from standard input and writes one JSON object a line to standard output, flushing each.
  2. Write a channels file, as processes, transports and lines says, naming the program's command and directory.
  3. teletext-server is built from neoteletext-app-server, and neottx from neoteletext-renderer-teletext, each with cargo build. Start the server: teletext-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8090 --origin http://127.0.0.1:8090 --channels channels.json --state state. The first line your program reads is start: stop if its protocol is not the version you wrote for, the one from the server to a program gives. A later start, when a program on a socket connects again, ends every connection you knew: forget them all, and keep what must last under the viewer's handle. Ignore a type you do not use, such as stats, every 10 seconds, and never stop on one.
  4. Answer describe, which comes second, with {"type":"description","page":"100","public":false}. Until you do, the channel does not count as ready.
  5. Make a sub-page. Every field is required but cursor, character_set, language, level and text. A row is base64 of 40 character codes, and a blank row is null: {"page":"100","sub":"0000","rows":[...],"links":[null,null,null,null,null,null],"display_row_24":false,"link_extension":{"keys":[],"numbers":[],"texts":[]},"control":{"erase":false,"newsflash":false,"subtitle":false,"suppress_header":false,"update":false,"interrupted_sequence":false,"inhibit_display":false,"magazine_serial":false},"enhancements":[],"packets":[],"cursor":null}. To write words, leave their rows blank and give them as text runs, such as "text":[{"row":1,"column":0,"text":"Hello"}], which the server encodes (text in any language).
  6. Make the index: [{"magazine":1,"name":"Example","pages":[{"page":"100","title":"Hello","section":null,"subpages":1}]}].
  7. On connected, read selection, which is null for the initial page, and answer with reply, copying connection and request, with the index and the sub-page as selected. A page that does not exist is selectednull, and a denied after it.
  8. On selected, answer {"type":"page","connections":[1],"request":2,"page":{...}} with the connection and number you were given, and keep each connection's latest number: redirect and denied copy it, and input gives you none, or {"type":"denied","connection":1,"request":2,"status":404}.
  9. For a page of several sub-pages, answer a selection whose sub is 3F7F with the first in ascending order, and send subpages with it. A selection of one sub-code gets that sub-page alone.
  10. When a page changes, send it again to the connections that show it, with requestnull. The server works out the changed rows.
  11. On input, act on the event, and send what changed: a key with Control held comes with mods 4 and no text. Move a viewer with redirect. On left and gone, let go of what you keep for that page or that connection.
  12. Print each refused line to standard error, which reaches the server's log. Its path and rule name the first fault, and its request the message refused. To find out before any viewer does whether a page's text fits, send it as measure (measuring a page).
  13. Run neottx probe http://127.0.0.1:8090/example/ --allow-local 127.0.0.1 --select 101 --select '100?a=1'. Each selection reports a page or DENIED, with its time, and a page your program did not answer in time fails with DENIED 503.

19 Troubleshooting

DOC-1789 · section

19.1 A channel will not open, and channel.ttx looks right

DOC-1874 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-507, REQ-513, REQ-516

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-507 Channels: a channel is a folder (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-513 A channel's entry file `channel.ttx` holds its settings as JSON (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-516 Media types of a channel's files (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. A receiver reports a failure on opening a channel, not the channel's pages.

Causes.

  • A member of channel.ttx is unknown or duplicated, which refuses the whole file: a misspelled name, or a member that was withdrawn, such as push.address or push.method.
  • The file answers with type text/html. A host often gives this for a missing file with status 200.
  • The address has no / at the end of its folder, or breaks the canonical form.

Fix. Run neottx probe on the channel's address. It names the step that failed. A folder holding only an older channel.json is not a fault: that file is never asked for, and the channel opens with the defaults, so rename it.

19.2 A page shows "not found", or a page is a failure

DOC-1875 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-313, REQ-508, REQ-516

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-508 The files of a channel (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-516 Media types of a channel's files (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. A page in the folder does not show.

Causes and fixes.

  • The name. A page file is exactly three digits and an extension, with A to F in capitals. Rename 1fe.t42 to 1FE.t42.
  • A failure, not "not found". The file answered 200 and failed its check: a TTI file with no PN line, a T42 file that is not whole packets, or a type of text/html. Run neottx check, and see media types and checks.
  • Another page's file. A page file fills only the page asked for, so a file named 100.tti that holds page 200 shows nothing at 100. Its PN line must match the name.
  • A hexadecimal number. A viewer cannot key a page with a digit from A to F. Link to it.

19.3 The upgrade is answered 426

DOC-1979 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. The push upgrade is answered 426 Upgrade Required, with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: neottx.10 when the request asked to upgrade, and with neither that nor Upgrade when it did not. A receiver reports the upgrade as refused, and does not try again.

Causes.

  • The request offers no Sec-WebSocket-Protocol, or offers another, such as neottx.8: the receiver is of another version than the server.
  • The request has no WebSocket upgrade at all: a browser or curl visited <channel>push.
  • The name differs in case. It is matched exactly.

Fix. Offer the name in the 426 response. There is no compatibility path, so receiver and server must speak one version: update the older. Run neottx probe on the channel's address, whose line handshake accepted: neottx.10 shows a good upgrade.

19.4 The upgrade is answered 403

DOC-1980 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-494

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-494 Server push over the channel's WebSocket (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. The push upgrade is answered 403 Forbidden, whatever the subprotocol.

Cause. The request carries Origin. A server refuses any push upgrade that does, whatever its value, null included. This is what stops a web page reaching a channel as the viewer, through the viewer's own receiver.

Fix. Send no Origin header. A web page's WebSocket always sends one and cannot be told not to, so a receiver cannot be written in a web page. A WebSocket library for a native program often has an option that adds one: turn it off. A proxy in front of the server must not add one either.

19.5 The connection closes with 4000 or 4001, and does not come back

DOC-1981 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-201

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-201 Input protocol unsigned varints: shortest encoding, at most 5 bytes, 32 bits (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. A connection closes, and a receiver does not reconnect, which is right: a stop code says the fault would be there on the next attempt.

Causes of 4001. HELLO named a version other than 7.

Causes of 4000. The channel read something it could not. These are the usual ones.

  • The retired PAGE event, FF 0A, or any other unknown core type.
  • A SELECT in the old binary form, FF 40 04 80 02 FF 7E. Its payload is the place as text now: FF 40 03 31 30 30.
  • A SELECT with small hexadecimal digits, a sub-code of 3F7F, or a query that is not pairs.
  • An event cut by the end of its message. A message holds whole events and whole characters.
  • A varint longer than it need be, or a mods flag set with a value of 0.
  • A control character in raw text. Enter and the like are KEY events.
  • A WebSocket fault: an unmasked frame, or a message over 8,192 bytes.

Fix. Run the message through the wire vectors' rows, whose refused rows are these faults.

A close of 4100 is not a fault: the server is restarting, and a receiver comes back by itself.

19.6 Every selection ends with DENIED 503

DOC-1982 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1481, REQ-1882

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1481 A selection the program does not answer in time ends with DENIED 503 and the connection stays open (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1882 `neottx probe` opens a channel as a receiver does and reports each step and how each selection ended (to be rechecked on livedevelopment).

Problem. A receiver reports that the channel's program is not answering, and neottx probe exits non-zero with DENIED 503: the channel's program did not answer.

Causes.

  • No program is running: the server's log says why it ended. DENIED then comes at once, not after 5 seconds.
  • The program answers selected but never answered connected, or the other way round. Both need an answer, and the server's log names which with the event program_late.
  • The answer does not flush. A line a program buffers does not reach the server.
  • The answer was refused. The program is sent refused, and nothing of the line is done: read the program's standard error or the server's log, event line_refused.
  • The answer carries an old request, and was dropped and counted as stale_answers. Copy the number from the message you are answering.
  • A reply with selectednull, and no page, redirect or denied after it.
  • The answer is a sub-page other than the one selected, which is not refused and goes nowhere. The log says only program_late.
  • A reply gives a page the index does not hold, which is refused with not_in_index.

Fix. Answer every connected and selected within 5,000 ms, with denied for a page that does not exist.

19.7 HELLO has no answer, or packets count as invalid

DOC-1983 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-210, REQ-1462

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-210 WELCOME travels as a control record of type 5 in one fragment (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-1462 Server sends only valid packets downstream (to be rechecked on main).

Problem. A receiver reports invalid packets on the push connection, or that the channel did not answer HELLO with WELCOME, on a server you wrote.

Causes.

  • The CRC-16 of a packet of data channel 12 is wrong. Its polynomial is that of EN 300 708 clause 6.5.8.1, x16 + x9 + x7 + x4 + 1, from a register of zeros, with no final inversion. It is not CRC-16-CCITT.
  • The record is not padded to 34 bytes, so the packet is not 42 bytes, and the whole message is discarded.
  • The Service Byte's bit 4 is clear, or the control byte's first and last bits are not set on a record of one fragment.
  • A message that is a text frame. A server sends binary alone.
  • The WELCOME sets a capability HELLO did not offer.

Fix. Compare your packet with the row welcome of the wire vectors, byte for byte.

19.8 Keys or clicks never reach the program

DOC-1984 · troubleshooting · informative · NeoTeletext's own: no standard defines it · requirements REQ-1555, REQ-1557, REQ-6523

Unfinished. The project's records do not show all of this as met, so it may not hold in full: REQ-1555 Every input event except focus and session events carries a page and sub-code stamp (to be rechecked on main); REQ-1557 Server checks input page stamp against the connection's selection (to be rechecked on livedevelopment); REQ-6523 The browser sends the server no input event for a page unless the page's rule table asks for it (tested, not recorded as met on main).

Problem. A channel shows its page, and a program hears no input, or hears only some.

Causes.

  • The page has no rule table, or its table has no rule that reports the event. Under push protocol 10 a receiver sends a page's input only when a rule of that page's table, fired by the event, runs a group that applies a REPORT of the firing (a page asks for input with its rule table). A page with no table sends nothing. Send the page its table at every selection of it: the server keeps none for a later viewer. A channel whose configuration gives it "default_rules": "send_all" is sent the default table at each selection, which reports every input.
  • The table is for another sub-page. A table belongs to one page number and one sub-code; a table sent for 101/0001 does nothing while 101/0002 is open.
  • The table was refused. A receiver that cannot decode a table reports a rules_fault of undecodable, and the server refuses one it would not send with a refused message naming the rule and the path.
  • The stamp is not the selection. A press stamped with another page or sub-code is dropped, and stale_input in the server's figures counts it. A page selected with 302 becomes a sub-page when it arrives: stamp the sub-code on screen, which is the header's, never 3F7F.
  • No selection was made, so every stamped event is dropped.
  • The event is one a program does not hear: what a program hears of input says which.
  • A click on a link the page declares, a key or click with the browser's own modifier, and the wheel over a page with several sub-codes where no wheel rule's target is under the pointer are the receiver's, and do not go to the channel.

Glossary

Active

What a selected page is to the back end: it receives the back end's updates, whatever the viewer's input is doing. A page can be active without being focused, for example in a tab behind another or with the pointer outside the page. It is not a word for a tab: a tab in front is "the tab in front" or "focused". The object kind "Active object" (TERM-1626) is a different thing, from EN 300 706. Source: DEC-1538 version 4, the owner's words of 30 October 2026.

TERM-1650

Active object

An object that behaves like extra local enhancement data of the page.

TERM-1626 · also active objects · broader term Object

Adaptive object

An object that adapts to the attributes under it.

TERM-1627 · also adaptive objects · broader term Object

Attribute

A change of colour or style on a teletext page: either a spacing attribute (a Level 1 control code that occupies a cell) or a non-spacing attribute (an X/26 triplet that uses no cell).

TERM-1602 · also attributes

Cell

One character position in a row of a teletext page; a row has 40 cells. A spacing attribute occupies a cell, which normally shows as a space; a non-spacing attribute does not use one up.

TERM-1588 · also cells, character cell · broader term Row

Character set

One of the sets of characters a teletext page draws from: G0 (the main text set), G1 (block mosaics), G2 (supplementary) and G3 (Level 2.5's smoothed mosaics and line drawing). DRCS characters were downloadable but are removed from the project.

TERM-1612 · also character sets

CLUT

Colour Look-Up Table: one of the four tables of 8 colours that make up the Colour Map. CLUT 0 is the classic 8 teletext colours. CLUT 1 is their half-intensity versions, with entry 0 meaning transparent. CLUTs 2 and 3 are 16 further colours.

TERM-1620 · also CLUTs, Colour Look-Up Table · broader term Colour Map

Colour Map

The 32-colour palette of Levels 2.5 and 3.5, organised as four CLUTs of 8 colours each.

TERM-1619

Default object

An object a page gets automatically from its magazine's table, the MOT.

TERM-1629 · also default objects · broader term Object

DRCS

Dynamically Redefinable Character Set: characters whose pixel patterns are downloaded from special pages. The project removed DRCS on 20 October 2026 (decision E.95).

TERM-1618 · also Dynamically Redefinable Character Set · broader term Character set

Enhancement data

Data carried in X/26 packets as triplets, each a command such as "at row 5, column 10, put character é" or "from here, background colour 19". Objects are reusable blocks of it.

TERM-1594

Focused

What a selected page is for the viewer's input, and only for input. Keys reach the page only while it holds the keyboard focus; mouse, wheel, touch and hover reach it only while the pointer is over the page area. Losing the focus never changes the selection and never stops updates. Source: DEC-1538 version 4, the owner's words of 30 October 2026.

TERM-1651

G0

The main text character set: Latin with a national option, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic or Hebrew.

TERM-1613 · broader term Character set

G1

The block-mosaic graphics character set.

TERM-1614 · broader term Character set

G2

The supplementary character set: accents and symbols.

TERM-1615 · broader term Character set

G3

Level 2.5's character set of smoothed mosaics and line-drawing shapes.

TERM-1616 · broader term Character set

GPOP

Global POP: a Public Object Page for the whole magazine.

TERM-1625 · also Global POP, Global Public Object Page · broader term Object page

Header

Row 0 of a teletext page, which carries the page number, the service name and the clock. The receiver's status area is part of it.

TERM-1589 · also header row, row 0 · broader term Row

Level 1

The basic teletext page: rows of characters with spacing attributes.

TERM-1608 · broader term Presentation Level

Level 1.5

Level 1 plus extra characters, such as accented letters, written by X/26.

TERM-1609 · broader term Presentation Level

Level 2.5

Level 1.5 plus non-spacing attributes, 32 colours (16 of them redefinable), side panels, objects and a few downloadable characters.

TERM-1610 · broader term Presentation Level

Level 3.5

Level 2.5 with all 32 colours redefinable, more downloadable characters, and bold, italic and proportional text.

TERM-1611 · broader term Presentation Level

M/29/0

Packet 29, designation 0, for a whole magazine: the settings X/28/0 carries for one page, applied to every page in the magazine.

TERM-1600 · broader term Packet

M/29/4

Packet 29, designation 4, for a whole magazine: the settings X/28/4 carries for one page, applied to every page in the magazine.

TERM-1601 · broader term Packet

Magazine

A group of teletext pages sharing their first digit: pages 100 to 199 are magazine 1. M/29 packets carry settings for every page in a magazine.

TERM-1592 · also magazines

MOT

Magazine Organization Table, page xFE: lists, for each page, which object pages and default objects it uses.

TERM-1630 · also Magazine Organization Table

National option

The variant of the Latin G0 set (English, German, French and so on), chosen by three bits, C12 to C14, in the page header.

TERM-1617 · also national options · broader term G0

Non-spacing attribute

An X/26 triplet that changes colour or style from a cell without using up that cell. It is the main feature of Level 2.5.

TERM-1606 · also non-spacing attributes · broader term Attribute

Object

A reusable block of enhancement data, kept on a separate object page. Objects are active, adaptive or passive; default objects come to a page automatically from its magazine's table (the MOT).

TERM-1622 · also objects · broader term Enhancement data

Object page

A page that holds objects rather than text: a POP (Public Object Page) or a GPOP (Global POP, for the whole magazine).

TERM-1623 · also object pages

Packet

A unit of 40 bytes in which a teletext page arrives, numbered. Packets 1 to 25 carry the rows' text. Packets 26 to 29 carry extra data that old receivers ignore. X/n names packet n of a page, where X is the magazine number; M/n names packet n for a whole magazine.

TERM-1591 · also packets

Page

A teletext page is 25 rows, numbered 0 to 24, of 40 character cells each. Row 0 is the header. A page arrives as numbered packets and belongs to a magazine.

TERM-1586 · also pages, teletext page

Passive object

An object that carries its own attributes.

TERM-1628 · also passive objects · broader term Object

PDC

Programme Delivery Control: video-recorder timing data that can also travel in X/26. It displays nothing.

TERM-1634 · also Programme Delivery Control

POP

Public Object Page: an object page whose objects the pages that link to it use.

TERM-1624 · also Public Object Page · broader term Object page

Presentation Level

One of the cumulative capability levels of a teletext receiver: Level 1, Level 1.5, Level 2.5 and Level 3.5. A Level 2.5 receiver also shows Level 1 and Level 1.5 pages.

TERM-1607 · also Presentation Levels

Row

One of the 25 lines of a teletext page, numbered 0 to 24, each of 40 character cells. Row 0 is the header; packets 1 to 25 carry the rows' text.

TERM-1587 · also rows · broader term Page

SAA5050

The Mullard/Philips Level 1 character generator chip in nearly every 1980s UK teletext set. Its behaviour is the project's rendering baseline (decisions E.12 and E.13).

TERM-1631

SAA5246A

A later Philips chip that decodes Level 1.5.

TERM-1632

Selected

The page and sub-page a tab shows, told to the back end with SELECT. A tab has at most one selection. A page selected is also active. "Selection" is the noun. Source: DEC-1538 version 4, the owner's words of 30 October 2026.

TERM-1649

Set-after

A spacing attribute that takes effect from the next cell, not its own.

TERM-1605 · also set after · broader term Spacing attribute

Set-at

A spacing attribute that takes effect in its own cell.

TERM-1604 · also set at · broader term Spacing attribute

Side panel

Up to 16 extra columns beside the 40-column page, at Level 2.5 and 3.5.

TERM-1621 · also side panels

Spacing attribute

A Level 1 control code, such as "red text", "flash" or "double height". It occupies a cell, which normally shows as a space. It is either set-at (it takes effect in its own cell) or set-after (it takes effect from the next cell).

TERM-1603 · also spacing attributes · broader term Attribute

Status area

The receiver's own part of the header: row 0, columns 0 to 7, where the receiver shows the page number being searched for.

TERM-1590 · broader term Header

Triplet

An 18-bit command of enhancement data, protected by Hamming 24/18 error correction. Each says, for example, "at row 5, column 10, put character é", or "from here, background colour 19".

TERM-1595 · also triplets · broader term Enhancement data

TTI

A common text file format for teletext pages.

TERM-1635

X/26

Packet 26 of a page (X is the magazine number). It carries the page's enhancement data, as triplets.

TERM-1593 · broader term Packet

X/27/4

Packet 27, designation 4, of a page: one of the two packets (with X/27/5) that carry a page's links to the pages that hold its objects.

TERM-1596 · broader term Packet

X/27/5

Packet 27, designation 5, of a page: one of the two packets (with X/27/4) that carry a page's links to the pages that hold its objects.

TERM-1597 · broader term Packet

X/28/0

Packet 28, designation 0, of a page: page-wide settings, namely character sets, the screen and row colours, the side panels and colour redefinitions (with X/28/4). M/29/0 carries the same settings for a whole magazine.

TERM-1598 · broader term Packet

X/28/4

Packet 28, designation 4, of a page: page-wide settings, namely character sets, the screen and row colours, the side panels and colour redefinitions (with X/28/0). M/29/4 carries the same settings for a whole magazine.

TERM-1599 · broader term Packet

Verified by inspection

No test can establish these requirements. Each was read, for the reason given.

  • REQ-1049 Nothing that identifies a viewer: Inspected 20 November 2026 in neoteletext-app-server at b7ec5f8 (TODO-6711, DEC-6471), read-only, for version 4. Every log write in crates was read: (1) the tracing calls in teletext-native (main.rs, apps.rs, apps/remote.rs, connection.rs, hub.rs, http.rs, state.rs, logging.rs) carry only the channel folder, connection numbers, counts, close codes, reasons, program command and socket path, state directory path, figures and fixed text; no tracing field takes a handle, proof, public key or secret, and there is no request-logging layer (no TraceLayer, no peer or forwarded address is logged). (2) Every runtime event goes through Channel::log and Effect::Log (teletext-runtime channel.rs and channel/*.rs), then logging::runtime in teletext-native and log() in teletext-cloudflare; the texts read are fixed phrases with connection numbers, page and sub-page codes, byte limits and fault names; the only Effect::Log built in viewers.rs says no random bytes were available, and the channel_address event names a channel address, not a viewer. (3) protocol/check.rs refusals (logged as line_refused) carry a field path, a rule name and numbers or one rejected character as U+XXXX or a language tag. Found: no event carries a viewer handle, proof, key or the handle secret. Caveats, not breaches: a program's own log lines and standard error are logged as they come (apps.rs line 405), which the requirement already assigns to the program; the redirect event names the address the program chose; and the stand_in event names one character code from text a program sent. No test asserts the absence; this is an inspection of the code at that commit only.
